**Impact.** The champion/challenger gate evaluates a policy that does not exist. emi_date_change and self_service_plan are precisely the two non-contacting, borrower-friendly actions the design note argues are the highest-ROI items in the ladder; systematically undervaluing them by 2-3x in the offline gate means the fitted scorer will be reported as no better than the hand-tuned EV scorer and will never be promoted, or will be promoted on a lift number computed from a different ranking than the one that goes live. A model-risk committee that later diffs the two scoring functions will treat every prior evaluation as void.

**Fix.** Do not re-implement the scoring formula in ope.py. Import EstimatorScorer's per-action value computation, or extract the formula into a single function in scoring.py (e.g. `scoring.ev_from_terms(action, exposure, recovery_fraction, p_reach, tau, decay, cost, fatigue)`) that both models.EstimatorScorer._rescore and ope.estimator_policy call. Add a test that asserts estimator_policy and EstimatorScorer produce the same ranking on a fixed logged candidate set.

### `ope-shadow-rows-pooled-with-live` — Shadow-mode decisions, which were never enacted, are pooled with live decisions by default

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:448** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:448: "modes: Sequence[str] = ('shadow', 'live')", repeated at ope.py:557 for treatment_effect, and evaluate_policy.py:74 "modes = ('shadow', 'live') + ...". engine.py:338-343 is explicit that "Shadow decides exactly as live does and then declines to act". The corpus holds 24 shadow rows against 201 live.

**Impact.** A shadow decision's outcome cannot have been caused by the action, because the action never happened - whatever the borrower did, they did for other reasons. Including these rows as if the logged action produced the reward is a straightforward causal error, and it biases toward whatever the base resolution rate is. In treatment_effect() it is worse: shadow rows are all effectively untreated but are counted in whichever arm their variant names, so the 'treated' rate is diluted by decisions that were never treatments. At 24/225 the distortion is ~11% today and grows with every shadow deployment a bank runs during onboarding - and onboarding at a bank is months of shadow running.

**Fix.** Default `modes=('live',)` for both observations() and treatment_effect(). Shadow rows are useful for measuring ranking agreement between a challenger and the champion, not for reward estimation; give them a separate entry point that computes agreement rate and never touches outcomes.

### `ope-observations-drops-every-suppressed-decision` — Every suppressed decision is silently dropped from the corpus, deleting the entire negative class

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:498** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:495-500: "# Within-arm propensity. The top-level column carries the arm factor / # too ... p_log = support.get(chosen) / if p_log is None or p_log <= 0: / continue". A suppressed decision is written with chosen_action='wait' and propensity=arm_probability on the column, but arbitration._hold (arbitration.py:195-201) constructs the Verdict with no `distribution`, so engine.py:566-574 ("if distribution: ... row['propensity'] = round(float(share), 8)") never writes a per-candidate propensity, and 'wait' is never a key in `support`. Every such row hits the `continue`. This directly contradicts engine.py:393-397: "Writing NULL instead would make every suppression invisible to an off-policy estimator, which is exactly the negative class the corpus exists to carry." The column was populated for a reader that does not read it.

**Impact.** The corpus already holds 106 null and 84 cancelled outcomes against 10 ptp and 7 paid. Suppression is the single most common thing the engine does, and it is the outcome a bank most needs evaluated - 'would a different policy have stayed silent here?' is the harassment question. OPE cannot see it. Any challenger that would contact more than the incumbent is scored only on the rows where the incumbent also acted, so the estimator is structurally blind to the cost of extra contact and will always favour the more aggressive policy. That is the exact failure mode that produces an RBI persistent-contact finding.

**Fix.** Have arbitration._hold carry a distribution of {A.WAIT: 1.0} (the suppressed verdict genuinely was pi(wait|x)=1 within the arm), so engine._candidate_log stamps a propensity on the wait row. Then in observations(), fall back to `row['propensity'] / arm_share` when `support.get(chosen)` is missing, and add an explicit `include_suppressed: bool = True` parameter so the exclusion is a choice rather than an accident. Add a test asserting that a suppressed decision with an outcome appears in observations().

### `ope-cancelled-and-superseded-scored-as-reward-zero` — Enactment failures are scored as borrower non-response, contaminating 70% of the labelled corpus

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:505** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:505: "reward=1.0 if str(row['outcome']) in CURED else 0.0" with CURED = frozenset({'paid','ptp'}) at ope.py:440. The only filter is "outcome IS NOT NULL" (ope.py:460). The live outcome distribution is 84 cancelled, 14 no_answer, 10 ptp, 7 paid, 4 superseded - and 'cancelled' is written by enact.py when enactment aborts, i.e. the treatment was never delivered to the borrower. 88 of the 119 non-null rows (74%) are execution artefacts, not responses.

**Impact.** The reward being estimated is not 'did the borrower resolve' but 'did the borrower resolve AND did the executor manage to send the message'. Cancellation rates are not uniform across actions - a human_call cancels when no agent is free, a mandate presentment cancels when the rail rejects it - so the contamination is action-correlated, which is the one direction of bias importance weighting cannot fix. Every reported lift, and the treatment effect, is dominated by executor reliability rather than by the decision. A challenger will be promoted for choosing whichever channel currently has the healthiest executor.

**Fix.** Introduce an explicit NON_OUTCOMES = frozenset({'cancelled','superseded'}) and exclude those rows in observations() and in treatment_effect()'s WHERE clause, or better, add a `delivered` boolean to the outcome model and make it a precondition of evaluability. Report the excluded count in the estimate so the shrinkage is visible rather than silent. Separately, cancelled rows are valuable as an executor-reliability signal and should be surfaced as their own metric.

### `ope-treatment-effect-null-variant-third-group` — NULL variant forms a third GROUP BY bucket and can be silently picked as the treated arm

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:572** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:571-578: "SELECT (variant = :arm) AS is_control, count(*)::int AS n, ... GROUP BY 1", then ope.py:583 "treated = next((r for r in rows if not r['is_control']), None)". In SQL, `NULL = 'null_treatment'` evaluates to NULL, so rows with variant IS NULL land in a distinct third group whose is_control is None. In Python `not None` is True, so `next()` matches whichever of the is_control=False group and the is_control=NULL group Postgres happens to return first. GROUP BY output order is unspecified.

**Impact.** The single causal number the whole system is built to produce - the ATE against the randomised control arm - can be computed from the wrong rows non-deterministically, with the real treated arm silently discarded from the numerator and denominator. Every decision logged before TREATMENT_AB_SPLIT was configured has variant NULL, as does every decision when the split is unset or when a variant name is typo'd (config.py:443 logs a warning and returns None). Two runs of evaluate_policy.py on the same database can print different ATEs. This is the number that gates promotion and the number a model-risk reviewer will ask to reproduce.

**Fix.** Use `COALESCE(variant, '') = :arm AS is_control`, or `(variant IS NOT DISTINCT FROM :arm)`, so the expression is never NULL. Then assert `len(rows) <= 2` and log loudly if a third group appears. Separately, treatment_effect() should restrict to variants that are actually in `config.ab_split()` rather than treating 'everything not the control arm' as treated.

### `enact-dial-fk-keyshare-vs-claim-for-update` — Every voice_bot enactment blocks on its own claim lock, times out after 60s and is recorded 'cancelled'

**backend/agent_core/treatment/enact.py:380** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T08-enact-contract`

process_one claims with `SELECT * FROM treatment_decisions ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` (decisions.py:380) and holds that lock on `conn` for the whole of enact_one. _dial_bot then opens a second connection — `with dbmod.engine.begin() as own:` (enact.py:358) — and calls `outbound.reserve(own, ..., decision_id=decision["id"], ...)` (enact.py:380-400), which INSERTs into call_attempts whose `decision_id TEXT REFERENCES treatment_decisions(id)` (21_outbound.sql:29). Postgres' RI trigger takes FOR KEY SHARE on the referenced row; FOR KEY SHARE conflicts with FOR UPDATE. The insert waits on `conn`, `conn` is waiting in Python for the handler, and the worker sets `statement_timeout=60000` (db_core.py:153-155,177). After 60s QueryCanceled propagates out of `own`, is caught by `except Exception` at enact.py:149 and the plan is written `cancelled` with note `enactment_failed` — after admit() has already booked the touch. _record_suppressed_dial (enact.py:441-454) has the same shape and stalls 60s on every gate-denied voice plan. No test drives _dial_bot against a database (test_outbound_gate_contract.py:46,196-200 are AST checks; test_phase4.py:174 monkeypatches handlers), so nothing would have caught it.

**Impact.** Voice — the highest-EV early-bucket channel — cannot be enacted through the executor at all; each attempt stalls the single bot_worker for a minute, then lands in the 'cancelled' bucket with the borrower's daily touch consumed and the case closed. This is the most likely single contributor to 84/225 cancelled. Refute by: `SELECT conname FROM pg_constraint WHERE confrelid='treatment_decisions'::regclass` on the live DB and grepping worker logs for 'treatment enactment failed' with 'canceling statement due to statement timeout'.

**Fix.** Change claim_due/claim_by_id to `FOR NO KEY UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` (it only updates non-key columns), and/or perform the reserve on `conn` and commit the claim before dialling (two-phase: claim → mark 'dialling' → commit → place → mark_enacted in a fresh txn). Add a DB-backed test that runs enact_one for VOICE_BOT with outbound.place stubbed and asserts it completes in <1s.

### `enact-whatsapp-double-gated-cooling-off` — Every treatment WhatsApp is denied by the cooling-off gate that its own enactment just tripped, and dead-letters within ~30s while the decision reads enacted

**backend/whatsapp_outbound.py:455** · correctness · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `T08-enact-contract`

The treatment WhatsApp path passes contact_policy.admit twice. First in enact_one: `contact_policy.admit(conn, customer_id=..., channel=spec.channel, purpose="outreach", session_key=decision_id, source="treatment", related_id=decision_id, ...)` (enact.py:122-132), which on success inserts a contact_events row with `outcome="allowed"` and `touch_counted=bool(counts)` (contact_policy.py:986-1000). _send_whatsapp then only enqueues a job: enact.py:293-305 -> promise_fulfillment.py:438-451 -> whatsapp_outbound.enqueue_agent_send, which persists purpose='outreach' and source='treatment' on whatsapp_outbound_jobs (whatsapp_outbound.py:88-105). A later bot_worker iteration drains that job (bot_worker.py:103) and calls admit AGAIN: `contact_policy.admit(conn, customer_id=job.get("customer_id"), channel="whatsapp", purpose=purpose, session_key=job.get("conversation_id"), source=source, related_id=job.get("message_id") or job.get("id"), actor_kind="system")` (whatsapp_outbound.py:455-465). Neither suppression path fires: _session_coalesced keys on session_key, which is conversation_id here versus decision_id there (contact_policy.py:386-409), and _already_counted_related keys on (source, related_id), which is (treatment, message_id) versus (treatment, decision_id) (contact_policy.py:413-437). So counts is True, purpose is 'outreach', and contact_policy.py:963-969 runs `last = _last_counted_at(conn, cid)` — the event enact just wrote, seconds ago — against `cool = cooling_off(rules)`, which defaults to 120 minutes (contact_policy.py:110-116, .env.example:468). Result: `_deny(REASON_COOLING)`. mark_failed_or_retry then backs off min(120, 2**attempt) seconds (whatsapp_outbound.py:373-374) for at most WHATSAPP_OUTBOUND_MAX_ATTEMPTS=5 (whatsapp_outbound.py:25-29), so all five attempts land inside ~30 seconds, entirely inside the 120-minute window, and the job goes status='dead' (whatsapp_outbound.py:353-367). Meanwhile enact_one has already run `decisions.mark_enacted(decision_id, ref=ref, ...)` (enact.py:155) with ref='whatsapp:<conversation_id>'. The suite cannot see this because the contact-policy tests set CONTACT_COOLING_OFF_MINUTES=0 (audit-reports/22-testing-quality.md:376 records tests/test_contact_policy.py:47-49 doing exactly that) and the enact tests monkeypatch admit (test_treatment_engine.py:1157-1161). No other channel double-gates: _send_sms calls twilio_sms.send directly (enact.py:327) and outbound.py has no admit call (its docstring at outbound.py:23 states callers gate themselves).

**Impact.** WhatsApp is the engine's rung-1 digital action and, in a default-configured deployment, none of its messages is ever delivered: the borrower is never contacted, a daily touch is consumed, the decision log asserts enacted=true with a whatsapp: reference, and the corpus learns that WhatsApp produces no response. This is simultaneously a silent outage of the primary channel and a false 'we contacted them' entry in the audit trail a regulator would read. It compounds with the FOR UPDATE/KEY SHARE blocker on voice: between them the two highest-volume contacting channels both fail while reporting success or a bare 'cancelled'.

**Fix.** Do not re-gate a send the engine already admitted. Either (a) have enact_one skip its own admit for WhatsApp and let whatsapp_outbound remain the single gate keyed on the message, or (b) carry the treatment decision id onto the job (a decision_id column on whatsapp_outbound_jobs) and pass session_key=decision_id, source='treatment', related_id=decision_id into the second admit so _session_coalesced and _already_counted_related both recognise it as the same touch. Add a db_tx test with CONTACT_COOLING_OFF_MINUTES at its production default that runs enact_one for WHATSAPP and then whatsapp_outbound.process_one and asserts the job reaches 'succeeded'.

### `attr-select-omits-variant` — attribute_outcomes never selects `variant`, so the control arm never receives its negative label

**backend/agent_core/treatment/followthrough.py:101** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T09-followthrough-decisions`

SELECT at 101-102: 'SELECT id, customer_id, account_id, trigger_kind, trigger_ref, chosen_action, enacted, enacted_at, created_at' — no 'variant'. _withheld_on_purpose at 218: 'config.variants().get(str(row.get("variant") or "")...)' is therefore always None → False, and the 'unresolved' branch at 192-193 is unreachable. Live DB confirms: 97 null_treatment rows, outcome distribution has no 'unresolved'. The only test (test_decision_intelligence_p1.py:502) calls _withheld_on_purpose with a hand-built dict.

**Impact.** The control arm contains only positives (paid/ptp) plus 'superseded'. metrics.causal (metrics.py:70-73) and ope.treatment_effect (ope.py:572-576) divide control cures by control labelled rows → control cure rate → 1.0 → ATE large and negative. This is precisely the pathology migration 0087's docstring says was found once already; it is back. Any go/no-go decision, any uplift model retrain on live data, and any regulator-facing 'the engine adds X' claim would be wrong.

**Fix.** Add `variant` (and `mode`) to the SELECT. Add an integration test: insert a null_treatment 'wait' row 15 days old on an open account, run attribute_outcomes, assert outcome == 'unresolved'. Add a metrics guard that refuses to report a control rate of exactly 1.0 with n > 10.

### `asymmetric-observation-window` — Treated rows are frozen at `no_answer` after hours; control rows are watched for 14 days — the arms are labelled on different clocks

**backend/agent_core/treatment/followthrough.py:201** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T09-followthrough-decisions`

201-203: 'grace = timedelta(hours=config.grace_hours(...)); if now - since >= grace: return "no_answer"' with sms/whatsapp 8h, voice_bot 2h (config.py:273-275). record_outcome (decisions.py:344) is 'WHERE id = :id AND outcome IS NULL' so the label is never upgraded. Control rows use OBSERVATION_WINDOW = 14 days (72, 192). The docstring at 160-165 ('a borrower who paid after an unanswered dial has paid') only holds if the payment lands inside the grace.

**Impact.** A borrower who ignores the SMS and pays on day 3 is a treated non-cure forever; the same borrower in the control arm is a cure. _label_cure (train_treatment_models.py:201-211) maps no_answer→0, paid→1. Uplift is biased downward, the reach model is fine but the timing/uplift models are trained on censored positives, and the causal scoreboard will report the engine as harmful. In a bank, salary-cycle payments routinely arrive 2-10 days after the nudge.

**Fix.** Split the label into two fields: contact_outcome (reached/no_answer/undeliverable/refused, decided at grace) and resolution_outcome (paid/ptp/unresolved, decided at one OBSERVATION_WINDOW for every arm and every action). Allow resolution to be written on rows that already have a contact label. Train reach on the first, cure/uplift on the second.

### `metrics-causal-unit-is-decision-not-customer` — Arms are randomised per customer but cure rates, MIN_ARM_N and the incremental estimate are computed per decision row

**backend/agent_core/treatment/metrics.py:70** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T10-sweep-timing-monitor-metrics`

metrics.py:66-95 counts `variant = :arm AND outcome IS NOT NULL` rows; config.py:498-505 'Hashed on the customer, not the event'; the sweep writes one row per delinquent account per day (sweep.py:14). Today's 97 control rows come from a 20-customer book with a 20% split, i.e. ~4 customers.

**Impact.** Pseudo-replication: 100 'labelled cases' can be 4 borrowers observed 25 times; the point estimate is a comparison of a handful of people, MIN_ARM_N passes on repeated observations, and any CI added later on rows would be wildly overconfident. Every rupee figure downstream (attributableRecoveryInr, incrementalRecoveryPerRupee) inherits this.

**Fix.** Aggregate to the customer (or customer-case) level first: cured = any paid/ptp in the window per customer per arm; compute rates and a cluster-robust/bootstrap-by-customer CI; set MIN_ARM_N in customers; add a power statement ('at 20% control and N customers the detectable lift is X points').

### `metrics-treated-definition-neither-itt-nor-per-protocol` — Treated = non-control rows with outcome and action != wait includes 'cancelled' and 'superseded' rows where nothing was sent, and excludes the policy's own wait decisions

**backend/agent_core/treatment/metrics.py:76** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T10-sweep-timing-monitor-metrics`

metrics.py:74-81 `variant <> :arm AND outcome IS NOT NULL AND chosen_action IS NOT NULL AND chosen_action <> 'wait'`; enact.py:89,93,103,108,141,147,152 write outcome='cancelled' without enacting; enact.py:114 writes 'superseded'. Established facts: 84 cancelled among 108 labelled rows. The control arm counts all its rows (waits included, :70-73).

**Impact.** The 'treated' cure rate is diluted by non-treatments, while the policy's deliberate waits (part of what the policy does) are dropped; the estimate is neither intent-to-treat (by arm) nor per-protocol (enacted only). The headline number the whole scoreboard exists for is not a treatment effect, and its sign can flip depending on how many plans the executor cancels that week.

**Fix.** Report ITT: all rows by assigned arm at customer level (the policy including its waits vs null_treatment). Report per-protocol separately: enacted rows only, with cancelled/superseded counted and shown as 'planned but not delivered'. Never mix.

### `no-policy-controls-at-all` — A collections head can change nothing about the engine from its own console

**Habibi/src/routes/treatment.lazy.tsx:264** · integration · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `U01-treatment-ui`

TreatmentPage's entire state is `const [days, setDays] = useState<number>(14); const [tab, setTab] = useState("insights");` (treatment.lazy.tsx:265-266). The only writes in the whole file are useCreateTreatmentHold and useReleaseTreatmentHold (lines 1283, 1448). There is no control for TREATMENT_MODE, TREATMENT_SWEEP, TREATMENT_GREEDINESS (0.7 today), TREATMENT_AB_SPLIT (control:80,null_treatment:20), TREATMENT_SCORER (ev), the daily contact cap, the calling window, or per-resource capacity — every one of which is an environment variable requiring a redeploy. `m.compliance.dailyCap` is displayed (line 524) and not editable; `m.capacity.resources` is displayed (577-592) and not editable.

**Impact.** In a bank, the collections head owns the contact strategy and the model-risk committee owns the exploration rate. Neither can act without raising a change request against a container's environment. There is no way to reduce greediness after a complaint spike, no way to widen the holdout arm for a validation exercise, no way to cut the daily cap during a festival period, and no way to pause the engine short of a deployment. An automated outbound decisioning system with no runtime controls will not pass operational readiness review.

**Fix.** Add a Policy tab backed by a `treatment_policy` table (versioned, maker-checker, effective-dated), with GET/PUT /treatment/policy. Surface mode, sweep, greediness, arm split, daily cap, calling window and per-resource capacity. Bump policy_version on every change so decision rows are attributable to the policy that produced them, and show the current version in the header.

### `feature-drift-psi-field-does-not-exist` — The drift table shows every feature as green 'Stable' with PSI '—', including features the backend flagged at alert level

**Habibi/src/routes/treatment.lazy.tsx:664** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `U01-treatment-ui`

`<TableCell ...>{fmtNum(f.psi, 3)}</TableCell>` and `<Lozenge tone={f.drifted ? "warning" : "success"}>{f.drifted ? "Drifted" : "Stable"}</Lozenge>` (treatment.lazy.tsx:668, 671-672), typed `{ feature: string; psi: number | null; drifted?: boolean }` (treatment.ts:127). The backend's feature_drift emits `{"feature", "trainedMean", "recentMean", "shiftSigma", "n", "level"}` (monitor.py:272-281) — there is no `psi` and no `drifted` key, and the backend does not compute PSI at all; the panel description 'PSI against the training distribution' (line 653) describes a statistic that does not exist. `f.drifted` is undefined for every row → falsy → green 'Stable'.

**Impact.** Combined with the blank alert banner above, the Model health tab renders an all-green drift board while the backend is emitting alert-level drift findings. This is not a missing number; it is an affirmative false assurance on the panel a bank's model-risk function will point at during validation. It fails in exactly the direction that lets a decayed model keep calling borrowers.

**Fix.** Type the row as `{ feature, trainedMean, recentMean, shiftSigma, n, level }`, render shiftSigma with its sign and the trained→recent means, derive the lozenge tone from `level` (ok=success, warn=warning, alert=danger), and retitle the panel 'Shift from training distribution (σ)'. Add a table row for the features monitor.py skips (n<30, or sigma≈0 'unmeasurable') rather than dropping them silently.

### `no-kill-switch` — No stop control — the only brake is a per-borrower hold placed one id at a time

**Habibi/src/routes/treatment.lazy.tsx:1149** · reliability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `U01-treatment-ui`

The HoldsTab (treatment.lazy.tsx:1149-1274) offers exactly one write path: place a hold for one customerId typed into a free-text box (line 1341-1346). There is no bulk hold, no segment hold, no channel-level suspension, and no engine stop. Nothing in the file references a pause, suspend, or disable action.

**Impact.** During an incident — a mis-scored segment dialling at 3x cap, a WhatsApp template getting a regulator's attention, a festival-day embargo — the operator's only tool is to type borrower ids one at a time. The realistic response becomes 'ring the SRE and stop the container', which loses the audit trail of who stopped what and when. Every bank ORM function will ask for a documented kill switch with a named owner before go-live.

**Fix.** Add a prominent, permission-gated 'Suspend engine' control (with scopes: all / one channel / one segment / one portfolio), requiring a reason, writing an audit row, and showing an unmistakable banner while active. Pair it with a scheduled-embargo calendar for festival days and regulatory blackout periods.

### `cancelled-enactments-counted-as-treated-failures-in-the-causal-arm` — The treated arm counts decisions that were never enacted as treated failures, so the causal headline will report a real number that is wrong

**backend/agent_core/treatment/metrics.py:74** · statistics · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `U01-treatment-ui`

The treated denominator is `count(*) FILTER (WHERE variant <> :arm AND outcome IS NOT NULL AND chosen_action IS NOT NULL AND chosen_action <> 'wait')::int AS treated_n` (metrics.py:74-77) and the numerator counts only `outcome IN ('paid','ptp')` (78-81). There is no `enacted` predicate. But enact.py writes `decisions.record_outcome(decision_id, "cancelled")` on seven distinct abort paths — plan_expired (89), no executor for a deferred action (93), unknown action (103), customer gone (108), contact-gate denial (141), NoExecutor (147) and a bare exception (152) — all of which leave `enacted` false while setting a non-null outcome on a row whose chosen_action is a real action. Every such row therefore enters treated_n as a failure. The corpus today holds 84 cancelled against 7 paid and 10 ptp, so `treated_rate = treated_cured / treated_n` (metrics.py:109) is computed over a denominator dominated by contacts that never happened. `attributable = recovered * (incremental / treated_rate)` (168) and `incrementalRecoveryPerRupee` (180-182) both inherit the error.

**Impact.** Once both arms clear MIN_ARM_N = 100 (metrics.py:50) the scoreboard will publish a causal number rather than withhold one — and that number will understate the treated cure rate by whatever share of decisions failed to execute, plausibly driving incrementalCureRate to zero or negative. The console will then tell a collections head and a model-risk committee that the engine is not working, or is harming recovery, when what it is measuring is its own enactment failure rate. This is the one failure mode this module exists to prevent, arriving through the denominator instead of through the metric, and it fails in the direction that gets a working engine switched off.

**Fix.** Restrict the treated arm to decisions that were actually carried out — add `AND enacted` to both treated filters — or, better, exclude the execution-failure outcomes explicitly (`AND outcome NOT IN ('cancelled','superseded')`) and report the excluded count alongside treatedN so the reader can see how many decisions never became contacts. Add an assertion test that a corpus of all-cancelled treated rows yields available:false rather than a negative ATE.

### `hold-dedupe-ignores-expiry` — An expired, unreleased hold blocks a new one and is handed back to the caller as active, while the engine correctly ignores it

**backend/db_treatment_holds.py:157** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`SELECT id FROM treatment_holds WHERE customer_id = :cid AND COALESCE(account_id,'') = COALESCE(:aid,'') AND kind = :kind AND released_at IS NULL` -> `if existing: return _treatment_hold(conn, existing["id"])` (db_treatment_holds.py:153-168). The partial unique index has the same predicate (`WHERE released_at IS NULL`, sql/05_collections.sql:302-304). But every consumer requires expiry too: `released_at IS NULL AND starts_at <= now() AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > now())` (agent_core/treatment/policy.py:516-521, features.py:1173, authority/features.py:140). And _treatment_hold reports `"active": row["released_at"] is None` (line 279), as does list_treatment_holds (line 116).

**Impact.** A borrower had a 30-day hardship hold last year that expired without being released. Today they tell the bot 'I lost my job again'. create_treatment_hold finds the stale row, places nothing, and returns it with active: true. The agent and the UI both believe a hold is in force. The treatment engine, applying the correct predicate, sees no active hold and resumes dunning a borrower who was just told they were protected. Two bugs pointing the same way, and the state is invisible from the screen. This is the failure mode a bank's conduct-risk review looks for first.

**Fix.** One predicate, one place: export `ACTIVE_HOLD_PREDICATE` from a single module and use it in the dedupe SELECT, in list_treatment_holds, in _treatment_hold's `active` field and in the unique index (make the index `WHERE released_at IS NULL AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > now())` is not possible — now() is not immutable — so instead expire holds by writing released_at from a sweep, and keep the index as is). Add a nightly sweep that releases expired holds with released_reason='expired'.

### `get-treatment-next-writes-the-training-corpus` — A GET endpoint commits a decision row indistinguishable from a policy decision, and the trainer consumes it

**backend/db_treatment_holds.py:302** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`with engine.begin() as conn: ... result = recommend_treatment(...)` (db_treatment_holds.py:302-311) behind `@app.get("/treatment/next")` (main.py:4764-4779). The rows carry a propensity and policy_version like any other. The trainer's corpus query filters only on mode and feature_schema_version: `WHERE mode = ANY(:modes) AND feature_schema_version = :schema` (scripts/train_treatment_models.py:127-137) — no trigger_kind filter. decisions.insights and metrics.report likewise do not exclude them.

**Impact.** Every screen refresh, every UI poll, every browser prefetch of a GET appends to the corpus the models are fitted on and the scoreboard is computed from. The book here is 20 customers and the corpus grows 19-42 rows/day (established fact) — a rate a 20-customer book cannot generate from real events alone. Off-policy evaluation is only valid over decisions the logging policy actually took; mixing in never-enacted UI queries biases coverage, action mix, expected value and the timing model's negatives (a never-enacted row with outcome 'cancelled' or 'unresolved' is labelled 0 at train_treatment_models.py:181-196). A model-risk reviewer will reject the corpus on this alone.

**Fix.** Two changes. (1) Tag the row: add a `decision_source` column ('policy' | 'inspection') and set it from the trigger site; exclude 'inspection' from the trainer, from insights and from metrics by default. (2) Make /treatment/next a POST, or make it not write at all and add an explicit POST /treatment/simulate for the supervisor question. Also rate-limit it.

### `get-treatment-next-mints-an-enactable-plan` — A read-scoped GET commits an unsuppressed plan that the executor then carries out, so opening a screen contacts a borrower

**backend/db_treatment_holds.py:302** · compliance · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `W01-triggers`

`GET /treatment/next` (main.py:4764-4779, mapped to COLLECTIONS_READ at authz.py:442) calls next_treatment, which commits the decision: `with engine.begin() as conn: ... result = recommend_treatment(customer_id=customer_id, account_id=account_id, trigger=Trigger(trigger), conn=conn)` (db_treatment_holds.py:302-311). In this deployment TREATMENT_MODE=live, so engine.py:340 `suppressed = verdict.suppressed or mode == config.MODE_SHADOW` leaves an approved decision unsuppressed and engine.py:391 writes `scheduled_at=(chosen.at if chosen and not suppressed else None)`. The executor's claim predicate has no trigger-kind filter: decisions.claim_due selects `WHERE enacted IS FALSE AND mode <> 'simulated' AND suppression_reason IS NULL AND outcome IS NULL AND chosen_action IS NOT NULL AND chosen_action <> 'wait' AND scheduled_at IS NOT NULL AND scheduled_at <= now()` (decisions.py:359-385), and enact_one likewise gates only on mode, plan age, deferred actions, customer existence, prior resolution and contact_policy (enact.py:81-142). bot_worker.py:125-127 runs treatment_enact.process_one every tick. The route docstring at main.py:4770-4772 asserts the opposite — 'outside TREATMENT_MODE=live the engine decides, logs and enacts nothing' — which is true of shadow and false of this deployment.

**Impact.** A supervisor opening the Floor screen, a browser prefetching a GET, a dashboard poller or a link crawler causes a real WhatsApp, SMS or bot call to a delinquent borrower, attributed to no case and no trigger_ref. GET is the one HTTP method every proxy, monitor and browser treats as free to repeat, and it is behind a read-only scope, so nobody in the deployment believes the read surface can contact anyone. Combined with the 'statutory' bypass and the phone_alt fallback this is a borrower contact with no operator intent behind it, which is exactly what an RBI conduct review and a DPDP processing-record audit ask about. The `trigger` query parameter is also caller-controlled (main.py:4767), so a screen can mint decisions under trigger_kind='bounce' with a NULL trigger_ref, polluting case aggregation as well.

**Fix.** Make inspection non-enactable at the source, not at the caller: pass a read_only flag into recommend_treatment so the logged row carries decision_source='inspection' and scheduled_at NULL, and add `AND decision_source = 'policy'` to claim_due and claim_by_id. Move the endpoint to POST /treatment/simulate, restrict the trigger parameter to 'manual', and add a test that a decision written by the read surface is never returned by claim_due.

### `bounce-return-code-discarded` — The NACH/NPCI return code is thrown away at the door and never stored anywhere

**backend/payment_events.py:81** · integration · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`reason = str(_pick(body, "reason") or "unknown").strip().lower()` then `if reason not in REASONS: reason = "unknown"` (payment_events.py:81-83), against REASONS = {insufficient_funds, account_closed, mandate_expired, technical, unknown} (line 30-32). The payload's raw code is never persisted; payment_events has no return_code column (sql/02_customer_account.sql:162-189). Meanwhile mandate_presentations.return_code exists with the comment 'Kept verbatim. The normalised reason below is a lossy projection, and a chargeback is argued from the original code' (sql/05_collections.sql:484-486) and is never written by this path.

**Impact.** A real NACH return file carries dozens of codes. 'Payment stopped by drawer' (a dispute signal that must suppress dunning), 'account frozen' (a legal signal), 'amount exceeds mandate limit' (a re-presentation opportunity at a lower amount) and 'signature mismatch' (a data-quality problem) all collapse to 'unknown' or 'technical'. The bank cannot reconcile our case list against its own return file, cannot argue a chargeback, and the treatment engine can never learn that account_closed and stopped-by-drawer deserve opposite treatments. This is the highest-value feature the engine is being denied, and it is free — the vendor already sends it.

**Fix.** Add `return_code TEXT` and `raw_payload jsonb` to payment_events, keep the code verbatim, and make REASONS a normalisation MAP (NPCI code -> reason) loaded from a per-rail config table rather than a hardcoded frozenset. Emit a metric and a work item on any code that does not map, so an unmapped code is visible instead of silently 'unknown'. Expose return_code as a treatment feature.

### `represented-bounce-silently-swallowed` — A second bounce on the same EMI is swallowed: no fee, no DPD bump, no new decision, and its source_ref is never recorded

**backend/payment_events.py:244** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`SELECT * FROM payment_events WHERE account_id = :aid AND emi_installment_id = :emi AND kind = 'bounce' AND status IN ('open','in_progress') FOR UPDATE` ... `if open_emi: ... return _result(event, idempotent=True)` (payment_events.py:244-266), enforced by uq_payment_events_open_emi (sql/02_customer_account.sql:192-196). Execution returns before the fee ledger insert (296-324), before the DPD/bucket update (284-294) and before _plan_next (416).

**Impact.** NACH re-presentation within a cycle is routine — an EMI commonly bounces twice or three times, each with its own bank charge and its own return code. Here the second and third bounces vanish: the bounce fee is never posted (the bank silently absorbs it or the reconciliation breaks), DPD never advances, the treatment engine is never re-asked, and because the second source_ref is never written, a later legitimate replay of that event re-enters this same branch forever and is never protected by the source_ref index. The 'idempotent: true' response tells the CBS everything was fine.

**Fix.** Separate the case from the event. Always insert a payment_events row per (tenant, source, source_ref) — that is the fact — and hang case state (first_touch, next_voice_at, status) off a separate case row keyed on (account, emi). Post the fee and re-ask the engine for every event; suppress only the borrower-facing send, not the record.

### `no-payment-received-trigger` — There is no ingest path for a payment that did not come through our own pay-link, so a borrower who pays at a branch keeps getting dunned

**backend/payment_events.py:342** · integration · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

The event kind is hardcoded to 'bounce' in the INSERT (payment_events.py:342) and the table CHECK allows nothing else: `kind TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (kind IN ('bounce'))` (sql/02_customer_account.sql:168). The only caller of cure_for_account is payments.py:231, inside the hosted-intent settlement path. followthrough.resolve_case is only reached from payments._close_treatment_cases (payments.py:240, 268-298).

**Impact.** In a bank, the large majority of cures arrive through the core banking system: branch cash, NEFT to the loan account, a successful NACH re-presentation, a UPI autopay retry, an agency deposit. None of those reach payments.py. The bounce stays 'open', next_voice_at stays set, the treatment plan stays scheduled, and at 18:00 the bot rings a borrower who paid at 15:00 — the exact scenario followthrough.py:475-477 names as 'the single worst thing a collections system can do'. It is also an RBI fair-practice complaint and, at scale, the thing that gets the pilot cancelled.

**Fix.** Widen payment_events.kind to include 'payment' and 'mandate_success', add a POST /webhooks/collections/payment-events path for credits (same HMAC, same idempotency on source_ref), and on ingest of a credit call cure_for_account + followthrough.resolve_case + cancel the open clerk work item. Treat 'no CBS credit feed configured' as a deployment blocker in the readiness checklist, not an optional integration.

### `debt-details-sent-to-phone-alt` — Debt amount, due date and failure reason are sent to phone_alt when phone_primary is missing, with no check that phone_alt belongs to the borrower

**backend/payment_events.py:578** · privacy · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`phone = account.get("phone_primary") or account.get("phone_alt")` (payment_events.py:578, again at 822 for the voice dial; promise_fulfillment.py:550 and 994 do the same). The body is built by _bounce_copy: `f"Your EMI of Rs.{rupees} due {date_s} did not go through ({why}). Pay securely here: {pay_url}. Do not share this link."` (payment_events.py:166-169), where `why` is the plain-language failure reason including 'account closed'.

**Impact.** In Indian lending, phone_alt is very often a reference, a spouse, an employer or a guarantor captured at origination. Disclosing that a named borrower's EMI bounced, for how much, and why, to a third party is a DPDP purpose-limitation breach and squarely against RBI's fair-practice prohibition on disclosing a borrower's default to third parties. On a 20-customer dev book with clean phone_primary values this never fires; on a real book with 5-15% missing primaries it fires thousands of times a day and each one is a complaint waiting to happen.

**Fix.** Never fall back to an alternate number for a debt-disclosing message. Add a phone_role/consent flag on the number and require role='self' with an unexpired consent basis for any message containing amount, reason or a pay link. If no compliant number exists, suppress with reason 'no_self_phone_on_file' and raise a data-quality work item.

### `statutory-bypasses-hours-dnd-and-window` — The bounce first touch declares itself 'statutory' in code, which skips DND, calling hours, the borrower's preferred window and allowed days

**backend/payment_events.py:588** · compliance · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

payment_events.py:588 `purpose="statutory"` (and promise_fulfillment.py:599 for the PTP confirm). contact_policy._veto gates every timing rule on outreach only: `if purpose == "outreach" and (customer.get("dnd") or customer.get("dnd_registry")): return REASON_CUSTOMER_DND` (contact_policy.py:487), the published/RBI calling window at 490-500, and the preferred window plus allowed_days at 502-525. admit() then reserves against `cap + 10_000` so the daily cap cannot stop it either (contact_policy.py:977-981).

**Impact.** A bounce file that lands at 02:30 IST — normal for NACH settlement — sends 'Your EMI of Rs.X due 05 Sep 2026 did not go through (account closed). Pay securely here...' to a DND-registered borrower at 02:30, outside their stated window, with no cap. Whether that is lawful turns entirely on a classification asserted by a Python keyword argument, with no rule engine, no per-tenant configuration and no legal sign-off recorded anywhere. RBI DOR.MCS.REC.No.199 (effective 2027-01-01) and TRAI DLT both make this the bank's liability, not ours, which is precisely why the bank's compliance team will not sign it off in this form.

**Fix.** Make the statutory exemption data, not code: a per-tenant statutory_rules row naming which purposes are exempt from which gates, with an effective date and an approver. Default the exemption to hours-only (never DND, never the borrower's explicit quiet hours), and queue anything that arrives outside 08:00-19:00 to the next window rather than sending immediately. Log the rule id that authorised each exempt send.

### `voice-dial-inside-ingest-transaction` — A PSTN call is placed synchronously inside the webhook's open transaction, on a second connection, while the account row is locked

**backend/payment_events.py:859** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`with dbmod.engine.begin() as own:` then mission_mod.build(own,...) and outbound.reserve(own,...) at payment_events.py:860-883, committed independently; then `placed = outbound.place(dbmod.engine, attempt, to_phone=phone)` at 886 — a carrier API call — and only afterwards `conn.execute(UPDATE payment_events ... first_touch_channel = 'voice')` at 897-910 on the outer transaction. All of this runs inside main.py:977 `with db.engine.begin() as conn:` while ingest still holds FOR UPDATE OF a on the account (line 199).

**Impact.** Three distinct failures. (1) If the outer transaction rolls back for any later reason, or the HTTP client disconnects, the borrower has already been rung and an outbound_attempt row is committed, but no payment_event exists — an outbound call with no case record, which under the RBI recording-retention rule is a call we cannot explain. (2) Anything inside mission.build or outbound.reserve that locks the same account row deadlocks against its own outer transaction and blocks until statement_timeout. (3) A slow carrier turns the CBS's webhook into a timeout; the CBS retries; retries pile up behind the row lock and the bounce file stalls. Under a morning bounce batch this is an outage.

**Fix.** Never dial inside the ingest transaction. Ingest should only set next_voice_at (even when the window is open) and let process_one_voice place the call from the worker, on its own connection, after the bounce has committed. Delete _try_voice_now's call from _digital_blocked.

### `settle-promises-one-giant-transaction` — settle_promises runs the entire book's breakage, N engine calls and N webhook dispatches in one unbounded transaction on the shared worker tick

**backend/promise_fulfillment.py:870** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`with engine.begin() as conn:` at promise_fulfillment.py:870 wraps: an unbounded `UPDATE promises SET status='due_today'` across all tenants (871-881), an unbounded intent-expiry UPDATE (882-892), an unbounded `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` of every overdue promise (893-905), and then a Python loop (906-961) that per row calls _next_action (a full recommend_treatment with feature queries), inserts a followup, records activity and dispatches a webhook. Invoked from bot_worker.py:89-90 on every 20th tick of the single-threaded worker.

**Impact.** On a 20-customer book this is instant. On a 50,000-account book with a 3% daily break rate it is ~1,500 engine invocations plus 1,500 webhook dispatches inside one transaction, holding row locks on every broken promise for minutes, blocking WhatsApp outbound, bot turns and every treatment queue behind it, generating replication lag and table bloat. If it fails at row 1,400 the whole thing rolls back and re-runs from scratch — and it will fail, because the per-statement timeout does not bound a transaction. There is also no advisory lock, so two workers do the same work.

**Fix.** Chunk it: claim N rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, commit per chunk, and return control to the tick between chunks. Scope every UPDATE by tenant and by a bounded window. Take a transaction-level advisory lock so only one worker settles at a time. Move it off the shared tick onto its own schedule.

### `clerk-hitl-approval-enacts-nothing` — An approved field visit / legal notice is marked done and never enacted

**backend/agent_core/clerk.py:145** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`if job.get("approvedBy"): return {"parked": False, "approved": True, "action": action, "enactedBy": "human"}` (clerk.py:145-146). The function returns before the enactment block at 165-179, so process_one calls finish(ok=True) and the job goes to 'completed'. The claim `"enactedBy": "human"` is false - nobody enacted anything. And the decision it refers to was already pushed 30 days out by _defer_hitl_plan (116-132) on the way in. Even if it did fall through, enact.py:41 `DEFERRED = frozenset({A.FIELD_VISIT, A.LEGAL_NOTICE})` and 92-99 would `record_outcome(decision_id, "cancelled")`.

**Impact.** A supervisor approves a legal notice or a field visit on the Floor; the UI shows the job completed and attributed to a human; nothing is sent, nobody visits, and the treatment decision sits unenacted with a scheduled_at a month away. The bank's recovery pipeline silently drops its most consequential actions, and the audit trail says they were approved and completed. This is both an operational loss and a false record in a regulated workflow.

**Fix.** Either implement the executors (a field-visit work order and a legal-notice document request) and route the approved job through them, or make the park terminal and honest: on approval, record_outcome('cancelled', reason='no_executor') and return {"acted": false, "reason": "no_executor"} so the Floor shows the approval as un-actionable. Never write enactedBy for an action that was not enacted.

### `clerk-completes-every-treatment-work-item-unactioned` — The clerk drains work_runtime_jobs regardless of workflow type and marks every LMS work item 'completed' without doing anything

**backend/agent_core/clerk.py:151** · correctness · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `W03-workers`

adapter_pg.claim_next (adapter_pg.py:164-176) selects `SELECT id FROM work_runtime_jobs WHERE tenant_id = :t AND status IN ('submitted','working') ORDER BY created_at ... LIMIT 1` with NO workflow_type predicate, so the clerk claims every row in the table. clerk._run (clerk.py:135-156) recognises a2a_remote, doc_sla, callback_diary and the HITL actions; everything else falls through to `action = str(payload.get("action") or "")` and then `if action in {A.WAIT, ""}: return {"skipped": True, "reason": "wait"}` (clerk.py:151-152). process_one then calls `finish(jid, ok=True, result=result)` (clerk.py:103) and adapter_pg.finish writes status='completed' (adapter_pg.py:202). The three work items the treatment executor hands to the lender's servicing system carry no 'action' key at all: `mandate_representment` (enact.py:720-733: presentationId, decisionId, accountId, amount, presentedFor, rationale), `emi_date_change` (enact.py:770-782: decisionId, accountId, proposedDueDay, salaryCreditDay, rationale) and `self_service_plan` (enact.py:825-838). The sweep's resume cursor row is claimed too - sweep._write_cursor writes it with `status="working"` (sweep.py:238-244).

**Impact.** enact.mark_enacted stamps the decision `enacted=true, enacted_ref='work:wrj-…'` (enact.py:70, 155) and the clerk then closes the work item as completed within one tick, so the platform's record says a mandate re-presentment was handed to the lender and finished when nobody was ever asked to present it - and a mandate presentment is a debit against a borrower's bank account, the one action enact.py:531-540 says there is no recoverable version of getting wrong. The same silently swallows every EMI-date-change request and every self-service repayment plan, which are candidate actions in the 0-30 and 31-60 buckets the engine spends most of its time in. Nothing on the Floor or in /work-runtime/jobs shows an outstanding item, because the item is green.

**Fix.** Give claim_next a workflow_type allow-list (or give work_runtime_jobs a queue/consumer column) so the clerk claims only the workflow types it implements; make the fall-through in clerk._run finish ok=False with reason='no_executor' instead of ok=True; and stop storing the sweep cursor as a claimable job row - or give it a status ('cursor') that no claimer selects. Add a test that enqueues each of the three treatment work types and asserts the clerk leaves them unclaimed.

### `worker-single-process-spof` — One un-replicated process performs every borrower-facing action, with a liveness check that only asks whether PID 1 exists

**backend/bot_worker.py:166** · reliability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

bot_worker.main() is a single-threaded while loop (bot_worker.py:217-233); docker-compose.yml:179-208 runs exactly one container with `command: ["python", "-m", "bot_worker"]` and `healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "kill -0 1"]`. There is no leader election, no replica, no readiness signal tied to progress, and no heartbeat row. claim_next's double-claim defect (above) blocks adding a replica anyway.

**Impact.** Every WhatsApp send, bot reply, PTP reminder, bounce voice, call close, cadence retry, campaign dial, treatment enactment, follow-through attribution, book sweep, webhook egress and clerk job stops when this one process stops - and the healthcheck will keep reporting healthy while it is wedged on a database lock. It compounds: enact.py:45,88-90 cancels any plan older than MAX_PLAN_AGE (12h), so a half-day outage does not just delay the day's plans, it stamps them outcome='cancelled' - which is why 84 of 108 outcomes on this book are already 'cancelled'. Worker availability is silently corrupting the label distribution the uplift model will be trained on.

**Fix.** Make the worker horizontally scalable (fix claim_next, add per-queue leases), run at least two replicas, and replace the healthcheck with a real liveness probe: a heartbeat row or file updated at the end of every tick plus a small HTTP /healthz that fails when the last tick is older than N seconds. Alert on the enact 'plan_expired' counter - a spike is an outage signature, not a modelling result.

### `payments-appenv-defaults-to-dev` — APP_ENV defaults to 'dev', so a missing env var turns on an unauthenticated 'mark paid' endpoint that writes the ledger

**backend/payments.py:40** · security · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`def app_env() -> str: return _env("APP_ENV", "dev").lower()` and `def is_production() -> bool: return app_env() in {"prod", "production"}` (payments.py:39-44). main.py:902 guards the sandbox completion with `if payments.is_production() or payments.provider() != "hosted": raise HTTPException(403)`, and '/pay' is in the unauthenticated public route list (main.py:269). So with APP_ENV unset, POST /pay/{token}/complete posts a ledger entry, reduces accounts.outstanding and marks promises kept, with the URL token as the only credential.

**Impact.** A money-affecting control fails OPEN on a missing environment variable, in a deployment model where the customer's ops team writes the env file. Anyone who obtains or observes a payment link (a shared phone, a forwarded WhatsApp message, a proxy log) can mark the debt paid. The bank's finance function will treat an unauthenticated ledger write as a P1 audit finding regardless of whether it was exploited.

**Fix.** Default APP_ENV to 'prod' (fail closed), require an explicit opt-in flag (PAYMENTS_SANDBOX_COMPLETE_ENABLED) for the sandbox route, and refuse to start the API when APP_ENV is unset.

### `payments-no-core-banking-ingress` — The only way money enters the system is a payment_intent this platform created

**backend/payments.py:117** · integration · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

record_payment resolves the payment strictly through payment_intents by id or public_token (payments.py:135-147: `raise ValueError("intent_not_specified")` otherwise, `raise KeyError("payment_intent_not_found")`), and both entry points (main.py:897 hosted sandbox, main.py:927 PSP webhook) go through it. There is no branch that accepts an account-level repayment with no intent.

**Impact.** In a bank most repayments arrive by NACH/e-mandate presentation, branch cash, UPI to the loan account, cheque clearing or a nightly CBS reconciliation file - none of which carry this platform's intent id. Every one of those is invisible: the ledger is not updated, promises are not marked kept, bounce cases are not cured, and treatments are not retired. On day one of a real deployment the engine is deciding against a stale balance and calling people who have paid.

**Fix.** Add an account-level ingest (batch file + webhook) keyed on (account_id, value_date, amount, bank_ref) with its own idempotency table, that posts the ledger entry, allocates to promises, cures bounces and closes treatment cases via the same code path. Treat payment_intents as one source among several, not the identity of a payment.

### `payments-no-reversal-path` — There is no reversal, refund or chargeback path, although payment.reversed is advertised to tenants

**backend/payments.py:117** · data-model · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

payments.py contains record_payment and allocate_to_promises and nothing that undoes either; ops_screens.py:110 publishes `{"key": "payment.reversed", "category": "Payments", "description": "Payment reversed."}` in the subscribable event catalog, and no code emits it.

**Impact.** Cheque returns, failed NACH presentations after provisional credit, PSP chargebacks and mistaken postings are routine in Indian collections. Today a reversal cannot be represented: the ledger entry stands, outstanding stays reduced, the promise stays 'kept', the treatment case stays closed as 'paid' and the account is never chased again. Money owed silently leaves the book, and the training corpus keeps a false positive forever.

**Fix.** Add reverse_payment(): a compensating ledger entry, intent status 'reversed', promise re-opened with paid_amount reduced, bounce case re-opened, treatment case re-decided, and emit payment.reversed. Make it idempotent on the provider's reversal reference.

### `payments-any-amount-marks-intent-paid` — Any positive amount marks the intent paid and closes the treatment case as 'paid', however small

**backend/payments.py:193** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

The only amount validation is `if paid <= 0: raise ValueError("invalid_payment_amount")` (payments.py:131-132). The intent is then set `status = 'paid'` unconditionally (193-210) with no comparison to intent['amount']; allocation makes the promise 'partial' (347-349); and _close_treatment_cases resolves the case with outcome='paid' for both 'kept' AND 'partial' (`if str(row.get("status")) not in {"kept", "partial"}: continue`, 289-290).

**Impact.** A one-rupee token payment against a 50,000-rupee promise closes the payment intent, retires the scheduled treatment, and labels the decision 'paid'. Collections stops chasing a barely-paying account, and the learning loop is told the action succeeded. Partial payment is the norm in Indian retail collections, not an edge case.

**Fix.** Compare paid against intent['amount']: keep the intent open (status 'partial') below a configurable materiality threshold, resolve the treatment case only on 'kept', and introduce a distinct outcome label ('part_paid') that the scorer and trainer treat separately from 'paid'.

### `payments-only-closes-bounce-and-ptp-cases` — A payment retires only bounce and broken-PTP cases; every sweep-generated plan survives and still dials

**backend/payments.py:284** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

_close_treatment_cases resolves exactly two trigger kinds - `trigger_kind="bounce"` (286) and `trigger_kind="broken_ptp"` (291) - and resolve_case matches on (trigger_kind, trigger_ref) (followthrough.py:486-487). The book sweep stamps its decisions with a different trigger entirely: `TRIGGER = "dpd_tick"` (agent_core/treatment/sweep.py:73), and the sweep is the dominant producer of live decisions on this deployment.

**Impact.** The docstring says 'The worst thing a collections system can do is ring somebody about a debt they have already paid' - and that is exactly what happens for the majority of scheduled plans. A borrower pays at 15:00 and the 18:00 dpd_tick plan still dials. Under RBI fair-practice / the 2027 directions this is the complaint that gets an NBFC's collections practice examined, and it is the fastest way to lose the customer's trust in the channel.

**Fix.** Close by ENTITY, not by trigger ref: after a payment, resolve all unenacted decisions for that account (or customer) whose predicate no longer holds - dpd_tick included - and re-run the decision instead of blindly cancelling where the account is still delinquent. Add a mandatory 'is this debt still owed?' re-check inside enact immediately before any contact.

### `payments-cleanup-poisons-the-payment-transaction` — The 'never raises' cleanup can abort the enclosing Postgres transaction and roll the whole payment back

**backend/payments.py:297** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`except Exception: logger.exception("closing treatment cases after payment failed")` (payments.py:297-298), documented at 279 as 'Never raises: a payment must record even if the cleanup does not'; the same pattern at 238-239 for cure_for_account. But conn is the caller's open transaction (main.py:944 `with db.engine.begin() as conn:`), and a failed statement puts Postgres into aborted-transaction state - catching the Python exception does not undo that. Everything after it, including webhooks_dispatch.dispatch (line 244) and the COMMIT, then fails. No SAVEPOINT / begin_nested anywhere in the module.

**Impact.** A borrower pays, the PSP webhook 200s or 500s depending on where the failure lands, and the ledger entry, the intent status, the promise allocation and the bounce cure all disappear together because a downstream cleanup query hit a bad column. The system then keeps chasing a borrower who has paid, and the bank's ledger disagrees with the PSP's settlement file. This is the single highest-consequence defect in the payments path.

**Fix.** Wrap each best-effort cleanup in `with conn.begin_nested():` so a failure rolls back only the savepoint, and add a test that injects a failing statement inside _close_treatment_cases and asserts the ledger entry still commits.

### `payments-production-has-no-checkout` — In production the pay page offers no way to pay, and Razorpay link creation is a stub

**backend/payments.py:445** · integration · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`if not paid and not expired and not is_production() and provider() == "hosted":` guards the ONLY interactive element on the page (payments.py:445-452); with APP_ENV=prod the page renders heading, amount and status and nothing else. checkout_url with PAYMENT_PROVIDER=razorpay logs 'checkout creation is stubbed; using hosted URL' and returns the hosted path anyway (52-59).

**Impact.** Every payment link the engine sends - and send_payment_link is one of the treatment actions whose expected value the scorer is optimising - lands a borrower on a dead page in production. The action's measured conversion will be zero, the model will learn (correctly, for the wrong reason) that payment links do not work, and the collections head will conclude the AI is useless.

**Fix.** Implement the Razorpay (and UPI intent / payment-link) order creation before any live deployment, or fail closed: refuse to create an intent when no real checkout is configured, so the engine never selects an action it cannot carry out.

### `frontend-fabricates-offer-in-browser` — The offline NBA derivation invents a Top-up Loan of ₹1,50,000 that no engine ever approved, and it renders on every first paint

**Habibi/src/lib/customerInsights.ts:213** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

mockOfferPolicy: `productId: "topup-loan", productName: "Top-up Loan", suggestedAmount: 150000, talkTrack: "You may be eligible for a Top-up Loan of about one point five lakh rupees.", presented: true` (customerInsights.ts:212-217), triggered by `const presented = customer.interactions.some((i) => i.intents?.upsellPresented)` (line 206). Its only guard is `if (customer.contact.dnd)` (line 197) — no channel consent, no hardship, no DPD, no 30-day cap, no eligibility. It is fed into offerNba (line 495) which renders 'Pitch Top-up Loan · ₹1,50,000'. This runs on the live path, not only in mock: `const insights = insightsQuery.data ?? deriveCustomerInsights(customer)` (customers.$customerId.lazy.tsx:114) renders it on every first paint before the query resolves, and api/customers.ts:44-57 falls back to it whenever /insights fails.

**Impact.** This is the duplicated hardcoded ladder that survives. The contact ladder was removed from both copies with great care; the product ladder was left behind in the browser. A rep opening any customer with a historical upsellPresented flag sees a ₹1.5 lakh pitch, with a talk track, attributed to no decision id and approved by no engine — and it persists for the whole session if the insights endpoint is down. In a bank that is an unapproved credit solicitation quoted to a borrower, with a rupee figure, sourced from a literal in a JavaScript bundle.

**Fix.** Delete mockOfferPolicy and pass `undefined` for offerPolicy in the offline derivation, exactly as the file already did for the authority matrix (customerInsights.ts:243-248). The offline path should render case handling plus the existing 'Recommendation unavailable' row and nothing commercial. Separately, stop rendering the offline derivation while the query is merely pending — show a skeleton — so it is reached only on genuine failure.

### `nba-no-outcome-feedback-loop` — decisionId reaches the card and is never sent back — no rep action is ever attributed to a decision

**Habibi/src/routes/customers.$customerId.lazy.tsx:184** · statistics · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

The id is produced (customer_insights.py:208 and 226 `"decisionId": treatment.get("decisionId")`), typed (customerInsights.ts:45 `decisionId?: string | null`), and serialised (schemas.py:211 `decisionId: str | None = None`). `onNbaAction = (action: NbaActionKind) => {...}` (customers.$customerId.lazy.tsx:184) takes only the action kind — the item, and therefore the id, is discarded at the call boundary. NextBestActionCard reads exactly one engine field: `{primary.advisory ? <StatusChip label="shadow" .../> : null}` (NextBestActionCard.tsx:75). No route or mutation posts an outcome.

**Impact.** This is the structural reason 106 of 225 treatment_decisions have a null outcome and offer_decisions has zero responses in its whole history. The engine writes decisions and never learns what happened; the fitted uplift model therefore has nothing but simulated corpus to train on (models/treatment_uplift.json 'corpus: simulated'), which is why it does not serve. A self-improving system that never observes its own actions is not self-improving. A model-risk reviewer will call this out before anything else.

**Fix.** Change onNbaAction's signature to take the NbaItem, and on every dispatch POST {decisionId, action, actorUserId, at} to a new outcome endpoint that writes treatment_decisions.outcome (accepted / overridden / dismissed) and offer_decisions.response. This one change converts the read-only decision log into a labelled training set and is the highest-leverage item in this report.

### `offer-policy-open-lead-overrides-suppression` — An open lead overwrites a suppressed status, so a DND borrower gets a 'Follow up' card and loses the DND warning

**backend/agent_core/reco/policy.py:140** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

policy._merge: `if lead: ... out["status"] = "open_lead"` (policy.py:133-140), applied after `out.update(_from_decision(decision))` which may have set status='suppressed' with suppressionReason='dnd' (policy.py:164-177, labels at policy.py:36-37). customer_insights._offer_nba accepts 'open_lead' (`if status not in {"ready","presented","interested","open_lead"}: return None`, customer_insights.py:107) and renders `'Follow up' if follow else 'Pitch'` (customer_insights.py:120). The protective bullet is gated on the overwritten value: `if offer_policy and offer_policy.get("status") == "suppressed": ... "Offer engine quiet: {label}. Do not freelance a product."` (customer_insights.py:461-466).

**Impact.** The two failure modes compound. A borrower who registered DND (or withdrew channel consent under DPDP) but has an old open lead is shown 'Follow up Top-up Loan · ₹1,50,000' as a ranked next-best action, and the 'DND is on — do not pitch' warning that would have stopped the rep is suppressed by the very same overwrite. A rep acting on the card makes a marketing contact to a DND number — a TRAI/DLT and RBI Fair Practices breach that a regulator can reconstruct from the decision log.

**Fix.** Make suppression dominant in _merge: when the latest decision has a suppression_reason, keep status='suppressed' and expose the lead separately (leadId/leadStage) rather than as a status. Independently, make the ins-offer-quiet bullet fire on `suppressionReason` being set rather than on the status string, so it cannot be masked by a later status transition.

### `offer-presented-double-counted` — A converted offer emits two offer_presented events, deflating the measured conversion rate

**backend/agent_core/tools/domain.py:558** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

capture_lead emits one: `capture.record_offer_presented(conn, interaction_id=interaction_id, product_id=pid, source="capture_lead", ...)` (domain.py:558-564). mark_upsell_presented emits another for the same interaction and product: `capture.record_offer_presented(conn, ..., source="voice_upsell", ...)` (domain.py:609-616), called from voice/tools.py:2035-2040, :2221-2226 and bot_tools.py:499-501. capture.record_offer_presented (capture.py:1505-1523) has no idempotency at all — it unconditionally marks the interaction and emits a commercial event.

**Impact.** Presented = actual presentations + conversions. Conversion rate = conversions / (presentations + conversions), understated by exactly the conversion rate itself — a true 20% reads as 16.7%. The funnel the collections head uses to decide whether to keep the offer engine is systematically wrong, and the error grows as the engine gets better, which is the worst possible direction.

**Fix.** Make record_offer_presented idempotent on (interaction_id, product_id) — the same treatment the CRM writes already get via idempotency keys — or drop the emit from capture_lead, since every lead is preceded by a presentation on every path that has one.

### `reco-write-txn-held-across-scoring` — Every reco call opens a write transaction and holds it for the whole scoring pass, against a 15-connection pool

**backend/voice/tools.py:1976** · scale · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

`with db.engine.begin() as conn: return reco_engine.recommend(...)` at voice/tools.py:1976, :2176, bot_tools.py:457 and insurance.py:122. engine.begin() is a write transaction (db_core.py:183-185 binds the tenant GUC on 'begin'). Pool is `pool_size=DB_POOL_SIZE` default 5 plus `max_overflow` default 10 (db_core.py:148-149, 172-173), and the comment there notes the sum across processes must stay under max_connections. _prepare_close_probe opens three such transactions in sequence — recommend (2176), present (2220), mark_upsell_presented (2221).

**Impact.** At 20 customers and a couple of concurrent calls, invisible. At a call-centre's concurrency — say 100 simultaneous voice legs — each in-flight recommendation pins a connection for the duration of feature assembly, candidate scoring and the decision-log insert, and the close probe pins three in a row at the exact moment every call converges on hangup. Pool exhaustion manifests as calls hanging on a tool result, which is the same symptom as the missing timeout above and compounds with it.

**Fix.** Split the read from the write: assemble features and score on engine.connect(), open engine.begin() only for the decision-log insert. Batch the close probe's three round trips into one transaction. Size the voice pool explicitly per process role rather than inheriting the API default.

### `reco-callsite-no-latency-guard` — The offer engine runs on the live audio path with no timeout at any layer

**backend/voice/tools.py:1988** · reliability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

`result = await asyncio.to_thread(_run)` (voice/tools.py:1988, repeated at 2188) wrapping `with db.engine.begin() as conn: return reco_engine.recommend(...)`. There is no asyncio.wait_for. The ToolSpec for recommend_next_offer declares no timeout (catalog.py:723-734: `args=(), channels=BOTH,` — no timeout_secs), and the ToolSpec default is None (schema.py:96 `timeout_secs: float | None = None`). The only backstop is Postgres statement_timeout, which in the voice process is 60000ms (db_core.py:152-154: `_DEFAULT_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS = 60000 if _PROCESS_ROLE in {"worker","bot_worker","voice"}`).

**Impact.** On a 20-customer dev book every query is instant. On a bank's book — offer_decisions with millions of rows, a shared Postgres under batch load, an eligibility join across products/consent — a slow plan turns into up to 60 seconds of dead air mid-call, and the close-probe path (2188) makes it up to 60 seconds of dead air on the hangup. The caller hangs up, the call is dispositioned as abandoned, and nothing in the trace says the offer engine caused it. This is the single most likely first-week outage on a pilot.

**Fix.** Set timeout_secs on the recommend_next_offer ToolSpec (Pipecat Flows already plumbs it, schema.py:174-175), and wrap both reco call sites in asyncio.wait_for with a hard budget (400-600ms) whose timeout branch returns the existing suppressed/engine_error payload at voice/tools.py:1993-1999. Add a per-role DB_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS for the reco query specifically. Record the timeout as a distinct suppression_reason so it is countable.

### `close-probe-presents-unspoken-offer` — The close probe marks an offer presented and burns 30-day quota before knowing whether it will be spoken

**backend/voice/tools.py:2203** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

_prepare_close_probe does `state.offers_presented += 1` (2203) and then `await asyncio.to_thread(reco_engine.present, result.decision_id, top.product_id)` plus mark_upsell_presented (2219-2226). The clause it builds is explicitly conditional: `f" If — and only if — they say there is nothing else, you may add ONE short sentence to this effect: ..."` (2211-2217). _record_close_probe is then called with `with_offer=bool(state.close_probe_offer_clause)` (2270) — true even when nothing is said. The comment at 2031-2032 states present() is 'the moment campaign quota is actually consumed'.

**Impact.** Structural downward bias on the one number that decides whether the offer engine keeps its budget: every caller who answers 'actually, one more thing' contributes a presented offer with no conversion. On a real floor most callers do raise another topic, so measured conversion could be halved. Worse, per-customer 30-day quota (SUPPRESS_CUSTOMER_CAP, arbitration.py:105) is spent on offers the borrower never heard, so the engine goes quiet for a month on customers it never actually pitched. Model-risk review will reject a conversion metric whose denominator counts non-events.

**Fix.** Split the decision from the presentation on this path. Prepare the clause and stash decision_id + product_id, but call present()/mark_upsell_presented only when the pre_close node's transcript shows the clause was actually spoken (or on the next tool call from that node). Until that plumbing exists, record the probe offer under a distinct status (e.g. 'offered_conditionally') and exclude it from both the presented denominator and the quota counter.

### `uplift-treated-arm-is-the-complement-of-the-control-arm` — The T-learner's treated half is every row that is not in the control arm, including shadow rows and suppressed 'wait' decisions

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:1054** · statistics · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `X01-tests-di`

train_treatment_models.py:1053-1054 reads `control_rows = [r for r in rows if str(r.get("variant") or "") == CONTROL_ARM]` and `treated_rows = [r for r in rows if str(r.get("variant") or "") != CONTROL_ARM]`, with `CONTROL_ARM = "null_treatment"` at :97. There is no filter on `enacted`, on `chosen_action`, or on `variant IS NOT NULL`, and `_rows` (:120-139) selects every shadow and live row at the current feature schema. `_label_cure` (:199-210) then labels `unresolved` as 0, so a non-control decision that was suppressed to `wait` and never enacted enters the treated half as a treatment that failed. Contrast `_label_timing` (:174-197), which does compute `acted = bool(row.get("enacted")) and str(row.get("chosen_action") or "") != "wait"` and restricts itself to the rows where nothing was done — the trainer knows how to ask this question and does not ask it for uplift.

**Impact.** The quantity the uplift artifact reports as tau is not P(cure|treated) - P(cure|control). Its treated half pools genuine contacts with borrowers the engine deliberately left alone: rows with variant NULL (every shadow decision written before an A/B split existed), rows suppressed below the value floor or by a veto, and rows the executor aborted. Those are the counterfactual population, so the treated rate is dragged toward the control rate and the fitted tau is biased toward zero on exactly the strata where the engine suppresses most — the thin-consent, low-exposure, high-fatigue accounts. The artifact still passes load_uplift (models.py:628-679), which only checks that a control arm is *named* and that control_n clears 500, and still passes registry.check, which never inspects how the treated arm was constructed. This is the same class of error as the 'cancelled' label but a distinct code site and a distinct mechanism: one poisons the labels, this one poisons the arm membership.

**Fix.** Define the treated arm positively: `variant IS NOT NULL AND variant <> CONTROL_ARM AND enacted AND chosen_action <> 'wait'`, matching the restriction `_label_timing` already applies in the opposite direction. Record the arm definition and both arm sizes in the artifact so registry.check can refuse an artifact whose treated half is not a treated half. Add a test that a suppressed non-control row is excluded from `_samples(treated_rows, _label_cure)`.

### `sweep-dedupes-per-customer-not-per-account` — The sweep's idempotence test cannot see the under-coverage it is masking

**backend/tests/test_decision_intelligence_p0.py:796** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X01-tests-di`

p0:796-809 asserts zero duplicates over `GROUP BY customer_id, COALESCE(account_id, ''), trigger_ref`. sweep._claim selects per account (sweep.py:145-158, 'FOR UPDATE OF a ... two accounts of one borrower are two decisions') but sweep._decided_today (sweep.py:194-204) matches on `customer_id = :cid AND trigger_kind = :kind AND trigger_ref = :ref` with no account_id. The second account of a borrower returns True from _decided_today and is skipped.

**Impact.** On the 20-customer dev book every borrower has one account, so the defect is invisible and the test is green. In a bank a delinquent customer routinely holds a personal loan, a card and an auto loan; only one of them is ever decided per day, and which one depends on the account-id collation order. The corpus silently loses a large fraction of the book, exactly the failure mode p3:974-988 documents costing 17% of a 60-account run.

**Fix.** Add account_id to _decided_today's predicate and to the trigger_ref key, then add a test that seeds one customer with two delinquent accounts and asserts two dpd_tick decisions on the same local day. Until then the duplicate assertion should be paired with a coverage assertion: decided count == claimed count.
