The source may be a bot: HOLD_SOURCES includes 'bot' (db_treatment_holds.py:39) and db_treatment_holds.py:126-128 describes the flow — "a bot that hears 'I lost my job' twice in one call". db_treatment_holds.py:104 returns `"reason": r["reason"]` to every COLLECTIONS_READ holder whose visibility scope includes the customer, and it never expires.

**Impact.** The bot writes the borrower's own words about job loss, illness, a death in the family or a legal matter into an unbounded, unredacted, permanently retained column. Health data and data about a death are the most sensitive categories a collections platform will ever hold; DPDP does not have a separate special-category regime but s.8(5) safeguards and the Significant Data Fiduciary obligations bite hardest exactly here, and a grievance or a DPB inspection will go looking for this column first. It is also the one place in the treatment engine where the 'no free text the borrower said' rule stated at features.py:326-328 is broken.

**Fix.** Cap reason at ~200 chars in schemas.py and run it through pii_redact.redact_text before the INSERT. Better: make the bot-sourced path write a closed reason code (hold_reason enum) and keep the verbatim quote, if it is needed at all, on the interaction transcript where the redaction and retention machinery already applies to it. Exclude `reason` from the list response unless the caller holds COMPLIANCE_READ.

### `trainers-read-unscoped-and-unfiltered` — The propensity trainer reads every tenant's offer decisions including simulated ones; the treatment trainer filters mode but still reads every tenant

**backend/scripts/train_propensity.py:80** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-security-privacy`

train_propensity.py:69-87: `SELECT ... FROM offer_decisions d LEFT JOIN leads l ON l.id = d.lead_id WHERE d.presented IS TRUE AND d.chosen_product_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY d.created_at DESC LIMIT :lim` — no `tenant_id = :tenant`, and no `mode <> 'simulated'` even though scripts/simulate_offer_decisions.py writes rows with mode='simulated' into the same table and reco/observability.py:57-58 defines _modes() precisely to exclude them from reporting. train_treatment_models.py:120-138 gets the mode filter right (`modes = ["shadow", "live"] + (["simulated"] if include_simulated else [])`) but the query is still `FROM treatment_decisions WHERE mode = ANY(:modes) AND feature_schema_version = :schema` with no tenant predicate.

**Impact.** Two failures. (1) The propensity model is fitted partly on synthetic rows, which is how models/propensity.json came to report AUC .758 on 1335 samples when offer_decisions holds 16 real rows with zero responses. (2) On a shared deployment, one bank's borrower behaviour trains the model that decides the other bank's offers — a DPDP purpose-limitation breach (data collected to service A's loans used to build B's commercial model) and a competitive-confidentiality problem no bank will accept.

**Fix.** Add `AND d.mode <> 'simulated'` (unless --include-simulated, matching the treatment trainer) and `AND d.tenant_id = :tenant` to train_propensity.fetch_rows, and `AND tenant_id = :tenant` to train_treatment_models._rows. Record the tenant and the mode set on the artifact alongside the corpus field so the artifact states its own training population.

### `reco-propensity-artifact-carries-no-corpus-provenance` — The reco loader has no equivalent of the treatment loader's `corpus == simulated` refusal, and train_propensity.py never writes the field, so a model of a synthetic book can serve real customers

**backend/agent_core/reco/models.py:204** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

agent_core/treatment/models.py:546-565 refuses an artifact whose `corpus` is `simulated` unless TREATMENT_ALLOW_SIMULATED_MODELS is set, with the reasoning that 'a model fitted on it also looks exactly like a real model -- same shape, same metrics block, plausible coefficients'. agent_core/reco/models.py:204-232 checks only `type == logistic`, vector version, schema version and age; there is no corpus field on ModelArtifact at all. train_propensity.py:364-384 writes the artifact dict and never emits `corpus`. The shipped backend/models/propensity.json has no `corpus` key and records `nSamples: 1335` against an offer_decisions table holding 16 rows -- the training corpus does not exist any more, and nothing in the file says where it came from.

**Impact.** Setting RECO_SCORER=propensity is a one-line env change that puts a model fitted on scripts/simulate_offer_decisions.py output in front of real borrowers, scoring which product to pitch. It would load cleanly: vectorVersion v1, featureSchemaVersion v1, trainedAt 2026-07-31 (36 days old against a 90-day limit). The asymmetry with the treatment engine is the tell -- the same team applied the right gate on one engine and not the other.

**Fix.** Add `corpus` to reco's ModelArtifact and to load_artifact's refusal list, mirroring treatment/models.py:546-565 with a RECO_ALLOW_SIMULATED_MODELS opt-in. Have train_propensity.py write `"corpus": "simulated" if <the rows carried mode='simulated'> else "live"` and record the mode mix it trained on. Retire the existing propensity.json, which cannot prove its provenance either way.

### `grace-period-exceeds-the-attribution-window` — emi_date_change and self_service_plan have a 35-day grace but attribution only looks at decisions from the last 30 days, so those two actions can never receive a negative label

**backend/agent_core/treatment/config.py:283** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

config.py:282-288: `"emi_date_change": 24.0 * 35` and `"self_service_plan": 24.0 * 35` -- 840 hours = 35 days. followthrough.attribute_outcomes selects `AND created_at >= now() - interval '30 days'` (followthrough.py:117). `_outcome_for` returns `no_answer` only when `now - since >= grace` (:201-203), and `since` is `enacted_at or created_at` (:168), so the clock starts no earlier than creation. A row therefore falls out of the query at day 30 having never reached its grace at day 35, and `record_outcome`'s `WHERE outcome IS NULL` (decisions.py:344) means it is never revisited.

**Impact.** The only labels those two actions can ever receive are `paid`, `ptp`, `superseded`, `reached` or `undeliverable` -- all positive or neutral. Their negative class is structurally empty. Any model fitted on this corpus learns that offering a date change or a self-service plan works essentially always, and the EV scorer already gives emi_date_change a 3x value horizon (scoring.py:90) and self_service_plan a 2x (:96). The engine will converge on rewriting borrowers' repayment schedules as its favourite action, on evidence that is missing by construction. That is a contract change to a lending agreement, and it is the action a DPO and a product-control function will ask about first.

**Fix.** Make the attribution window a function of the longest grace rather than a constant: replace the literal 30 days at followthrough.py:117 with `now() - make_interval(days => :horizon)` where horizon = max(grace_hours over all actions)/24 + slack. Add a startup assertion that `max(_GRACE_DEFAULTS.values()) / 24 < ATTRIBUTION_WINDOW_DAYS`, so the next grace change cannot silently reintroduce this.

### `suppressed-decisions-dropped-by-the-estimator-built-to-read-them` — The engine deliberately records a propensity on every suppressed decision so the negative class is off-policy evaluable, and ope.observations then silently drops all of them

**backend/agent_core/treatment/engine.py:396** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

engine.py:393-398: 'A suppressed decision has a propensity of 1.0 and that is not a placeholder ... Writing NULL instead would make every suppression invisible to an off-policy estimator, which is exactly the negative class the corpus exists to carry.' But arbitration._hold (arbitration.py:188-201) constructs a Verdict with `propensity=max(1e-9, min(1.0, arm_probability))` and leaves `distribution` at its dataclass default of `{}` (arbitration.py:50). engine._candidate_log guards on `if distribution:` at :567, so no per-candidate `propensity` key is written for a hold. ope.observations then builds `support` only from entries that carry that key (:489-493) and does `p_log = support.get(chosen)` / `if p_log is None or p_log <= 0: continue` (:498-500). Every suppressed row is skipped.

**Impact.** The corpus's negative class -- 'we looked at this borrower and decided silence was worth more' -- is exactly what distinguishes a decision engine from a dialler, and it is invisible to IPS, SNIPS and DR. Any challenger policy that would have acted where the champion held is evaluated only on the rows where the champion also acted, which is the selection the estimator's own docstring (ope.py:29-34) warns about. The `unsupported` diagnostic will not catch it, because the rows are not counted as unsupported -- they are not counted at all.

**Fix.** Have `_hold` set `distribution={A.WAIT: 1.0}` (or the within-arm share when an arm is in play) so a suppressed decision carries a real one-point distribution over the only action available to it. Then ope.observations picks it up with p_log = 1.0 and a candidate policy that would have acted there is correctly scored as unsupported rather than silently dropped. Also reconcile the two floors: arbitration.py:200 uses 1e-9 while explore.MIN_PROPENSITY (explore.py:67) is 1e-6, so a hold can log a propensity 1000x below the value the clipping argument was written for.

### `paid-and-ptp-labels-are-customer-level-and-unbounded` — Any payment or promise on any account of the customer after a decision labels that decision `paid`/`ptp`, so one payment can mark many concurrent decisions as successes

**backend/agent_core/treatment/followthrough.py:285** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

followthrough.py:285-297 `_promised_since` queries `promises WHERE customer_id = :cid AND created_at > :since` -- no account filter, no trigger filter, no link to the decision. `_paid_since` (:257-282) checks `ledger_entries` on the decision's account but falls back to `payment_intents WHERE customer_id = :cid AND status = 'paid'` (:271-281), again customer-level. Neither has an upper time bound. With `dpd_tick` in LOOPED_TRIGGERS (followthrough.py:60-62) the sweep opens one case per customer per day, so a customer can carry several open decisions at once; a single payment satisfies `_paid_since` for all of them on the next attribution pass.

**Impact.** Positives are duplicated across correlated rows while negatives are not, which inflates the cure rate in whichever arm has more open decisions per customer -- and the treated arm has more, because the control arm suppresses discretionary action and produces fewer ladder rungs. That is a differential measurement error pointing the same way as the metrics.causal selection bug. It also breaks the independence assumption every SE in the codebase already assumes. And there is no attribution at all: a payment triggered by the borrower's own standing instruction credits whichever decisions happen to be open.

**Fix.** Attribute at the case level, not the customer level: match the payment to the account and to the instalment or bounce the case was opened against (`trigger_ref` already carries the payment_events / promises / emi_installments id, and `_case_still_open` at :401-421 already knows how to resolve each kind). Where several decisions share a case, credit the most recent enacted one and mark the others `superseded` -- the machinery for that already exists at :222-254. Bound the lookback to the observation window.

### `control-arm-cannot-power-its-own-measurement-on-this-book` — TREATMENT_AB_SPLIT is live and withholding outreach from 20% of a 20-customer book for a measurement that needs roughly twenty years, while MIN_ARM_N=100 lets the dashboard print a causal number long before either arm can support one

**backend/agent_core/treatment/metrics.py:50** · statistics · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

The arm is running now: TREATMENT_AB_SPLIT=control:80,null_treatment:20, 97 of 225 decisions in null_treatment. metrics.py:46-50 gates the causal block at `MIN_ARM_N = 100` labelled cases per arm -- a raw count, not a power calculation. Running the repository's own formula (power_control_arm.py:105-131) at p_control = 0.45, MDE = 0.05, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80: at an 80/20 split the requirement is 974 control + 3,896 treated = 4,870 CASES with no clustering, and 2,920 + 11,680 = 14,600 cases at the design effect this book actually exhibits (~11 cases/customer, ICC 0.2). A 20-customer book at one delinquency episode per EMI cycle yields ~4.6 cases/week, giving 1,054 weeks at DE=1 and 3,161 weeks (61 years) at DE=3. A 50,000-account book at 5% delinquency yields ~577 cases/week: 8 weeks at DE=1, 25 weeks at DE=3.

**Impact.** Every borrower in null_treatment is a borrower who received no discretionary outreach in exchange for information the book cannot produce. That is a real cost carried by real customers, and it is the exact failure power_control_arm.py:9-14 was written to prevent -- 'the failure mode here is not choosing wrong. It is running a control arm for six months, withholding treatment from thousands of borrowers, and discovering that the book could never have detected the effect being looked for.' Worse, MIN_ARM_N=100 means the dashboard will publish `incrementalCureRate` once ~9 customers' worth of decisions have labels, and that number will be quoted.

**Fix.** Gate the causal block on power, not on a row count: call power_control_arm.sample_size with the measured control cure rate and the measured cases-per-customer, and refuse the number until n_control is met -- reporting 'this book needs N more cases at the current MDE' instead. For a pilot-sized book, do not run a within-tenant control arm at all; run the engine in shadow, publish the priors as priors, and state that the first quarter is calibration (which is option three in power_control_arm.py:389-392). Reserve the arm for the 50k deployment where the arithmetic closes in a quarter.

### `segment-promoted-on-noise-then-given-86-percent-of-the-weight` — The segment holdout gate has no margin and no standard error, and the shrinkage weight that follows is computed on total n rather than on the control n the estimate's variance actually depends on

**backend/agent_core/treatment/models.py:160** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

train_treatment_models.py:927-931: `if lift <= 0: entry.update({"verdict": "rejected", "reason": "no_holdout_lift"})` -- any positive lift promotes. The one segment in the shipped artifact, `b0030/open/timing`, won on `holdoutLift: 0.000765` (eight ten-thousandths of a nat of log loss). It is then blended by models.py:268-276 with `w = segment.weight(self.shrinkage_k)` and models.py:158-160 `return self.n / (self.n + max(1.0, k))` -- n = 4612, k = 750, so w = 0.86. Meanwhile the power gate that admitted it is on the *control* side: models.py:390 `if model.control_n < MIN_SEGMENT_CONTROL_N` with MIN_SEGMENT_CONTROL_N = 200 (:87). tau is a difference of two quantities and its variance is dominated by the smaller half, so a segment with control_n = 200 and n = 20,000 would receive weight 0.96 on the strength of 200 control observations.

**Impact.** The ladder is the mechanism by which the engine gets to say 'this stratum responds differently'. As written it will promote strata that beat the pooled model by rounding error and then let them displace 86-96% of the pooled answer. On a bank's book that surfaces as a segment of borrowers -- here, 0-30 DPD reachable salary-timing accounts -- being treated on a tau fitted to noise, with a model card that says the segment 'beat the population model on the holdout' and is technically true.

**Fix.** Two changes. (1) Require a material and significant lift: compare log losses with a paired bootstrap over the held-out rows and require the lower bound of the lift interval to exceed a stated floor, not merely lift > 0. (2) Compute the shrinkage weight on the harmonic mean of the treated and control counts (or on control_n alone), since that is what bounds Var(tau_segment): `w = harmonic(n, control_n) / (harmonic(n, control_n) + k)`. Report the resulting weight per segment in the artifact so a reviewer can see how much of the answer each segment is taking.

### `tau-double-discounted-by-reach-and-timing` — tau already averages over non-answer and over self-cure, and the EV formula then multiplies it by P(reach) and by P(not self-cured) a second time

**backend/agent_core/treatment/models.py:820** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

models.py:820: `gross = value * reach * resolve * decay`, where `resolve` is tau from the uplift model (:804) and `decay = 1.0 - already` with `already = self._timing.predict(vec)` (:812-813). The docstring at :708-716 claims these compose. They do not, on this corpus. tau is fitted from `_label_cure` over decisions (train_treatment_models.py:203-212), which counts `no_answer` as 0 -- so the probability of not reaching the borrower is already inside tau. The timing model is fitted only on control-arm and un-enacted rows (`_label_timing`, :174-196) and its shipped artifact records nSamples 3668 and baseRate 0.34133, exactly the uplift artifact's controlN and controlRate -- i.e. the timing model predicts the same self-cure the T-learner's control half already subtracts.

**Impact.** For a WhatsApp with prior reach 0.55 and a timing model predicting 0.34 self-cure, the served gross is tau * 0.55 * 0.66 = 0.36 * tau. Stacked on the 3.4x calibration compression this makes the served expected value roughly an order of magnitude below the causal truth. The discount is also channel-differential -- voice at 0.30, WhatsApp at 0.55, and non-contacting actions at 1.0 (scoring.py:226) -- so it does not merely scale the ladder, it reorders it, systematically toward represent_mandate and emi_date_change and away from every contact channel. That may look like the intended behaviour (fewer calls) while being an arithmetic error.

**Fix.** Pick one convention and enforce it in the artifact. Either estimate tau conditional on reach and on the account still being open (restrict `_label_cure` to enacted-and-reached rows and record `conditioning: 'reached'` on the artifact), so the multiplication is legitimate; or keep tau marginal and drop the `reach` and `decay` factors from the uplift branch of `_rescore` entirely. Record the choice as a field on the artifact and have `_rescore` branch on it, so the two can never drift apart silently.

### `uplift-calibration-monitor-compares-two-different-populations` — The one check that can detect a response model wearing an uplift label averages predicted tau over a population that includes `wait` rows and differences it against an ATE computed with `wait` rows excluded

**backend/agent_core/treatment/monitor.py:424** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

monitor.py:419-437. The measured side counts a treated row only `elif str(row.get("chosen_action") or "") not in ("", "wait")` (:424). The predicted side skips only the control arm (`if arm == control_arm: continue`, :427) and then appends `p_resolve` for every remaining row (:429-437), including rows whose chosen action was `wait` -- whose logged pResolve is 0.0 by construction (scoring.py:394-406 returns `p_resolve=0.0` for WAIT). `mean_tau = sum(predicted) / len(predicted)` (:449) is therefore diluted by zeros from a population the `measured` figure excludes.

**Impact.** `gap = mean_tau - measured` (:451) drives the alert at :484 and the note at :453-470. Diluting the predicted side toward zero makes the gap look smaller -- or negative -- which produces the reassuring branch ('the engine is leaving lift on the table rather than inventing it', :465-467) precisely when a response model would be inflating tau. This is the check monitor.py:21-28 calls 'the only check that sees it', and it is calibrated to under-fire.

**Fix.** Apply the same population filter to both sides: skip `wait` rows when building `predicted`, exactly as :424 skips them when building `treated_n`. Add a minimum-n guard (the module has none -- `reach_calibration` at :350-383 will compute and alert on an ECE from five attempts) and report the count next to the gap.

### `ope-estimator-policy-scores-a-different-formula-than-the-serving-scorer` — The challenger policy the promotion gate evaluates drops VALUE_HORIZON and both probability clamps, so the SNIPS lift describes a ranking the engine would never produce

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:396** · statistics · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `L-statistics`

`ope.estimator_policy`'s inner `_score` returns `exposure * recovery_fraction * p_reach * tau * decay - cost - fatigue`. The serving path computes `value = exposure * policy.recovery_fraction * scoring.VALUE_HORIZON.get(s.action, 1.0)` then `gross = value * reach * resolve * decay` (models.py:817-820), and the baseline EVScorer does the same at scoring.py:429. Grepping the package, `VALUE_HORIZON` appears only at scoring.py:89, scoring.py:429 and models.py:817 -- never in ope.py. scoring.VALUE_HORIZON is 3.0 for emi_date_change and 2.0 for self_service_plan (scoring.py:89-97). Two further divergences in the same function: models._rescore clamps `reach = max(0.01, min(0.95, ...))` and only substitutes it `if A.spec(s.action).channel is not None` (models.py:797-800), while ope applies `reach.predict(vec)` unclamped to every action including channel-less ones, whose true p_reach is 1.0 by construction (scoring.py:226); and models._rescore clamps `resolve = max(0.0, min(0.95, ...))` (:803) while ope does not.

**Impact.** The baseline policy in the same comparison, `greedy_on_logged_ev`, ranks on the logged `expectedValue`, which DOES contain VALUE_HORIZON -- so the challenger is systematically penalised by 3x on emi_date_change and 2x on self_service_plan relative to the policy it is being compared against, and represent_mandate is additionally discounted by a reach probability it should not carry at all. `Estimate.lift` is therefore not the lift of any policy the engine can run, and it is the single scalar registry.check thresholds at 0.005 to decide whether a model may serve. The bias is action-differential, so it does not cancel: it makes the fitted scorer look worse than it is on exactly the actions the fitted scorer would otherwise favour, and no diagnostic in the report would reveal it.

**Fix.** Extract one scoring function used by both paths. `models.EstimatorScorer._rescore` and `ope.estimator_policy._score` should call a shared `expected_value(vec, entry, artifacts, recovery_fraction)` that owns VALUE_HORIZON, the channel test and both clamps, so an offline estimate and a live decision cannot diverge silently. Add a test that scores one logged candidate through both paths and asserts equality to within floating point.

### `analysis-queries-carry-no-tenant-predicate` — None of the causal or model-health queries scope by tenant_id, so on a multi-tenant deployment without RLS enforced they pool every lender's book into one ATE

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:469** · privacy · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

ope.observations (:469-478) filters on mode, outcome, propensity and variant only. ope.treatment_effect (:571-579) filters on mode and outcome only. metrics.causal (:66-88, :122-160), metrics.efficiency (:197-236), metrics.borrower_experience (:419-439), monitor._calibration_rows (:124-152), monitor._drift_rows (:174-201) and the trainer's `_rows` (train_treatment_models.py:127-136) are all the same. treatment_decisions has a tenant_id column and an index on it (20260814_0069_treatment_engine.py:211). RLS exists but is an explicitly opt-in switch (scripts/rls.py:9-24: 'apply installs policies without turning row security on ... enable is the switch'), and scripts/train_treatment_models.py:1044 opens `db.engine.connect()` directly rather than a tenant-scoped session.

**Impact.** A causal number computed across tenants is not a causal number for any of them -- the arms are balanced within a tenant, not across a mix of lenders with different books, different products and different delinquency profiles. Worse, a model fitted this way encodes one bank's borrower behaviour into the coefficients that score another's, which is a data-sharing question before it is a statistics one and one an Indian bank's DPO will ask about DPDP consent. The trainer is the sharpest case: the artifact it writes is a single file served to every tenant.

**Fix.** Add an explicit `AND tenant_id = :tenant` to every query in ope.py, metrics.py and monitor.py, taking the tenant from db.current_tenant() the way agent_core/reco/decisions.py:82 already does. For the trainer, either require `--tenant` and write per-tenant artifacts, or make cross-tenant pooling an explicit, logged, contractual opt-in with the shrinkage machinery models.SegmentModel.weight already provides (its docstring at :155-156 already anticipates 'cross-tenant priors -- the only thing that changes there is what the pool means').

### `treatment-effect-counts-shadow-and-holdout-rows-as-treated` — ope.treatment_effect buckets on `variant = control_arm` alone, so the deliberately-untreated `holdout` arm and every shadow-mode decision land in the treated numerator

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:572** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

ope.py:571-581: `SELECT (variant = :arm) AS is_control, count(*) ... WHERE mode = ANY(:modes) AND outcome IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1` with `modes: Sequence[str] = ("shadow", "live")` (:557). config.py:353-360 defines `holdout` as `Variant(name="holdout", mode=MODE_SHADOW)` -- 'An explicit do-nothing arm ... Note what this arm actually withholds: *everything*'. ope.observations at :448 excludes it explicitly (`exclude_variants: Sequence[str] = ("null_treatment", "holdout")`); treatment_effect does not. Separately, every shadow-mode row in any arm is by definition unenacted (enact.py:80-83 refuses non-live) and is counted as treated.

**Impact.** Two untreated populations are added to the treated arm's denominator with their base-rate cure counts, pulling the treated rate toward the control rate and biasing the ATE toward zero. On the live corpus 24 of 225 rows are shadow, ~11%. The inconsistency between the two functions in the same module is the tell: whoever reads `evaluate_policy.py`'s output sees an ATE computed on one population and an off-policy lift computed on another, and the two are presented side by side as if they described the same rows.

**Fix.** Give treatment_effect the same `exclude_variants` parameter observations already has and default it to `('holdout',)`; add `AND enacted` or an explicit `AND mode = 'live'` to the treated bucket, or -- better, since the correct estimand is intent-to-treat -- restrict the whole query to live mode so both arms describe borrowers who could actually have been contacted. Assert in a test that treated_n + control_n equals the row count the observations query would return.

### `promotion-gate-is-a-point-estimate-threshold` — A challenger is promoted on a SNIPS point estimate crossing 0.005 with no confidence interval, no multiplicity correction, and the ATE significance flag the evaluator computes is never read

**backend/agent_core/treatment/registry.py:236** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

registry.py:234-237: `lift = evaluation.get("lift")` ... `elif float(lift) < MIN_HOLDOUT_LIFT:` with MIN_HOLDOUT_LIFT = 0.005 (:60). `Estimate.stderr` exists (ope.py:112, computed at :270) and is carried into the evaluation block by `to_log()` (ope.py:148), and no gate reads it. evaluate_policy.py:147-155 picks `best = max(challengers, key=lambda k: report["policies"][k]["snips"]["lift"])` -- an argmax over challengers, with no correction for having taken a maximum -- and attaches `snips["ateSignificant"] = effect.significant` at :154. Grepping the repository, `ateSignificant` appears only at that line; registry.check reads `evaluation.get("ate")` and gates only on `<= 0` (registry.py:263-268).

**Impact.** The gate the design note describes as 'promoted on holdout lift, never on offline metrics alone' is a threshold on a noisy scalar. With the corpus sizes this book will hold for months, the SNIPS standard error will comfortably exceed 0.005, so the gate is approximately a coin flip that says yes about half the time regardless of whether the challenger is better. Combined with the winner's-curse selection at evaluate_policy.py:147, the expected lift of whatever gets promoted is biased upward. That is how a model that is not better than the champion ends up deciding who gets dialled.

**Fix.** Gate on the interval, not the point: require `lift - 1.96 * stderr > MIN_HOLDOUT_LIFT`. Read the `ateSignificant` flag that is already being computed and refuse an uplift promotion when the ATE is not clear of zero (after the clustering correction above). Apply a Bonferroni or Holm correction across the challengers compared in one run -- the same discipline heterogeneity_z (train_treatment_models.py:202-217) already applies inside the segment ladder.

### `represent-mandate-tau-is-pure-extrapolation` — represent_mandate has never been a candidate on any of the 225 decisions, yet the uplift model will happily produce a tau for it, because the vector encodes the action only as a rung and an intrusiveness score

**backend/agent_core/treatment/scoring.py:512** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

The action encoding available to any fitted model is `"rung": float(A.rung(scored.action))` and `"intrusiveness": A.spec(scored.action).intrusiveness` (scoring.py:512-513), plus `this_action_tried` (:528) and `connect_rate_channel` (:524-526). There is no one-hot for the action itself. models._rescore calls `self._uplift.predict(vec)` for every candidate (models.py:804) with no check that the action was ever observed. On the live corpus represent_mandate was excluded on every one of the 225 decisions (124 `no_mandate_on_file`, 97 `control_arm`), so it contributes zero rows to any half of the T-learner. Its tau is whatever the coefficient on `rung` extrapolates to.

**Impact.** The design note calls represent_mandate the highest-ROI action in the system, and config.py:186-195 prices it at Rs.0.50 against a 0.35 resolve prior -- so a tau extrapolated even slightly high makes it dominate the ranking on cost alone. Presenting a NACH debit against a borrower's account is an irreversible financial act with a bounce charge attached when it fails. A model-risk reviewer will ask 'how many observations support this action's effect estimate' and the answer is zero, with nothing in the artifact or the decision log saying so.

**Fix.** Record per-action support in the uplift artifact (`observedByAction: {action: {treatedN, controlN}}`) and have `_rescore` fall back to the EV prior for any action below a minimum support, tagging the reason code `uplift_unsupported_action` so the decision log says which term was modelled and which was a prior. Separately, one-hot the action in the vector so the model cannot silently interpolate between rungs that are not on a continuum.

### `reco-propensity-fitted-on-a-doubly-selected-sample` — The propensity model estimates P(interested | the offer was presented AND the customer responded) and is served as P(convert | customer), with no correction and no way to build one

**backend/scripts/train_propensity.py:83** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

train_propensity.py:83-87 selects `WHERE d.presented IS TRUE AND d.chosen_product_id IS NOT NULL`. `label()` (:94-108) then drops `deferred`, `not_reached`, and still-open leads -- deliberately and correctly for the label's own validity ('An offer nobody made is not an offer that was refused', :24-27). But presentation is decided by agent_core/reco/arbitration.py's eleven gates (DND, consent, escalation, dispute, hardship, sentiment floor, commitment, caps, score threshold) and by whether the conversation reached that point at all, and response is decided by whether the borrower engaged. Neither selection is modelled. `comparable_score` (models.py:118-121) then divides by `base_rate`, which is the *holdout* base rate (train_propensity.py:344), a further-selected subsample of 333 rows.

**Impact.** The model is served on every customer the engine scores, including the ones the gates would have suppressed and the ones who would not have engaged -- the exact populations excluded from its training set. Because the gates suppress on hardship, dispute and negative sentiment, the excluded population is systematically the distressed one, so the model's estimate of conversion probability is optimistic precisely where a bank is most exposed to a mis-selling finding under the Digital Lending Guidelines. There is no logging propensity in the reco corpus (previous finding), so the standard fix -- inverse-probability-of-selection weighting -- is not available and cannot be retrofitted.

**Fix.** This is a second, independent reason to add a logging propensity to offer_decisions. With one, weight the training rows by the inverse probability of presentation to recover a population-level estimate. Until then, document on the model card that the quantity is P(interested | presented and responded), and clamp its use to ranking within the presented population rather than to any absolute expected-value figure (`expected_value = p * margin * amount` at reco/models.py:335 is currently an absolute rupee number built on a conditional probability).

### `random-row-split-on-a-clustered-corpus` — The treatment trainer holds out random rows, not random customers and not later dates, so every reported AUC is optimistic -- while the reco trainer in the same repository does it correctly

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:510** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

train_treatment_models.py:510 `train_idx, test_idx = _split(len(X), holdout, seed)` with `_split` (:436-441) being `random.Random(seed).shuffle(idx)`. With ~11 decisions per customer, the same borrower's rows appear on both sides of the split, and the vector carries persistent borrower-level features -- `secured`, `promises_total`, `promises_broken`, `ptp_keep_rate`, `has_mandate`, `salary_timing_gap_days` (scoring.py:517-587) -- that make the split leak identity. There is also no temporal ordering. train_propensity.py:321-330 does the right thing for reco and says why: 'Split by recency, not at random: the question a holdout has to answer is does this generalise to next month, and a random split answers does it interpolate within the same month, which it always does.'

**Impact.** The AUCs on the model cards -- reach 0.7306 (holdoutN 1314), timing 0.8125 (holdoutN 917), uplift 0.7191 (holdoutN 3583) -- are the numbers a model-risk reviewer will be shown and the numbers `registry.check` implicitly relies on. They measure interpolation within the same borrowers and the same fortnight. The real generalisation gap is unknown and, on a corpus this clustered, likely large. A model validated this way will underperform the moment the book turns over, and the failure will be attributed to drift rather than to the split.

**Fix.** Change `_split` to a grouped, time-ordered split: sort rows by created_at, cut at a date, and additionally ensure no customer_id spans the cut (hold out whole customers). `_rows` already selects `customer_id` and `created_at` (train_treatment_models.py:128-130) so both are available; they just are not carried into `_samples` (:976-996). Carry them, and report both a temporal-holdout AUC and a grouped-holdout AUC on the model card.

### `uplift-control-half-has-no-holdout-at-all` — The T-learner's control half is fitted on 100% of the control rows and never evaluated, and the artifact's holdoutAuc describes only the treated response model

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:606** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

train_treatment_models.py:604-606: `t_idx, t_test = _split(len(X_t), holdout, seed)` splits only the treated half; the control half is `zw_c, zb_c = fit_logistic(Z_c, y_c, seed=seed + 1)` over the entire `Z_c`. The metrics block at :621-629 computes `holdoutAuc` from `probs` built from `w_t, b_t` on `t_test` alone (:613-617). The shipped artifact records `holdoutAuc: 0.7191, holdoutN: 3583` against `controlN: 3668` -- the control half's 3,668 rows are entirely in-sample. Those same rows are then reused by fit_segments as `buckets[key]["c"]` for the heterogeneity gate (:833-841).

**Impact.** tau is the difference of the two halves, so an unvalidated control half is half an unvalidated tau. The number on the model card looks like a validation of the causal estimator and is a validation of one arm's response model. Nothing in the pipeline would detect a control half that had overfitted -- which is the likelier of the two, because the control arm is always the smaller and its labels come from the 14-day `unresolved` path with far less variety.

**Fix.** Split the control half on the same holdout fraction, fit on its training slice, and report `controlHoldoutAuc` and `controlHoldoutBrier` on the artifact. Better still, report a tau-level diagnostic that does not need per-row counterfactuals: the Qini/uplift-decile curve computed by binning holdout rows on predicted tau and differencing the realised treated and control rates within each bin. That is the metric that would have caught the calibration compression at the top of this report.

### `reco-cooldown-keyed-on-wrong-timestamp` — The per-product decline cooldown is measured from the most recent offer of *any* product, so a declined product can never leave cooldown

**backend/agent_core/reco/candidates.py:152** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`if pid in features.declined_product_ids and features.last_offer_at: if features.last_offer_at > cooldown_cutoff: excluded[pid] = REASON_DECLINED_COOLDOWN` (candidates.py:152-155), and the family variant at 158-164. `_offer_history` returns `declined` as a bare `set[str]` with no timestamps and `last_offer_at` as `max` over every presented offer regardless of product (reco/features.py:413-414, 444, 472).

**Impact.** A customer who declined a top-up in January and has been offered a card every month since has `last_offer_at` = last month, so the top-up stays suppressed indefinitely — the cooldown resets every time any unrelated offer is made. The higher the offer volume, the more permanently products are excluded. The family cooldown (`family_cooldown_days`) fails the same way and takes a whole product family with it. Over a year this silently narrows the sellable catalogue to whatever has never been declined, and the exclusion reason logged is `declined_cooldown`, which reads as intentional.

**Fix.** Make `_offer_history` return `declined: dict[str, datetime]` — the timestamp of each product's most recent decline — and compare that per product against `cooldown_cutoff`. Source it from `offer_decisions.responded_at` (which decisions.py:139 already writes) rather than `created_at`. Keep `last_offer_at` for global frequency only.

### `reco-no-point-in-time` — The reco engine has no injectable clock and no timezone awareness at all — it cannot be replayed, backtested, or window-gated

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:416** · statistics · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`cutoff = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=30)` (reco/features.py:416) sitting two statements away from `WHERE customer_id = :cid AND created_at > now() - interval '180 days'` (line 424) — an app-clock cutoff applied to a DB-clock-filtered set. Same pattern at lines 289 and 520, and at reco/candidates.py:105. `recommend` takes no `now`. There is no `ZoneInfo` import anywhere in agent_core/reco, and the package's only contact_policy import is `BLOCKING_CONSENT` (reco/arbitration.py:20) — never `evaluate` or `admit`.

**Impact.** Three consequences. (1) No offer decision can be replayed, so there is no way to answer 'what would the engine have offered in July' — and with offer_decisions holding 16 rows and 0 responses ever, replay is the only route to any evidence at all. (2) App/DB clock skew silently miscounts `offers_30d`, which is the frequency cap on cross-sell. (3) Nothing in reco consults the calling window, the daily cap, or the borrower's consent hours; the collections gate's protections simply do not exist on the upsell path. Under DPDP purpose limitation and the Digital Lending Guidelines separation the offer path is the one that most needs a gate.

**Fix.** Add `now: datetime | None = None` to `recommend` and thread it through features, candidates and scoring exactly as the treatment engine does. Replace every `now()` in reco SQL with a bound `:now`. Route offer delivery through `contact_policy.admit(..., data_purpose='promotional')` — the parameter and the REASON_NO_PROMO_CONSENT path already exist (contact_policy.py:477-482) and reco is the caller they were built for.

### `talk-track-promises-unpermitted-window` — The bot reads the raw preferred_window back to the borrower as a callback promise without intersecting it with the statutory window or the recorded consent hours

**backend/agent_core/reco/talk.py:118** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`window = (preferred_window or '').strip()` then `ask += f' between {window}'` (reco/talk.py:118-127), fed straight from `features.preferred_window` (reco/engine.py:214), which is the unprocessed `customers.preferred_window` column (reco/features.py:396). The seeded book contains `"preferredWindow": "18:00–21:00 IST"`, and contact_policy.py:256-257 calls that row out by name: 'the seeded book contains an ``18:00-21:00 IST`` preference, and intersecting it with the statutory 19:00 cut-off is what stops that row buying a nine o'clock call.'

**Impact.** The voice bot says, out loud and on a recorded line, 'Would you like a specialist to call you between 18:00–21:00 IST?' — offering a 21:00 recovery call that RBI DOR.MCS.REC.No.199 forbids after 19:00. The gate will then correctly refuse to make it, so the borrower is promised a callback that cannot legally happen and never comes. Under the 2027 direction's six-month recording retention that sentence is in the evidence file. The intersection helper the treatment side uses (`contact_policy.preferred_hours`) is exported and public; reco simply does not call it.

**Fix.** Have engine.recommend pass `contact_policy.preferred_hours(customer_row)` intersected with the statutory voice window, rendered as a string, instead of the raw column — and refuse to name a window at all when the intersection is empty ('Would you like a specialist to call you back?'). Add a test asserting no talk track can name an hour outside RBI_VOICE_START..RBI_VOICE_END.

### `cancelled-closes-the-case` — A plan the executor reached more than 12 hours late is marked `cancelled`, which followthrough treats as resolving — worker latency permanently closes borrower cases

**backend/agent_core/treatment/enact.py:88** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`if datetime.now(timezone.utc) - at > MAX_PLAN_AGE: decisions.record_outcome(decision_id, 'cancelled', conn=conn); return False, 'plan_expired'` with `MAX_PLAN_AGE = timedelta(hours=12)` (enact.py:45, 88-90). `RESOLVING = frozenset({'paid','ptp','superseded','cancelled'})` (followthrough.py:65) and `open_cases` only returns cases whose latest outcome is in `UNRESOLVED` (followthrough.py:387), which does not contain `cancelled`.

**Impact.** The executor is the last of eleven stages in bot_worker's priority chain (bot_worker.py:126) and returns after the first stage that does work (line 101 onward), so a busy tick starves it. Twelve hours of backlog — one long weekend of queue depth, one deploy window, one incident — converts every pending plan into `cancelled`, and `cancelled` is read downstream as 'this case is finished'. The borrower is dropped from the ladder for a reason that has nothing to do with them, and 84 of the 108 labelled decisions in the live corpus already carry this outcome. Combined with finding `cancelled-is-a-negative-class`, our own outage becomes the training signal.

**Fix.** Introduce a distinct terminal-vs-retryable distinction: `expired` should re-open the case for re-decision (the situation has moved on, which is exactly the argument for re-deciding, per the constant's own comment at enact.py:43-44), not close it. Remove `cancelled` from RESOLVING, or split it into `cancelled_resolved` (borrower paid, consent withdrawn) and `cancelled_operational` (expired, no executor, error) and put only the former in RESOLVING. Alert when the operational share exceeds a threshold.

### `features-wall-clock-not-decision-now` — days_overdue and bounce_age_hours are computed from the process wall clock, not the decision's `now`, so the engine is not replayable and a backfill leaks the future

**backend/agent_core/treatment/features.py:612** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`days = int((datetime.now(timezone.utc) - due).total_seconds() // 86400)` (features.py:612, inside `_instalment`, which is not even passed `now`) and `age = ... max(0.0, (datetime.now(timezone.utc) - occurred).total_seconds() / 3600.0)` (features.py:757, inside `_bounce`). Every sibling method takes `now` explicitly — `_promises(..., now)` at 767, `_contact(..., now, tz)` at 836, `_reachability(..., now, tz)` at 890, `_treatment_history(..., now)` at 1198, `_case_history(..., now)` at 1234.

**Impact.** `bounce_age_hours` is what `_legal_veto` uses to decide whether the NI Act s.138 21-day position is real (`features.bounce_age_hours or 0) >= 24 * 21`, policy.py:458) and what the scorer's urgency term reads. `days_overdue` drives bucket-adjacent logic. Any offline replay, any backfill of the corpus, and any unit test that injects `now` gets today's value for a decision dated March — which is textbook target leakage, since the bounce aged partly *because* of the decision being replayed. It also means the engine cannot be dry-run against a historical date to answer 'what would we have done', which is the first thing a collections head will ask before switching TREATMENT_MODE to live on a real book.

**Fix.** Thread `now` into `_instalment` and `_bounce` (both already have the call site in `_build`, features.py:470/479) and replace both `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` calls with it. Add a test that builds features twice with two different injected `now` values and asserts `days_overdue` and `bounce_age_hours` differ accordingly. Then grep the package for `datetime.now(` and make its absence a lint rule inside agent_core/treatment/features.py.

### `attribution-30-day-cliff` — Outcome attribution has a hard 30-day cutoff with no backfill, so a labelling backlog destroys training data permanently

**backend/agent_core/treatment/followthrough.py:117** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`AND created_at >= now() - interval '30 days'` inside `attribute_outcomes` (followthrough.py:117), with `BATCH = 25` (line 81) and `LIMIT :limit` (line 129). A row that ages past 30 days with `outcome IS NULL` can never be selected again — there is no backfill path and no alert.

**Impact.** Compounded by starvation: `process_one` runs attribution and returns immediately if it labelled anything (`if attribute_outcomes(conn): return True`, line 514-515), and bot_worker runs the whole treatment follow-through only after ten higher-priority stages (bot_worker.py:131). At 19-42 new decisions a day and 25 per pass this is survivable on 20 customers; on a real book of tens of thousands of daily decisions the queue never drains and rows fall off the 30-day cliff continuously. The corpus loses labels in a way that is *correlated with load* — the busiest weeks lose the most — which biases every model fitted on it. Established fact: 117 of 225 rows already have no outcome.

**Fix.** Make the cutoff a configurable horizon that is strictly longer than the longest label window (OBSERVATION_WINDOW=14d plus slack), and emit a metric for 'rows that expired unlabelled' so the cliff is visible. Size BATCH from the arrival rate rather than a constant. Change `process_one` to run attribution and re-decision in the same tick rather than returning after the first, so the ladder is not starved by the labeller.

### `followthrough-dpd-tick-never-advances` — dpd_tick is in LOOPED_TRIGGERS but _case_still_open has no branch for it, so the sweep population never gets a second rung

**backend/agent_core/treatment/followthrough.py:421** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`_case_still_open` handles `bounce` (line 406), `broken_ptp` (411), `pre_due` (416) and then `return False` (line 421). `open_cases` filters on it: `return [dict(r) for r in rows if _case_still_open(conn, dict(r))]` (line 398). Meanwhile `LOOPED_TRIGGERS = frozenset({'bounce','broken_ptp','pre_due','dpd_tick'})` (line 61) carries a nine-line comment ending 'Leaving it out gave the largest population in the book exactly one decision a day and no escalation at all' (lines 48-54).

**Impact.** The fix that comment describes was never completed. `dpd_tick` cases are selected by the SQL and then unconditionally discarded in Python, so the largest population in the book still gets exactly one decision a day and no escalation — the stated defect, still live, now with a comment claiming it is fixed. On the live corpus this is the whole sweep population (TREATMENT_SWEEP=1, 19-42 rows/day). A silent roller at 30 DPD gets one SMS a day forever and never reaches a human.

**Fix.** Add a `dpd_tick` branch. The case is open while the account is still delinquent and the local day has not rolled: `SELECT 1 FROM accounts a JOIN customers c ON c.id=a.customer_id WHERE a.customer_id=:cid AND a.dpd>0 AND a.status='active'` plus a check that `trigger_ref` equals today's local date in the customer's zone (otherwise a stale case from yesterday would be re-opened, which sweep.py:20-22 explicitly forbids). Add a regression test that a dpd_tick decision labelled `no_answer` produces a case from open_cases.

### `breach-auditor-third-window-rule` — The compliance breach auditor is a third, weaker implementation of the window rule that resolves a different timezone from the gate it audits

**backend/agent_core/treatment/metrics.py:357** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`EXTRACT(HOUR FROM ce.occurred_at AT TIME ZONE ` + _SAFE_TZ + `) < :start OR ... >= :end_h` (metrics.py:357-360) with `_SAFE_TZ` = the suffix-stripping SQL zone, against a gate that uses the non-stripping Python `_zone` (contact_policy.py:553). The query filters `ce.channel = 'voice'` (line 354) and compares only against RBI_VOICE_START/END; it never checks `allowed_hours`, `preferred_window`, or `allowed_days`. The cap check uses `daily_cap()` with no rules argument (line 367) while `admit` uses `daily_cap(rules)` (contact_policy.py:919).

**Impact.** Its docstring says the target is zero and that 'Anything counted here got past contact_policy.evaluate()' — but it cannot see three of the four rules the gate enforces. A WhatsApp sent at 03:00 to a borrower whose consent says 09:00-20:00 is a real breach of REASON_WINDOW and is invisible here. A Sunday contact against a Mon-Sat consent is invisible. A breach of a *published* rule cap lower than the env cap is invisible. And where the two timezone resolutions disagree it will report phantom breaches or miss real ones. This is the number a compliance officer will put in front of a regulator.

**Fix.** Audit against the same predicate the gate applies: join `consent_records` and `customers.preferred_window`, apply the intersection, cover every channel not just voice, include the day-of-week check, and resolve the zone with the same helper the gate uses (once findings 1 is fixed, that is one helper). Break the result out by rule so 'window' and 'statutory hours' are separate counters.

### `uplift-calibration-borrowed-across-arms` — tau is a difference of two probabilities passed through a Platt map fitted only on the treated arm, over two logits that were class-reweighted separately

**backend/agent_core/treatment/models.py:300** · statistics · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `L-time`

`treated = _sigmoid(self.calibration_a * treated_logit + self.calibration_b)` and `untreated = _sigmoid(self.calibration_a * control_logit + self.calibration_b)` (models.py:300-301) — one `(a, b)` pair applied to both halves. That pair comes from the treated arm alone: `logits = [sum(a * c for a, c in zip(X_t[i], w_t)) + b_t for i in t_idx]; cal = platt_calibrate(logits, [y_t[i] for i in t_idx])` (train_treatment_models.py:609-610), and the artifact carries exactly one `calibration` block (`_artifact`, :477). The two halves' raw logits are not on a common scale to begin with, because `fit_logistic` rebalances each fit to its own class ratio: `positives = sum(y) or 1; negatives = (n - sum(y)) or 1; pos_w = n / (2.0 * positives); neg_w = n / (2.0 * negatives)` (:248-251), and platt_calibrate's own docstring at :272-277 says the class weighting 'made the raw scores good at *ranking* and useless as probabilities'. The treated and control arms have materially different cure rates by construction — that difference is the ATE — so the two rebalancings differ, and the single Platt map corrects only one of them. `predict` returns this tau (models.py:260-278) and EstimatorScorer feeds it straight into the EV formula as `resolve` (models.py:804).

**Impact.** The uplift number the engine would allocate on carries a systematic bias whose sign and size are set by the class-balance difference between the arms rather than by any treatment effect — the very confound the T-learner design exists to remove. It is invisible in every reported metric: `holdoutAuc` (train_treatment_models.py:626) is rank-based and computed on the treated half only, so it is unaffected by a monotone miscalibration of either half, and `ate` (:625) is computed from raw label rates and never touches the fitted halves at all. A model-risk reviewer asked to reproduce tau from the artifact cannot, because the artifact ships one calibration for two models. The segment ladder inherits it: `_predict(x, w, b, cal)` is applied with the same `cal` to both treated and control halves at :915 and :918.

**Fix.** Fit and ship a second Platt map on the control half's own training logits (`controlCalibration`), and apply each half its own. Add an assertion that the two calibrated halves reproduce their arms' observed base rates on held-out rows to within tolerance — a T-learner whose halves do not recover their own base rates cannot produce a meaningful difference. Until then, record on the artifact that the control half is uncalibrated, so nothing downstream reads tau as a probability difference.

### `holds-not-evaluated-at-planned-instant` — Treatment holds are evaluated at decision time, not at the planned instant, so a hold that starts before the slot does not block it

**backend/agent_core/treatment/policy.py:154** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`held = _hold_veto(action, features)` (policy.py:154) — `_hold_veto` takes no `at`, and `features.holds` was built by `_holds` with `starts_at <= now() AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > now())` (features.py:1176-1177). Every other veto in the same function is explicitly given the planned instant: `_legal_veto(features, at)` (197), `_mandate_veto(conn, features, at=at)` (202), `_contact_veto(..., at=at)` (227-229). `veto`'s own docstring says '``at`` is the *planned* instant, not now: an action scheduled for tomorrow 08:15 is checked against the calling window it will actually land in' (policy.py:142-144).

**Impact.** The planning horizon is up to 72 hours. A hardship, bereavement, complaint or legal hold scheduled to begin tomorrow morning (a supervisor placing a hold with a future `starts_at`) does not block an action planned for tomorrow afternoon; the plan is written, the executor claims it, and `contact_policy.admit` does not check treatment_holds at all. A bereavement hold placed a day in advance is exactly the case where a dunning call is most damaging and most likely to become a complaint to the grievance officer.

**Fix.** Pass `at` to `_hold_veto` and re-evaluate holds against it — either by having `_holds` return the hold intervals rather than a bare set of kinds, or by adding an explicit hold check inside `contact_policy.evaluate` (which already receives `now=at` and is already the one authoritative feasibility check per timing.py:15-17). The second is better: it also closes the gap at enact time, where holds are never re-checked.

### `sweep-decided-today-ignores-account` — The sweep's 'already decided today' check is keyed on customer alone, so a borrower with two delinquent loans gets one decision a day, contradicting the module's own design note

**backend/agent_core/treatment/sweep.py:195** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`SELECT 1 FROM treatment_decisions WHERE customer_id = :cid AND trigger_kind = :kind AND trigger_ref = :ref LIMIT 1` (sweep.py:198-205) — no `account_id`. `_claim` locks per account and its docstring states '``FOR UPDATE OF a SKIP LOCKED`` on the account, not the customer: two accounts of one borrower are two decisions, and locking the customer would serialise a household behind whichever of its loans was claimed first' (sweep.py:140-143). `trigger_ref` is the local date, identical for both accounts.

**Impact.** Whichever account sorts first by `a.id` wins the day; the other is silently skipped forever. In Indian retail lending a delinquent borrower routinely holds a personal loan and a card, or two vehicle loans. The second exposure never enters the corpus, never gets a decision, and never appears in any coverage metric — the sweep reports success. The lock design pays the cost of per-account concurrency and gets none of the benefit.

**Fix.** Add `AND (account_id = :aid OR (:aid IS NULL AND account_id IS NULL))` to `_decided_today` and pass `account['id']`. Note the CAST-for-NULL-parameter hazard the codebase has already hit twice (features.py:683-693, 736-738) — write it as `AND account_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM CAST(:aid AS TEXT)`. Add a test with two delinquent accounts on one customer asserting two decisions in one sweep day.

### `tz-python-sql-divergence` — Python resolves customers.timezone differently from the SQL twin, so every non-IST borrower is silently gated in IST

**backend/contact_policy.py:156** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`def _zone(name): label = (name or '').strip() or DEFAULT_TZ; try: return ZoneInfo(label) except (ZoneInfoNotFoundError, ValueError): return ZoneInfo(DEFAULT_TZ)` (contact_policy.py:156-161; identical copy at agent_core/treatment/features.py:116-121). The SQL twin thirty lines below strips the display suffix first: `btrim(split_part(COALESCE(c.timezone, ''), '(', 1))` (contact_policy.py:195), and its docstring claims at line 180 'Same policy as :func:`_zone`, expressed once here so both paths agree' and at line 185 warns that falling back 'would be right by accident for an Indian borrower and wrong for anyone else'. That is exactly what _zone does. All six seeded customers carry `"timezone": "Asia/Kolkata (IST)"`, so the exception path is the only path exercised in production today and nothing logs it.

**Impact.** The gate that enforces RBI's 08:00-19:00 calling window (contact_policy._veto:499) reads `now_local.hour` from `_zone()`. Load a book with an NRI or a Gulf-based borrower whose timezone reads 'Asia/Dubai (GST)' or 'America/New_York (EST)' and the window is enforced in IST: a call at 08:00 IST reaches a New York borrower at 21:30 the previous evening. Meanwhile the breach auditor (metrics._breaches:357) uses the stripped zone and would score that same call as compliant, so the violation is invisible in the compliance report. Under the 2027 RBI direction this is a reportable conduct breach with no detection.

**Fix.** Give _zone/zone the same two-step as safe_tz_sql: strip everything from the first '(' and btrim before ZoneInfo(), then fall back. Delete the duplicate in features.py and import contact_policy._zone. Log at WARNING (rate-limited, customer-id only) every time the fallback fires, and add a startup check that counts customers whose timezone does not resolve — a book where that count is nonzero is a book the window cannot be enforced on.

### `window-parse-drops-minutes-and-accepts-inverted` — The consent-window parser discards minutes and happily returns an inverted window from a 12-hour string its own docstring advertises

**backend/contact_window.py:55** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`return int(match.group(1)), int(match.group(3))` (contact_window.py:55; identical regex and identical truncation at contact_policy.py:212-218). The docstring three lines above lists the supported forms: '``09:00-20:00 IST``, ``9:00 – 8:00 pm``, ``10:00–19:00``' (contact_window.py:39). Feed it `9:00 – 8:00 pm` and it returns (9, 8): start greater than end. There is no validation that end > start.

**Impact.** Two separate failures. (1) Minute truncation: a borrower whose consent reads '09:30-18:30' is callable from 09:00 — half an hour before they consented, every day, on every channel; and is refused between 18:00 and 18:30 which they did consent to. Half-hour windows are normal in Indian CRM extracts. (2) An inverted window makes the borrower permanently uncontactable: `_veto` computes `hour < 9 or hour >= 8` which is always true (contact_policy.py:520), and timing._window_for produces start>=end so _first_instant_in_window returns None (timing.py:114-116) and every action is planned as 'no consented slot'. The borrower drops silently out of collections — the failure mode contact_window.py:84 already names, 'they are simply never contacted, which is the kind of wrong that does not raise'.

**Fix.** Return `(start_hour, start_minute, end_hour, end_minute)` and compare minute-precise instants, not bare hours. Detect and reject an inverted or empty parse explicitly — return None and let callers fall back to DEFAULT_START_HOUR/DEFAULT_END_HOUR with a WARNING naming the customer, rather than emitting (9,8). Add am/pm handling or refuse the form and drop it from the docstring; advertising `9:00 – 8:00 pm` as supported when it produces a null window is worse than not supporting it.

### `insights-does-not-exclude-simulated` — /treatment/insights — the report the go-live gate is written against — has no mode filter, so the synthetic corpus counts toward the shadow-fortnight exit criterion

**backend/agent_core/treatment/decisions.py:437** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

All five queries in insights() filter only on the window: `WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '{window}'` (decisions.py:437, 446, 457, 467, 476). Its sibling endpoints both take the flag — `treatment_metrics(days, include_simulated=includeSimulated)` (main.py:4806) and `treatment_model_health(... include_simulated=...)` (main.py:4815) — and /offers/health has it too (main.py:1104-1116, with the comment 'so nobody makes a call on a number that came out of the simulator'). /treatment/insights has no such parameter (main.py:4782-4789, db_treatment_holds.py:433-440). 0085:90-92 claims 'simulated' can be 'excluded everywhere by one predicate'.

**Impact.** main.py:4785-4787 states the endpoint's purpose: 'The report the roadmap's exit criterion is written against: two weeks of shadow logs with a suppression breakdown before any live auto-act.' scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py exists and writes into this table. The one number that authorises the engine to start contacting real borrowers unsupervised can therefore be met with generated rows, and the byMode breakdown at decisions.py:463-471 is the only place the contamination would be visible — as a line the reader has to notice.

**Fix.** Add `include_simulated: bool = False` to insights() and default the five predicates to `AND mode <> 'simulated'`, matching metrics/model-health/offer_health. Plumb it through db.treatment_insights and add `includeSimulated` to the route. Additionally, have the endpoint refuse to report coverage at all when any simulated row falls in the window and the flag is off, rather than silently filtering — an operator asking the go-live question should be told the corpus is mixed.

### `offer-decisions-has-no-propensity-or-policy-version` — offer_decisions never received the propensity / policy_version / explore_kind columns that made treatment_decisions learnable, so the reco engine's log is permanently unusable for off-policy evaluation

**backend/alembic/versions/20260731_0051_upsell_nbo_engine.py:189** · statistics · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

The offer_decisions table as created (0051:189-263) carries mode, variant, recommender, features, candidates, excluded, score — and no propensity, no policy_version, no explore_kind. 0052 and 0053 add only mode='simulated' and variant. No later migration adds them (grep for offer_decisions across alembic/versions returns only 0051, 0052, 0053, and comment mentions in 0069/0070/0085/0063). 0085's own docstring explains why this matters — 'A deterministic argmax assigns every action it took a probability of 1.0, which makes the log unusable for off-policy estimation... One column, and it cannot be added retroactively' (0085:16-21) — and applies the lesson to treatment_decisions only.

**Impact.** RECO_SCORER is unset so RuleScorer serves, RECO_AB_SPLIT is unset so there is no holdout arm, and 16 logged decisions carry no propensity. Every day the reco engine runs is a day of data that can never support a counterfactual claim about what a different offer policy would have earned. The migration that diagnosed this problem for one engine did not fix it for the other, and unlike a model this cannot be backfilled.

**Fix.** Add propensity double precision (with the same >0 CHECK), policy_version integer and explore_kind TEXT to offer_decisions in one migration, and make agent_core/reco/engine.py record them — even a fixed exploration epsilon over the approved candidate set is enough to make the log estimable. Do it before the corpus grows, not after.

### `no-tenant-leading-index-on-either-decision-log` — offer_decisions has no tenant_id index at all and treatment_decisions has no composite with tenant leading, so every windowed dashboard query scans the whole corpus

**backend/alembic/versions/20260731_0051_upsell_nbo_engine.py:264** · scale · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

offer_decisions indexes: customer, interaction, lead, (customer, chosen_product_id, created_at DESC), and the partial variant index (0051:264-270, 0053:30-35). No tenant_id index, and none in sql/06_sales.sql:143-152 either. treatment_decisions gets `idx_treatment_decisions_tenant_id` on tenant_id ALONE (0069:210-212) plus (customer_id, created_at) (:213-217), (mode, created_at) (:219-223) and the partial due index (:225-232) — nothing leads with tenant.

**Impact.** Every /offers/health query is `WHERE mode = ANY(:modes) AND created_at > now() - interval '30 days'` (observability.py:122-123) with no index that can serve it: a sequential scan of every offer decision ever written, nine times per page load, under the API's 15-second statement_timeout (db_core.py:154). /treatment/insights is the same shape. This is fine at 225 and 16 rows; at a bank's volume the observability pages time out first and then, because they hold a connection from a pool of 15 (db_core.py:149-150), they take the API down with them. A DBA reviewing this schema rejects it on this alone.

**Fix.** Add `(tenant_id, created_at DESC)` to both decision tables and `(tenant_id, mode, created_at DESC)` to treatment_decisions; drop the single-column idx_treatment_decisions_tenant_id it subsumes. Then add the tenant predicate to the queries (see reads-have-no-tenant-predicate-and-rls-is-off) so the index is usable. Build them CONCURRENTLY.

### `no-retention-or-partitioning-on-the-decision-logs` — Three append-only logs with three unbounded JSONB columns each, no partitioning, no retention job, and a policy kind called 'recording_retention' that governs nothing here

**backend/alembic/versions/20260814_0069_treatment_engine.py:142** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

treatment_decisions carries features, candidates and excluded as `postgresql.JSONB()` with no size bound (0069:142-159); offer_decisions the same (0051:215-232); authority_decisions carries features and reason_codes (0070:43-58). No migration partitions any of them and no purge exists (grep for retention/purge across backend/*.py finds nothing in db.py). policy_rules.kind includes 'recording_retention' (0085:327) and RuleSet exposes recording_retention_months() (policy_rules.py:172-173), but no caller applies it to these tables.

**Impact.** Volume: the sweep writes one decision per delinquent account per day. A 2-million-account book at 10% delinquency is ~200k rows/day, each carrying a features map and a candidates array of up to nine scored actions — realistically 5-15 GB/month in TOAST alone, growing forever, on the same tablespace as the live collections tables. Legally: DPDP storage limitation requires a defined retention period and RBI's 2027 direction sets 6 months for call recordings; a bank's DPO will ask what the retention period of the decision log is and the answer is 'unbounded'. Operationally: VACUUM and backup windows scale with it, and the observability queries above scan all of it.

**Fix.** Partition all three decision logs by RANGE (created_at) monthly (pg_partman or a scheduled migration), so retention is a DETACH rather than a DELETE. Define a retention period per table in the policy rule set and add a worker that detaches and archives expired partitions to object storage. Separately, cap the JSONB: store the top-N candidates rather than all, and move the full feature vector to a compressed archive keyed by decision id.

### `erasure-cascades-destroy-the-regulatory-decision-log` — customer_id ON DELETE CASCADE on every decision and hold table means a DPDP erasure silently deletes the audit trail the bank must retain

**backend/alembic/versions/20260814_0069_treatment_engine.py:181** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

`sa.ForeignKeyConstraint(["customer_id"], ["customers.id"], ondelete="CASCADE")` on treatment_decisions (0069:181) and treatment_holds (0069:79); the same on authority_decisions (0070:73) and offer_decisions (0051:199-202). Combined with the docstrings that call these tables append-only (0069:9, 0070:7-10), and with main.py:423 listing append-only enforcement as a deferred control.

**Impact.** A DPDP Act erasure request, a mis-run data-subject job, or an operator cleaning test data deletes: every treatment decision for that borrower (including the evidence for 'why did you dial at 19:15'), every hardship/bereavement/legal HOLD ever placed on them, every authority decision that waived a fee, and the mandate presentations that recorded debits against their bank account. RBI record-retention and DPDP erasure are in direct tension here, and the schema resolves it silently in favour of destruction, with no tombstone and no log. It also silently deletes rows out from under an in-flight uplift training run.

**Fix.** Change these four FKs to ON DELETE RESTRICT and introduce an explicit erasure path that pseudonymises rather than deletes: null/redact the free-text columns (rationale, reason, features->PII keys), keep the decision id, timestamps, action, propensity, policy_version and outcome, and record the erasure in a dedicated table. Pair it with a documented retention schedule so retention and erasure are one reviewed policy rather than two accidental ones.

### `due-index-predicate-never-sheds-dead-rows` — idx_treatment_decisions_due keeps every never-enacted decision forever, including shadow and suppressed rows that can never be claimed, so the executor's index grows without bound

**backend/alembic/versions/20260814_0069_treatment_engine.py:225** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

`CREATE INDEX idx_treatment_decisions_due ON treatment_decisions (scheduled_at) WHERE enacted IS FALSE AND chosen_action IS NOT NULL AND chosen_action <> 'wait'` (0069:225-232). claim_due filters far more narrowly: `AND mode <> 'simulated' AND suppression_reason IS NULL AND outcome IS NULL AND scheduled_at IS NOT NULL AND scheduled_at <= now() AND created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'` (decisions.py:363-378). Every shadow-mode actionable decision (suppression_reason='shadow_mode', per decisions.py:422-426) and every suppressed decision satisfies the index predicate and never satisfies the claim.

**Impact.** The index accumulates one entry per actionable decision for the life of the deployment and sheds only the ones that are actually enacted. In shadow mode — the mode the rollout prescribes for a fortnight, and the mode the 24 shadow rows are in — NOTHING is enacted, so the index is pure growth. The executor then scans an ever-longer scheduled_at prefix of permanently-unclaimable rows on every poll, and the poll is on the outbound hot path.

**Fix.** Rebuild as `WHERE enacted IS FALSE AND outcome IS NULL AND suppression_reason IS NULL AND chosen_action IS NOT NULL AND chosen_action <> 'wait' AND mode <> 'simulated'` — every one of those is either immutable or monotone toward exclusion, so entries leave the index as rows are resolved. Add created_at to the index key so the 7-day bound is usable.

### `ddl-takes-access-exclusive-locks-with-no-not-valid-or-concurrently` — 0085/0087/0090 add validating CHECK constraints and build non-concurrent indexes on the hot decision and accounts tables, ignoring the NOT VALID pattern the repo already established

**backend/alembic/versions/20260820_0085_decision_intelligence_p0.py:96** · scale · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

`"ALTER TABLE treatment_decisions ADD CONSTRAINT treatment_decisions_mode_check CHECK (mode IN (...))"` (0085:96-99) and the action check at :108-114 — a plain ADD CONSTRAINT holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for a full table scan. Same in 0087:47-53 and 0090:52-57. Indexes are built without CONCURRENTLY: `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_treatment_decisions_sweep ...` (0085:130-134), `idx_treatment_decisions_ope` (0085:138-142), and worst of all `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_accounts_delinquent ON accounts (id) WHERE status = 'active' AND dpd > 0` (0085:150-153) on the accounts table. 0063:23-26 already spelled out the correct pattern — 'Added NOT VALID and then validated. The two steps take a weaker lock than a plain ADD CONSTRAINT, which holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for a full table scan. Both tables are small today; the pattern costs nothing here and is the one that stays safe when they are not.' — and 0085 does not use it.

**Impact.** On a bank's accounts table (tens of millions of rows) a non-concurrent partial index blocks every write to accounts for the duration of the build; on a decision log at 5M rows/month a validating CHECK blocks the collections engine outright. No migration sets lock_timeout, so a blocked ALTER queues behind a long-running read and then blocks every subsequent query on the table — the classic Postgres lock-queue outage. This is a deployment-window outage in the customer's environment, and it will happen on the first upgrade after go-live.

**Fix.** Set `lock_timeout` and `statement_timeout` at the top of every migration. Replace plain ADD CONSTRAINT with ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID followed by a separate VALIDATE CONSTRAINT step (0063 shows the DO-block form). Build indexes with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside `with op.get_context().autocommit_block():`, and add a repeatable check that no new migration touches accounts/interactions/treatment_decisions/offer_decisions without one of these forms.

### `policy-rule-sets-permit-overlapping-windows` — Nothing prevents two rule sets of the same scope being in force at once, and the resolver silently intersects them while stamping only one version on the decision

**backend/alembic/versions/20260820_0085_decision_intelligence_p0.py:293** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

policy_rule_sets constrains only the window's internal ordering (`ck_policy_rule_sets_window CHECK (effective_to IS NULL OR effective_to > effective_from)`, 0085:293-295) and version uniqueness (0085:308-312). There is no exclusion constraint on overlapping [effective_from, effective_to) per (tenant, scope, product) and no trigger that closes the previous row. The docstring asserts the outcome anyway: 'A rule set is never edited once effective; it is superseded, and the superseded row keeps answering "what was in force in March"' (0085:284-287). policy_rules.py:351-353 admits the gap and claims a tie-break — 'Latest effective_from wins within a scope' — that the code does not implement: _resolve_uncached folds every matching set through _tighten (policy_rules.py:389-401) and sets statutory_version from the last statutory entry in version order (:393-394).

**Impact.** Publishing a corrected statutory set without closing the old one leaves both live. Calling windows intersect, caps take the minimum, cooling-off takes the maximum — the engine becomes stricter in a way nobody authorised and nobody can reproduce — and treatment_decisions.policy_version names one of the two sets, so the answer to 'which rules governed this call' is wrong. That is the exact question 0085:20-27 built this table to answer, and the RBI 2027 calling-window change (08:00-19:00, effective 2027-01-01) is the first real publication event.

**Fix.** Enable btree_gist and add `EXCLUDE USING gist (COALESCE(tenant_id,'') WITH =, scope WITH =, COALESCE(product_id,'') WITH =, tstzrange(effective_from, effective_to) WITH &&)`. Make publication a single transaction that closes the incumbent (`UPDATE ... SET effective_to = :new_from WHERE effective_to IS NULL AND ...`). Change RuleSet.version to carry the full (scope, version) tuple, or store the resolved rule-set ids on the decision, so the stamped provenance is unambiguous.

### `policy-rules-params-is-schemaless` — The RBI calling window and every other statutory limit live in an unvalidated jsonb blob with no schema, no defaults and no round-trip test

**backend/alembic/versions/20260820_0085_decision_intelligence_p0.py:335** · data-model · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

`params jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb` (0085:335) is the entire specification. The readers are defensive but silent: `calling_window()` returns None unless both startHour and endHour parse as ints (policy_rules.py:118-126), `_opt_int` swallows every TypeError/ValueError (policy_rules.py:186-192), and resolve() returns EMPTY on any exception (policy_rules.py:325-327). The module then documents that EMPTY means 'unregulated by this table' and each caller falls back to its own constant (policy_rules.py:32-37).
