**Fix.** Require lift > MIN_HOLDOUT_LIFT AND lift > 2 * stderr (or a one-sided lower confidence bound above the floor), and require ateSignificant is True for uplift. Add a minimum-n objection so a gate cannot fire on a corpus too small to measure anything.

### `evaluate-policy-cannot-score-a-challenger` — The evaluation the promotion gate requires can only ever describe the model already serving

**backend/scripts/evaluate_policy.py:96** · integration · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`reach, timing, uplift = models.load_reach(), models.load_timing(), models.load_uplift()` — evaluate_policy has no --artifact argument. models.load_* resolve TREATMENT_*_MODEL_PATH or the fixed serving paths. So the report evaluate_policy emits, which promote_model.py:129 requires and registry.check refuses to promote without (registry.py:226-231), scores whatever is already champion. To evaluate a challenger you must first install it as champion, which is the act promotion is supposed to gate.

**Impact.** The learning loop has no working middle. Either operators promote on a report about the wrong model (the gate becomes theatre), or they copy the challenger over the serving file to evaluate it (the gate is bypassed and borrowers are exposed to an unevaluated model in the meantime). Either way the audit trail asserts something false.

**Fix.** Add `--artifact target=path` (repeatable) to evaluate_policy so it loads named candidate files via models.load_artifact, and record every loaded artifact's sha256 and version in report['artifacts']. Then have registry.check refuse an evaluation whose artifacts block does not contain the sha of the file being promoted.

### `ate-fabricated-when-no-control-arm` — With no control arm the reported ATE equals the raw treated cure rate, and the uplift gate passes on it

**backend/scripts/evaluate_policy.py:153** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`snips["ate"] = effect.ate` (line 153). TreatmentEffect.ate is `self.treated_rate - self.control_rate` and control_rate is `(int(control["cured"]) / c_n) if c_n else 0.0` (ope.py:590-591). With control_n == 0 the ATE is the treated cure rate — a large positive number. registry.check's uplift gate is `if ate is not None and float(ate) <= 0` (registry.py:263-269), so it passes. The human-readable warning that this is 'a response rate, not a treatment effect' is printed only in the non-JSON branch (evaluate_policy.py:170-174) — and `--json` returns at line 159 before reaching it, which is precisely the mode promote_model consumes. `snips["ateSignificant"] = effect.significant` is carried at line 154 and never read by any gate.

**Impact.** A tenant who never configures TREATMENT_AB_SPLIT (the default: RECO_AB_SPLIT unset already produces no holdout arm on the sibling engine) gets an uplift model promoted against a fabricated causal number. That model then ranks self-curers first — exactly the failure models.load_uplift's docstring says is 'invisible in every offline metric except the one that compares against a control arm' (models.py:628-641) — and the bank spends its most expensive capacity on borrowers who needed nothing.

**Fix.** Make TreatmentEffect.ate return None when control_n == 0 (or add an explicit `measurable` property), emit that in to_log(), and add objections in registry.check for a missing/None ATE and for `ateSignificant is False`. Also move the no-control-arm warning into the JSON report so it survives --json.

### `promoted-by-is-unauthenticated-free-text` — Model promotion has no authenticated identity and no second approver

**backend/scripts/promote_model.py:87** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`ap.add_argument("--by", default="", help="who is promoting this, for the ledger")` and `if not args.by: ap.error("--by is required to promote: the ledger records who decided")` (line 161-162). The string goes straight into treatment_model_registry.promoted_by (registry.py:347-352). Anyone with shell access and the DB URL can promote any file as anyone. There is no approver column, no maker-checker, and no --list of who approved what beyond a free-text reason.

**Impact.** RBI model-governance expectations and every internal audit standard require segregation of duties for a model that decides how a borrower is contacted, plus an identified approver. 'susanth.p typed his own name' is not an approval record. This blocks the go-live sign-off regardless of how good the statistics are.

**Fix.** Promotion should be an authenticated API action, not a CLI flag: record the caller's identity from the session/service account, add `approved_by` distinct from `requested_by` with a DB constraint that they differ, and store the evaluation report inline in the ledger row (it already has an `evaluation` jsonb column). Emit an immutable audit event to the platform's audit log on every promote, reject and rollback.

### `no-rollback-and-champion-bytes-are-lost` — There is no rollback command, and promotion overwrites the previous champion's file irrecoverably

**backend/scripts/promote_model.py:164** · reliability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

promote_model.py exposes --list, --verify, --check, --register and promote. There is no --rollback and no CLI for registry.reject (registry.py:376-396, defined and never called from anywhere). registry.promote ends with `shutil.copyfile(p, destination)` (registry.py:362), overwriting the serving file in place; the retired row keeps only `artifact_path` (registry.py:117), a path that may already have been overwritten — and if the operator promoted directly from the serving path, `p.resolve() != destination.resolve()` is False (line 361) and the old bytes never existed anywhere else.

**Impact.** When a promoted model misbehaves on Monday morning, the recovery procedure is 'find last week's file' and there may not be one. Meanwhile the trainer overwrites those same paths by default (see trainer-overwrites-serving-models). A bank will not approve a model that cannot be reverted within an agreed RTO, and an incident here means every borrower contacted while it serves.

**Fix.** Archive every promoted artifact under models/archive/<target>/<version>-<sha12>.json before copying, and store the archive path in the ledger. Add `promote_model.py --rollback --target X` that re-promotes the most recent retired champion from its archive, writes a new ledger row (never mutating history), and requires --by and --reason. Add `--reject` to drive registry.reject.

### `control-arm-demand-inflates-dual-prices` — The capacity solve counts the control arm's candidate lists as real demand

**backend/scripts/solve_capacity.py:76** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`SELECT DISTINCT ON (COALESCE(account_id, customer_id)) COALESCE(account_id, customer_id) AS key, candidates FROM treatment_decisions WHERE mode = ANY(:modes) AND created_at >= now() - make_interval(hours => :hours)` (lines 79-85) — no variant filter and no enacted filter, so every null_treatment row's scored candidate list becomes an allocate.Demand. The engine scores and logs candidates for control rows (the established corpus shows 97 control-arm rows each carrying the represent_mandate exclusion, i.e. a full candidate list), but by definition nothing will be enacted for them. Shadow rows are included too via `modes = ["shadow", "live"]` (line 113).

**Impact.** With TREATMENT_AB_SPLIT at control:80,null_treatment:20, a fifth of the book's demand for agent minutes and field slots is phantom. The LP therefore prices scarcity that does not exist; those duals go into capacity_duals and, once TREATMENT_DUAL_PRICING is on, into costs.for_action, suppressing real actions on real borrowers because imaginary ones were counted. Shadow rows compound it. The failure is silent and its size is exactly the holdout fraction — so making the experiment more powerful makes the allocator more wrong.

**Fix.** Exclude rows whose variant is a suppress_discretionary arm (config.variants()) and rows with mode <> 'live' from demands(). Log the counts included and excluded by arm so the plan's denominator is inspectable, and cross-check the account count against the active book size before writing prices.

### `extraction-materialises-whole-corpus-in-memory` — The trainer reads the entire decision log — every candidate's feature vector included — into one Python list with the statement timeout switched off

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:120** · scale · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`def _rows(conn, *, include_simulated): _lift_timeout(conn); ... return [dict(r) for r in conn.execute(text("SELECT id, customer_id, account_id, variant, mode, chosen_action, chosen_channel, enacted, outcome, scheduled_at, created_at, candidates, features FROM treatment_decisions WHERE mode = ANY(:modes) AND feature_schema_version = :schema ORDER BY created_at ASC"), ...).mappings()]` (train_treatment_models.py:120-136). No LIMIT, no OFFSET, no server-side cursor, no streaming, no date bound. `candidates` is the full ranked list — one entry per scored action, each carrying a complete feature vector (engine.py:382-385, `_candidate_log`) — and `features` is a second jsonb blob per row. _lift_timeout (:104-117) explicitly runs `SET statement_timeout = 0`, removing the only backstop, and its own docstring anticipates 'eighteen thousand decisions, each carrying a feature vector per scored action'. The same shape appears in evaluate_policy via ope.observations (ope.py:478-479, `for row in conn.execute(...).mappings()` accumulating into `out`) with `--limit` defaulting to None. Contrast monitor.py, which does bound itself: SAMPLE_LIMIT / DRIFT_SAMPLE with an explicit `"truncated": len(rows) >= limit` field (monitor.py:494-520).

**Impact.** The reader's scale finding is about fit time; this is about the process dying before the fit starts. A 50k-account book decided daily by the sweep produces on the order of a million decision rows a month, each with seven candidate entries of ~30 floats plus a features blob — tens of gigabytes of Python dicts. The trainer OOMs, and because the statement timeout was deliberately removed there is no server-side failure to catch either; the symptom is a killed process or an unbounded-duration query holding a connection out of a pool sized at 5+10 (db_core.py:148-149). Nothing paginates, checkpoints or samples, so there is no partial result and no way to run the job at all on a real book. It also collides with the sweep and the corpus simulator on the same table with no advisory lock.

**Fix.** Stream the extraction: use `conn.execution_options(stream_results=True, yield_per=N)` (or keyset-paginate on (created_at, id)) and build samples incrementally rather than materialising rows. Select only the chosen action's vector rather than the whole `candidates` blob — the trainer discards the rest immediately in _vector_for (:142-160) — and drop `features`, which is selected and never read. Bound the extraction with `--since-days` and a row cap that is reported when hit, the way monitor.report already does. Replace `SET statement_timeout = 0` with a large but finite budget so a runaway query fails loudly.

### `no-tenant-filter-in-trainer` — The trainer reads every tenant's decision log into one model while the registry books the champion per tenant

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:126** · privacy · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

The extraction is `SELECT ... FROM treatment_decisions WHERE mode = ANY(:modes) AND feature_schema_version = :schema` (lines 127-135) with no tenant predicate, although decisions.py:100 inserts `tenant_id` on every row and promote_model.py:104 does `tenant = db.current_tenant()` and registry keys champion/challenger on tenant_id (registry.py:148-158). solve_capacity has the same asymmetry: `demands()` has no tenant clause (solve_capacity.py:79-88) but `allocate.persist(conn, allocation, tenant_id=db.current_tenant())` (line 178) writes per-tenant duals.

**Impact.** In a multi-entity deployment — an NBFC and its bank partner, or two portfolios under one platform — coefficients fitted on entity A's borrowers decide contact strategy for entity B's. That is a purpose-limitation breach under the DPDP Act and a contractual breach in essentially every Indian BFSI data-processing agreement. It is also silently wrong: one tenant's book drift moves another's model, and neither ledger records it. On a single-tenant dev box the bug is invisible.

**Fix.** Add `AND tenant_id = :tenant` (from db.current_tenant()) to _rows() and to solve_capacity.demands(), require --tenant explicitly rather than defaulting, record tenant_id on the artifact and add a registry.check objection when the artifact's tenant does not match the promoting tenant. Verify RLS is enforced on treatment_decisions for the batch role rather than relying on the predicate.

### `pure-python-fit-does-not-scale` — 2000 fixed epochs of interpreted batch gradient descent, run up to ~120 times by the segment ladder

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:253** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`for _ in range(epochs): grad_w = [0.0]*d ... for xi, yi in zip(X, y): ... for j in range(d): grad_w[j] += err * xi[j]` with epochs=2000, no convergence check, no early stop, no loss tracking. fit_segments calls _fit_half twice for the population, twice per stratum for the verdict and twice more per promoted stratum for the shipped halves (lines 830-831, 903-904, 935-936) — up to ~4 fits per stratum across a 30-cell partition. The repo's own tests record the cost: 'the alternative was a six-minute run for five assertions' for a 5,400-row two-stratum ladder (test_decision_intelligence_p3.py:818-819). _lift_timeout's docstring anticipates 'eighteen thousand decisions' (line 111).

**Impact.** A 50k-account book at 5% delinquency generates ~2,500 delinquent accounts a month across seven actions — hundreds of thousands of candidate rows within a year. Retraining becomes a multi-hour to overnight job with no checkpointing, no progress output and no timeout, run by a cron that cannot tell success from a hang. The retraining cadence the product's self-improvement claim depends on becomes 'when someone has a spare evening'.

**Fix.** Add a convergence criterion (relative change in the weighted log-loss below a tolerance) with a max-epoch cap, and log the epoch count and final loss into metrics so a stalled fit is visible. Vectorise the inner loop over rows using array module or accept numpy as a build-time-only dependency for the trainer (it never has to enter the serving image — the artifact is JSON). Cache the standardised design matrix across the ladder's repeated fits instead of rebuilding it per _fit_half.

### `no-training-provenance-record` — Given an artifact, the training set that produced it cannot be reconstructed

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:443** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

_artifact (lines 443-488) records name, target, version, trainedAt, featureNames, coefficients, means, stdevs, calibration, metrics, nSamples, vectorVersion, featureSchemaVersion and corpus. It records no date range, no row-id set or hash, no tenant, no mode/variant composition, no code version, no hyperparameters (epochs, lr, l2, holdout, seed are all invisible on the artifact), and no environment. The run itself logs only `logger.info("%d decisions in scope", len(rows))` (line 1027).

**Impact.** Model reproducibility is a hard requirement of any bank's model risk policy and of any RBI supervisory review. Nobody can answer 'rebuild this artifact and show me the same coefficients' or 'which borrowers' data is in this model' — the second of which is a DPDP data-subject question, not just a governance one. It also blocks debugging: when the ATE flips sign next quarter there is no way to diff the two training populations.

**Fix.** Add a `training` block to the artifact: tenant, corpus counts by mode and variant, min/max created_at, decision-id count plus a sha256 over the sorted id list, the full hyperparameter set, the git sha of the trainer, and the SCHEMA_VERSION/SEGMENT_VERSION in force. registry.register should copy it into the ledger row.

### `platt-fitted-on-training-logits` — Platt calibration is fitted on the same rows the model overfit

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:522** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`logits = [sum(a*c for a,c in zip(X[i], w)) + b for i in train_idx]` then `cal = platt_calibrate(logits, [y[i] for i in train_idx])` (lines 521-522); identical pattern at 609-610 for uplift. platt_calibrate itself (lines 269-290) is 300 fixed steps of unregularised gradient descent with no convergence check, no divergence guard and no bound on `a` — a negative `a` would silently invert every probability the artifact serves.

**Impact.** The docstring is explicit that calibration exists because 'Expected value multiplies this by a rupee amount' (lines 276-278). Calibrating on training logits reproduces the model's training-set optimism, so the p that multiplies exposure is overconfident on exactly the borrowers the model overfit. On a thin book the effect is large. And nothing detects the inverted-calibration failure: train_one writes the artifact regardless of what holdoutAuc comes out as, including below 0.5.

**Fix.** Fit Platt on a dedicated calibration fold (or out-of-fold predictions from a small k-fold), assert `a > 0` and refuse the artifact otherwise, add a convergence check to platt_calibrate, and refuse to write any artifact whose holdout AUC is below a floor (0.55 say) or whose holdout Brier exceeds the base-rate Brier.

### `no-fairness-or-disparate-impact-test` — No trainer or gate measures differential treatment across borrower populations

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:529** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

The metrics block is `{"baseRate", "holdoutAuc", "holdoutBrier", "holdoutN"}` (lines 529-534) plus `segmentLadder`/`segmentsPromoted` for uplift. registry.check's objections (registry.py:200-274) cover corpus, evaluation, lift, trustworthiness, control arm, control_n, ATE sign and age. Nothing anywhere partitions performance or contact intensity by geography, product, ticket size band, language or any proxy for a protected characteristic.

**Impact.** RBI's Fair Practices Code and the fair-lending expectations behind it require that a collections strategy not systematically disadvantage a class of borrowers, and the new DOR.MCS circular effective 2027-01-01 raises the supervisory attention on contact practice specifically. An uplift model trained on a book where some geographies were historically under-contacted will learn that they do not respond and will stop contacting them — a self-fulfilling loop that shows up in a supervisory review as differential servicing, not as a modelling artefact.

**Fix.** Add a fairness block to the artifact: per-slice AUC, base rate, predicted contact intensity and mean tau across configured slices (state/region, product, ticket band, language, channel availability). Add registry.check objections for a slice whose predicted contact rate deviates beyond a configured tolerance from the population, and require the slice definition to be tenant-configurable so the bank chooses its own protected dimensions.

### `nan-and-inf-unguarded-end-to-end` — NaN metrics and NaN coefficients are written to the artifact, load into the serving path, and break the registry

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:531** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`auc()` returns `float("nan")` when the holdout has one class (line 298-299), and train_one writes it unguarded: `"holdoutAuc": round(auc(probs, truth), 4)` (line 531). `json.dumps` then emits the non-RFC literal `NaN` (line 1067). Nothing validates coefficient finiteness either — a single inf/NaN in a logged vector propagates through fit_logistic (lines 253-266, no isfinite check) into `"coefficients": [round(w, 8) for w in weights]`. models.load_artifact does `tuple(float(c) for c in coefficients)` (models.py:476) which accepts NaN happily, while registry.register does `CAST(:metrics AS jsonb)` (registry.py:123) which Postgres rejects outright.

**Impact.** Three failure modes, all bad. A NaN AUC artifact loads and serves but cannot be registered, so the ledger and the serving path diverge. NaN coefficients produce NaN probabilities; every `>` comparison in the argmax is False, so the engine silently picks the first action in sorted order for every borrower on the book — a total loss of decision quality with no error anywhere. And on a 20-customer book with 7 'paid' outcomes, a one-class 25% holdout is not a hypothetical.

**Fix.** Refuse to write an artifact whose coefficients, intercept, calibration or metrics are not all math.isfinite; refuse when the holdout contains fewer than (say) 10 positives and 10 negatives rather than emitting NaN; use json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False) so the failure is loud; and add an isfinite check to models.load_artifact so a hand-edited or truncated file cannot reach the audio path.

### `control-imputed-with-treated-means` — The T-learner's shared imputation is the treated arm's means, applied to control rows

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:589** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`X_t, y_t, means = _design(treated, names)` (line 589) — means come from the treated arm alone — followed by `X_c = [[float(v[n]) if v.get(n) is not None else means[n] for n in names] for v, _ in control]` (lines 590-593). The docstring claims only that both halves 'share one feature list and one imputation' (line 570-572), which is true but says nothing about whose. `_dispersions(X_t + X_c, mu)` at line 701 likewise measures pooled spread about the treated mean.

**Impact.** Missingness is not arm-independent here: a null_treatment row is never enacted, so channel-, attempt- and delivery-derived features are absent far more often in the control arm. Filling those gaps with treated-arm means pulls control predictions toward the treated distribution, which shrinks tau toward zero in a way that varies by feature coverage — an effect that will look like heterogeneity to the segment ladder. The shipped `stdevs`, used as the drift monitor's denominator, are also centred on the wrong mean.

**Fix.** Compute imputation means on the pooled treated+control training fold, record per-arm coverage per feature on the artifact, and drop any feature whose coverage differs between arms by more than a threshold — a feature only observable when we act cannot be a covariate in a causal contrast.

### `control-half-fitted-on-all-rows-and-uplift-auc-is-a-response-auc` — The control half sees every control row, and the artifact's headline AUC measures response, not uplift

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:606** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`zw_c, zb_c = fit_logistic(Z_c, y_c, seed=seed + 1)` (line 606) — the full control set, while the treated half is fitted on `t_idx` only (line 604). The reported metric is then computed from the treated half alone: `probs = [_sigmoid(cal[0] * (sum(a*c for a,c in zip(X_t[i], w_t)) + b_t) + cal[1]) for i in t_test]` and `"holdoutAuc": round(auc(probs, truth), 4) if t_test else None` (lines 612-626). Nothing anywhere evaluates tau — no Qini coefficient, no uplift-at-k, no calibration of the difference.

**Impact.** The uplift artifact on disk advertises AUC 0.72 and a reviewer will read it as 'the uplift model discriminates at 0.72'. It does not — that is the treated arm's response model, and a response model with excellent AUC can have a useless or inverted tau. Meanwhile the control half has no holdout at all, so its contribution to tau is unvalidated and asymmetrically overfit relative to the treated half, which biases tau in a fixed direction.

**Fix.** Split the control arm too, fit the control half on its training fold, and report an uplift-specific metric on the joint holdout: Qini/uplift curve and the top-decile ATE difference. Rename the response metric to `treatedResponseAuc` so no one mistakes it for evidence about tau.

### `single-platt-applied-to-both-arms` — One Platt calibration is fitted on the treated arm and then applied to the control half, biasing tau by construction

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:610** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`cal = platt_calibrate(logits, [y_t[i] for i in t_idx])` (line 610) — logits from the TREATED half only. The artifact carries exactly one calibration block (`"calibration": {"a": ..., "b": ...}`, line 477) and no control calibration. At serving, models.ModelArtifact._tau applies it to both: `treated = _sigmoid(self.calibration_a * treated_logit + self.calibration_b)` and `untreated = _sigmoid(self.calibration_a * control_logit + self.calibration_b)` (models.py:300-301). The same single `cal` is also used for both halves inside the ladder's holdout comparison (`_predict(x, w, b, cal)` at lines 915 and 918).

**Impact.** The two arms have different base rates by design — that difference IS the treatment effect. Platt scaling fitted on the treated arm's base rate and applied to the control logit shifts P(cure|untreated) systematically, so tau is biased everywhere, in a direction that depends on the sign of the ATE. tau is then multiplied by exposure in the EV formula, so the bias is denominated in rupees and drives which borrowers get called and which get a field visit. This is a defect a model validator will find in an afternoon and it invalidates the causal claim.

**Fix.** Fit and store two calibrations — controlCalibration alongside calibration — and apply each to its own half in _tau. Fit both on held-out folds (see platt-fitted-on-training-logits). If a single calibration must be kept for compatibility, calibrate the difference directly against observed segment-level ATEs rather than calibrating each arm's probability.

### `heterogeneity-gate-is-in-sample-and-subset-vs-pool` — The ladder's causal gate tests a subgroup against a pooled estimate that contains it, in-sample, with the wrong standard error

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:874** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`p_t = sum(label for _, label in rows_t) / len(rows_t)` / `p_c = ...` over the FULL stratum (lines 874-875), then `se = _ate_stderr(p_t, len(rows_t), p_c, len(rows_c))` and `z = abs(ate - population_ate) / se` (lines 877-878). `_ate_stderr` is the SE of the segment's own ATE (lines 744-748); the variance of `population_ate` is never included, and population_ate (passed at line 661 as `treated_rate - control_rate` over everything) contains the stratum being tested.

**Impact.** The gate the docstring calls 'the load-bearing one... backed by the randomisation rather than by a model' (lines 777-781) is none of those things as implemented: it is an in-sample comparison of overlapping estimates with an SE that ignores one of them. Bonferroni corrects for how many cells were tried but not for the fact that the cells are evaluated on the same data that defined them. Segment models are the finest-grained thing this engine ships and they change contact strategy for a named stratum of borrowers, so a spurious promotion is directly actionable harm.

**Fix.** Test the stratum against its complement, not against the pool: ate_seg vs ate_rest, with SE = sqrt(se_seg^2 + se_rest^2) — two independent estimates. Compute the z on the training fold and confirm it on the holdout fold before promoting. Report the segment's ATE confidence interval in the report rows so a reviewer can see the width, not just the verdict.

### `no-retraining-schedule-and-models-expire-silently` — Nothing schedules any of these four jobs, and at 90 days the models vanish from the serving path with a log line nobody sees

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:999** · reliability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

There is no cron entry, systemd unit, Airflow DAG, compose service or Makefile target referencing train_treatment_models.py, evaluate_policy.py, promote_model.py or solve_capacity.py — the only references in the repository are the scripts themselves and two test files. Meanwhile models._max_age_days() defaults to 90 (models.py:595-599) and load_artifact refuses anything older with `_warn_once(f"stale:{p}", ...)` (models.py:574-582). Per the operator's own notes, the API and voice services install no root log handler, so that warning never prints. No script takes an advisory lock, so a training run, the corpus simulator and the sweep can contend on the same rows.

**Impact.** Ninety days after go-live the treatment engine silently reverts to the hand-tuned EV priors — losing every point of lift that justified the project — and nothing on any dashboard changes. There is no runbook for 'the model expired', no alert, and no retraining cadence tied to the outcome-maturity window. Concurrency is unguarded, so the first collision between a solve and a sweep produces a lock timeout at the worst moment.

**Fix.** Ship the loop as scheduled units with the correct order (attribute outcomes -> train -> evaluate -> check -> human promote -> solve capacity), each taking a pg_advisory_lock keyed on tenant+job. Emit a metric for model age and alert at 0.7 * max_age. Make the engine emit a loud, rate-limited error (not a warning through a discarded logger) the first time it falls back to priors, and surface champion age and verify() state on an operator screen.

### `corpus-label-from-flag-not-data` — The artifact's provenance stamp is derived from a CLI flag, and --include-simulated silently blends synthetic and live rows in one fit

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:1029** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`corpus = "simulated" if args.include_simulated else "live"` (line 1029) and `modes = ["shadow", "live"] + (["simulated"] if include_simulated else [])` (line 122). The flag adds simulated rows to the live ones rather than selecting them, and the stamp reflects the flag rather than the rows returned. The whole downstream provenance chain — models.load_artifact's refusal (models.py:549-565) and registry.check's objection (registry.py:216-224) — trusts this one string.

**Impact.** Two ways to get it wrong. (1) `--include-simulated` on a box that has both corpora fits one model across a synthetic latent-truth book and a real one; the resulting coefficients are a blend of a book that exists and one that does not, and the shrinkage/segment machinery averages across them. (2) Any UAT or migrated dev extract written under mode='live' yields an artifact stamped 'live' that clears the provenance gate. In a bank, 'which data was this model trained on' is question one of the model inventory.

**Fix.** Compute the stamp from the rows actually used — count by mode and set corpus='simulated' if any simulated row is present, corpus='mixed' being disallowed outright. Record `rowsByMode`, `rowsByVariant`, min/max created_at, the decision-id count and the code git sha on the artifact. Make --include-simulated select only simulated rows rather than adding them.

### `shadow-rows-counted-as-treated` — The treated arm is defined solely by variant, so shadow and cancelled rows enter it as treated

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:1054** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S01-train-treatment`

`treated_rows = [r for r in rows if str(r.get("variant") or "") != CONTROL_ARM]` (line 1054), applied to rows drawn from `modes = ["shadow", "live"]` (line 122). A shadow decision was scored but never enacted; a cancelled decision was withdrawn by the executor before dispatch (enact.py:89-152). Both land in the treated half with a _label_cure of 0 unless the borrower happened to pay. On this corpus that is 24 shadow rows plus 84 cancelled rows out of 225.

**Impact.** The 'treated' arm is contaminated with untreated observations, so the measured ATE — the number registry.check gates uplift promotion on — is biased downward by roughly the share of non-enactment. On a real book, non-enactment rates vary by day (rail outages, DND refreshes, capacity), so the causal estimate moves with operational noise rather than with treatment. Either arm-level ITT or per-protocol is defensible; silently mixing them is not.

**Fix.** Decide and document the estimand. For ITT, restrict to mode='live' and count every assigned row including non-enacted ones, and label a non-enacted treated row by the same 14-day silence rule the control arm uses. For per-protocol, require `enacted` on the treated side and report the compliance rate on the artifact. Either way, drop mode='shadow' from the uplift extraction and record the mode composition in metrics.

### `label-loop-never-closes` — Nothing ever closes an unanswered offer, so the corpus can never acquire enough labels to train on

**backend/agent_core/reco/decisions.py:126** · integration · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

record_response accepts 'interested'/'declined'/'deferred'/'not_reached' (line 130), but the only production callers are record_response(..., 'declined') at bot_tools.py:518 and voice/tools.py:2087, and attach_lead(..., response='interested') at agent_core/tools/domain.py:575 and db.py:5087. Grep across backend/*.py finds no writer of 'deferred' or 'not_reached' outside the simulator, and no scheduled sweep. The treatment engine has exactly this component (agent_core/treatment/followthrough.py:14: 'the whole shadow corpus is missing without it'); reco has no equivalent. The live evidence: offer_decisions holds 16 rows and 0 responses, ever.

**Impact.** train_propensity correctly excludes unlabelled rows (:106-108), so the trainable corpus grows only from offers that either produced a lead or were explicitly declined in-call. Every offer where the call dropped, the customer said 'send me details', or the rep moved on is lost forever. The engine therefore cannot self-improve at any traffic volume, and the 200-row floor may never be reached. It simultaneously makes the replay baseline bug above fire on every run.

**Fix.** Add a followthrough sweep for reco mirroring the treatment one: after a configurable horizon (e.g. 14 days), close any presented decision with response IS NULL and no lead to 'not_reached', and close one whose lead is still open past the horizon to 'deferred'. Record the closure timestamp and reason so a censored label is distinguishable from an observed one, and teach the trainer to treat 'not_reached' as censored (excluded) but 'deferred' as a weak negative or a separate class — a decision the design doc should make explicitly rather than by omission.

### `features-offer-history-ignores-mode-and-tenant` — The live offer-history read has no mode and no tenant predicate, so simulated rows drive real borrowers' fatigue and cooldowns

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:419** · correctness · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `S02-train-reco`

features.py:419-430 issues "SELECT chosen_product_id, response, presented, created_at FROM offer_decisions WHERE customer_id = :cid AND created_at > now() - interval '180 days' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 200" with params {"cid": customer_id} — no mode filter and no tenant_id filter. The results set features.declined_products, features.last_offer_at and features.offers_last_30d (:437-446), which feed the decline/family cooldowns in candidates.generate (candidates.py:106-107,153), the fatigue sub-score (scoring.py:229-234 'fatigue = _clamp01(features.offers_last_30d / 3.0)'), the fatigue and offers_last_30d model features (vectorize.py:62,81), and the hard per-customer frequency cap in arbitration.py:104 'if features.offers_last_30d >= policy.max_offers_per_customer_30d: return _no(SUPPRESS_CUSTOMER_CAP)'. The simulator marks ~85% of its decisions presented (simulate_offer_decisions.py:201-204) and writes real responses (:221) against real seeded customer ids (:110,142). This directly contradicts the contract asserted three times elsewhere: sql/06_sales.sql:107-110, alembic/versions/20260731_0052:5-7, simulate_offer_decisions.py:12-14 ('the trainer, the replay harness and the dashboards can all exclude it with one predicate'). observability.py:57-58,104 and replay_offers.py:64,77 do honour it; the feature builder — the one read that changes a live borrower's outcome — does not.

**Impact.** A simulated or otherwise non-real decision row raises a real customer's offers_last_30d and last_offer_at, and adds its chosen product to their declined set. That suppresses genuine offers through the per-customer 30-day cap, silences a whole product family through the cooldown, and shifts the fatigue penalty in the rule score and the fatigue feature in the model. Unlike the trainer's missing predicate this one affects a live decision on the audio path, not an offline artifact. On a shared UAT or dev database seeded from production — the normal bank pattern — one simulator run at --calls 800 over twenty customers pushes every one of them past RECO_MAX_PER_CUSTOMER_30D=3 and the engine goes quiet for real people, with the suppression logged as a legitimate customer cap. The missing tenant predicate has the same shape as the offline-jobs finding but here it is on the serving path.

**Fix.** Add "AND mode <> 'simulated' AND tenant_id = :tenant" to the query at features.py:421-427, matching what policy.py:293-296 already does on its own decision read, and pass db.current_tenant(). Add a test that seeds one simulated row and asserts offers_last_30d and declined_products are unchanged. Longer term, make the mode predicate structural: expose a single `real_decisions` view (or a helper in decisions.py) that every reader must go through, so 'exclude it with one predicate' becomes true by construction rather than by each caller remembering.

### `rule-version-constant-hides-weight-changes` — RuleScorer's logged version is a hard-coded constant while its weights are env-tunable, so replay cannot identify the logging policy

**backend/agent_core/reco/scoring.py:241** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

"name = \"rule\"\n    version = \"1.0.0\"" (scoring.py:240-241), written into offer_decisions.recommender_version on every decision (engine.py:232). config.py:1-6 states the opposite intent: 'Changing how much sentiment matters must not require a code review, a build and a deploy — it has to be a config change someone can make on a Tuesday afternoon.' replay_offers.build_ranker then calls 'weights = config.weights()' (:104) — today's environment — and scores decisions made under whatever weights were live at the time.

**Impact.** Replaying '--scorer rule' against decisions logged before a weight change silently compares two different policies and attributes the difference to nothing. Worse, the operational premise is that weights change often, so this will be the normal case. Nothing in the decision row records the weights, so the drift is not merely unattributed — it is undetectable after the fact. That also undermines the A/B design, since two arms can share recommender_version='1.0.0' while running different weights.

**Fix.** Derive RuleScorer.version from a hash of the Weights dataclass (e.g. 'rule@' + short digest of the sorted weight tuple), and additionally write the full weights snapshot into offer_decisions.features under a 'policy' key. Have replay read the logged weights per row rather than the current environment, and refuse to aggregate across differing policy versions without an explicit flag.

### `no-exploration-no-propensity-in-reco` — The reco loop logs no propensity and does no exploration, so no offline estimator it produces has valid support

**backend/scripts/replay_offers.py:22** · statistics · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

The docstring admits it: 'That estimator is only unbiased if the logging policy explored randomly, and this one does not — it is deterministic' (:22-23). RuleScorer.score sorts deterministically with ties broken on product id (scoring.py:252-256, 'offline replay depends on' it). offer_decisions has no propensity, policy_version or explore_kind column (sql/06_sales.sql:99-137), while treatment_decisions has all three. RECO_AB_SPLIT is unset, so config.assign_variant produces no holdout arm (engine.py:112).

**Impact.** Every candidate product other than the rule scorer's argmax has zero probability of ever being offered, so the corpus contains no counterfactual for it and no amount of data will ever reveal that product 4 would have converted. The trainer learns P(convert | chosen by the rule scorer), replay's rejection sampling has empty support outside the logged action, and there is no unbiased way to decide whether to promote a model. This is the difference between the treatment engine (ranked exploration running, non-degenerate propensity on every live row) and the reco engine, and it is the reason 'plugs in and self-improves' is not true of reco today.

**Fix.** Add propensity, policy_version and explore_kind columns to offer_decisions; put a small epsilon-greedy or ranked-exploration layer between scoring and arbitration (post-veto, so exploration can never surface an ineligible product); log the sampling probability of the chosen action. Then replace replay's rejection sampling with a self-normalised IPS estimator with a clipped weight and a bootstrap interval. Configure a null_offer control arm via RECO_AB_SPLIT so there is an untreated baseline at all.

### `replay-ranks-by-p-not-ev` — Replay evaluates a propensity ranking that production never produces

**backend/scripts/replay_offers.py:124** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

build_ranker: '(lambda vec: artifact.comparable_score(artifact.predict(vec)))' (line 124), and main sorts by that alone (:180-183). Production PropensityScorer ranks by expected value: models.py:335 'expected = p * candidate.margin_score * base.suggested_amount' and models.py:318 'scored.sort(key=lambda o: (-(o.expected_value or o.score), -o.score, o.product_id))'. The class docstring makes the point explicitly (models.py:268-270): 'a 20% chance on Rs 5 lakh beats a 45% chance on Rs 25,000, and ranking on probability alone gets that backwards.'

**Impact.** The offline harness that exists to answer 'would this scorer have done better?' answers it for a scorer that will never ship. Whenever the ticket sizes across the catalogue differ — which is the entire reason expected-value ranking was built — the replayed argmax differs from the production argmax, so 'matched', replayConversion, lift and precision@1 all describe a different policy. A committee approving RECO_SCORER=propensity on these numbers would be approving an untested ranking. The same applies to --scorer hybrid at :132-134, which blends the rule score with comparable_score rather than reproducing HybridScorer's blend over the EV-sorted output.

**Fix.** Have replay reconstruct the production ranking: log suggestedAmount and margin_score per candidate in the decision row (suggestedAmount is already in ScoredOffer.to_log, scoring.py:60), then rank by p * margin * amount with a documented fallback to comparable_score when the amount is absent — the same 'expected_value or score' fallback models.py:318 uses. Better still, expose one ranking function that both PropensityScorer._score_one and replay call, the way rule_score_from_vector already pairs with RuleScorer.

### `replay-baseline-denominator-mismatch` — replayConversion and baselineConversion have incompatible denominators, so 'lift' is systematically inflated

**backend/scripts/replay_offers.py:213** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

Lines 191-194: 'if row.get("presented") and chosen: logged_presented += 1; if label is not None: logged_positive += label'. Lines 198-200: 'if label is not None and chosen and top_score >= floor: if top_product == chosen: matched += 1; matched_positive += label'. Then :213-214 'baseline = (logged_positive / logged_presented)' and 'replayed = (matched_positive / matched)', and :226-230 'lift = replayed / baseline - 1.0'. The baseline denominator counts unlabelled presented rows; the replay denominator does not.

**Impact.** This is the single number a collections head or a model-risk committee will read when deciding whether to switch RECO_SCORER. Because nothing in production ever writes 'deferred' or 'not_reached' and there is no sweep that closes an unanswered offer (see label-loop-never-closes), the unlabelled fraction of presented offers in a real deployment will be large — plausibly the majority. If 60% of presented offers stay unlabelled, the baseline is deflated by 2.5x and the reported lift is inflated by 150 percentage points of pure arithmetic. The docstring's honest caveats are about sampling bias; this one is a bug, and it points the same direction every time.

**Fix.** Compute the baseline over the same labelled population: 'if row.get("presented") and chosen and label is not None: logged_labelled += 1; logged_positive += label' and divide by logged_labelled. Report the unlabelled count separately as a first-class metric ('presented but never labelled'), because that number is itself the health signal for the learning loop.

### `simulator-truth-is-the-fitted-model-class` — The latent truth is a logistic-linear function of exactly the logged vector — the trainer is guaranteed to recover it

**backend/scripts/simulate_offer_decisions.py:55** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

_accept_probability builds 'z = -4.6 + 2.4*get("in_call_intent", 0.25) + 1.6*get("affordability") + ... - 1.0*get("utilization")' from the same dict that is logged and trained on, then '1.0 / (1.0 + pow(2.718281828, -z))' (:55-68). The docstring claims independence only from the rule scorer: 'deliberately a different function from the rule scorer ... so there is something for a model to find' (:16-19).

**Impact.** The corpus is a well-specified recovery problem for the exact hypothesis class fit_logistic implements, with no unobserved confounder, no customer or product random effect, no temporal drift and no measurement noise on the features. The achieved holdout AUC is bounded only by Bernoulli sampling noise, so 0.758 is close to the theoretical ceiling of that corpus and says nothing about achievable performance on real borrowers, where most of the variance in whether someone accepts a top-up loan is unobservable. Reporting it as evidence that the propensity pipeline works is circular, and it is the number that would appear in a readiness deck.

**Fix.** Add irreducible noise the model cannot fit: a per-customer random intercept, a per-product effect, an unobserved 'household income shock' latent that is drawn but never written into the vector, and a mild non-linearity (an interaction the linear model cannot express). Then report the oracle AUC of the true generating function alongside the fitted AUC, so the readiness question becomes 'how much of the recoverable signal did we recover' rather than 'did we recover a function we planted'.

### `offline-jobs-cross-tenant` — Every offline job reads across all tenants; there is no RLS to catch it

**backend/scripts/train_propensity.py:72** · privacy · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

train_propensity.py:71-88, replay_offers.py:70-84, bench_recommender.py:147 ('SELECT id FROM customers ORDER BY id') and simulate_offer_decisions.py:110-115 all issue tenant-free SQL. offer_decisions.tenant_id is NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id) (sql/06_sales.sql:101) and every serving read scopes it — agent_core/reco/policy.py:280-296: 'WHERE d.customer_id = :cid AND d.tenant_id = :tenant AND d.mode <> \'simulated\''. There is no ROW LEVEL SECURITY or CREATE POLICY anywhere under backend/sql or backend/alembic/versions, so nothing in the database enforces what the application forgot; tenant_context.py:5-13 states this explicitly ('one process serves one tenant ... the policies already read the GUC' — but no policies exist).

**Impact.** A bank hosting two entities (e.g. the bank arm and the NBFC) in one database gets one model fitted on both books and served to both, and a replay report that mixes them. Under DPDP that is a purpose-limitation and data-segregation failure; contractually it is co-mingling of two regulated entities' borrower data in a derived artifact that cannot be un-mixed after the fact. It also makes every offline number wrong the day the deployment stops being single-tenant, with no error to signal it.

**Fix.** Add 'AND d.tenant_id = :tenant' (from db.current_tenant(), overridable by a required --tenant argument) to all four scripts, refuse to run without one, and record the tenant in the artifact. Separately, enable RLS with FORCE on offer_decisions/customers/leads against the app.tenant_id GUC that db_core.py:169-181 already sets, so an offline job that forgets the predicate returns zero rows instead of everyone's.

### `no-tests-for-any-of-the-four-scripts` — None of the four scripts has any test; the trainer's statistics are entirely unverified

**backend/scripts/train_propensity.py:254** · testing · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

A repo-wide grep for train_propensity / replay_offers / bench_recommender / simulate_offer_decisions matches only main.py (a docstring), the scripts themselves, two SQL files, train_treatment_models.py, two alembic migrations and observability.py — no file under backend/tests. Yet auc (:254-274), platt_calibrate (:226-245), brier (:248-251), fit_logistic (:181-223), label (:94-108), extract (:123-152) and column_means (:155-165) are pure functions with no I/O, trivially testable, and every one of them is load-bearing for a model that will price offers to borrowers.

**Impact.** The tie-handling in auc, the class-weight normalisation in fit_logistic and the labelling precedence in label are the kind of code where an off-by-one is silent and permanently biases every model the system produces. The 216 passing tests give a false sense of coverage: they cover the serving path, not the learning path. In a bank, an unvalidated metric implementation used to gate a model's release is itself an audit finding.

**Fix.** Add unit tests with hand-computed expectations: auc against a known ranking including ties and against the degenerate one-class case; platt_calibrate recovering a known (a,b) on synthetic logits; fit_logistic recovering known coefficients on separable and on noisy data; label precedence when response and lead_stage disagree; extract's three skip counters; column_means with an all-missing column. Add an end-to-end test that runs the trainer against a small fixture corpus containing simulated rows and asserts they are excluded.

### `force-flag-leaves-no-trace` — --force bypasses both quality gates and the resulting artifact is indistinguishable from a validated one

**backend/scripts/train_propensity.py:283** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

"ap.add_argument(\"--force\", action=\"store_true\", help=\"write the artifact even if it is below the sample floor or fails to beat a coin flip\")" (:283-287), consumed at :303 and :355. The artifact dict at :364-384 contains no field recording that --force was used, who ran it, or what it overrode.

**Impact.** An engineer under deadline pressure can ship a model with AUC 0.48 — an inverted model that systematically ranks the worst prospects first — and neither the file, the log retained afterwards, nor models.load_artifact can tell. For a bank's model-risk function, the ability to override a validation gate without leaving an auditable record is itself the finding; RBI-style model governance requires the override, the justification and the approver to be recorded with the model.

**Fix.** Require --force to carry a reason string ('--force "reason"'), write 'forced': true, 'forcedReason', 'trainedBy' (os.getlogin / an explicit --operator) and the failed gate values into the artifact, and have models.load_artifact refuse a forced artifact unless RECO_ALLOW_FORCED_MODELS=1. Emit the whole artifact header as a structured log line at ERROR level when forcing.

### `customer-level-leakage-in-split` — The holdout is not grouped by customer, so per-customer features are memorised and the AUC is inflated

**backend/scripts/train_propensity.py:328** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

"cut = max(1, int(len(X) * args.holdout))\n    X_test, y_test = X[:cut], labels[:cut]\n    X_train, y_train = X[cut:], labels[cut:]" (:328-330). customer_id is not even selected in fetch_rows (:72-81), so grouping is impossible without a schema change to the query. Roughly a third of the 23 features are customer-level constants within a short window — dpd_worst, utilization, relationship_months, account_count, months_since_last_payment, open_disputes, prior_win_rate.

**Impact.** The book here is ~20 customers against 1335 training rows, so each customer contributes ~67 rows split across train and test. The model can memorise 'this particular customer converts' from their fixed attributes and be rewarded for it on the holdout. The reported AUC 0.7584 is therefore an upper bound that will not reproduce on unseen customers — which is the only population that matters, since a real book turns over. This is the classic reason a model looks strong in validation and flat in an A/B.

**Fix.** Select d.customer_id, and split by customer with a time cut: hold out the most recent window AND restrict the holdout to customers absent from training where the book allows it. Report both the grouped and ungrouped AUC in the artifact so the gap is visible. Add nCustomers to the artifact and refuse to fit when nCustomers is below a floor (a 20-customer corpus cannot support 23 coefficients regardless of row count).

### `train-on-test-fallback-silent` — A warning-only fallback makes the holdout the training set, and the artifact does not say so

**backend/scripts/train_propensity.py:331** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

"if not X_train or not sum(y_train):\n        logger.warning(\"holdout split left no positive training rows — training on everything\")\n        X_train, y_train = X, labels\n        X_test, y_test = X, labels" (lines 331-334). Every metric below — model_auc, model_brier, baseline_brier, base_rate — is then in-sample, and it is model_auc that the ship/no-ship gate at :355 evaluates.

**Impact.** A logistic regression with 23 coefficients on a few hundred rows will comfortably exceed 0.55 AUC in-sample, so the one quantitative gate protecting the serving path is disabled precisely in the case where the data is thinnest. The artifact records metrics.auc and metrics.holdoutN with no flag distinguishing this; the only tell is holdoutN == nSamples, which nothing checks. base_rate, which becomes the divisor in comparable_score at serve time (models.py:118-121, :181), is also computed in-sample.

**Fix.** Make this path fatal by default (return a distinct exit code and no artifact) with an explicit --allow-insample override. Whenever it is taken, stamp 'validation': 'in_sample' into the artifact and have models.load_artifact refuse such an artifact unless RECO_ALLOW_INSAMPLE_MODELS is set. Log the positive counts on each side of the split so the operator can see why.

### `platt-calibrated-in-sample` — Platt scaling is fitted on the training logits, so p_convert is overconfident by construction

**backend/scripts/train_propensity.py:338** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

"train_logits = [sum(a * c for a, c in zip(xi, w)) + b for xi in X_train]\n    cal_a, cal_b = platt_calibrate(train_logits, y_train)" (:337-338). The calibrator's own docstring states the stakes: 'Expected value multiplies p by an amount, so an uncalibrated p would put a confident rupee figure on a number that does not mean what it says' (:229-232).

**Impact.** Fitting the sigmoid on the same rows the coefficients were fitted on is the textbook way to get an overconfident calibrator: the training logits are already separated more than out-of-sample logits will be, so cal_a is too large and p is pushed toward 0 and 1. p_convert then feeds expected_value = p * margin * amount (models.py:335), which is the number production ranks by and which appears in the explanation string shown to the operator ('{p:.0%} modelled conversion, expected value {expected:,.0f}', models.py:350-354). An overstated probability attached to a rupee figure in a collections context is a number a supervisor will act on and a regulator will ask about.

**Fix.** Carve a dedicated calibration slice out of the training tail (a three-way split: fit / calibrate / test), or use cross-fitted out-of-fold logits for the Platt fit. Report a reliability-curve summary (expected calibration error in a handful of bins) in the artifact metrics alongside Brier, and gate on it — an artifact whose ECE exceeds a threshold should not ship even if the AUC is fine.

### `artifact-has-no-provenance` — The artifact carries no corpus, tenant, date window or class counts — there is no model card

**backend/scripts/train_propensity.py:364** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

The artifact dict (:364-384) is name, version, type, featureNames, coefficients, intercept, means, calibration, trainedAt, nSamples, vectorVersion, featureSchemaVersion, metrics{holdoutN, auc, brier, baselineBrier, baseRate}. models/propensity.json confirms nothing more is present. The treatment-side artifacts, by contrast, record 'corpus: simulated' and are gated by TREATMENT_ALLOW_SIMULATED_MODELS; agent_core/reco/models.py:135-234 has no analogous check.

**Impact.** Nobody can answer, from the artifact alone: which tenant, which date range, how many positives, live or simulated traffic, which rule weights produced the logging policy, was a gate overridden. Those are exactly the questions a model-risk reviewer asks first, and 'check the shell history of whoever ran it' is not an answer. It is also why the simulated-corpus defect above went unnoticed for five weeks.

**Fix.** Add corpus (list of modes), tenantId, dataWindow {from, to}, nPositives/nNegatives, nCustomers, rowsSkipped by reason, ruleWeights snapshot, trainerGitSha, trainedBy, and a 'validation' field. Have models.load_artifact log the full header once at load and refuse artifacts whose corpus includes 'simulated' or whose tenantId disagrees with the process tenant, unless explicitly allowed.

### `no-model-registry-or-rollback` — The trainer overwrites the live serving artifact in place, with no versioned history, approval step or rollback

**backend/scripts/train_propensity.py:386** · reliability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `S02-train-reco`

"out = Path(args.out)" defaulting to 'os.getenv(\"RECO_MODEL_PATH\", \"models/propensity.json\")' (:279), which is exactly the path models._model_path() serves from (models.py:237-238), written via tmp.replace(out) (:389-391). The artifact carries a 'version' timestamp field but the file name never changes, so the previous model is gone. models.load_propensity is invoked from build_scorer on every recommend() call (scoring.py:431), so the swap takes effect between two turns of a live conversation.

**Impact.** There is no champion/challenger step, no shadow evaluation of the new artifact against the old, no approval record, and no way to roll back other than restoring a file from git or backup. A retraining run at 14:00 changes the model mid-call for customers already in conversation, with no canary and no announcement. For a bank this is an uncontrolled production model change; RBI-style governance expects versioned artifacts, an approval trail and a documented rollback.

**Fix.** Write to models/propensity/<version>.json and maintain 'current.json' as an explicit, separately-approved pointer that a human or a promotion job flips after the challenger has been replayed and shadow-scored. Cache the loaded artifact in the process behind an mtime check so a swap takes effect at a defined boundary rather than mid-conversation, and log a structured 'model promoted' event with the old and new versions.

### `metrics-and-trainer-read-across-tenants` — The recovery sum and the model trainer both read every tenant's rows with no tenant predicate

**backend/agent_core/treatment/metrics.py:226** · privacy · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `S03-simulator`

metrics.efficiency's money query is `SELECT COALESCE(sum(amount), 0)::float AS recovered FROM ledger_entries WHERE type = 'payment' AND posted_at >= now() - make_interval(days => :days)` (metrics.py:226-236) — no tenant join and no tenant filter, feeding recoveredInr and voiceMinutesPerLakhRecovered (:251-254). The same file's voice query (:213-224) reads `FROM interactions WHERE channel = 'voice' ...` with no tenant predicate either, and _breaches (:345-390) joins customers but filters only on contact_events. train_treatment_models._rows (:120-139) selects `FROM treatment_decisions WHERE mode = ANY(:modes) AND feature_schema_version = :schema` — no tenant predicate — so a model is fitted across every tenant's decisions at once.

**Impact.** On a multi-entity NBFC or a shared platform install, tenant A's §17 scoreboard reports tenant B's recovered rupees and voice minutes, and a model promoted for tenant A is fitted on tenant B's borrowers. That is a cross-tenant disclosure of financial aggregates and a model trained on data the tenant has no basis to process — a DPDP purpose-limitation problem and the kind of finding that ends a security review, independent of the simulator entirely.

**Fix.** Add `JOIN accounts a ON a.id = le.account_id JOIN customers c ON c.id = a.customer_id WHERE c.tenant_id = :tenant` to the recovery sum and an equivalent predicate to the voice and interaction reads; add `AND tenant_id = :tenant` to train_treatment_models._rows and stamp the tenant on every artifact. Better, run both under the application's RLS role rather than a bypass connection, so the predicate cannot be forgotten.

### `sim-no-tenant-scoping-anywhere` — Synthetic ids are global, the sweep and purge queries carry no tenant predicate, and a second tenant's run silently produces nothing

**backend/scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py:313** · data-model · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S03-simulator`

`customer_id = f"{TAG}C{index:06d}"` / `account_id = f"{TAG}A{index:06d}"` (:313-314) - identical for every tenant. customers.id is a global primary key (02_customer_account.sql:45) and every INSERT uses `ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING`. accounts has no tenant_id at all (02_customer_account.sql:81-95). sweep_day selects `WHERE a.id LIKE :tag` with no tenant filter (:574); purge deletes `WHERE mode = 'simulated' OR customer_id LIKE :tag` and `WHERE id LIKE :tag`, also with no tenant filter (:853-859).

**Impact.** Run the simulator for tenant B after tenant A and every INSERT is a no-op while the script still reports success; the sweep then writes tenant-B-context decisions against tenant-A customers, and the resulting corpus crosses a tenant boundary that RLS exists to enforce. Purge deletes every tenant's corpus. On a shared staging or a multi-entity NBFC deployment this is both a data-integrity and an isolation failure, and it is the kind of finding that ends a security review.

**Fix.** Prefix the tag with the tenant (`SIM-{tenant}-C000001`), add `AND c.tenant_id = :tenant` to sweep_day's join and to both purge DELETEs, and run the whole script through the same RLS role the application uses rather than a bypass connection.

### `sim-thin-support-for-field-and-legal` — Ticket sizes are too small for the expensive actions to be chosen, so the corpus has almost no support for the two actions its own latent truth says work best on avoidant borrowers

**backend/scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py:326** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `S03-simulator`

`instalment = round(rng.lognormvariate(8.3, 0.55), 2)` (:326) gives a median instalment of about Rs 4,000. config.py:183-184 prices a field visit at Rs 1,150 and a legal notice at Rs 2,500 against TREATMENT_RECOVERY_FRACTION 0.35 (config.py:250). Meanwhile ACTION_EFFICACY gives avoidant borrowers field_visit 1.00 and legal_notice 0.90 (:181-182) - the highest in the table.

**Impact.** The EV scorer will almost never choose the two actions the simulator says are the only things that move an avoidant borrower, so those cells get only the exploration floor (MIN_PROPENSITY 1e-6, explore.py:67) worth of data. The positivity/overlap assumption that every off-policy estimator in ope.py depends on is thin exactly where the effect is largest, and the resulting importance weights are enormous. The corpus quietly cannot answer the question it was built to answer for the hardest segment.

**Fix.** Generate a realistic product mix including larger secured and higher-ticket accounts (currently `secured` is false for every row), and report per-action support and the maximum importance weight alongside each artifact so a thin cell is visible before the model ships.

### `sim-no-consent-dnd-or-hold-rows` — dnd is hardcoded false and no consent, hold, dispute or preferred-window row is ever written, so the compliance vetoes are never exercised

**backend/scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py:344** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `S03-simulator`

The customers INSERT hardcodes `'Asia/Kolkata', :segment, :risk, :score, false` (:344) for dnd, sets `language` to a literal 'en' (:343), and leaves preferred_window null. The script writes only customers, accounts, emi_installments, mandates, payment_events, promises and ledger_entries - no consent table, no holds, no disputes, no complaints. features.py's `consent_by_channel`, `allowed_hours`, `allowed_days`, `holds` and `open_dispute_count` are therefore at their defaults for every one of the 14,331 rows.

**Impact.** The docstring claims the corpus runs 'through the real vetoes' (:27). It does not run through the ones that matter to a DPO: DPDP consent by purpose and channel, TRAI DLT registration state, the DND registry, borrower-set contact windows, legal holds and open disputes. On a real book these suppress a large and non-random share of decisions, so the corpus's action mix, propensity distribution and cost profile are all unrepresentative - and there is no regression evidence anywhere that the consent path behaves correctly at volume. `secured`, `on_hold`, `open_disputes` and `field_visits_90d` are additionally zero-variance columns in the vector, so the artifacts ship coefficients for a support the corpus never observed.

**Fix.** Generate consent rows with realistic per-channel coverage and expiry, a DND subpopulation, borrower-set windows, a share of accounts under hold or with an open dispute, and a vernacular language mix. Assert in a test that every suppression_reason the engine can emit appears at least once in a generated corpus - a veto with zero corpus coverage is a veto nobody has tested.

### `sim-risk-score-encodes-the-latent-reach` — risk_score is a near-deterministic encoding of latent reachability, and it is in the model vector - the reach AUC of .73 is largely a self-fulfilling feature

**backend/scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py:366** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `S03-simulator`

`"score": max(300, min(850, int(300 + 500 * reachability + rng.gauss(0, 55))))` with the comment 'A *noisy proxy* for reachability, not a copy of it' (:361-368). scoring.py:534 includes `"risk_score": float(features.risk_score)` in the model vector. Within-segment reach variation comes only from latent_reach's id hash (:289), which no other feature sees.

**Impact.** The reach model's headline AUC is mostly the recovery of an engineered channel from the label's own driver. A bureau score in an Indian book correlates with willingness and with capacity; it does not correlate with contactability at rho ~0.93 - the number that actually predicts contactability is attempt history, and that is the thing the corpus makes constant. The reach model will be materially worse on a real book than the artifact advertises, and the champion/challenger gate has no way to notice because it compares against the same corpus.

**Fix.** Make reachability observable only through behavioural traces that a real book also carries - attempt/connect history, hour-of-day response, channel-specific bounces - and let risk_score correlate with willingness/capacity instead. Then report the reach AUC with and without risk_score in the artifact so the dependence is visible.

### `sim-days-overdue-uses-wall-clock-not-simulated-now` — The simulator passes a past `now` but the feature builder computes days_overdue from the wall clock, so a logged point-in-time feature is anchored to the run time

**backend/scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py:602** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S03-simulator`

The simulator calls `recommend_treatment(..., trigger=Trigger(kind="dpd_tick", at=day, ref=ref), now=day, ...)` (:602-604) with `day` up to `--days` in the past. features.py:614 computes `days = int((datetime.now(timezone.utc) - due).total_seconds() // 86400)` using the process clock, ignoring the injected `now`.

**Impact.** Two features that must agree - `dpd` (frozen at book build) and `days_overdue` (wall clock minus a fixed due date) - are both constant across the run and disagree with each other. The point-in-time discipline that scoring.vector's docstring (scoring.py:503-509) and segments.py's header both claim as the corpus's central guarantee is broken for this column. It is also a live bug outside the simulator: any replay or backfill that injects `now` gets today's days_overdue.

**Fix.** Thread `now` through FeatureProvider.build into the instalment query (it is already a parameter) and use it instead of datetime.now(). Add a test that builds features twice with two different injected `now` values and asserts days_overdue differs.

### `sim-no-harm-outcomes-at-all` — The latent truth has no downside: no complaint, no dispute, no opt-out, no consent withdrawal, no goodwill cost - every model fitted here concludes that contact is free

**backend/scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py:637** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `S03-simulator`

_settle's entire outcome vocabulary is {paid, unresolved, reached, ptp, refused, no_answer} (:682, :693-697). A 'refused' never withdraws consent, never opens a dispute, never raises a complaint. There is no channel in the script by which a treatment can make things worse. ACTION_EFFICACY's comments describe legal notice and field visits as costing goodwill (:122-123, :184-186) but no code implements it.

**Impact.** Contact fatigue, the daily cap, `fatigue_cost` (config.py:255) and the whole intrusiveness ladder exist to price a harm the corpus asserts is zero. An uplift model fitted here will always favour more contact and the harsher rung, because the corpus contains no evidence against it. The engine's most consequential safety parameters are therefore unfalsifiable on the only data that exists. In a bank this is the failure mode that produces an RBI fair-practices finding, and the model-risk file would have nothing to show that the harm side was ever modelled.

**Fix.** Add a harm process to the latent truth: probability of complaint / opt-out / dispute rising with intrusiveness, with cumulative touches, and with segment (distressed and avoidant highest), and let it terminate future reachability for that borrower. Then the fatigue cost and the caps become measurable, and 'the model wanted to call them a sixth time' becomes a thing the corpus can refute.

### `sim-latent-truth-ignores-every-context-feature` — Uplift depends only on segment x action x reach - no dpd, no bucket, no timing gap, no attempt history, no mandate state, no time

**backend/scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py:663** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `S03-simulator`

`efficacy = ACTION_EFFICACY.get(segment, {}).get(action, 0.2)` then `incremental = profile["uplift"] * efficacy * _reach_probability(action, reachability)` (:663-670). Nothing else enters. Notably, `salary_timing_gap_days` - the one feature built expressly to make emi_date_change causal (features.py:299-316) - has no role in the latent truth, so emi_date_change 'works' on forgetful borrowers at efficacy 0.80 whether or not there is any timing gap to close.

**Impact.** The granularity ladder's third rung (individual CATE) has almost nothing to discover beyond re-learning risk_score, and no interaction term is learnable at all. The engine's policy layer reasons about mandate state, timing tolerance, attempt history and bucket; the corpus asserts none of them modifies the treatment effect. So the corpus cannot refute a wrong policy rule, and the segment-vs-population promotion test it was used to calibrate is measuring a world where segment is the only true moderator - which is exactly the answer the segment ladder was built to produce.

**Fix.** Make efficacy conditional: emi_date_change effective only when |salary_timing_gap_days| is large, represent_mandate effective only for insufficient-funds returns with a live mandate near the salary credit, human_call decaying with prior unanswered attempts. Then the ladder has something real to climb and the policy rules become testable.

### `sim-no-fatigue-or-decay` — The thirtieth consecutive daily contact is exactly as effective as the first

**backend/scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py:668** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `S03-simulator`

`incremental = profile["uplift"] * efficacy * _reach_probability(action, reachability)` (:668-670) carries no term for prior attempts, and `_reach_probability` (:806-816) depends only on the action's channel and the borrower's static reachability. `features.digital_attempts_since_connect` and `case_attempts` are in the vector (scoring.py:520-527) and have zero causal weight in the latent truth.

**Impact.** Response decay under repeated contact is one of the two or three strongest empirical regularities in collections, and it is the justification for the daily cap, the intrusiveness ladder and TREATMENT_FATIGUE_COST=6. On this corpus, an optimiser that contacts everyone every day dominates - and neither the EV scorer's fatigue term nor the caps can be validated or falsified. The collections head is being asked to trust a contact policy whose restraint has never been priced against evidence.

**Fix.** Multiply efficacy and reach by a decay in unanswered attempts since last connect, and make the decay segment-dependent (avoidant fastest). Add a corpus-level assertion that a saturating contact policy underperforms a paced one - if it does not, the corpus is not modelling fatigue.

### `sim-no-mandate-presentation-rows` — represent_mandate is 'enacted' without a mandate_presentations row, so the presentment-limit and retry-backoff vetoes never fire and the corpus teaches unlimited daily re-presentment

**backend/scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py:689** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S03-simulator`

`decisions.mark_enacted(result.decision_id, ref=f"{TAG}SIM", conn=conn, enacted_by="treatment_executor")` is the whole of enactment. features.py:695-720 derives `mandate_attempts_this_cycle` and `mandate_last_presented_at` from `mandate_presentations`, which the script never writes. policy.py:261 (`if features.mandate_attempts_this_cycle >= limit: return MANDATE_LIMIT_REACHED`) and policy.py:265-266 (MANDATE_TOO_SOON, whose comment says a premature re-presentment 'debits the borrower twice for one EMI, which is the single worst thing this action can do') therefore never trigger on a single simulated row.

**Impact.** 72% of simulated accounts have an active mandate (:417-418) and ACTION_EFFICACY makes represent_mandate the strongest instrument for the two largest segments (1.00 forgetful, 0.95 squeezed, :145 and :158) with guaranteed reach. The corpus consequently rewards presenting the same mandate every day for thirty days - a policy that breaches NACH/NPCI presentment limits, that double-debits borrowers, and that is the fastest route to a mandate revocation and an RBI complaint. Any model fitted on this corpus learns that represent_mandate is nearly free and nearly always right, and the two vetoes that stand between that belief and a compliance incident have zero test coverage in the corpus.

**Fix.** Insert a mandate_presentations row for every enacted represent_mandate, with presented_for = the mandate cycle, a realistic settle delay and a return_reason drawn from RETURN_MIX. That single change exercises MANDATE_LIMIT_REACHED, MANDATE_TOO_SOON and _mandate_return_permits_retry, and stops the corpus from rewarding a scheme violation.

### `sim-enactment-path-bypassed-label-distribution-wrong` — _settle calls mark_enacted directly instead of the executor, so the corpus's outcome distribution is nothing like the live one

**backend/scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py:689** · testing · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S03-simulator`

`decisions.mark_enacted(result.decision_id, ref=f"{TAG}SIM", conn=conn, enacted_by="treatment_executor")` (:689-691). The real path is agent_core/treatment/enact.py, gated at enact.py:80 on `config.mode() != config.MODE_LIVE` - which force_mode='simulated' never satisfies. Established fact: 84 of the 108 labelled live outcomes are 'cancelled', written by enact.py when enactment aborts. The corpus produces zero 'cancelled' rows.

**Impact.** 78% of the live label mass is a class the training corpus does not contain. _label_cure maps 'cancelled' to 0 (train_treatment_models.py:206) and _label_timing maps it to 0 as well (:186-187), so on live data the models will be scoring a regime whose dominant outcome they never saw. Capacity reservation, send-time consent re-checks, template/DLT selection and channel fallback are likewise untested by the corpus - and those are precisely the failure paths that generate the 'cancelled' rows.

**Fix.** Route _settle through a simulated executor that shares enact.py's abort logic (or make enact.py accept a pluggable transport), so aborts produce 'cancelled' at a realistic rate and the corpus's label distribution resembles the live one. Report the label histogram of the corpus alongside the live histogram in every artifact.

### `sim-ledger-payments-leak-into-live-recovery-kpi` — Simulated cures post untagged ledger_entries rows that the live recovery metric sums unconditionally

**backend/scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py:748** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `S03-simulator`
