A regulator or an internal auditor asking 'show me the exact model that decided to call this borrower on 12 March, and reproduce the score' cannot be answered, and RBI's recording/traceability expectations for automated customer treatment point the same way as the DI design's own audit ambitions.

**Fix.** Store the artifact bytes (compressed) in the registry row or in a content-addressed store keyed by sha, written in the same transaction as the promotion. Retain for the regulatory retention period. This also makes rollback and offline replay possible.

### `registry-evaluation-is-unverified-operator-json` — The promotion gate trusts an unsigned, unbound JSON blob the operator supplies

**backend/agent_core/treatment/registry.py:226** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T04-models-registry`

`if evaluation is None: objections.append("no evaluation attached...")` else `lift = evaluation.get("lift")`. The Mapping comes from `_load_evaluation(args.evaluation)` (scripts/promote_model.py:63-79), which reads any file path and accepts `{"lift": ...}` at the top level. Nothing binds the evaluation to the artifact's sha, to the target, to the row window it was computed over, or to when it was computed.

**Impact.** `echo '{"lift":0.9,"trustworthy":true,"ate":0.2}' > ok.json` promotes any loadable artifact. The gate that a compliance committee is told is the control is defeated by a text editor, and the ledger records the fabricated evidence verbatim into treatment_model_registry.evaluation as if it were provenance. In an RBI/internal-audit model review this is the finding that fails the whole learning loop.

**Fix.** Have evaluate_policy stamp into its report the artifact sha it scored, the target, the decision-id range / as-of timestamp, the row count and an HMAC over those fields keyed by a deployment secret. check() must recompute the HMAC, refuse a sha mismatch, and refuse an evaluation older than N days. Better still: have check() recompute the OPE estimate itself from treatment_decisions inside the same transaction so there is no blob to forge.

### `registry-no-significance-test-on-lift` — Promotion gates on a point estimate and ignores the standard error it is handed

**backend/agent_core/treatment/registry.py:236** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T04-models-registry`

`elif float(lift) < MIN_HOLDOUT_LIFT:` — the only numeric test. ope.Estimate carries `stderr` (ope.py:106) and to_log() emits it (ope.py:150), and check() never reads it. `Estimate.trustworthy` (ope.py:129-141) tests ESS fraction and unsupported fraction only, not whether the lift is distinguishable from zero.

**Impact.** lift=+0.006 with stderr=0.40 promotes. On a 20-customer dev book, and on a real book for the first several months, the standard error will routinely dwarf 0.005, so the gate is effectively a coin flip dressed as a control. A bank's model-risk function will not accept a promotion criterion with no confidence interval, and the engine will churn champions on noise — each churn resetting whatever learning the previous champion had accumulated.

**Fix.** Require `lift - z * stderr > MIN_HOLDOUT_LIFT` with z from a configurable one-sided level (1.645 default), refuse when stderr is absent, and record the interval in the ledger. Add a minimum n and a minimum ESS in absolute terms, not just the fraction ope.py already checks.

### `registry-promoted-by-unauthenticated` — promoted_by is free text from a CLI flag, and there is no maker-checker

**backend/agent_core/treatment/registry.py:284** · security · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `T04-models-registry`

`promoted_by: str,` written straight into the ledger at registry.py:353 (`"by": promoted_by`). Its only source is `--by` (scripts/promote_model.py:87), validated by `if not args.by: ap.error("--by is required to promote: the ledger records who decided")` (161-162) — non-emptiness, nothing more.

**Impact.** The model-approval audit trail records whatever string the person with shell access typed. There is no authentication, no role check, no second approver, and no UI — the same individual proposes the challenger, computes its evaluation, writes the evaluation JSON and approves the promotion. Under RBI outsourcing/IT governance and any internal audit of an automated customer-treatment system, a single-actor irreversible change to a production decision model with a self-asserted approver name is a finding on its own, before anyone looks at the statistics.

**Fix.** Move promotion behind the authenticated API with the existing _authz_guard (main.py:616) and a dedicated role; record the authenticated principal, not a parameter. Require a distinct second principal to approve (status 'approved' between 'challenger' and 'champion'), and record both in the ledger with timestamps.

### `registry-no-rollback-path` — There is no demote or rollback, and the staleness gate can make the previous champion unrestorable

**backend/agent_core/treatment/registry.py:376** · reliability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `T04-models-registry`

The module exposes register, champion, history, check, promote, reject, verify. `reject()` acts only on challengers (`AND status = 'challenger'`, registry.py:393). Reverting means re-promoting the old artifact through check(), which calls models.load_artifact (registry.py:212), which refuses any artifact older than TREATMENT_MODEL_MAX_AGE_DAYS (models.py:569).

**Impact.** The bad promotion is discovered a week later from a contact-rate or complaint spike. The correct incident action — put yesterday's model back — has no command, and if the previous champion is now past 90 days the gate refuses it outright. The operator's only options are to hand-copy the file (defeating the ledger and leaving verify() reporting 'unregistered'), to set TREATMENT_MODEL_MAX_AGE_DAYS higher globally (weakening the staleness guard for everything), or to delete the serving file and fall back to priors. All three are worse than a rollback command.

**Fix.** Add `rollback(conn, tenant_id, target, to_version=None)` that restores the most recent retired champion from a registry-owned artifact store, bypasses the staleness check with an explicit reason recorded in the ledger, and records a 'rolled back from X' row. Keep every promoted artifact's bytes so this is always possible.

### `registry-no-auto-verify-or-auto-demote` — Nothing runs verify() on a schedule, and nothing demotes a champion that goes bad

**backend/agent_core/treatment/registry.py:399** · observability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `T04-models-registry`

verify()'s only callers are `db_treatment_holds.treatment_models` (db_treatment_holds.py:490) behind `GET /treatment/models` (main.py:4818) and `scripts/promote_model.py --verify` (109). No worker job, no cron, no alert.

**Impact.** Every drift condition the function was written to detect — a swapped file, a deleted file, an unregistered file — is detected only when a human happens to open a page. And the reverse control is missing entirely: monitor.py computes feature drift and calibration, and nothing connects a broken calibration or a post-promotion ATE turning negative back to a demotion. A model that degrades after promotion stays champion until someone notices the business metric.

**Fix.** Run verify() from the worker on an interval, emit its states as metrics, and alert on anything but 'ok'. Add an automatic demotion (to the previous champion, or to priors) when monitor's calibration or drift checks breach an alert threshold for N consecutive runs, recording the demotion and its evidence in the ledger.

### `registry-verify-inspects-the-wrong-machine` — verify() reports on the filesystem of whichever process answered the HTTP request

**backend/agent_core/treatment/registry.py:410** · observability · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `T04-models-registry`

`serving = Path(SERVING_PATHS[target])` inside verify(), reached from `db_treatment_holds.treatment_models` (db_treatment_holds.py:486-491) behind `GET /treatment/models` (main.py:4818-4824).

**Impact.** With more than one replica, the answer depends on which pod the load balancer picked, and it says nothing about the voice workers that actually score live-call decisions. An operator can refresh the page and get different answers, or get a green 'ok' from an API pod while every voice worker is serving a stale file (see registry-file-copy-does-not-reach-replicas). The check that exists to detect drift is itself the least reliable observation in the system.

**Fix.** Have every serving process report its loaded artifact sha, version and load verdict as a heartbeat row or a labelled metric, and make verify() aggregate across processes: 'reach: 7 of 9 workers serving sha abc123, 2 serving def456'.

### `registry-verify-does-not-verify-serving` — verify() reports 'ok' for a champion the loader currently refuses

**backend/agent_core/treatment/registry.py:430** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T04-models-registry`

`actual = _sha(serving)` / `matches = actual == record["artifact_sha"]` / `"state": "ok" if matches else "drifted"`. It compares bytes and never calls models.load_artifact.

**Impact.** Every refusal path in load_artifact is invisible to the health check: stale past TREATMENT_MODEL_MAX_AGE_DAYS (models.py:569), vectorVersion mismatch after a t2→t3 bump (525), featureSchemaVersion mismatch (535), and corpus='simulated' without the opt-in (549). Today all three shipped artifacts are corpus='simulated' and the flag is not set, so verify() would print 'ok — serving what was promoted' for three models that are answering nothing. The one dashboard a collections head or an SRE would look at to ask 'is the model live?' answers the wrong question with a green light.

**Fix.** verify() must load the serving file through models.load_artifact with production settings (allow_simulated=None so the env gate applies) and report a third axis: sha-matches, loads, and the loader's refusal reason when it does not. Expose it as a metric, not only as a GET endpoint.

### `reach-artifact-is-an-action-lookup-not-a-borrower-model` — The shipped reach model is a near-deterministic function of the action, and the 0.95 clamp binds on every voice and field decision

**backend/models/treatment_reach.json:1** · statistics · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `T04-models-registry`

The artifact carries intercept 1.99012709 with coefficient +15.00346947 on `intrusiveness` and -4.44753632 on `rung`; every other coefficient is <= 0.266 in magnitude (next largest: bucket_curability -2.425, then ptp_keep_rate +0.265). `intrusiveness` and `rung` are both deterministic per-action constants from actions.SPECS (actions.py:80-124) and are collinear by construction. Scoring at the artifact's own training means gives p_reach = 0.068 at intrusiveness 0.0, 0.256 at SMS (0.10), 0.426 at WhatsApp (0.15), 0.987 at voice_bot (0.45), 0.994 at human_call (0.50) and 0.99997 at field_visit (0.85); models.py:795 then clamps to `min(0.95, ...)`. load_artifact (models.py:467-500) applies no bound to coefficient magnitude and registry.check() (registry.py:192-274) never reads the artifact's own metrics, so it passes every gate at holdoutAuc 0.7306.

**Impact.** For the three most expensive actions the reach term is a constant 0.95 for every borrower, so all borrower-level discrimination inside those strata is destroyed and the ranking among them collapses onto cost and fatigue — the opposite of what a reach model is for, and it makes the dialler spend decisions on the cost side of the formula alone. Nothing reports it: the reason code says 'reach_from_model' (models.py:796), the components record the clamped value (830-836), and monitor.py measures drift and calibration but not clamp incidence. A near-perfect apparent AUC accompanies it, because predicting reach from the channel is easy.

**Fix.** Refuse |coefficient| above a configurable bound at load and add the same objection to check(); drop one of the collinear action constants from the feature set or regularise them together; and add a clamped-fraction counter per target with an alert above a few percent. Report per-action reach spread in the model card so 'this model has learned the channel and nothing else' is visible before promotion, not after.

### `evaluation-selects-the-max-lift-challenger-with-no-correction` — The promotion block is the argmax over candidate policies, handed to a gate that tests a point estimate

**backend/scripts/evaluate_policy.py:147** · statistics · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `T04-models-registry`

`best = max(challengers, key=lambda k: report["policies"][k]["snips"]["lift"])` (evaluate_policy.py:147-150), then `snips["ate"] = effect.ate` and `snips["ateSignificant"] = effect.significant` (153-154) and `report["promotion"] = snips` (155). registry.check() reads only `lift` against MIN_HOLDOUT_LIFT (registry.py:236), `trustworthy is False` (242) and `ate <= 0` (264) — it never reads the `stderr` that ope.Estimate.to_log put in the same dict (ope.py:149) nor the `ateSignificant` flag two lines above the lift it does read.

**Impact.** Selecting the maximum of several noisy off-policy estimates biases the reported lift upward by roughly the spread of the candidate set, and the gate then compares that inflated point estimate to a fixed 0.005 floor with no interval and no multiple-comparison correction. On a corpus growing 19-42 rows a day this reliably promotes noise, and each promotion churns the champion, resets whatever the previous one had accumulated, and — because no artifact version lands on the decision row — cannot afterwards be evaluated against its own outcomes. A model-risk reviewer will read 'we picked the best of five and promoted it because it cleared 0.005' as a textbook selection-bias finding.

**Fix.** Report every challenger's interval rather than only the winner's point estimate; require `lift - z*stderr > MIN_HOLDOUT_LIFT` in check() with z configurable (1.645 default) and refuse when stderr is absent; apply a Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment for the number of challengers compared, recording the count in the evaluation; and make check() honour the `ateSignificant` flag it is already handed instead of only testing the sign of the ATE.

### `explore-seed-is-deterministic-per-customer-not-per-decision` — The exploration draw is a fixed function of the customer, so the logged propensity is not the conditional probability of the action

**backend/agent_core/treatment/explore.py:199** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

explore.py:208-210: "return '|'.join([customer_id, trigger_kind, trigger_ref or '', ','.join(actions)])" with the docstring at explore.py:206 stating "Excludes the clock, so the same decision replays to the same answer." _draw (explore.py:186-189) derives its entire randomness from that seed. So for a fixed customer, trigger kind, trigger ref and surviving candidate list, the chosen index is constant across every repetition. The logged propensity w_i is a population-marginal, not pi(a|x): conditional on x the action was taken with probability 1.

**Impact.** IPS and SNIPS assume the log is a draw from pi(.|x). Here the randomisation is across customers, not across decisions, so the effective sample size for exploration is the number of distinct (customer, trigger, candidate-set) tuples - roughly 20 on this book, not 225 - while ESS is computed from weights and reports a much larger number. Worse, the assignment is confounded with the customer: whichever customers happen to hash into 'try WhatsApp' are permanently the WhatsApp cohort, so any measured difference between actions is a difference between customer cohorts. On a real book of 200k accounts the law of large numbers rescues the marginal, but only if each account contributes one decision; collections re-decides the same account daily for 90 days, so the correlation never washes out. Every confidence interval the system prints is too narrow by roughly sqrt(decisions per account).

**Fix.** Include a per-decision nonce in the seed - the decision id is not available before the draw, so use the trigger's timestamp bucket or a monotonic attempt counter: seed_for(..., attempt=features.case_attempts, at=now.isoformat(timespec='hours')). Reproducibility for replay is preserved because the same inputs are recoverable from the logged row; what is lost is the accidental per-customer stratification. Also persist the seed in the candidate log so an auditor can verify the draw.

### `followthrough-reward-attribution-is-customer-level-not-decision-level` — One payment labels every open decision for that borrower 'paid', so the OPE reward is a borrower-level fact replicated across correlated rows

**backend/agent_core/treatment/followthrough.py:257** · statistics · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `T05-explore-ope`

_paid_since queries "SELECT 1 FROM ledger_entries WHERE account_id = :aid AND type = 'payment' AND posted_at > :since" and falls back to "SELECT 1 FROM payment_intents WHERE customer_id = :cid AND status = 'paid' AND paid_at > :since" (followthrough.py:257-282); _promised_since is "SELECT 1 FROM promises WHERE customer_id = :cid AND created_at > :since AND status IN (...)" (followthrough.py:285-297). Neither joins on the decision, the case (trigger_kind, trigger_ref), the channel or the action, and `since` is the decision's own enacted_at or created_at (followthrough.py:168) with no upper bound. ope.observations() then turns each such row into an independent Observation with reward 1.0 (ope.py:501-511), and every variance formula treats them as independent (ope.py:232, 266, 309, 532-535).

**Impact.** On this book, ~11 decisions per customer means one payment can flip many rows to reward 1.0 simultaneously. The rewards are then not merely correlated within a borrower, they are frequently identical by construction, so the true design effect on every reported standard error is far larger than the naive count implies and TreatmentEffect.significant will fire on a handful of paying borrowers. It also destroys the attribution the gate depends on: a payment triggered by an SMS is credited equally to the WhatsApp, the bot call and the mandate presentment decided in the same window, so no challenger can be distinguished from any other on the evidence the corpus carries. In a bank, one large borrower curing can move the reported ATE on its own.

**Fix.** Attribute at the case level and bound the window: require the payment or promise to fall inside a per-action attribution window measured from enacted_at (the same shape as config.grace_hours already used at followthrough.py:201), and credit at most one decision per case per resolving event — the most recent enacted attempt. Persist customer_id on ope.Observation and report the distinct-customer count alongside n in Estimate.to_log so the clustering is at least visible while the attribution is being fixed.

### `ope-action-label-is-coarser-than-the-treatment` — The evaluated action space is the action label only; timing, channel and content are treated as fixed

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:95** · correctness · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:92-95: "#: A candidate policy: given the logged candidates, what would it have done? / #: Returns a distribution over actions." Every policy in the module maps to a bare action string (ope.py:335 "return {best: 1.0} if best else {}"). But the thing actually enacted is (action, channel, scheduled_at) - engine.py:520-525 calls `timing.plan(action, features, now=now, horizon_hours=...)` before the veto, and engine.py:387-391 records chosen_channel and scheduled_at. explore.choose() draws over actions only; the slot is a deterministic function of the action.

**Impact.** Two challengers that pick whatsapp are scored as identical even if one would send it at 09:00 and the other at 18:30, and the timing model - one of the three fitted estimators, AUC .81 - is precisely a claim about when. So the gate cannot measure the value of the model most likely to be right. Conversely, when the incumbent's timing changes (a new calling-window rule, a salary-credit signal), the logged propensity is unchanged while the treatment materially changed, so historical rows are silently reinterpreted. Under the RBI 08:00-19:00 calling window effective 2027-01-01 the feasible slot set will shift for the whole book, and every pre-2027 row will describe a treatment that can no longer be delivered.

**Fix.** Either widen the logged action key to (action, hour bucket) so the propensity and the policy agree on what an action is, or state the restriction explicitly in Estimate as an `action_space` field and refuse to compare policies that differ in timing. At minimum, log the planned slot on each candidate so a future estimator can condition on it, and record the timing policy version alongside policy_version.

### `ope-promotion-on-max-lift-with-no-uncertainty-gate` — There is no standard error on the lift, and the promotion block selects the argmax challenger without checking trustworthy or significance

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:125** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:125-127: "@property / def lift(self) -> float: / return self.value - self.baseline" - a point estimate with no variance. The consumer at evaluate_policy.py:145-155 does "best = max(challengers, key=lambda k: report['policies'][k]['snips']['lift'])" and writes it straight into report['promotion'], which the comment at evaluate_policy.py:136-139 describes as "the input to promote_model.py without anybody reshaping JSON by hand". Nothing in that path consults `est.trustworthy` (ope.py:129-140), and nothing compares lift to stderr.

**Impact.** Three compounding errors in one promotion decision. First, `stderr` describes `value`, not `lift`, and value and baseline are computed from correlated rows, so no valid interval exists. Second, taking the max over challengers is the winner's curse - the selected lift is biased upward by roughly the spread of the candidates. Third, evaluate_policy.py is a CLI a human or a cron can run repeatedly against a corpus that grows 19-42 rows/day, so a 2-SE threshold peeked at daily will eventually fire on pure noise. A bank promoting a collections model on this evidence has no defensible model-validation record, and the model would not survive an RBI model-risk review.

**Fix.** Add `lift_stderr` computed as the SE of the paired per-row difference (w*r - r), which is the correct variance for a paired comparison on the same rows. Make `trustworthy` a hard precondition of the promotion block, add `lift > 2 * lift_stderr` as a second, and record the number of challengers compared so a Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment can be applied. Persist every evaluation run with its timestamp and corpus bounds so sequential peeking is at least auditable.

### `ope-challenger-space-truncated-to-incumbent-approved-set` — A challenger can only be evaluated inside the incumbent's approved set, so no challenger with a different value floor or ladder is measurable

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:196** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:195-198 tests support against `obs.support`, which observations() (ope.py:489-493) builds from the per-candidate propensities - and engine.py:566-574 writes those only for actions present in `verdict.distribution`, which arbitration.py:170 populates from `affordable`, i.e. after the value floor (arbitration.py:138), the reserve (arbitration.py:155-163) and the already-planned check (arbitration.py:125-136). `wait` is removed even earlier at arbitration.py:97 "contenders = [s for s in scored if s.action != A.WAIT]", so no policy that would wait can ever be supported.

**Impact.** The most valuable challenger questions a collections head asks are 'should the floor be lower?', 'should we contact less?', and 'should we skip a rung?' - and every one of them is unanswerable here, because every such policy is 100% unsupported and fails MAX_UNSUPPORTED_FRACTION. The engine can only ever learn to reorder within the choices the incumbent's hand-tuned thresholds already permit, which is a local search around TREATMENT_GREEDINESS and the EV floor. Combined with the suppressed-decision drop, the system cannot self-improve along the axis regulators and borrowers care most about.

**Fix.** Log a propensity for every scored action, including the below-floor and reserve-filtered ones and `wait` - the propensity is genuinely 0 for those under the current policy, but recording the full scored set with an explicit zero (plus the gate that zeroed it) lets a doubly-robust estimator carry them on the direct term instead of discarding them. Then explicitly randomise the floor itself in a small arm so a lower floor becomes supported at all.

### `ope-baseline-over-different-population-than-value` — lift compares the candidate scored on its agreement subset against the logged average over all rows

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:217** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:217-220: "def _baseline(observations): / return (sum(o.reward for o in observations) / len(observations) if observations else 0.0)" versus ope.py:230-232 "terms = [w * r for w, r in zip(weights, rewards)] / value = sum(terms) / n", where w is 0 on every row the deterministic candidate disagrees with. The docstring at ope.py:110-114 claims "Computing it here rather than leaving it to the caller means the two numbers always come from exactly the same rows."

**Impact.** With a deterministic candidate that agrees with the log on, say, 40% of decisions, `value` is an estimate over that 40% while `baseline` averages all 100%. `lift` therefore mixes a policy-comparison signal with a selection difference between the agreement subset and the rest of the book - and the agreement subset is exactly the population where the incumbent already did what the challenger wanted, i.e. the easy cases. A challenger that agrees only on the easiest decisions will show a large positive lift for no reason. This is the number evaluate_policy.py:149 ranks challengers by.

**Fix.** For a like-for-like comparison, compute the baseline over the same rows that carry nonzero weight, and additionally report the coverage fraction (rows with w>0 / n) as a first-class diagnostic. Better: report the paired per-row difference and its SE rather than the difference of two separately-computed means.

### `ope-estimator-policy-drops-shipped-clamps` — The OPE re-scorer applies none of the clamps the shipped scorer applies, and applies reach to channel-less actions

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:371** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:370-383: "p_reach = (reach.predict(vec) if reach is not None else ...)", "tau = (uplift.predict(vec) ... )", "decay = (1.0 - timing.predict(vec) ...)". The shipped scorer clamps every one: models.py:795 "reach = max(0.01, min(0.95, self._reach.predict(vec)))", models.py:804 "resolve = max(0.0, min(0.95, self._uplift.predict(vec)))", models.py:812 "already = max(0.0, min(0.99, self._timing.predict(vec)))". models.py:794 also guards reach substitution with "if self._reach is not None and A.spec(s.action).channel is not None" - ope.py applies the reach model to represent_mandate and emi_date_change, which have no channel and for which the reach model was never fitted.

**Impact.** models.py:256 notes that a negative tau is a real and expected finding. Unclamped, a negative tau multiplied by a large exposure produces a large negative score in OPE that the shipped scorer would have floored at 0.0, so the two rank differently on exactly the segments where the uplift model is most informative. Applying a channel reach model to a mandate presentment produces a number with no meaning and pushes the single highest-ROI action around the ranking arbitrarily - relevant here because represent_mandate has been excluded on all 225 decisions and is the action most in need of an honest counterfactual.

**Fix.** Fold into the same shared scoring function as the previous finding, so the clamps and the channel guard live in one place. Until then, replicate models.py:794-813 exactly in ope.py:363-388 and add a property test asserting parity.

### `ope-logged-ev-reward-scale-mismatch` — The DR reward model's default recovery_fraction is 1.0 while the scorer's is 0.35, so the direct term is ~3x too small

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:410** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:410 "def logged_ev_reward(recovery_fraction: float = 1.0) -> RewardModel:" and ope.py:427 "return min(1.0, gross / (exposure * recovery_fraction)) if exposure else 0.0", called with no argument at evaluate_policy.py:122 "reward_model = ope.logged_ev_reward()". But gross was produced by scoring.py:429-430 as exposure * policy.recovery_fraction * VALUE_HORIZON * reach * resolve * decay, so dividing by exposure * 1.0 leaves recovery_fraction (0.35, and estimator_policy's own default at ope.py:353 is 0.35) baked in. The docstring at ope.py:425-427 claims the result is "Normalised to a cure-probability scale so it is comparable with a 0/1 reward". It is not; it is about a third of one.

**Impact.** In doubly_robust (ope.py:300-306) the direct term is systematically ~0.35x the true modelled cure probability and the residual correction w*(r - taken) is correspondingly inflated, so DR - the estimator the module docstring at ope.py:18-20 says is "The one to quote when a reward model exists" - is biased low by an amount that depends on the agreement rate. Because the bias is not constant across policies, the ranking of challengers under DR is not even order-preserving. Also, the VALUE_HORIZON multiplier is still inside gross but not in the denominator, so date-change rows are biased in the opposite direction from everything else.

**Fix.** Default `recovery_fraction` to `config.policy().recovery_fraction`, or have evaluate_policy.py pass it as it already does for estimator_policy (evaluate_policy.py:112). Divide by `exposure * recovery_fraction * VALUE_HORIZON.get(action, 1.0)` to invert the scorer exactly. Add a unit test asserting that logged_ev_reward on a candidate produced by EVScorer returns reach*resolve*decay.

### `ope-ptp-scored-equal-to-paid` — A promise to pay is scored identically to a payment, creating a direct incentive to optimise for promises that break

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:440** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:436-440: "#: Outcomes that count as the borrower resolving. ``ptp`` is included because a / #: promise is what a collections floor is measured on ... CURED = frozenset({'paid','ptp'})". The corpus has 10 ptp against 7 paid, so PTPs are already the majority of positive labels, and no PTP-kept/PTP-broken outcome exists in the model at all.

**Impact.** PTP break rates in Indian retail collections run 40-60%. A challenger that maximises the reward defined here is a challenger that maximises promise extraction, and the fastest way to extract a promise is pressure. This is the single most well-known gaming vector in collections analytics, and it points the model at behaviour that RBI's fair-practices guidance treats as coercive. Because PTPs already outnumber payments in the label set, the gate is majority-driven by the softer signal today, and a promotion made now would bake it in.

**Fix.** Split the reward: `paid` at 1.0, `ptp` at its empirically-measured kept rate (and at 0 until that rate can be measured, since assuming 1.0 is the aggressive assumption). Add a `ptp_kept` / `ptp_broken` outcome so the rate becomes measurable, and make the discount a named, logged constant rather than set membership so a model-risk reviewer can see the assumption. Report cure-on-payment and cure-on-promise as separate estimates.

### `ope-no-policy-version-or-recommender-filter` — The corpus is pooled across policy versions, scorers and feature schema versions, so the logging policy is an undocumented mixture

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:460** · statistics · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:460: "clauses = ['mode = ANY(:modes)', 'outcome IS NOT NULL', 'propensity IS NOT NULL']" - nothing else. The columns exist and are deliberately populated: decisions.py:105 inserts `policy_version`, `recommender`, `recommender_version`, `feature_schema_version`, and models.py:736-739 is explicit that the recommender name exists so "a corpus spanning a rollout cannot be split by which model produced each row, and the champion/challenger comparison silently mixes them".

**Impact.** OPE's validity rests on the logged propensities describing one policy. A corpus spanning a scorer change or a rule-version change is a mixture whose components have different propensities for the same x, and the importance weights are then wrong in a direction nobody can sign. The code that writes these columns states the exact hazard; the code that reads the corpus ignores them. In a bank, policy_version changes every time legal updates the calling-window or notice rules - which, with RBI DOR.MCS.REC.No.199 landing 2027-01-01, is guaranteed to happen mid-corpus.

**Fix.** Add `policy_version`, `recommender`, `recommender_version` and `feature_schema_version` filters to observations(), default them to the currently-live values, and record the distinct values found in Estimate.to_log() so a mixed corpus is visible rather than assumed away. Refuse to compute (or mark untrustworthy) when more than one recommender_version is present without an explicit override.

### `ope-no-tenant-scoping` — Neither observations() nor treatment_effect() filters by tenant, pooling every client's book into one estimate

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:469** · privacy · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:469-474: "SELECT id, chosen_action, outcome, propensity, variant, candidates / FROM treatment_decisions / WHERE {' AND '.join(clauses)} / ORDER BY created_at ASC" - the clause list (ope.py:460) is only mode / outcome / propensity / variant. treatment_effect (ope.py:571-578) is the same. The column exists and is populated: decisions.py:100 and :133 insert `tenant_id`, and the engine resolves it from features (engine.py:360).

**Impact.** Two distinct failures. Governance: a policy is promoted for tenant A on evidence drawn partly from tenant B's borrowers, so no tenant can be told what evidence supports the model acting on their book, and the DPDP purpose-limitation position is that borrower outcome data from one lender was processed to build another lender's model. Statistics: books differ in product mix, ticket size and collection culture, so pooling produces an estimate that describes no actual book and Simpson's paradox is live - a challenger better for every tenant separately can look worse pooled, and vice versa. This is invisible on a single-tenant 20-customer dev book and immediate on the first two-client deployment.

**Fix.** Make `tenant_id` a required keyword argument of both functions, add it to the WHERE clause, and put it in the Estimate/TreatmentEffect log payload. Fail loudly rather than defaulting to all tenants. If a cross-tenant pooled model is ever wanted it must be an explicit, separately-consented mode.

### `ope-loads-whole-corpus-into-memory` — The whole decision corpus including candidate JSONB is materialised in Python, with the statement timeout disabled

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:479** · scale · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:479-512: "out: list[Observation] = [] / for row in conn.execute(text(sql), params).mappings():" builds a list of every matching row, each holding the full `candidates` JSON array with a feature vector per action (engine.py:596-599 writes a `vector` dict onto every candidate row when log_vectors() is on). The caller disables the safety net: evaluate_policy.py:79 "conn.execute(text('SET statement_timeout = 0'))". There is no server-side cursor, no yield_per, no chunking.

**Impact.** At 19-42 rows/day on a 20-customer book this is invisible. A real book of 200k accounts decided daily produces millions of rows per quarter, each carrying a multi-hundred-byte candidate array with vectors - tens of gigabytes materialised in one Python list. The job OOMs, and because statement_timeout is 0 it will hold a Postgres connection open indefinitely first, on the same database serving the collections floor. The failure arrives exactly when the corpus finally becomes large enough for OPE to be worth running.

**Fix.** Stream with `conn.execution_options(stream_results=True, yield_per=1000)` and make the estimators consume an iterable rather than a Sequence (they currently need two passes; restructure to accumulate sums in one pass). Keep a bounded statement_timeout rather than zero. Consider pushing reward and support extraction into SQL so the vectors never cross the wire for estimators that do not need them - only DR does.

### `ope-reward-is-binary-and-ignores-amount` — OPE optimises cure count while the engine optimises rupees, so the gate promotes on a different objective than the policy pursues

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:505** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:505: "reward=1.0 if str(row['outcome']) in CURED else 0.0". The serving scorer is explicitly monetary: scoring.py:429-433 "value = exposure * policy.recovery_fraction * VALUE_HORIZON.get(action, 1.0) / gross = value * reach * resolve * decay / cost = costs.for_action(action) / fatigue = fatigue_cost(...) / ev = gross - cost - fatigue", and explore.py:27 states "The scores are rupees, and rupees are unbounded."

**Impact.** A challenger that cures fifty 8,000-rupee accounts scores five times better than one that cures ten 2,00,000-rupee accounts, while the business recovers half as much. Collections books are extremely heavy-tailed in exposure, so this is not a rounding difference - it inverts the ranking of any policy that trades volume for value. The collections head's target is recovery in rupees; the gate hands them a cure-count optimiser and calls it a lift. It also means the OPE reward has no cost or fatigue term at all, so the estimator can never see that a policy contacts more, which is the harassment dimension.

**Fix.** Add a monetary reward alongside the binary one - amount recovered within a fixed window, net of the logged action cost - and report both estimates. Winsorise the monetary reward (or evaluate on log-rupees) so a single large account does not dominate. Keep the binary cure rate as a secondary metric, not the promotion criterion. Whichever is chosen, the reward must include the cost side, or the gate structurally prefers contacting everyone.

### `ope-no-clustering-by-customer` — Every estimator treats decisions as independent observations when they are repeated measures on the same borrowers

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:535** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `T05-explore-ope`

ope.py:532-535: "def _var(p: float, n: int) -> float: / return p * (1 - p) / n if n else 0.0 / return math.sqrt(_var(self.treated_rate, self.treated_n) + _var(self.control_rate, self.control_n))", where treated_n and control_n are decision counts from "count(*)::int AS n" (ope.py:574). The same iid assumption is in ips (ope.py:232 "variance = sum((t - value) ** 2 for t in terms) / max(1, n - 1)"), snips (ope.py:266) and doubly_robust (ope.py:309). Observation (ope.py:74-89) carries decision_id but no customer_id, so clustering is not even possible downstream.

**Impact.** 225 decisions over ~20 customers is ~11 correlated observations per cluster; the design effect inflates the true variance by roughly 1 + (m-1)*rho, easily 3-5x for collections outcomes where a borrower's ability to pay is the dominant factor. `TreatmentEffect.significant` (ope.py:538-540) will declare a two-SE result on what is really under one SE. Randomisation is at the customer level (config.py:498-516) while inference is at the decision level - the classic unit-of-analysis error, and the first thing a bank's model validation team looks for.

**Fix.** Add customer_id to Observation and to the treatment_effect query. Compute cluster-robust standard errors (a customer-level bootstrap is enough and needs no scipy: resample customers with replacement 2000 times and take the 2.5/97.5 percentiles of the statistic). Report both the naive and clustered SE so the design effect is visible. Report the number of distinct customers alongside n in Estimate.to_log().

### `ope-treatment-effect-counts-the-holdout-arm-as-treated` — The holdout arm — defined to run in shadow and never act — is counted in the treated group of the ATE

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:557** · correctness · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `T05-explore-ope`

treatment_effect takes "modes: Sequence[str] = ('shadow', 'live')" and "control_arm: str = 'null_treatment'" (ope.py:557-558) and splits the corpus on "(variant = :arm) AS is_control" alone (ope.py:572), so every arm that is not null_treatment lands in the treated group via "treated = next((r for r in rows if not r['is_control']), None)" (ope.py:583). The built-in holdout arm is declared "holdout": Variant(name="holdout", mode=MODE_SHADOW) (config.py:360), and engine.py:188-190 lets the arm's mode override the process mode, so every holdout decision is a shadow decision that engine.py:338-343 declines to act on. observations() knows this and excludes holdout explicitly (ope.py:448); treatment_effect does not.

**Impact.** The arm whose entire purpose is to withhold treatment is counted as treated in the one number that measures whether treatment works — and because un-enacted rows can only be labelled paid/ptp/superseded (followthrough.py:19-20, 179-194), those rows enter the treated numerator positively selected. The ATE is corrupted in the direction that favours acting, and it is the number registry.check tests for uplift promotion (registry.py:263-269). The two functions in the same module disagree about which arms are comparable, so the report's own lift and ATE describe incompatible arm sets while being printed and persisted as one experiment.

**Fix.** Derive both the control and the excluded arms from config: control = the arms with suppress_discretionary, excluded = every arm whose mode forces shadow, and restrict the treated group to variants actually present in config.ab_split(). Assert the GROUP BY returns at most two buckets and log loudly otherwise. Report the per-arm row counts in TreatmentEffect.to_log so a third arm cannot enter silently.

### `evaluate-policy-simulated-corpus-passes-the-promotion-gate` — --include-simulated pools synthetic decisions into the promotion evidence, and the gate that refuses simulated artifacts has no equivalent check on a simulated evaluation

**backend/scripts/evaluate_policy.py:74** · correctness · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `T05-explore-ope`

evaluate_policy.py:74: "modes = ('shadow', 'live') + (('simulated',) if args.include_simulated else ())", passed to both treatment_effect and observations (evaluate_policy.py:80-81), and advertised in the usage block at evaluate_policy.py:5. Simulated rows carry outcomes the simulator wrote from a latent truth it controls — followthrough.py:105-110 excludes them from real attribution for exactly that reason ("The synthetic corpus writes its own outcomes, sampled from a latent truth it controls"), and simulate_treatment_corpus.py:683,698 writes them. The resulting report['promotion'] block (evaluate_policy.py:151-155) is Estimate.to_log() plus policy/ate/ateSignificant (ope.py:142-155) and carries no mode, no corpus and no provenance field. registry.check refuses a simulated *artifact* — "if artifact.corpus != 'live' and not allow_simulated" (registry.py:216-224) — but applies no such test to the evaluation, checking only lift, trustworthy and ate (registry.py:232-269).

**Impact.** A live-fitted artifact can be promoted on an evaluation computed wholly or partly from synthetic decisions, and nothing in the ledger records that it was: promote_model.py --evaluation report.json passes registry.check with no objection, and treatment_model_registry.evaluation stores the payload with no way to tell (registry.py:342). The one flag the gate is built around — 'do not serve a model of a book that does not exist' — is enforced on the model and not on the evidence, which is the half a model-risk reviewer will actually audit. It is also an easy accident: --include-simulated is the second line of the script's own usage text.

**Fix.** Have observations() and treatment_effect() return the mode set they actually read and have evaluate_policy.py stamp it into the promotion block (plus the corpus row count and created_at bounds). Then add an objection in registry.check refusing any evaluation whose mode set is not exactly ('live',) unless --allow-simulated is passed, mirroring the artifact rule. Default evaluate_policy.py to live-only rather than shadow+live.

### `allocate-no-legal-or-digital-resource` — The resource set omits every constraint that actually binds in an Indian NBFC

**backend/agent_core/treatment/allocate.py:67** · integration · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `T06-allocate-config`

USAGE at allocate.py:67-77 covers exactly agent_minutes, field_slots, bot_minutes and mandate_presentations. `legal_notice` — the most consequential and most externally rate-limited action in the ladder, at Rs 2,500 a shot (config.py:184) — consumes nothing. `sms` and `whatsapp` consume nothing. RESOURCES is derived from USAGE at allocate.py:79 and both are module constants.

**Impact.** The constraints an Indian collections floor actually hits are not in the model: TRAI DLT template throughput and per-header daily SMS caps, WhatsApp BSP tier limits and template-quality throttling, the legal team's capacity to review and dispatch notices, the print/dispatch vendor's daily volume, and — critically — the sponsor bank's NACH file cut-off, which differs per sponsor and is modelled here as a single tenant-wide `mandate_presentations` number. The optimiser will therefore happily plan 40,000 legal notices for a team that can issue 300, and the dual prices it produces are optimal against a fiction. A collections head shown a plan that ignores the DLT ceiling loses confidence in the whole layer.

**Fix.** Make the resource set data rather than code: a `capacity_resources` table (tenant_id, resource, unit, active) and a `resource_usage` table (resource, action, units_consumed), read at solve time, so a deployment adds `legal_dispatch`, `sms_dlt_throughput` or `nach_file_slots_<sponsor>` without a redeploy. RESOURCES and USAGE become the seeded defaults. This also fixes the per-sponsor mandate cap, which cannot be expressed as one scalar.

### `allocate-solve-is-504-passes-not-one` — The solve is O(sweeps x resources x bisect x n x actions x resources) of pure Python, not the advertised single O(n) parallel pass

**backend/agent_core/treatment/allocate.py:225** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T06-allocate-config`

allocate.py:16-17 claims 'One pass is O(n), it parallelises trivially'. The implementation runs `for sweep in range(MAX_SWEEPS)` (allocate.py:225, MAX_SWEEPS=6) x `for resource in RESOURCES` (allocate.py:228, 4) x [1 free probe at allocate.py:250 + `for _ in range(BISECT_STEPS)` at allocate.py:258, 20] = 504 calls to _demand_at. _demand_at (allocate.py:182-194) is a serial `for demand in demands` loop, and _adjusted_choice inside it recomputes `sorted(values)` (allocate.py:164) and an inner `sum(... for resource, usage in USAGE.items())` (allocate.py:165-168) per account per action. There is no numpy/scipy in the dependency set and no thread/process pool anywhere in the module.

**Impact.** At the two-million-account book the module's own docstring names (allocate.py:4-5, 11-12), one pass is 2e6 accounts x ~9 actions x 4 resources = 7.2e7 inner dict lookups plus 2e6 list sorts; 504 passes is ~3.6e10 operations in CPython. That is roughly 10-30 hours on one core for a job the CLI header says 'Runs once a day, before the sweep' (solve_capacity.py:11). The daily plan would never be ready, and the batch would hold a DB connection (solve_capacity.py:122) the whole time. It is fine on this 20-customer dev book and on the 200-account test book (test_decision_intelligence_p2.py:179-195), which is why it has never been noticed.

**Fix.** Three cheap fixes recover ~50x before any parallelism: (1) hoist the price->action surcharge into a table computed once per price vector — there are at most 9 actions, so `surcharge = {a: sum(prices[r]*USAGE[r].get(a,0) for r in USAGE) for a in ALL_ACTIONS}` replaces the inner loop at allocate.py:165-168 with one lookup; (2) pre-sort each Demand's action list once at construction instead of re-sorting 504 times at allocate.py:164; (3) collapse identical accounts — a real book has far fewer distinct value vectors than accounts, so bucket demands by rounded value signature and carry a weight. Then chunk _demand_at across a process pool. Add a book-size guard that refuses to start a solve above a configured n without the fast path.

### `allocate-cache-not-tenant-keyed` — The dual-price cache is a process global but the query it caches is tenant-scoped

**backend/agent_core/treatment/allocate.py:418** · privacy · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T06-allocate-config`

allocate.py:416-419 `global _CACHE; now = time.monotonic(); if _CACHE and now - _CACHE[0] < _CACHE_TTL: return _CACHE[1]` — the key is time only. The query it memoises is parameterised by `dbmod.current_tenant()` (allocate.py:433), and current_tenant() is request-scoped: db_core.py:127-138 `return tenant_context.current_tenant()`, documented as 'the tenant this call is acting for' replacing the process-level TENANT_ID fallback.

**Impact.** In any multi-tenant deployment (the platform is explicitly tenanted — tenants table FK at migration:43, tenant_id on every row), the first request in each 60s window populates _CACHE for whichever tenant happened to arrive first, and every other tenant's decisions for the next 60 seconds are priced with a different bank's capacity duals. A large NBFC's scarcity signal silently governs a small one's contact strategy, and the cross-tenant read is invisible in logs because the query looks correct. For a bank's DPO this is a tenant-isolation failure on operational data; for the collections head it is unexplainable channel suppression.

**Fix.** Key the cache on tenant: `_CACHE: dict[str, tuple[float, dict[str, float]]]`, read/write under `_CACHE.setdefault(tenant, ...)`, and resolve `tenant = dbmod.current_tenant()` before the cache lookup rather than after. Bound the dict size and make reset_cache() clear all entries.

### `allocate-nonconverged-prices-are-served` — A dual price the solver declared meaningless is persisted and read into every cost term

**backend/agent_core/treatment/allocate.py:429** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T06-allocate-config`

allocate.py:425-434 reads `SELECT resource, dual_price FROM capacity_duals WHERE tenant_id = :tenant AND plan_date = CURRENT_DATE` with no `converged` predicate and no upper bound. persist() at allocate.py:347-382 writes every resource unconditionally, and solve_capacity.py:177-178 calls it after printing 'DID NOT CONVERGE ... The prices below it are not meaningful' (solve_capacity.py:160-165). When bisection never satisfies demand, `hi` stays at its initial MAX_PRICE and allocate.py:268 assigns `prices[resource] = hi` = 100_000.0.

**Impact.** One mistyped capacity number — TREATMENT_CAPACITY_AGENT_MINUTES=240 instead of 24000 — produces a non-converged solve with dual_price 100000. price_for_action('field_visit') then returns 100000 * 45 = Rs 4,500,000 and human_call Rs 600,000, both applied inside Costs.for_action (config.py:167) on the path that decides whether a borrower is contacted. Every human contact on the entire book falls below min_expected_value and the engine goes silent for a full day, with no alert, no suppression_reason that names capacity, and a dashboard (metrics.py:471) that reports it only as a nonConvergedDays count nobody is paged on. This is exactly the 'makes the same mistake two million times, efficiently, with a confident dual price attached to it' failure the module docstring at allocate.py:32-35 warns about.

**Fix.** Add `AND converged` to the read at allocate.py:430 and clamp the result: `price = min(float(r['dual_price'] or 0.0), MAX_SANE_PRICE_PER_UNIT)` with the sane cap derived from the ledger cost of the most expensive action consuming that resource (e.g. never let the surcharge exceed N x Costs.field_visit). Refuse to persist a non-converged solve unless `--force`, and emit a metric/alert when price_for_action would return a surcharge greater than the ledger cost.

### `config-for-action-silent-zero-cost` — An action absent from the Costs dataclass silently costs zero rupees

**backend/agent_core/treatment/config.py:167** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T06-allocate-config`

config.py:167 `return float(getattr(self, action, 0.0)) + allocate.price_for_action(action)`. The default swallows any mismatch between the action-name constants in actions.py:47-56 and the field names of Costs (config.py:140-149). There is no test asserting `set(A.ALL) - {A.WAIT} == set(Costs.__dataclass_fields__)`.

**Impact.** Adding a tenth action — a payment-link nudge, a UPI collect request, an IVR blast — without also adding the field makes that action free. In an expected-value scorer, a free action dominates everything with any cost, so the engine would route the entire book down the new channel from the first deploy, with no error, no warning, and a rationale that looks arithmetically sound. Given the module's whole thesis is that the money constants are the first thing a collections head corrects (config.py:9-14), silently defaulting the most important input to zero is the worst possible failure mode. A typo in a variant's scorer or a rename in actions.py has the same effect.

**Fix.** Replace getattr-with-default by an explicit lookup that raises for unknown actions, and add a startup assertion (and a unit test) that Costs covers exactly A.ALL minus A.WAIT. If a soft failure is genuinely wanted on the hot path, return a large sentinel cost (so the action is suppressed) and log at ERROR, never 0.0.

### `config-costs-and-floors-unvalidated` — Unit costs, min_expected_value and fatigue_cost accept negative values with no clamp

**backend/agent_core/treatment/config.py:172** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T06-allocate-config`

costs() at config.py:171-203 is nine bare `env_float(...)` calls with no bound: `field_visit=env_float('TREATMENT_COST_FIELD_VISIT', 1150.0)`. policy() clamps recovery_fraction to [0,1] (config.py:249-251), urgency_halflife to >=1 (config.py:252-254), max_rung_advance to >=1 (config.py:256), reserve_margin to >=1 (config.py:258), retry_backoff to >=0 (config.py:264) — but leaves `min_expected_value=env_float('TREATMENT_MIN_EV', 2.0)` (config.py:248) and `fatigue_cost=env_float('TREATMENT_FATIGUE_COST', 6.0)` (config.py:255) unclamped.

**Impact.** The design deliberately routes 'a field visit is worth Rs 1,100 not Rs 800' to an env edit by a collections head (config.py:9-14), so a sign error is an expected human input, not an exotic one. TREATMENT_COST_FIELD_VISIT=-1150 makes field visits pay the engine to make them and they win every ranking. TREATMENT_FATIGUE_COST=-6 inverts the one term that stops the engine spending a day's budget on repeated touches — negative fatigue rewards each additional contact, which is textbook harassment under RBI's fair-practices expectations and would be visible in the call log as an escalating same-day sequence. TREATMENT_MIN_EV=-1 disables the floor entirely. Every one of these is a one-character edit with no validation, no warning and no reject.

**Fix.** Clamp every money input at the boundary the way policy() already clamps its ratios: `max(0.0, env_float(...))` for all nine costs and for fatigue_cost and min_expected_value, and log a WARNING naming the variable when a supplied value is rejected. Add an upper sanity bound too (a Rs 100,000 SMS is also a typo). Longer term, validate the whole config on process start and refuse to serve `live` with an out-of-range value.

### `config-no-parameter-provenance-on-decision-rows` — The tunables that produced a decision are not recorded with it, so no decision is reproducible

**backend/agent_core/treatment/config.py:246** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `T06-allocate-config`

policy() (config.py:246-265) and costs() (config.py:170-203) resolve twenty-odd numbers from the environment at call time. engine.py:358-403 records tenant, customer, trigger, mode, variant name, recommender name+version, feature_schema_version, the veto policy provenance (engine.py:379 `'policy': rules.to_log()`), policy_version, candidates, propensity and explore_kind — but no min_expected_value, no fatigue_cost, no recovery_fraction, no urgency halflife, and none of the nine unit costs. The dual price added at config.py:167 is likewise not recorded on the row.

**Impact.** The corpus reports policy_version=1 on all 225 rows, so the indexed version column carries the statutory veto layer only. When a model-risk reviewer or an RBI inspector asks 'why did the engine decide to send a field agent to this borrower on 14 September', the answer requires the cost of a field visit and the EV floor in force at that instant, and both are recoverable only from whatever the env file happened to contain. The same gap breaks the engine's own self-improvement story: the fitted uplift model is trained on decisions whose reward threshold silently moved, and off-policy evaluation compares policies that were never separated in the log.

**Fix.** Hash the resolved (Costs, Policy, dual-price vector) tuple at decision time and write both the hash and the full dict into the decision's features/policy blob — the row already carries a JSON policy field, so this is cheap. Persist each distinct hash once in a `treatment_policy_snapshots` table. Then 'what was the configuration on the 14th' is a join, and a config change becomes visible in the corpus as a new snapshot id rather than as unexplained drift.

### `config-variants-can-redefine-the-control-arm` — TREATMENT_VARIANTS can silently redefine the built-in arms, including null_treatment and holdout

**backend/agent_core/treatment/config.py:428** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T06-allocate-config`

config.py:428 `return {**_BUILTIN_VARIANTS, **(_parse_variants(raw) if raw else {})}` — the env JSON is merged second, so it wins. _parse_variants lower-cases the key at config.py:394 and constructs a full Variant at config.py:403-412 with no protection for reserved names. `{"null_treatment": {"suppressDiscretionary": false}}` turns the randomised control arm into an ordinary treated arm; `{"holdout": {"mode": "live"}}` turns the do-nothing arm live.

**Impact.** The decision row stores only the arm name (engine.py:367), and the whole NAMING HAZARD argument at config.py:333-343 rests on that name meaning something fixed. After an env edit, 20% of the book is stamped `null_treatment` while being contacted normally, and every incremental-uplift number computed off those rows is zero-by-construction and looks like a finding — the exact error the comment warns about. In the other direction, redefining `holdout` to live enacts on a population a model-risk committee signed off as untreated. Neither change leaves any trace: no version, no hash, no audit row.

**Fix.** Refuse to override reserved names — in _parse_variants, skip and warn loudly on any key already in _BUILTIN_VARIANTS, or invert the merge to `{**parsed, **_BUILTIN_VARIANTS}`. Then move variant definitions out of env into a versioned `treatment_variants` table with an id stamped on every decision row alongside the name, so 'what was null_treatment on 14 Sept' is answerable from the row.

### `config-ab-split-drops-typos-silently` — A mistyped arm name in TREATMENT_AB_SPLIT deletes that arm and renormalises the rest to 100%

**backend/agent_core/treatment/config.py:462** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T06-allocate-config`

config.py:461-463 `if key not in known: logger.warning('TREATMENT_AB_SPLIT names unknown variant %r — dropped', key); continue`, followed by config.py:474-477 which renormalises whatever survived: `return [(name, share / total) for name, share in buckets]`. `TREATMENT_AB_SPLIT=control:80,nul_treatment:20` therefore yields `[('control', 1.0)]` — one arm, 100% treated, no control group.

**Impact.** The only signal is a WARNING, and per this deployment's own operational notes the root logger in the api/voice services has no handler, so logger.warning never reaches anybody. The experiment quietly ceases to exist: assign_variant returns `control` for every customer, arm_probability returns 1.0, every row is stamped `control`, and the incremental-uplift readout is zero because there is nothing to difference against. Weeks of book time are spent producing a measurement that cannot be made, and the failure is only discoverable by counting distinct variants in the table.

**Fix.** Fail loudly rather than silently renormalising: if any named arm is unknown, log at ERROR and return [] (no split, process defaults, which is at least an honest state), or refuse to start in `live` mode. Add a startup self-check that logs the resolved split and its bucket boundaries once per process, so the effective experiment is visible in the boot log.

### `config-no-experiment-epoch` — Arm assignment has no experiment salt, so any split change re-buckets live customers mid-experiment

**backend/agent_core/treatment/config.py:513** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `T06-allocate-config`

config.py:513-516 `digest = hashlib.blake2b(customer_id.encode('utf-8'), digest_size=8, person=b'treatmnt').digest(); position = int.from_bytes(digest, 'big') / float(1 << 64)`. The personalisation is a module constant; nothing about the experiment, the split string, or a start date enters the hash. Assignment is then `position < cumulative` over the current split's boundaries (config.py:518-523).

**Impact.** Two consequences a model-risk reviewer will find. First, changing weights (80/20 -> 50/50) moves the boundary and silently migrates every customer with position in [0.50, 0.80) from control to null_treatment while their earlier rows say control — contaminating both arms and violating the docstring's own invariant at config.py:502-505. Second, a *later* experiment reuses the same positions, so arm assignment is perfectly correlated across experiments: whoever was in null_treatment last quarter is in the first bucket of the next split too, and any customer-level heterogeneity is confounded between the two studies for the life of the deployment. With ~20 customers today this is invisible; on a real book it is the difference between an auditable causal claim and a correlation.

**Fix.** Add an experiment epoch to the hash: `person=b'treatmnt'` plus an `TREATMENT_EXPERIMENT_ID` (or the id of a row in a `treatment_experiments` table) folded into the hashed payload, so a new split is a new randomisation and an old one is reproducible. Stamp that experiment id on every decision row next to `variant`, and treat a change to the split without a new experiment id as an error.

### `metrics-capacity-no-tenant-filter` — The capacity dashboard aggregates capacity_duals across every tenant

**backend/agent_core/treatment/metrics.py:461** · privacy · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T06-allocate-config`

metrics.py:461-478 `SELECT resource, count(*), avg(dual_price), min(dual_price), max(dual_price), avg(CASE WHEN capacity > 0 THEN demand / capacity END), count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT converged) FROM capacity_duals WHERE plan_date >= (now() - make_interval(days => :days))::date GROUP BY 1` — there is no `tenant_id = :tenant` predicate, unlike every other tenant-scoped query in the codebase. No RLS policy exists for this table: sql/05_collections.sql:568-591 creates the table and two indexes and nothing else, and the migration (20260821_0088) does the same.

**Impact.** capacity_duals carries `capacity` (how many agent-minutes and field slots a lender has), `accounts` (book size), `demand` and the dual price — a fairly complete picture of a competitor's collections operation. On a shared deployment every tenant's dashboard shows the blended figure, and the 'should we hire' number (migration:22-23) is computed off another bank's roster. db_core.py:130-137 explicitly notes that a tenancy disagreement 'is not a visible error', which is what makes this class of omission dangerous.

**Fix.** Add `WHERE tenant_id = :tenant` (parameterised from db.current_tenant()) to metrics.capacity(), and enable row-level security on capacity_duals with a policy on `app.tenant_id` so the next query that forgets is caught by the database rather than by a reviewer.

### `solve-capacity-not-scheduled` — The daily solve is a hand-run script with no scheduler, no lock, no alert, and a one-day price validity window

**backend/scripts/solve_capacity.py:11** · reliability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `T06-allocate-config`

solve_capacity.py:11 says 'Runs once a day, before the sweep', but a repo-wide search for `solve_capacity` finds it only in the script itself, an audit report and git-status snapshots — no cron entry, no compose service, no Makefile target, no scheduler registration. The prices it writes are valid for exactly one date (plan_date = tomorrow, solve_capacity.py:134) and are read only for CURRENT_DATE (allocate.py:430). There is no advisory lock, so two concurrent runs both solve and race on the upsert.

**Impact.** With TREATMENT_DUAL_PRICING on, a missed nightly run means every dual price silently becomes zero the next morning: capacity ceases to be priced, the ladder stops throttling, and the floor is over-planned against a roster it does not have — with no alert, because the fail-open path at allocate.py:436-438 and the empty-dict default are indistinguishable from 'nothing is scarce'. That is a fail-open on a control the bank was told throttles intrusive contact. Conversely a run that is late by hours plans a day already half-spent.

**Fix.** Register it as a scheduled job with the rest of the platform's timers, take a Postgres advisory lock for the tenant, and emit a heartbeat. Then close the fail-open: when TREATMENT_DUAL_PRICING is on and no row exists for CURRENT_DATE, log at ERROR and expose a health signal rather than returning {} silently — either fall back to the previous day's prices with a staleness flag, or refuse to serve `live` until a solve exists.

### `solve-capacity-counts-suppressed-accounts-as-demand` — The demand curve includes accounts the engine decided not to contact

**backend/scripts/solve_capacity.py:76** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T06-allocate-config`

solve_capacity.py:76-88 selects `DISTINCT ON (COALESCE(account_id, customer_id)) ... candidates FROM treatment_decisions WHERE mode = ANY(:modes) AND created_at >= now() - make_interval(hours => :hours)` with no filter on `suppression_reason` or `chosen_action`. It then takes every candidate with a non-zero expectedValue (solve_capacity.py:95-99). But arbitration suppresses for attempts-exhausted, backoff, already-planned, below-floor and budget-reserved (arbitration.py:100-165) *after* scoring, and engine.py:387 writes `chosen_action=A.WAIT` for those rows while the full scored candidate list is still logged (engine.py:383, _candidate_log at engine.py:557-565).

**Impact.** On the live corpus 106 of 225 rows have a null outcome and the engine's own README describes wait/suppression as a first-class verdict, so roughly half the demand fed to the solver is from accounts under retry backoff or at their attempt cap — accounts that cannot be contacted tomorrow whatever the price. Their agent-minutes and field-slots are counted as competing for capacity, the dual price comes out too high, and contactable accounts are throttled to make room for demand that will never materialise. The bank sees fewer contacts than its roster supports and a scarcity price that says it should hire.

**Fix.** Filter to decisions the engine would actually act on: add `AND suppression_reason IS NULL AND chosen_action <> 'wait'` to the query at solve_capacity.py:83, or better, restrict each account's `values` to actions that were not vetoed and that clear the arm's floor. Log the count dropped so the operator can see how much of the book is currently un-actionable — that number is itself a useful management signal.

### `allocate-dual-price-double-counted-in-next-days-demand` — Tomorrow's solve reads expected values that already have today's dual price subtracted, so the surcharge compounds and the price oscillates

**backend/scripts/solve_capacity.py:96** · statistics · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `T06-allocate-config`

allocate.Demand documents its contract as `#: action -> expected value in rupees, before any capacity price.` (allocate.py:107-108). The pipeline breaks it as soon as dual pricing is on. scoring.py:431-433 computes `cost = costs.for_action(action)` then `ev = gross - cost - fatigue`, and Costs.for_action is `float(getattr(self, action, 0.0)) + allocate.price_for_action(action)` (config.py:167). That ev is what is logged: scoring.py:156-167 `to_log()` emits `"expectedValue": round(self.expected_value, 2)`, written into the candidates blob at engine.py:383. solve_capacity.py:95-99 then reads exactly that field back as the pre-price value: `values = {str(e["action"]): float(e.get("expectedValue") or 0.0) for e in entries ...}`. Nothing subtracts the embedded surcharge out again — the solver has no record of what price was in force when each row was scored, because it is not on the row (engine.py:358-404).

**Impact.** A positive feedback loop on the one number Layer 3 exists to produce. Day 1 prices agent_minutes at p; day 2's logged expected values are all p x usage lower, so the binding pre-check at allocate.py:249-251 — which asks for demand at a price of zero for that resource, holding others fixed — cannot undo the surcharge already baked into `values`, sees suppressed demand, declares the resource non-binding and sets the price to 0. Day 3's values carry no surcharge, demand floods back, and the price jumps again. The dual price becomes a two-cycle whose amplitude has nothing to do with scarcity, the ladder throttles hard on alternate days, and metrics.py:494-498 will label the resource `volatile` without anyone being able to say why. It also invalidates the 'should we hire, stated in rupees' claim (migration:22-23): the marginal value of an agent-hour is being computed from values that were already discounted by the previous marginal value.

**Fix.** Make the invariant enforceable rather than assumed. Log the pre-capacity gross and the applied dual surcharge separately on each candidate (ScoredAction already carries `cost` and a `components` dict at scoring.py:164-166 — add `dualPrice` and `ledgerCost` there), and have solve_capacity reconstruct `values` as expectedValue + the recorded surcharge before solving. Until that lands, refuse to solve from rows written while TREATMENT_DUAL_PRICING was on, or require a `--assume-unpriced` flag so the operator has to state the assumption out loud.

### `mandate-intrusiveness-zero-ignores-borrower-fees` — represent_mandate is priced at ₹0.50 and intrusiveness 0.0, ignoring the ₹200-750 return fee the borrower pays per failed presentment

**backend/agent_core/treatment/actions.py:86** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `T07-policy-arb-actions`

actions.py:86-88 `REPRESENT_MANDATE: ActionSpec(REPRESENT_MANDATE, None, "system", 0, 0.0, False, requires_phone=False)` and actions.py:13 'costs approximately nothing, annoys nobody'; config.py:195 `represent_mandate=env_float("TREATMENT_COST_REPRESENT_MANDATE", 0.50)` with :186-187 'it spends no goodwill at all, so there is no fatigue term'. timing.py:242-243 contradicts: 'every failed presentation costs a bounce charge the borrower pays and resents'. Default limit 3 per cycle (policy.py:320).

**Impact.** The scorer sees a near-free action with a real chance of a whole EMI and ranks it first every time it is legal; on an insufficient-funds account without a salary-credit hint the borrower can be charged three return fees per cycle by their own bank plus the lender's bounce charge. RBI's 2023 penal-charges circular and fair-practice code treat repeated presentments known to fail as harassment; it is also the reason borrowers revoke mandates (policy.py:268-270 says so).

**Fix.** Add a borrower-side cost term: expected fee × P(return) into the action's cost and a non-zero intrusiveness that rises with `mandate_attempts_this_cycle`; default `TREATMENT_MANDATE_MAX_PRESENTATIONS` to 2 for insufficient_funds and require a credit hint or debit-day alignment for the second.

### `case-attempts-counts-non-contacts-and-blocks-statutory` — Case-level guards count mandate presentments as 'contacts' and stop the statutory notice and the mandate the engine elsewhere says nothing may stop

**backend/agent_core/treatment/arbitration.py:102** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T07-policy-arb-actions`

arbitration.py:102-106 `if features.case_attempts >= policy.max_attempts_per_case: return _hold(... SUPPRESS_ATTEMPTS_EXHAUSTED ...)` with the comment 'RBI reads a sixth as persistent calling'. `case_attempts` is `count(*) ... WHERE ... enacted IS TRUE` with no channel filter (features.py:1256-1267), so three `represent_mandate` presentments plus two SMS = 5. The same guard, `retry_backoff` (:108-116), `already_planned` (:125-136) and the value floor (:138-142) apply to LEGAL_NOTICE and REPRESENT_MANDATE, contradicting engine.py:62-65 (`CONTROL_ARM_PERMITS` keeps legal_notice because 'a statutory demand runs on a clock that a measurement does not get to stop') and actions.py:119-121.

**Impact.** A borrower who was presented three times and messaged twice is 'exhausted' without ever being called; conversely a s.138/PSS-s.25 notice due this week is withheld because an SMS went out 6 hours ago or because its EV is below ₹2. Missed limitation windows are unrecoverable.

**Fix.** Count only `A.CONTACTING` actions toward `case_attempts` (add `chosen_channel IS NOT NULL` to the query). In `arbitrate`, partition contenders into contacting and non-contacting; apply attempts/backoff/reserve only to contacting ones, and exempt LEGAL_NOTICE from the value floor (or give it an EV floor of its own tied to the limitation deadline).

### `non-contacting-actions-enact-45-days-later-with-no-revalidation` — MAX_PLAN_AGE measures lateness, not lead time, so a self-service plan or EMI date change decided today is enacted up to 45 days later against zero re-validation

**backend/agent_core/treatment/enact.py:88** · reliability · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `T07-policy-arb-actions`

engine.py:440-447 NON_CONTACT_HORIZON_MULTIPLIER = 15 and _horizon_for returns policy.planning_horizon_hours * 15 for every action in A.NON_CONTACTING (actions.py:141-143: represent_mandate, emi_date_change, self_service_plan) - 72 * 15 = 1080 hours = 45 days. enact.py:85-91 then tests 'datetime.now(timezone.utc) - at > MAX_PLAN_AGE' where at is scheduled_at and MAX_PLAN_AGE is 12 hours (:45), so it only cancels plans that are more than 12h LATE and never one made 45 days early. Because spec.channel is None for all three, enact.py:121-142 skips contact_policy.admit entirely; _resolved_since (:178-192) only inspects the bounce or promise status; and no handler re-reads holds, account status, bucket or dpd. Only _represent_mandate re-reads its own object (:548-576).

**Impact.** A self-service repayment plan decided for a borrower today is opened 45 days later on an account that may since have been settled, disputed, put on a bereavement hold, written off or moved to legal - none of which anything checks. An EMI date change work item lands at the LMS with reasoning six weeks stale. The 45-day horizon was introduced deliberately (engine.py:426-439) to let a mandate presentment reach the borrower's payday; the same multiplier was applied to two actions that have no payday to wait for.

**Fix.** Give MAX_PLAN_AGE a lead-time twin: refuse to enact a plan whose decision row is older than N hours regardless of its scheduled_at, and re-run policy.veto with freshly built features before any non-contacting handler. Apply NON_CONTACT_HORIZON_MULTIPLIER only to REPRESENT_MANDATE, which is the action the comment at engine.py:426-439 is actually about; emi_date_change and self_service_plan have no monthly cycle to wait for and timing.py:160-164 already schedules the date change at now.

### `vetoes-not-rechecked-at-enactment` — Holds and mandate vetoes are evaluated only at decision time; a plan can sit up to 72h (contacts) or 1080h (non-contacting) and enactment never re-runs them

**backend/agent_core/treatment/enact.py:119** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `T07-policy-arb-actions`

enact.py:119-143 re-checks only `contact_policy.admit` for `spec.channel` actions (consent/DND/window/caps); grep for `treatment_holds`, `_mandate_veto`, `policy_mod` in enact.py returns nothing (only prose at :790). `_resolved_since` (enact.py:178-192) checks bounce/PTP status only. Non-contacting actions get `hours * NON_CONTACT_HORIZON_MULTIPLIER` = 72*15 = 1080h (engine.py:440-447). policy.py:130-145 is the only place `_hold_veto` runs.

**Impact.** A bereavement or hardship hold placed by a supervisor at 10:00 does not stop the WhatsApp the engine planned at 09:00 for 18:00; a mandate the borrower cancels on day 3 of a 30-day-out presentment plan is still presented (with `TREATMENT_MANDATE_EXECUTOR=rail`) or handed to the LMS as an instruction. RBI complaint pattern: 'we told you to stop and you sent another message'.

**Fix.** Enactment must call `policy.veto(conn, action, features_now, at=now, ...)` (or at minimum `_hold_veto` + `_mandate_veto` + `bucket`/`account_status` checks) with freshly built features before every handler, and record `cancelled:<reason>` on refusal. Add a `treatment_holds` insert trigger/worker that cancels unspent plans for the customer.
