### `create-hold-not-concurrency-safe` — create_treatment_hold is a check-then-insert with no ON CONFLICT and no IntegrityError handler, contradicting its own docstring

**backend/db_treatment_holds.py:171** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

The docstring promises 'Re-placing an active one is a no-op, not an error... The partial unique index is what enforces it' (lines 124-129), but the code does `existing = _one(conn.execute(SELECT ...))` (153-166) and then a bare `conn.execute(text("INSERT INTO treatment_holds ..."))` (171-198) with no ON CONFLICT clause and no try/except. Two callers racing — which the docstring's own example creates: 'a bot that hears "I lost my job" twice in one call, and an agent who clicks twice' — both see no row and both insert.

**Impact.** The loser gets a unique-violation 500. On the bot path that surfaces mid-call as a tool failure; the bot may then tell the borrower the hold could not be placed, or retry and fail again. The one operation in the system whose entire purpose is to stop contact is the one that throws under exactly the concurrency its docstring anticipates.

**Fix.** `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT uq_treatment_holds_active DO NOTHING RETURNING id`, and when nothing is returned, re-select and return the existing row. Belt and braces: catch IntegrityError and re-select.

### `hold-release-has-no-dual-control` — Any authenticated caller can release any hold, including legal and regulator-sourced ones, with no role check and no maker-checker

**backend/db_treatment_holds.py:211** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

release_treatment_hold's only guard is `_assert_tenant_owns(conn, "treatment_holds", hold_id)` (db_treatment_holds.py:222). There is no check on hold.kind, hold.source, the actor's role, or a second approver. A 'legal' or source='regulator' hold releases exactly like a bot-placed hardship hold.

**Impact.** A hold placed because a regulator asked, or because legal is running a matter, is a control. Controls that any user can silently switch off are not controls, and an internal auditor will say so. Worse, releasing a hold immediately re-opens automated outreach to a borrower who may be in an ombudsman process. There is not even an alert on the event.

**Fix.** Gate release by kind: hardship/dispute releasable by a collections supervisor; complaint/legal/regulator-sourced requiring a second approver recorded on the row (released_approved_by_user_id) and an entry in the compliance log. Require a non-empty released_reason for those kinds.

### `list-treatment-cases-unbounded-aggregate` — The cases view is a full-table GROUP BY with four array_agg ORDER BYs and a correlated NOT EXISTS, paged with OFFSET

**backend/db_treatment_holds.py:376** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

db_treatment_holds.py:376-410: `FROM treatment_decisions td JOIN customers c ... GROUP BY td.customer_id, c.name, td.account_id, td.trigger_kind, td.trigger_ref ORDER BY max(td.created_at) DESC LIMIT :limit OFFSET :offset`, with four `(array_agg(... ORDER BY td.created_at DESC))[1]` projections, an `array_remove(array_agg(...) FILTER (WHERE td.enacted), NULL)` and, under open_only, a per-group correlated NOT EXISTS subquery (369-373).

**Impact.** There is no time window and no index that can serve this. At 225 rows it is instant; treatment_decisions is append-only and every decision from every sweep lands in it, so on a real book it is millions of rows within months. Every open of the Cases screen then scans the table, sorts it and pages with OFFSET, at a per-connection statement_timeout of 15s on the API path — meaning the screen simply starts failing one day, with no warning and no gradual degradation.

**Fix.** Add a bounded default window (e.g. created_at >= now() - interval '90 days'), keyset pagination instead of OFFSET, and a covering index on (tenant, trigger_kind, trigger_ref, created_at DESC). Longer term, maintain a treatment_cases table updated on decision write rather than aggregating the log on read.

### `insights-metrics-not-tenant-scoped` — The treatment scoreboards aggregate every tenant's decisions with no tenant predicate

**backend/db_treatment_holds.py:439** · privacy · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`with engine.connect() as conn: return treatment_decisions.insights(conn, days=days)` (db_treatment_holds.py:439-440) and the same shape for treatment_metrics (457-460) and treatment_model_health (469-470) — none passes a tenant, unlike treatment_models on line 486 which does. decisions.insights runs `FROM treatment_decisions WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '...'` (agent_core/treatment/decisions.py:436-437) with no tenant clause. `grep -c tenant` returns 0 for both metrics.py and monitor.py.

**Impact.** GET /treatment/insights and /treatment/metrics are the screens a collections head and a model-risk reviewer read. On a shared deployment they show a blend of every tenant's coverage, suppression mix, incremental recovery and model drift, and the numbers are wrong for everyone. If any tenant's volumes are commercially sensitive — they always are — this is a confidentiality incident, not just a bug. Only RLS is standing between this and a cross-tenant read, and RLS is not proven on in this deployment.

**Fix.** Thread tenant_id into insights/report/monitor.report as a required argument, add `AND tenant_id = :tenant` to every aggregate, and add a test that each function's SQL contains a tenant predicate (the same shape of test rls.py already uses for policy coverage).

### `webhook-binds-no-tenant` — The bounce webhook binds no tenant: one global HMAC secret, and every write lands under the process-default tenant

**backend/main.py:977** · security · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

The route is in the API-key exempt list (main.py:273) and authenticates only with a single process-wide secret: `webhook_secret()` reads PAYMENT_EVENTS_WEBHOOK_SECRET / PAYMENT_WEBHOOK_SECRET (payment_events.py:54-55). It then runs `with db.engine.begin() as conn: pe.ingest(conn, body)` (main.py:977-979) with nothing calling tenant_context.set_tenant. tenant_context.current_tenant() returns 'the process default outside one' (tenant_context.py:75-77), and the engine's begin listener only issues SET LOCAL when a tenant was bound (db_core.py:184-199). ingest derives tenant_id from the joined customer row (payment_events.py:207) but the account lookup at 190-203 is `WHERE a.id = :id` with no tenant predicate.

**Impact.** Two mutually exclusive failure modes, both bad. With RLS enabled (the module rls.py exists precisely to enable it), every account belonging to any tenant other than the process default returns zero rows and the webhook 400s 'account_required' — a silent, total outage for every tenant but one, that looks like bad data. With RLS disabled, any party holding the one shared secret can post bounce events against any tenant's account id and cause an automated WhatsApp/SMS/voice contact to that tenant's borrower. For a bank running this per-entity or an NBFC running it multi-brand, either is a go-live blocker.

**Fix.** Require a tenant identifier in the signed body (or a per-tenant secret keyed by a tenant header), resolve and validate it before the transaction, wrap ingest in tenant_context.bind(tenant), and add `AND a.tenant_id = :tenant` to the account lookup. Rotate to per-tenant secrets stored in the tenant row, not the environment.

### `webhook-has-no-replay-window-or-rate-limit` — The HMAC covers the body only: no timestamp, no nonce, no rate limit, and the route is exempt from the API key

**backend/payment_events.py:58** · security · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`expected = hmac.new(secret.encode("utf-8"), raw_body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()` (payment_events.py:58-66) — nothing binds the signature to a time or a delivery id. The route is in the API-key exempt tuple (main.py:273) and main.py:959-981 applies no throttle. The whole of ingest, including sends and possibly a dial, runs inline in the request.

**Impact.** A captured request is replayable forever; idempotency limits the damage to the DB but a replay of a not-yet-first-touched event will still perform a send. More practically, there is no backpressure: a CBS pushing an overnight bounce file of 100k rows opens 100k transactions, each doing consent lookups, an intent insert, a WhatsApp/SMS enqueue and an engine decision, against a 15-connection pool. The first production morning is an outage.

**Fix.** Require a signed timestamp header inside the HMAC with a 5-minute tolerance and a replayed-delivery-id cache. Rate-limit per tenant. Accept the webhook by writing a raw inbox row and returning 202, then process from a worker with bounded concurrency — the ingest work does not belong in the request.

### `occurred-at-unbounded-and-load-bearing` — Vendor-supplied occurredAt is accepted without any sanity bound and then drives EMI selection, the fee posting date and the engine's trigger age

**backend/payment_events.py:108** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`_parse_dt` accepts any ISO-8601 value and falls back only on a parse error (payment_events.py:108-117). The value is then used for EMI resolution (`AND due_date <= :occurred`, line 503), the ledger posting date (`"posted_at": occurred`, line 312), the stored occurred_at (line 360) and the treatment trigger (`at=event.get("occurred_at") or now`, line 446). Trigger.age_hours clamps negatives to 0 but does not bound the positive side (features.py:143-147).

**Impact.** CBS reconciliation replays are routine and carry historical timestamps. A month-old occurredAt makes the engine believe the case has been rotting for 720 hours and escalates the ladder accordingly, selects the wrong EMI (the oldest one still due before that date), and back-dates a bounce-fee ledger entry into a closed accounting period. A future-dated value silently disables the age feature. None of these fail loudly; they produce confidently wrong decisions.

**Fix.** Reject or clamp occurred_at outside a configured window (say now-30d to now+1h), record the received_at separately, and use received_at for the ledger posting date. Emit a counter on clamped values so a misbehaving upstream is visible.

### `bounce-never-writes-mandate-presentation` — Bounce ingest never touches mandates or mandate_presentations, which is why represent_mandate has never been a candidate

**backend/payment_events.py:333** · integration · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

The INSERT at payment_events.py:333-362 writes payment_events only. The word 'mandate' appears in the whole file exactly twice, both times as the string literal 'mandate_expired' (lines 31, 37). enact.py:573-578 raises `NoExecutor("no_mandate_on_file")` when it cannot find a mandate row for the account, and represent_mandate has been excluded on all 124 non-control decisions for exactly that reason (established fact).

**Impact.** Re-presentation is the cheapest and highest-yield action in Indian collections — it costs nothing, needs no borrower contact, and cures a large share of insufficient-funds bounces on the salary-credit date. The engine has the action, the veto ladder for it (policy.py:53-58: NO_MANDATE, MANDATE_NOT_ACTIVE, MANDATE_NO_CYCLE, MANDATE_RETURN_BLOCKS, MANDATE_LIMIT_REACHED, MANDATE_TOO_SOON) and the attribution column (mandate_presentations.decision_id), and it has never once been able to choose it. On a real book this is most of the recoverable value the product claims.

**Fix.** In ingest(), resolve the mandate for the account (by rail + account) and write a mandate_presentations row with status='returned', return_code, presented_for = the EMI cycle, attempt_no derived from the existing rows for that cycle, and payment_event_id = the new event. That single insert makes represent_mandate a live candidate, makes the presentation limit countable, and closes the attribution loop.

### `activity-rows-wrong-tenant-and-fake-actor` — Every audit row written by the bounce trigger claims the wrong tenant and claims a human did it

**backend/payment_events.py:406** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

payment_events.py calls dbmod.record_activity four times (406-414 bounce_ingested, 714-722 bounce_first_touch, 779-787 and 802-810 bounce_suppressed). record_activity delegates to db_core._activity, which hardcodes `'human'` as actor_kind and fills tenant_id from `_tenant()` and actor from `_actor_user_id()` (db_core.py:375-386) — neither of which is bound on this route, so both fall back to process defaults, while the event's real tenant is sitting in a local variable at payment_events.py:207.

**Impact.** The borrower's timeline is the artefact an internal auditor, an ombudsman and a consumer court all read. Here it says a named human triggered an automated statutory notice, in the wrong tenant. Under RLS the row is invisible to the tenant who owns the borrower and visible to the one who does not. Any 'who contacted this borrower and on whose authority' question gets a wrong answer, and DPDP processing-record obligations are not met by a log that misattributes the controller.

**Fix.** Give record_activity explicit tenant_id and actor_kind parameters; pass the event's tenant_id and actor_kind='system' from every payment_events call site. Add a test asserting that no activity_events row written by a webhook carries actor_kind='human'.

### `trigger-failures-are-log-only` — Every failure path on the trigger surface is a log line: no counter, no state on the row, no alert, no dead letter

**backend/payment_events.py:460** · observability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

payment_events.py:460-463 (treatment planning failed), 680-682 (bounce sms send failed), 888-896 (dial not placed / dial failed); promise_fulfillment.py:697-700 (fulfill enqueue failed), 850-852 (treatment lookup failed), 1065-1067 (reminder send failed); db.py:1005-1007 (treatment snapshot failed); db_treatment_holds.py:327-329 (action contract build failed). All are `logger.exception(...)` or `logger.warning(...)` with no metric emission and, except for the reminder row, no persisted status.

**Impact.** These are the eight places where the engine stops being asked or a borrower stops being contacted. If the treatment planner has been failing on every bounce for three days, nothing on any screen says so — coverage in /treatment/insights simply drifts down and looks like the engine deciding to wait. An SRE has no signal, a collections head has no signal, and the model-risk reviewer has no evidence the pipeline ran. This is the difference between a system that self-improves and one that quietly stops.

**Fix.** Emit a named counter at each site (treatment_trigger_failed{trigger=...}, bounce_send_failed{channel=...}, bounce_dial_failed{reason=...}) through observability.py, persist a failure reason on the row where one exists, and alert on rate. Add a daily reconciliation: bounces ingested vs decisions written vs first touches sent, per tenant.

### `holds-do-not-bind-the-statutory-sender` — treatment_holds bind the treatment engine and nothing else; the bounce first touch and the PTP confirm never read them

**backend/payment_events.py:533** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

_first_touch (payment_events.py:533-733) and promise_fulfillment.fulfill (519-761) contain no reference to treatment_holds; the only veto they consult is contact_policy.admit, whose _veto does not read the hold table either (contact_policy.py:460-526). The correct read exists three modules away: agent_core/treatment/policy.py:513-524. The table's own comment claims the opposite: 'As rows they bind the bot at 02:00 exactly as they bind a supervisor' (db_treatment_holds.py:35-36).

**Impact.** A borrower on a bereavement hold, or with an open dispute on the very EMI that bounced, or with a regulatory complaint in flight, still receives an automated 'your EMI did not go through, pay here' message within seconds of the bounce. That is the single most reputationally damaging message a collections system can send, it is the case the hold table was built to prevent, and the hold gives false assurance to the supervisor who placed it.

**Fix.** Promote the hold read to a shared veto (one function, the policy.py predicate) called by contact_policy.admit for every purpose including statutory, with a narrow, explicitly configured carve-out for a genuine statutory demand under 'legal' holds only. Add a test that a bereavement hold blocks a bounce first touch.

### `session-key-merges-unrelated-whatsapp-notices` — Using the long-lived WhatsApp conversation id as the contact session key merges unrelated notices into one counted touch

**backend/payment_events.py:582** · compliance · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`session_key = event["id"]; if ch == "whatsapp": session_key = dbmod._open_whatsapp_conversation(conn, customer_id)` (payment_events.py:581-584); the same choice at promise_fulfillment.py:592-594. contact_policy._session_coalesced treats any allowed event on that key within session_window() — 30 minutes by default (contact_policy.py:119-120) — as the same session, which sets counts=False and skips the daily/weekly/cooling checks entirely (contact_policy.py:959-976).

**Impact.** The WhatsApp conversation is per customer and effectively permanent (_open_whatsapp_conversation reuses it), so a bounce notice at 10:00 and a PTP confirm at 10:20 are recorded as one touch, and any outreach in that window skips the cap and cooling-off checks. The daily contact count the bank reports is therefore an undercount, and the cap is softer than the policy document says. On a 20-customer book with sparse events this never triggers; on a real book with several concurrent cases per borrower it triggers constantly.

**Fix.** Key the session on the case (payment_event id / promise id) for outbound notices and reserve the conversation id for genuinely in-session replies, or make the coalescing key (conversation_id, source) so different purposes never merge.

### `voice-failure-abandons-the-case` — Any failure of the last-resort voice attempt permanently abandons the bounce with no retry, no backoff and no alert

**backend/payment_events.py:957** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`if not _try_voice_now(conn, event, account=account, now=when): conn.execute(text("UPDATE payment_events SET next_voice_at = NULL WHERE id = :id"), {"id": event["id"]})` (payment_events.py:957-961). _try_voice_now returns False for a missing phone, a denied policy decision, `attempt is None` from the fleet gate, `not placed.get("placed")` from the carrier, and any exception (lines 823, 850, 885, 893, 896) — all indistinguishable at the call site.

**Impact.** These are overwhelmingly transient conditions: the outbound fleet gate is momentarily full, the carrier 503s, the trunk is saturated at 09:00. One bad ten minutes silently and permanently abandons every bounce case scheduled for voice that morning. The borrower is never contacted, the case sits 'open' with next_voice_at NULL so nothing will ever pick it up again, and the only trace is a logger.info line (888-892) in a process whose root logger may have no handler.

**Fix.** Distinguish permanent from transient. Permanent (no phone, consent denied) -> set a suppression_reason and close. Transient -> reschedule next_voice_at with exponential backoff and an attempt counter, dead-letter after N, and emit a counter per reason. Never NULL the schedule without recording why.

### `voice-hours-reschedule-destroyed-by-caller` — process_one_voice NULLs the next_voice_at that _try_voice_now just wrote for an out-of-hours dial, deleting the only reschedule in the system

**backend/payment_events.py:957** · correctness · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `W01-triggers`

_try_voice_now handles the calling-window denial by scheduling the retry: `if decision.reason == contact_policy.REASON_HOURS: nxt = next_voice_window(...); conn.execute(text("UPDATE payment_events SET next_voice_at = :nxt, suppression_reason = :reason WHERE id = :id"), ...)` and then `return False` (payment_events.py:837-850). process_one_voice treats that False identically to every other failure: `if not _try_voice_now(conn, event, account=account, now=when): conn.execute(text("UPDATE payment_events SET next_voice_at = NULL WHERE id = :id"), {"id": event["id"]})` (:957-961), on the same transaction, overwriting the value written moments earlier. The sibling caller does not make this mistake — _digital_blocked re-reads the row and preserves an existing next_voice_at (:764-788).

**Impact.** The one behaviour process_one_voice's own docstring says it exists to implement — 'a bounce that arrived at night is scheduled for 08:00 and dialled when the window opens' (:918-921) — is destroyed whenever the window closes between scheduling and draining, which is every case dialled near 19:00 IST or drained after a worker restart. The claim predicate requires `next_voice_at IS NOT NULL` (:939), so the case can never be reclaimed: the borrower is never contacted, the case stays 'open' forever, and the only trace is a logger line. It also means the RBI calling-window compliance path silently degrades into permanent non-contact rather than deferred contact.

**Fix.** Have _try_voice_now return a tri-state (placed / retry-scheduled / permanently-failed) instead of a bare bool, and only clear next_voice_at on the permanent case. Add a regression test that drains a bounce at 19:30 IST and asserts next_voice_at is the next 08:00 rather than NULL.

### `broken-ptp-trigger-at-is-processing-time` — The broken-PTP trigger reports processing time as the event time, so trigger age is constant zero for every broken promise

**backend/promise_fulfillment.py:837** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`trigger=Trigger(kind="broken_ptp", at=datetime.now(timezone.utc), ref=promise["id"])` (promise_fulfillment.py:837), against features.Trigger's contract: '`at` is when the *event* happened, not when we got round to it. The gap between the two is the delay this whole product exists to close, so the scorer reads it directly' (features.py:128-130). Trigger.age_hours clamps at 0.0 (features.py:143-147). The bounce trigger does it correctly: payment_events.py:446.

**Impact.** Trigger age is a scoring feature and a monitoring signal. Here it is a constant, so the engine cannot distinguish a promise that broke last night from one that broke four days ago because the settle job was down over a weekend or the worker was starved by the previous finding. Every uplift and timing model trained on this corpus sees a feature with zero variance for the entire broken_ptp population, and the operational signal 'we are running behind on settlement' never surfaces.

**Fix.** Pass the end of the promised IST day as `at`: `datetime(promised_day.year, ..., 23,59,59, tzinfo=IST)`. The row is already selected on that predicate (lines 900-901), so the value is available. Add a monitor alerting when median (now - trigger.at) for broken_ptp exceeds a few hours.

### `broken-ptp-followup-ignores-suppression` — A suppressed or held decision still produces a high-priority voice follow-up for a human to action

**backend/promise_fulfillment.py:854** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W01-triggers`

`if not result.actionable: return {**fallback, "note": note}` (promise_fulfillment.py:854-855) where fallback is `{"due_at": None, "note": "Broken promise follow-up", "channel": "voice"}` (826-830). The caller then unconditionally inserts `... 'open', 'high', COALESCE(:due_at, now() + interval '1 day'), :note, :channel` (917-939). TreatmentResult.actionable is false exactly when the decision was suppressed — including by a hardship, bereavement, complaint or legal hold.

**Impact.** The hold stops the bot and then hands the same borrower to a human as a high-priority voice task tomorrow. From the borrower's side nothing changed except who is calling — and a telecaller calling a bereaved family the day after a hold was placed is worse than a bot doing it, because it looks deliberate. The hold's whole promise ('binds the bot at 02:00 exactly as it binds a supervisor') fails at the one point where the queue meets a person.

**Fix.** Branch on the suppression reason. Hold-derived suppressions must produce either no followup or a followup addressed to the hold's specialist_user_id with status 'snoozed' until the hold expires, never an open high-priority outreach task. Carry result.reason into the followup row so the queue can filter on it.

### `contact-events-has-no-policy-version` — The contact ledger does not record which rule set approved the contact

**backend/alembic/versions/20260813_0066_contact_events.py:29** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W02-contact-policy`

The contact_events table (lines 28-97) has no policy_version, rule_set_id, data_purpose, or resolved-window column, and _insert_event (contact_policy.py:776-807) binds none. Meanwhile policy_rules.py:25-30 states the whole point: 'the version stamped on a decision is the statutory one ... the indexed column still answers the question it exists for' — and treatment_decisions does carry policy_version while contact_events does not.

**Impact.** The regulator's question is 'why did you dial this borrower at 18:55 last March', and the answer requires the window that was in force then. Reconstructing it means re-resolving policy_rules against a historical instant and hoping no row was edited in place — policy_rule_sets has no immutability guarantee and overlapping validity windows are explicitly not constrained (policy_rules.py:351-353). The ledger cannot be used as evidence, which defeats its stated purpose.

**Fix.** Add policy_version int, rule_provenance jsonb (RuleSet.to_log() already produces it), data_purpose text and window_start/window_end smallint to contact_events; populate them in _insert_event from the already-resolved `rules` object. Make policy_rule_sets append-only with a trigger.

### `bot-gate-fails-open-on-exception` — The WhatsApp bot's contact gate swallows its own exception and then allows the send

**backend/bot_runtime.py:158** · reliability · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `W02-contact-policy`

_policy_gate wraps the admit call in `try: ... with engine.begin() as conn: decision = contact_policy.admit(...) ; if not decision.allowed: return decision.reason` and then `except Exception: logger.exception("contact_policy bot gate failed conversation=%s", conv.get("id"))` (bot_runtime.py:142-159), after which control falls to `return None` at bot_runtime.py:160 — and the function's own docstring is 'Return abort reason or None if send is allowed' (line 128). contact_policy.admit itself never raises (contact_policy.py:1014-1016), but `engine.begin()` does: a pool exhaustion, a statement timeout (db_core.py:155 sets 15-60s) or a database restart raises here. Both call sites treat None as permission (bot_runtime.py:679-684 and 1075-1079).

**Impact.** The whole module is built fail-closed — contact_policy.py:1-4 and policy_rules.py:303-310 both argue at length that an unreadable consent table must block contact rather than raise. This caller inverts that guarantee for the highest-volume automated channel: during exactly the incident where consent cannot be read, the bot keeps replying to every conversation and nothing in the ledger records that the gate was never consulted. A DB blip becomes a book-wide unvetted send instead of a book-wide safe stop.

**Fix.** Return a reason from the except block — `return "contact_policy_unavailable"` — so a gate failure cancels the job the way every other refusal does, and count the reason so the incident is visible. The fail-closed default belongs in the caller that consumes the verdict, not only in the module that produces it.

### `gate-enforced-by-convention-and-a-lint-test` — Nothing structurally prevents a send path from skipping the veto

**backend/contact_policy.py:3** · maintainability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W02-contact-policy`

The docstring asserts 'Every outbound path calls admit before a dial or a send' (line 3), while outbound.py:23 documents the actual contract: 'Callers run contact_policy.admit themselves — it is their responsibility'. The only enforcement is test_outbound_gate_contract.py, an AST walker over a hardcoded module list checking the reserve/admit/suppress/place ordering around outbound.place (lines 112-160). Nineteen distinct call sites currently do this by hand.

**Impact.** The one control that stands between the platform and a conduct breach is upheld by author discipline plus a static test that only knows about today's modules. The next channel integration — an agency dialler, an IVR blast, a push notification, an email vendor — is compliant only if its author remembers. In a bank this is not an acceptable control design; the auditor's question is 'what stops it', and 'a unit test that lists the files' is not an answer.

**Fix.** Invert the dependency: make admit return an opaque admission token and have every dispatch primitive (outbound.place, the WhatsApp drain, twilio_sms.send, the email sender, the field dispatcher) require and consume one, rejecting a send without it. Then the lint test becomes a backstop rather than the control.

### `field-visits-have-no-prerequisites-at-the-gate` — channel='field' passes the same veto as an SMS: no intimation, no identification, no digital-exhaustion check

**backend/contact_policy.py:40** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W02-contact-policy`

'field' is a first-class channel (line 40, and the CHECK constraint at the migration line 78) and enact.py:121-132 calls admit with `channel=spec.channel` where FIELD_VISIT maps to 'field' (actions.py:116). In _veto, a field visit takes exactly the same path as email: no statutory window, borrower-preference default 09:00-20:00, done. policy_rules declares KIND_FIELD_PREREQS ('field_prerequisites', policy_rules.py:67) and KIND_VISIT_INTIMATION (line 69) but RuleSet has no accessor for the former and visit_intimation_hours() (line 169) has no caller anywhere in the tree.

**Impact.** The 2027 circular's prior-visit intimation requirement is declarable as a row and enforced by nothing. A field visit is the highest-risk, most-complained-about contact type in Indian collections, and the shared veto treats it as the cheapest. The digital-exhaustion rule exists only inside the treatment engine (config.py:233), so any non-treatment caller — an agency portal, a manual dispatch, a bulk allocation — gets a field visit with no prerequisites at all.

**Fix.** Add `field_prerequisites()` and enforce visit_intimation_hours() inside _veto for channel='field': require a recorded intimation contact_event at least N hours old, deny with a new REASON_NO_VISIT_INTIMATION otherwise, and record the intimation reference on the event. Move the digital-exhaustion check out of the treatment engine and into the shared veto so every caller inherits it.

### `no-tenant-predicate-on-any-query` — Every read and write is keyed on customer_id alone, with no tenant scoping

**backend/contact_policy.py:288** · security · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W02-contact-policy`

_load_customer (`WHERE c.id = :id`, line 296), _today_count (line 358), _week_counted (line 375), _session_coalesced (line 402), _already_counted_related (line 428), _last_counted_at (line 447) and ledger_usage (`customer_id = ANY(:ids)`, line 1038) all omit tenant_id. _insert_event then writes `"tenant_id": customer["tenant_id"]` (line 792) — the *loaded* customer's tenant, not the caller's.

**Impact.** A caller in tenant A passing a customer_id belonging to tenant B gets a real admission decision, reserves a slot against B's borrower, and writes an audit row into B's tenant partition. In a hosted multi-tenant deployment that is cross-tenant data modification; in a single-bank on-prem install with multiple business units it is a segregation-of-duties failure. The gate is the last place that should trust the caller's parameter.

**Fix.** Thread tenant_id into admit/evaluate as a required argument and add `AND c.tenant_id = :tid` to _load_customer, returning None (hence REASON_NO_CUSTOMER, fail-closed) on mismatch. Enable Postgres RLS on contact_events and contact_day_counters as defence in depth.

### `consent-expiry-never-checked` — consent_records.expires_at is selected and never read

**backend/contact_policy.py:293** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W02-contact-policy`

_load_customer selects `cr.allowed_days, cr.allowed_hours, cr.dnd_registry, cr.expires_at` (line 293). grep for expires_at across contact_policy.py returns exactly that one line. _veto (lines 460-526) never compares it to now_local, and the only 'expired' block comes from channel_consents.status via BLOCKING_CONSENT (lines 38, 474).

**Impact.** Under DPDP a consent has a validity period and expiry must withdraw the basis for processing. Here a consent record that expired two years ago still permits outreach as long as the per-channel status column was never flipped, and nothing in this module flips it. A DPO auditing the gate will find the expiry date loaded into memory and thrown away.

**Fix.** In _veto, after the BLOCKING_CONSENT check: `exp = customer.get('expires_at'); if exp is not None and _aware(exp) <= now_local.astimezone(timezone.utc): return REASON_EXPIRED`. Do it for all three purposes — an expired basis is not cured by the borrower being on the line. Add a nightly job that materialises expiry into channel_consents.status so the screen agrees.

### `no-suppression-states` — The veto has no concept of deceased, disputed, litigation, insolvency, or cease-and-desist

**backend/contact_policy.py:460** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W02-contact-policy`

_veto's complete list of blocking conditions is: no customer, channel consent status in {opted_out, dnd, expired}, missing promotional consent, customers.dnd or dnd_registry, statutory hours, borrower window, consent days (lines 460-526). Nothing else can stop a contact.

**Impact.** Real collections books carry hard suppressions that no cap or window expresses: deceased borrower, account in SARFAESI or DRT proceedings, an active ombudsman or grievance complaint, a solicitor's cease-and-desist, insolvency moratorium, and a fraud/dispute hold. Contacting into any of these is a serious conduct matter and, for a moratorium, potentially contempt. On a 20-customer dev book none of these states exist, so the gap is invisible; on a real book several percent of accounts carry one at any time.

**Fix.** Add a customer/account-level suppression table with a reason code, an effective range and a source, checked in _veto before every other rule and returning a distinct reason per code so the ledger is queryable by suppression type. Make it apply to all three purposes — a legal hold is not lifted by the borrower being on the line.

### `consent-days-unparseable-fails-open` — An unrecognised allowed_days string removes the day restriction instead of defaulting it

**backend/contact_policy.py:522** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W02-contact-policy`

`days = _parse_days(customer.get("allowed_days"))` (line 518) then `if days is not None:` (line 522). contact_window.allowed_days returns None both when nothing was recorded and when the string named no recognisable day (`return days or None`, contact_window.py:119). So 'Weekdays', 'All days', 'Working days', 'Lun-Vie', or a Hindi/Tamil day name yields None and the check at line 523-524 never runs. The sibling hours rule does the opposite, falling back to `contact_window.window_hours(None)` at line 517 with a five-line comment explaining why absence must not mean unrestricted.

**Impact.** A borrower who consented to weekday contact only gets dialled on Sunday, and the ledger records it as allowed. Free-text day columns are the norm in migrated CRM data. This is a conduct breach that the system will never flag, on the same line of code where the neighbouring rule fails closed.

**Fix.** Make the absent case explicit and non-permissive at the gate: `days = _parse_days(...) ; if days is None: days = DEFAULT_CONTACT_DAYS` with a named constant, and log at WARNING when the raw string was non-empty but unparsed so data quality is visible. Distinguish 'no column value' from 'value we could not read' by returning [] for the latter (see the next finding).

### `statutory-purpose-is-unauthenticated` — Any caller can pass purpose='statutory' and bypass hours, DND, cooling-off and both caps

**backend/contact_policy.py:898** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W02-contact-policy`

`purpose = purpose if purpose in PURPOSES else "outreach"` (line 898) is the only validation. There is no allow-list of sources, no assertion that a statutory contact corresponds to an actual PTP confirmation or payment receipt, and no distinct actor requirement. _veto skips every hours and DND branch for it (lines 487-502) and admit skips every volume limit (line 965).

**Impact.** The strongest exemption in the compliance gate is granted on the honour system by a string literal. One mislabelled call site — or one API surface that forwards a client-supplied purpose — turns unrestricted 22:00 dialling into a supported feature with clean audit rows saying 'statutory'. In a bank this is the finding that closes the deployment.

**Fix.** Require a corroborating reference for statutory: `related_id` must resolve to a promise/payment row, checked in admit. Maintain an explicit allow-list of (source, purpose) pairs and downgrade anything else to outreach with a WARNING. Never accept purpose from an HTTP payload.

### `related-id-bypasses-every-volume-limit` — A repeated (source, related_id) pair skips cooling-off, weekly cap and daily cap entirely

**backend/contact_policy.py:963** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W02-contact-policy`

`counts = purpose in {"outreach", "statutory"} and not coalesced and not related_done` (line 963), then `if purpose == "outreach" and counts:` guards the cooling-off check (967), the weekly check (970-972) and _reserve_day (973-975). When related_done is True the function falls straight through to _insert_event and returns Decision(True). De-duplicating the *count* silently also disables the *veto*. main.py:3918 supplies `related_id=attempt["id"] if attempt else to` — the fallback is the borrower's phone number, so two manual dials to the same number with no reserved attempt share (source='voice_outbound', related_id=<phone>) and the second one is admitted with no cap check of any kind.

**Impact.** The cross-channel contact cap — the control the whole module exists to provide, and the one a bank will point an RBI inspector at — is bypassable by any caller that reuses a related_id. Retry loops, webhook redeliveries and operator double-clicks all reuse it. On a real book this is unlimited dialling of a single borrower with a clean audit trail saying every touch was allowed.

**Fix.** Separate the two questions. Keep `related_done` as the reason not to *increment* the counter, but always run the cooling-off, weekly and daily *reads* for purpose='outreach' and deny on them. Concretely: hoist the checks out of the `and counts` guard, and only skip `_reserve_day` when related_done or coalesced. Add a regression test that a second admit with the same related_id after the daily cap is exhausted is denied.

### `cooling-off-and-weekly-are-toctou` — Only the daily cap is serialised; cooling-off and the weekly cap are unlocked reads

**backend/contact_policy.py:965** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W02-contact-policy`

Lines 966-972 read `_last_counted_at` and `_week_counted` against the transaction snapshot, and only afterwards does line 973 call `_reserve_day`, which is the sole statement taking `FOR UPDATE` (line 828). The module docstring advertises the lock as if it covered the budget generally (lines 16-17).

**Impact.** Two concurrent admits for the same borrower on *different* channels both pass the weekly and cooling-off checks and then contend only on the day counter — so with a daily cap of 3, three simultaneous sends land inside the 120-minute cooling-off period. A campaign sweep, a cadence tick and a treatment enactment firing in the same second is the normal case at book scale, not a race you have to engineer.

**Fix.** Take the per-customer lock first: `SELECT ... FROM contact_day_counters WHERE customer_id = :cid AND local_date = :d FOR UPDATE` (or a pg_advisory_xact_lock on hash(customer_id)) before the cooling-off read, and hold it across the weekly check and the increment. The lock is already per-customer-per-day so this adds no new contention class.

### `deny-audit-rolled-back-by-require-admit` — require_admit raises after writing the denial event, so the caller's rollback erases it

**backend/contact_policy.py:1019** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W02-contact-policy`

`decision = admit(conn, **kwargs); if not decision.allowed: raise ValueError(decision.reason or REASON_UNREADABLE)` (lines 1021-1023). admit's _deny already inserted the outcome='denied' contact_event on the same `conn` (lines 937-953). Callers raise out of a transaction block — db.py:5698 calls require_admit inside the document-delivery transaction and db_inbox.py:1897/1939 do the same — and the exception unwinds the block, discarding the insert.

**Impact.** Precisely the denials that produced a user-visible 409 are the ones missing from the ledger. The 'why did nobody contact this borrower' query that enact.py's comment celebrates is systematically blind to the HTTP path. A complaint investigation finds no record that the system refused, which reads as the system never having been asked.

**Fix.** Write contact_events through an autonomous path — a separate short-lived connection, or an outbox row committed by a SAVEPOINT released before the raise (the same begin_nested pattern already used at line 1000). Alternatively have require_admit return the Decision and make callers translate to 409 after the transaction commits.

### `window-regex-ignores-am-pm` — The window regex drops am/pm, silently inverting a 12-hour window

**backend/contact_window.py:41** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W02-contact-policy`

`_WINDOW_RE = re.compile(r"(\d{1,2}):(\d{2}).*?(\d{1,2}):(\d{2})")` (line 41) captures only hour digits, yet the docstring on line 39 advertises '9:00 - 8:00 pm' as a supported form. window_hours returns (9, 8); outside_preferred_window then computes `hour < 9 or hour >= 8`, true for all 24 hours.

**Impact.** A borrower whose window was captured in 12-hour form is either never contactable (fail-closed, so nobody notices until the recovery rate on that segment is queried) or, if the inverted pair reaches contact_policy._veto, produces REASON_WINDOW on every attempt. CRM and telephony imports routinely carry am/pm strings; the seeded book does not, which is why 216 passing tests do not catch it.

**Fix.** Extend the regex to capture an optional am/pm after each pair and normalise to 24-hour. Reject and log any parsed pair where start >= end rather than returning it, and fall back to the documented defaults — matching the module's own 'unparseable is not a licence' stance.

### `demo-waiver-leaves-the-ledger-saying-denied` — A waived demo call is placed while contact_events records outcome='denied' and no allowed row

**backend/main.py:4268** · compliance · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `W02-contact-policy`

admit denies, and _deny has already written `outcome="denied"` with the reason onto contact_events (contact_policy.py:937-953). main.py:4263-4267 then computes `waived = not decision.allowed and waivable_for_demo and platform_switches.demo_ignores_window()`, main.py:4284 skips the 409 when waived, and main.py:4289-4295 calls outbound.place. _DEMO_WAIVABLE_REASONS includes REASON_HOURS — the statutory 08:00-19:00 window — along with REASON_WINDOW, REASON_COOLING, REASON_DAILY and REASON_WEEKLY (main.py:4007-4013). No compensating contact_event is written, no day counter is incremented (contact_policy.py:973 was never reached), and the only trace is a record_activity row (main.py:4272-4280) on a different table.

**Impact.** The contact ledger — the artefact main.py:3866-3869 and enact.py:134-138 both nominate as the compliance record of record — asserts the system refused a call that it in fact placed, outside statutory hours, against a real borrower's customer_id. That is an audit trail that is wrong in the unsafe direction, and the borrower's daily budget is silently under-counted afterwards. The blast radius is contained by the endpoint dialling one env-configured handset (main.py:4020-4021, 4194-4202), but the switch platform_switches.demo_ignores_window() is a runtime setting on a production build, not a compile-time flag.

**Fix.** When a waiver fires, write a second contact_event with outcome='allowed', reason='demo_waiver:<original>' and touch_counted true (or a new outcome value 'waived' plus a CHECK update), and reserve the day slot, so the ledger reflects what physically happened. Better: give admit an explicit `override=(actor, justification)` parameter so the waiver is a first-class, attributable ledger fact rather than a caller ignoring a denial.

### `recording-retention-unenforced` — recording_retention_months() is declarable, seeded, echoed by a script, and enforced nowhere

**backend/policy_rules.py:172** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W02-contact-policy`

`def recording_retention_months(self) -> int | None: return _opt_int((self._params(KIND_RECORDING_RETENTION) or {}).get("months"))` (lines 172-173). The only caller in the tree is scripts/seed_policy_rules.py:218, which prints it back after seeding. No retention job, no deletion path, no reference from contact_policy or the voice stack.

**Impact.** The 2027 circular mandates six-month recording retention; DPDP mandates erasure once the purpose is served. A rule that is expressible but unenforced is worse than an absent one, because the seeded row will be shown to an auditor as evidence of a control that does not exist. Recordings accumulating indefinitely is simultaneously a retention breach and an unbounded storage cost.

**Fix.** Add a scheduled retention job that resolves the rule per tenant and hard-deletes recordings past the window, writing a deletion audit row. Surface the resolved retention on the Consent/compliance screen so it is visible, and fail the deployment health check if the rule resolves to None.

### `field-channel-cannot-hold-consent-or-an-opt-out` — 'field' is a contactable channel that the consent schema cannot represent, so a doorstep visit can never be opted out of

**backend/sql/03_consent.sql:20** · data-model · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `W02-contact-policy`

contact_events accepts `channel IN ('voice','whatsapp','sms','email','chat','field')` (sql/03_consent.sql:55, mirrored at alembic/versions/20260813_0066_contact_events.py:78) and contact_policy.CHANNELS includes 'field' (contact_policy.py:40). But channel_consents is `channel TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (channel IN ('voice','whatsapp','sms','email','chat'))` (sql/03_consent.sql:20) and optout_events is `CHECK (channel IN ('voice','whatsapp','sms','email','chat','all'))` (sql/03_consent.sql:37). Consequently capture.latest_consent_by_channel (capture.py:394-406) can never return a row for 'field', so _channel_status returns None (contact_policy.py:304-308), None is not in BLOCKING_CONSENT (contact_policy.py:38), and the status check at contact_policy.py:474 can never fire for a field visit.

**Impact.** A borrower who tells an agent 'do not send anyone to my house' has nowhere for that to be recorded except the blanket 'all' opt-out, which also silences the servicing SMS they may still want. The one contact type with the highest complaint and physical-safety exposure in Indian collections is the one the consent model cannot express, and enact.py:122-132 will admit it. This is upstream of the field-prerequisites gap: even a correct prerequisite check would have no consent row to consult.

**Fix.** Add 'field' to both CHECK constraints (and to the opt-out writer's channel map in db.opt_out), backfill nothing, and make _veto treat a missing field consent as a refusal rather than as silence — a doorstep visit is the one channel where absence of a recorded basis should not mean permission.

### `clerk-enqueue-failure-invisible` — enqueue_chase returns None on any failure and every caller ignores the return value

**backend/agent_core/clerk.py:68** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`except Exception: logger.exception("clerk enqueue failed type=%s ref=%s", workflow_type, trigger_ref); return None` (clerk.py:68-70). payment_events.py:452 and promise_fulfillment.py:842 call enqueue_from_treatment without inspecting the result, inside their own broad try/except.

**Impact.** A schema drift, a tenant FK violation or a full disk makes every chase enqueue silently return None while bounce ingest reports success. The system looks healthy and does nothing. On this book the volume is low enough that somebody would notice; at 40k bounces a month nobody would.

**Fix.** Return a typed result and count failures on a metric the on-call sees; keep the swallow (bounce ingest must survive) but make the swallow loud.

### `clerk-failure-is-terminal` — One transient error permanently drops a bounce or broken-PTP chase - no attempt counter, no backoff, no dead-letter, no alert

**backend/agent_core/clerk.py:106** · reliability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`except Exception as exc: logger.exception(...); finish(jid, ok=False, error=str(exc)[:500])` (clerk.py:106-108). adapter_pg.finish sets status='failed', which is in TERMINAL (adapter_pg.py:12) and outside claim_next's `status IN ('submitted','working')` selection. The job is never retried and nothing watches the failed count.

**Impact.** A five-second database failover, a lock timeout, or a momentarily unavailable downstream turns into a permanently un-chased bounce - the borrower is never contacted about a cheque return whose statutory pay-link the system was supposed to send. Nobody finds out; there is no queue-health alert anywhere in this path.

**Fix.** Add attempt_count and next_retry_at to work_runtime_jobs, classify errors (transient vs terminal), retry transient ones with capped exponential backoff up to a cap, and move exhausted jobs to a 'dead' status that a Floor widget and an alert both watch.

### `clerk-error-string-leaks-pii` — Failed clerk jobs persist a raw exception string (SQL + bound parameters) that is served over the API

**backend/agent_core/clerk.py:107** · privacy · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`logger.exception("clerk job %s failed", jid)` then `finish(jid, ok=False, error=str(exc)[:500])` (clerk.py:107-108). A SQLAlchemy StatementError stringifies as the statement plus `[parameters: {...}]`, which for these workflows contains customer_id, phone numbers, amounts and note text. adapter_pg.finish writes it to work_runtime_jobs.error, and _public exposes it as `error` through GET /work-runtime/jobs/{id} and GET /floor/approvals (main.py:1019-1024, 1494-1498).

**Impact.** Borrower phone numbers and identifiers land in an operational table and in worker stdout, both of which are shipped to log aggregation. This is precisely the class of leak the platform already fixed elsewhere; DPDP purpose-limitation and the bank's own log-hygiene controls make an unredacted borrower identifier in a log line a finding, and it is uncontrolled by retention.

**Fix.** Store a short classified reason (exception type + a stable code) in the error column, put the detail behind pii_redact.redact() before logging, and never surface the raw string on an API response.

### `clerk-defer-30-days-rewrites-schedule` — Parking a HITL plan silently rewrites the decision's scheduled_at to now()+30 days and never restores it

**backend/agent_core/clerk.py:116** · data-model · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`UPDATE treatment_decisions SET scheduled_at = now() + interval '30 days' WHERE id = :id AND enacted IS FALSE AND outcome IS NULL` (clerk.py:125-131), described only as 'Keep claim_due from cancelling a parked field/legal plan'. Nothing restores the original time on approval, nothing records that it was moved, and a job re-claimed after a reject/approve cycle would move it again. It is also not atomic with the park: _defer_hitl_plan commits its own transaction (122) before park_input_required (148) commits its own, so a crash between them leaves the plan deferred and the job still 'working' - to be re-claimed and deferred another 30 days.

**Impact.** scheduled_at is the decision's own record of when the engine intended to act, and it is a feature the timing model and every audit reconstruction rely on. Overwriting it to hide the plan from claim_due destroys that evidence, hard-codes a 30-day SLA nobody agreed to, and makes 'when did the system decide to act on this borrower' unanswerable to a model-risk reviewer.

**Fix.** Add an explicit state (e.g. status='awaiting_approval' or held_until + hold_reason) instead of moving scheduled_at, exclude that state in claim_due, and do the hold and the park in ONE transaction (pass the conn through to park_input_required). Record the original scheduled_at.

### `clerk-doc-sla-and-callback-are-noops` — Overdue document SLAs and due callbacks complete as 'noted' with no action taken

**backend/agent_core/clerk.py:140** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`if wf in {DOC_SLA, CALLBACK}: return {"noted": True, "workflowType": wf, "ref": payload.get("triggerRef")}` (clerk.py:140-141). The job is finished ok=True. Nothing chases the document, nothing reminds the assignee, nothing changes document_requests.status or followups.status.

**Impact.** The clerk agent is presented as the thing that chases SLA breaches and callback diaries. In production a breached document SLA (a borrower waiting on a statement or an NOC) and a promised callback both produce a green completed job and no contact. Missed callbacks are a standard source of RBI ombudsman complaints; a 'completed' record for a contact that never happened is the worst possible artefact to hand a grievance officer.

**Fix.** Implement the two handlers (enqueue a WhatsApp/SMS chase or reassign to the queue owner; escalate on second breach) or remove the workflow types so the sweep stops manufacturing no-op jobs. If they must remain stubs, finish them with ok=False/'no_executor' so they are visibly outstanding.

### `clerk-sweep-head-of-line-block` — sweep_overdue re-reads the same oldest 20 rows forever because nothing marks a row swept

**backend/agent_core/clerk.py:219** · scale · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`SELECT id, customer_id FROM document_requests WHERE status = 'requested' AND sla_due_at IS NOT NULL AND sla_due_at <= now() ORDER BY sla_due_at LIMIT 20` (clerk.py:220-229) and the same shape for followups (232-245). The enqueue is idempotent per row, and no code path changes document_requests.status or followups.status - the handler is the no-op above. So every sweep returns the identical 20 rows and rows 21..N are never enqueued.

**Impact.** On this 20-customer book the whole overdue set fits in 20 rows, so the bug is invisible. On a real book with thousands of overdue documents and callbacks, only the oldest 20 are ever considered and they are considered forever; everything else is invisible to the clerk permanently. There is also no index on (status, sla_due_at) or (status, due_at) (sql/05_collections.sql:180-181), so each sweep sorts a large filtered set.

**Fix.** Keyset-paginate on (sla_due_at, id) with a cursor, or mark the source row (swept_at / escalated_at) when a job is created and exclude it. Add the composite indexes. Make the LIMIT a config, not a literal.

### `clerk-sweep-cross-tenant` — sweep_overdue queries document_requests and followups with no tenant predicate, then stamps the jobs with the worker's tenant

**backend/agent_core/clerk.py:220** · privacy · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

Neither query has a tenant filter (clerk.py:220-229, 234-243) and neither table has a tenant_id column (sql/05_collections.sql:157-181, 247-261); the resulting jobs are written by adapter_pg.start_workflow with `db._tenant()` (adapter_pg.py:57,68), the worker process's own tenant.

**Impact.** The deployment model is one process per tenant against a shared database (tenant_context.py:1-13). The moment a second tenant's rows exist, tenant A's worker enqueues chase jobs carrying tenant B's customer_id and document id, stored under tenant A's tenant_id - a cross-tenant record that RLS will then happily show to tenant A's operators. For a bank running two entities (NBFC + bank book) in one platform that is a reportable data incident under DPDP.

**Fix.** Join through customers/accounts to filter by tenant explicitly, or add tenant_id to document_requests and followups and make it NOT NULL with an RLS policy. Assert in enqueue_chase that the customer's tenant equals db.current_tenant().

### `self-service-open-veto-defeated-by-clerk` — The 'one open self-service plan per borrower' veto never fires, because the clerk completes the job it looks for

**backend/agent_core/treatment/policy.py:402** · correctness · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `W03-workers`

policy.py:402-415 `SELECT 1 FROM work_runtime_jobs WHERE tenant_id = :tenant AND workflow_type = 'self_service_plan' AND customer_id = :cid AND status NOT IN ('completed','failed','cancelled') LIMIT 1`, returning SELF_SERVICE_OPEN with the comment 'Offering a second plan while the first is still open is how a borrower ends up with two schedules and a dispute about which one they were on' (policy.py:416-418). The clerk marks exactly that job 'completed' on the next idle tick (clerk.py:151-152 -> clerk.py:103 -> adapter_pg.py:202), so the predicate is false within seconds of the plan being opened. The fallback the code relies on does not cover it: policy.py:392-398 says a duplicate is 'refused by the database' via the idempotency key, but enact._open_self_service_plan keys on `f"self-service-plan:{decision['id']}"` (enact.py:837) - a NEW decision on a later day has a new id and a new key.

**Impact.** A borrower can be put on a second self-service repayment plan while the first is still live, which is precisely the dispute the veto was written to prevent, and it will present as the borrower's word against two conflicting schedules in a grievance. It also silently removes a veto from the policy layer that a compliance reviewer would count as an active control when reading policy.py.

**Fix.** Fix the clerk's over-claiming (see clerk-completes-every-treatment-work-item-unactioned) so the job stays 'submitted' until the servicing system settles it, and additionally key the open-plan check on the account/plan state in the LMS rather than on a queue row's status. Add a regression test that opens a plan, runs the clerk, and asserts the veto still fires on the next day's decision.

### `worker-no-metrics-or-queue-depth` — A failing queue and an empty queue are indistinguishable, and no stage emits a metric

**backend/bot_worker.py:74** · observability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`except Exception: logger.exception("queue=%s failed", queue); return False` (bot_worker.py:76-78) returns the same False as 'nothing to do'. The module imports no metrics client and observability.py is never referenced; there are no counters for jobs processed, per-stage latency, queue depth, oldest-pending age, or error rate. The only signals are ad-hoc log lines.

**Impact.** An SRE cannot answer 'is the treatment queue draining?', 'how old is the oldest unsent WhatsApp?', or 'which stage is failing?' without opening psql. A stuck queue looks like an idle system, so the first symptom is a collections head noticing yesterday's plans never went out. In a bank this is the difference between a five-minute page and a next-day post-mortem.

**Fix.** Emit per-stage counters and histograms (processed, failed, seconds), plus gauges for pending depth and oldest-pending age per queue, and expose /metrics from the worker. Distinguish the empty and error returns in the loop so 'idle' means idle.

### `worker-single-tenant-loop` — The worker drains exactly one tenant and the deployment has no story for the second one

**backend/bot_worker.py:81** · scale · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

process_one_any takes no tenant argument; the clerk path resolves tenancy through `db._tenant()` (work_runtime/adapter_pg.py:167) which is the process-wide default (tenant_context.py:9-13: 'one process serves one tenant'), and the sweep resolves its own tenant per batch (sweep.py:89-91). docker-compose.yml:1-6 budgets connections for exactly one worker: 'api 5+5=10 + worker 3+2=5 + bot_worker 3+2=5 + voice 3+2=5 ... Stay under Postgres max_connections (100)'.

**Impact.** An Indian bank or NBFC will run at least two books (retail unsecured vs secured, or bank + NBFC entity) and expects one platform. Today that means N worker containers with N times the connection budget and no shared fairness - one noisy tenant's sweep starves nothing for another tenant only because they are different processes, while the connection ceiling is a hard 100. There is no per-tenant rate limiting, quota, or isolation in the loop.

**Fix.** Make the tenant an explicit parameter of the tick and round-robin tenants inside one process (fair share per tenant), or formalise the sharded deployment: one worker per tenant with a documented connection budget, PgBouncer in front, and a per-tenant queue-depth metric.

### `worker-clerk-and-canary-starved` — The clerk, the doc-SLA sweep and the canary rollback sweep only run when every other stage is idle

**backend/bot_worker.py:146** · reliability · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

The clerk block (bot_worker.py:146-160) sits below nine `if _run_stage(...): return True` short-circuits. Any stage above returning True ends the tick before the clerk is reached. treatment_sweep (line 138) is the corpus generator and returns True whenever it decided any account in its 50-row batch (sweep.py:76-109). Note bot_jobs got an explicit fairness counter for exactly this reason (bot_worker.py:55-59) and the clerk did not.

**Impact.** On a real book the sweep has work almost every iteration, so the clerk never drains: supervisor approvals sit in 'input_required' forever, bounce and broken-PTP chases never enact, doc SLAs are never swept, and - worst - agent_core.canary.sweep_rollbacks (line 152-156), the automatic rollback of a bad model or prompt, never runs. A safety mechanism that is starved by load is a safety mechanism that fails exactly when it is needed.

**Fix.** Give the clerk the same treatment as bot_jobs: a CLERK_PRIORITY_EVERY first-look, or a round-robin over stages instead of a fixed priority chain. Move the periodic sweeps (settle, clerk_overdue, canary) out of the priority chain entirely into an unconditional time-based section at the top of the tick.

### `worker-settle-cadence-coupled-to-unreached-code` — The clerk_overdue / canary cadence uses a global iteration counter inside a branch that is not evaluated every iteration

**backend/bot_worker.py:149** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`if _iteration % SETTLE_EVERY == 1:` at line 149 sits inside the clerk block that is only reached on an otherwise-idle tick, while _iteration is incremented on every tick (line 85). The identical condition at line 89 is at the top of the function and is therefore evaluated every tick. So the line-149 block fires only when idleness happens to coincide with _iteration ≡ 1 (mod 20).

**Impact.** On a bursty book the doc-SLA sweep and the canary rollback sweep can go hours or days without executing even when the worker has idle ticks, and nothing reports that they did not run. The cadence is unpredictable and untestable, and it degrades precisely as load rises.

**Fix.** Schedule periodic work on wall-clock deadlines (next_run_at per periodic task, checked unconditionally at the top of the tick), not on a modulo of an iteration counter that different code paths observe differently.

### `worker-poison-row-hot-loop` — A persistently failing row is retried at full loop speed with a full traceback each time, with no per-queue backoff or circuit breaker

**backend/bot_worker.py:224** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`if not did:` guards the sleep (bot_worker.py:224-233), so when any stage returns True the tick repeats immediately. _run_stage logs a full `logger.exception` for every failure with no rate limit, no per-queue backoff, no dead-letter, and no use of the circuit_breaker.py that already exists in this backend.

**Impact.** One malformed row in whatsapp_outbound while the sweep keeps the loop hot produces thousands of stack traces per minute - filling the log volume, hiding every other signal, and burning CPU that the borrower-facing queues need. During a database outage all twelve stages raise every tick. The docstring's fix (don't abort the tick) is right; the missing half is not to retry the same failure at maximum rate.

**Fix.** Track consecutive failures per queue and apply exponential backoff to that queue only; rate-limit identical exceptions to one traceback per interval with a count; wire circuit_breaker.py in front of stages with external dependencies; and give each queue a dead-letter path after N failures on the same row id.

### `ops-floor-snapshot-unbounded` — The Floor snapshot has no row limit and no reaper for interactions stuck 'active'

**backend/ops_screens.py:447** · scale · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`WHERE i.tenant_id = :tenant AND i.status = 'active' ORDER BY i.started_at ASC NULLS LAST` with no LIMIT (ops_screens.py:447-449); the result set then drives four correlated batch queries (flags, last-two sentiments, last-four transcript turns, alerts) and three policy modules (offer, authority, live_qa) before being returned whole to a polled screen.

**Impact.** A bank floor runs hundreds to thousands of concurrent interactions, and any call whose closer never ran (a crashed voice container, a dropped carrier callback) stays 'active' forever - there is nothing in this module that ages one out. The Floor payload therefore grows without bound, and the supervisor screen becomes the heaviest query in the system exactly when the floor is busiest.

**Fix.** Cap the query (LIMIT + server-side pagination or a risk-ordered top-N), add `AND i.started_at > now() - interval '4 hours'`, and add a sweeper that closes interactions with no activity past a threshold. Consider a materialised snapshot refreshed on a cadence instead of a per-poll full scan.

### `ops-barge-commits-state-before-audio` — Barge reassigns the call to a human and commits, then tries to join audio - and never compensates on failure

**backend/ops_screens.py:878** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

The `UPDATE interactions SET handler_kind = 'human', handler_user_id = :uid, handler_bot_id = NULL` plus the accepted handoff row are inside the transaction that closes at ops_screens.py:877; only afterwards does `result = barge_audio(interaction_id, reason=action)` run under `except Exception: logger.exception("supervisor barge audio failed for %s", interaction_id)` (880-886), recording `audio_joined = False` (897) while leaving the reassignment in place.

**Impact.** When the audio join fails the database says a named human owns the call - so the Floor stops showing it as a bot call, the bot-at-risk count drops, and any routing that keys on handler_kind treats it as supervised - while the bot is still talking to the borrower unattended. That is the exact scenario a supervisor barges to prevent, and the screen now says it was handled.

**Fix.** Attempt the audio join first (or in the same unit of work with compensation): on failure roll the handler reassignment back, mark the supervisor action as failed, and raise a visible alert on the Floor instead of returning ok:true with audioJoined:false.

### `ops-webhook-config-changes-unaudited` — Creating, re-pointing, rotating or deleting a webhook endpoint writes no audit record, and delete is a hard DELETE

**backend/ops_screens.py:1197** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

patch_webhook_endpoint updates url/target/status/algo/name (ops_screens.py:1197-1237) with no activity or audit write; create (1141), rotate (1250) and `DELETE FROM webhook_endpoints WHERE id = :id AND tenant_id = :tenant` (1240-1247) likewise. Compare payments.py:362 which does call db.record_activity for a promise allocation.

**Impact.** The webhook URL is the destination of customer data (payment.updated carries account and amount; call.summary.ready carries call content). Changing it is a data-export change, and there is no record of who changed it, from what, to what, or when. Deleting an endpoint also removes its delivery history (the audit of what was sent), which conflicts with the retention expectations around collections records.

**Fix.** Write an immutable audit row for every endpoint mutation (actor, before, after) and soft-delete endpoints (status='deleted') so the delivery log survives its retention window.

### `ops-sandbox-and-prod-share-credentials` — Sandbox and production share one process-wide credential set, so the environment toggle is cosmetic

**backend/ops_screens.py:1618** · security · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`# Credentials are process-wide env vars, so 'values' is shared; only the DB-backed status is per-environment.` (ops_screens.py:1618-1619); `values = _env_values(pid)` is computed once per provider and handed to both perEnv entries (1610-1651), and the 'region' difference is a hard-coded literal `"centralindia" if for_env == "production" else "eastus"` (1620-1621).

**Impact.** A bank will not accept one Twilio account and one Azure key serving both its test and live collections traffic, and its separation-of-duties policy requires that the people who can see sandbox credentials cannot see production ones. As built, flipping 'production' on the screen changes a database flag and nothing about which account is dialled - so a test campaign can dial live borrowers.

**Fix.** Key credentials by (tenant, environment) in a secret store, resolve them per environment at call time, and make the environment toggle actually switch the credential set. Fail closed when the production credential set is absent.

### `ops-secrets-vault-attestation-false` — The Integrations screen attests to controls the code does not implement (ops vault, locked credentials)

**backend/ops_screens.py:1626** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`"usageStats": [{"label": "Source", "value": "env"}, {"label": "Secrets", "value": "ops vault"}, {"label": "Editable", "value": "no"}], "costMonth": "—", "unitLabel": "ops", "credentialsLocked": True` (ops_screens.py:1625-1632). The values actually come from `os.getenv` (1515-1525) populated by env_loader from a plaintext backend/.env (env_loader.py:8-27), and the webhook 'vault' reference is the literal string `f"vault://local/{eid}"` (1144).

**Impact.** A bank's information-security review and its auditors read these screens as control evidence. Stating 'Secrets: ops vault' when the secrets are a plaintext file mounted into four containers (docker-compose.yml:8-11 admits worker, bot_worker and voice all receive the full .env) is a false control attestation - the kind of thing that turns a technical finding into a governance one.

**Fix.** Either integrate a real secret store (Azure Key Vault / HashiCorp Vault) and resolve secret_ref through it, or change the labels to state the truth ('Source: process environment'). Split the env files per service so a sidecar does not receive credentials it never uses.

### `ops-test-provider-fabricates-health` — 'Test connection' checks that env strings are non-empty and then reports a green health and an invented latency

**backend/ops_screens.py:1717** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`missing = [env_name for field in meta["fields"] if field.get("secret") ... if env_name and not (os.getenv(env_name) or "").strip()]`, `ok = not missing`, `latency = int((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000) + (12 if ok else 3)`, `message = "Connection config present"` (ops_screens.py:1723-1732), then `"health": "healthy" if ok else "degraded"` is written to provider_configs (1795) and an integration_test_logs row with status 'ok' is persisted (1801-1819).

**Impact.** During a bank go-live the Integrations screen is the first thing the customer's ops team looks at. It will show Azure OpenAI, Azure Speech, Twilio and WhatsApp as healthy with ~12ms latency while the keys are wrong, the tenant's egress proxy blocks the endpoint, or the deployment name does not exist - and the persisted latency then feeds any dashboard. The screen actively suppresses the signal it exists to provide.

**Fix.** Perform a real, cheap, timed round trip per provider (Azure OpenAI models list, Speech token endpoint, Twilio account fetch, WhatsApp phone-number GET) with a short timeout, store the real latency and the real status code, and label a config-only check as 'config present' with health 'unknown' rather than 'healthy'.

### `payments-public-base-url-localhost-default` — PUBLIC_BASE_URL silently defaults to http://127.0.0.1:8000 for links sent to borrowers

**backend/payments.py:47** · integration · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`base = _env("PUBLIC_BASE_URL") or "http://127.0.0.1:8000"` (payments.py:47-49); checkout_url interpolates it (59) and promise_fulfillment.py:272 stores the result as payment_intents.pay_url, which is what goes out over WhatsApp/SMS.

**Impact.** An unset variable in the bank's environment means every statutory bounce pay-link and every PTP link sent to a borrower is a localhost URL - dead for the borrower, and a support and compliance problem when the message claims to be a payment facility. The default is also plain http, so even a mis-set public value would carry the token in cleartext.

**Fix.** No default: raise at startup if PUBLIC_BASE_URL is unset or is not https, and validate it once in a config check rather than per call.

### `payments-no-provider-event-idempotency` — Webhook replay protection is the intent status alone, so a second genuine payment is swallowed as 'idempotent'

**backend/payments.py:149** · reliability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`if intent["status"] == "paid": return {"ok": True, "intentId": intent["id"], "status": "paid", "idempotent": True}` (payments.py:149-150). There is no table of processed provider event ids and provider_ref is only recorded with COALESCE (200), never compared.

**Impact.** Two different real payments against the same intent (common when a borrower retries after a timeout, or pays twice) are indistinguishable from a duplicate webhook: the second is acknowledged with ok:true and never posted. The money is with the PSP and not on the bank's ledger, and the borrower's statement disagrees with the bank's. Reconciliation will find it weeks later.

**Fix.** Add a payment_provider_events table keyed on (provider, event_id) with a unique constraint, insert before processing, and treat a conflict as the replay case; when a NEW provider_ref arrives for an already-paid intent, post it as an over-payment/unapplied credit rather than discarding it.

### `payments-paid-label-on-unenacted-decisions` — 'paid' outcomes are written onto decisions that were never enacted, contaminating the training labels

**backend/payments.py:285** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

payments.py:285-296 calls `followthrough.resolve_case(conn, trigger_kind=..., trigger_ref=..., outcome="paid")`, and resolve_case updates `WHERE trigger_kind = :kind AND trigger_ref = :ref AND outcome IS NULL AND enacted IS FALSE` (followthrough.py:484-492). By construction it labels only decisions whose action was never carried out.

**Impact.** The corpus that the uplift/reach models learn from now contains rows where the recommended action was never taken and the outcome is 'paid'. Any estimator that treats outcome as the response to the recorded action will over-credit whatever action happened to be recommended when a borrower paid spontaneously. With 7 'paid' rows out of 108 outcomes today, this is a material fraction of the entire positive class. A model-risk reviewer will reject a model trained on it.

**Fix.** Use a distinct terminal label for 'the reason for the case went away before we acted' (e.g. 'superseded_paid' - resolve_case already defaults to 'superseded'), and exclude non-enacted rows from the training set at the query level in the trainers.

### `workrt-claim-next-double-claims` — claim_next re-selects 'working' rows and releases its row lock before the job body runs, so two workers execute the same job

**backend/work_runtime/adapter_pg.py:157** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W03-workers`

`SELECT id FROM work_runtime_jobs WHERE tenant_id = :t AND status IN ('submitted','working') ORDER BY created_at FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1` inside `with db.engine.begin() as conn:` (adapter_pg.py:158-176). The transaction commits at the end of the with-block, releasing the lock; the job body then runs in clerk._run under a separate connection. A second worker's claim_next sees the same row (status 'working' is in the selection set, and nothing holds a lock) and claims it too.

**Impact.** This is the reason the platform cannot run two bot_worker replicas - i.e. cannot have HA on the process that performs every borrower-facing action. If someone scales it anyway (the obvious response to a slow queue), the same treatment decision is enacted twice: two dials, two SMS, two field-visit orders. Duplicate contact on the same day is exactly what the RBI harassment provisions and the contact-frequency policy exist to prevent. The only thing standing between this and a double dial today is decisions.claim_by_id's own lock inside enact.

**Fix.** Either hold the transaction for the life of the job (claim, run, finish in one transaction with the FOR UPDATE lock held) or add a lease: locked_by/locked_at + heartbeat, select only 'submitted' plus 'working' rows whose lease expired, and make finish() assert the lease is still ours. webhooks_dispatch.claim_next (locked_at/locked_by + STALE_CLAIM_SECONDS) already does this correctly in the same codebase - copy it.

### `nba-engine-actions-not-actionable` — Eight of the fourteen NBA action kinds — every one the treatment engine emits — land on 'coming soon'

**Habibi/src/routes/customers.$customerId.lazy.tsx:202** · ux · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`
