`resolve_case` runs `UPDATE treatment_decisions SET outcome = :outcome, outcome_at = now() WHERE trigger_kind = :kind AND trigger_ref = :ref AND outcome IS NULL AND enacted IS FALSE` (backend/agent_core/treatment/followthrough.py:481-493) — no customer_id, no tenant_id. It is safe today only because both live callers pass a globally unique id: `trigger_ref=event_id` for 'bounce' and `trigger_ref=promise_id` for 'broken_ptp' (backend/payments.py:285-295). But the sweep's case key is deliberately not unique: `trigger_ref` is the borrower's local ISO date, so every account swept on the same day shares `('dpd_tick', '2026-09-05')` — stated as the design at backend/agent_core/treatment/sweep.py:14-16 and implemented at sweep.py:180 (`Trigger(kind=TRIGGER, at=now, ref=local_day)`). The function's signature accepts any trigger_kind and its docstring invites the usage ('Called when a bounce cures or a promise is kept'), and 'dpd_tick' is in the ladder's LOOPED_TRIGGERS.

**Impact.** One call to resolve_case with trigger_kind='dpd_tick' — added by anyone wiring a cure event, a hardship hold or a payment webhook to the sweep case, which is the obvious next integration — would mark every unenacted sweep decision for that calendar day as superseded, across every borrower and every tenant. On a 2M-account book that is a whole day of planned contact silently cancelled, with no error, no count that looks wrong, and rowcount returned to a caller that ignores it. It is a loaded gun with the safety on only because of who happens to be holding it.

**Fix.** Require `customer_id` (and the tenant) as parameters on resolve_case and add them to the WHERE clause; the two current callers already have the customer in hand. Failing that, refuse trigger kinds whose ref is not an entity id with an explicit allow-list, so the function states the assumption instead of depending on it. A test that writes sweep decisions for two customers on the same local day and asserts resolve_case cannot touch both would pin it.

### `warn-once-hides-recurring-degradation` — _warn_once turns a persistent model-serving degradation into a single log line for the life of the process, with no recovery signal

**backend/agent_core/treatment/models.py:93** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-failure`

`_warn_once` records the key in a process-global set and never emits again (models.py:93-104), and every artifact rejection path uses it — missing (441), unreadable (444), shape (448), arity (457), target (515), vector version (526), schema version (536), simulated corpus (558), stale (574). The same pattern is in reco/models.py:58. There is no counter, no gauge, and no corresponding 'artifact recovered' line, so a process that logged 'refusing' at 03:00 during a deploy is serving priors at 15:00 with nothing in the log to say so.

**Impact.** The bank's model-risk function asks 'which model decided this contact?' The decision row records the scorer name (models.py:740 — 'ev' vs 'ev+reach+uplift'), which is good, but the operational question 'is the champion actually serving right now, across the fleet?' has no live answer. A stale-artifact refusal at 90 days (models.py:567-582) silently reverts the whole engine to hand-tuned priors and the only evidence is one line in whichever process noticed first.

**Fix.** Keep the once-per-reason suppression for the log line but pair it with a counter and a current-state gauge per (target, state), exported on the health endpoint. Re-emit at a low rate (once an hour) while the condition persists, and emit an INFO line when an artifact that was refused begins loading again.

### `duplicate-workers-thrash-shared-cursor` — Two sweep workers share one unsynchronised cursor row, so the slower one rewinds the faster one's progress

**backend/agent_core/treatment/sweep.py:106** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-failure`

The cursor is a single row keyed on `(tenant_id, CURSOR_KEY)` (sweep.py:70-71) read without a lock at sweep.py:221-232 and written last-writer-wins at sweep.py:106 / 235-244. SKIP LOCKED means worker A claims accounts 1-50 and worker B claims 51-100 concurrently; whichever commits last stamps its own `accounts[-1]["id"]`. If A commits second, the cursor rewinds from 100 to 50. The module documents concurrency safety only for the account lock ('Concurrency is the account row lock, not a unique index', sweep.py:30-36) and never addresses the cursor.

**Impact.** Horizontal scaling of the sweep — the obvious response to a book that will not finish in a day — makes it slower rather than faster, and can prevent a pass from ever completing. The `_decided_today` guard keeps it correct, so the failure shows up only as a sweep that never reaches the end of the book, with no error anywhere.

**Fix.** Take the cursor row `FOR UPDATE` at the start of the batch so cursor advancement is serialised, or advance it with `GREATEST(existing, new)` semantics. Better: partition the book by `hashtext(a.id) % workers = :shard` so each worker owns a disjoint slice and needs no shared cursor at all.

### `sweep-single-tenant-executor-all-tenant` — The sweep decides for exactly one tenant — the worker's process default — while the executor enacts for all of them

**backend/agent_core/treatment/sweep.py:128** · integration · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-failure`

`_tenant` returns `dbmod.current_tenant()` (sweep.py:126-132), which with nothing bound is the process TENANT_ID (db_core.py:117-138). Every downstream query is scoped to that one value: `_claim` filters `c.tenant_id = :tenant` (sweep.py:150), and the resume cursor is a single work_runtime_jobs row under one well-known idempotency key (sweep.py:70-71, 221-244). There is no loop over tenants anywhere in the module. By contrast decisions.claim_due (decisions.py:359-386) and followthrough.open_cases have no tenant predicate at all.

**Impact.** True today because the deployment is single-tenant, false the moment the platform serves a second NBFC or a second book within one bank. Every tenant except the process default receives zero sweep decisions — no corpus, no ladder on the silent roller, no coverage — and this failure is completely silent: the sweep reports success and 'decided N accounts' every tick. Meanwhile the executor happily enacts across all tenants, so the two halves disagree about what the deployment is.

**Fix.** Enumerate active tenants and sweep each in turn with tenant_context bound, one cursor per tenant (the cursor key already has a tenant column at sweep.py:227). Add a per-tenant 'accounts swept today / accounts eligible' gauge so a tenant receiving no decisions is visible on day one rather than at the first quarterly review.

### `no-worker-liveness-or-queue-metrics` — The worker that carries both engines exposes no health endpoint, no heartbeat and no queue-depth metric

**backend/bot_worker.py:217** · observability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-failure`

main() is a bare `while not stop:` loop (bot_worker.py:217-233) with a SIGTERM handler (207-215). There is no liveness file, no heartbeat row, no /health, and no per-stage timing. The only per-tick output is `logger.info("treatment sweep decided %s account(s)", decided)` (sweep.py:109) and the enactment info line (enact.py:873).

**Impact.** If the process dies, wedges on a stage, or is simply never started in the customer's environment, nothing anywhere says so. Due contacts stop being enacted and the sweep stops generating decisions, and the first signal is a collections head noticing the queue is quiet — days later. An on-call rotation cannot be built on this.

**Fix.** Write a heartbeat row (tenant, worker id, last tick, last stage, iteration count) every tick, expose oldest-due-plan-age and per-stage last-success-at, and alert on staleness. A worker whose absence is undetectable is not a production worker.

### `artifacts-reloaded-per-decision-non-atomic-write` — The treatment trainer overwrites the serving artifact non-atomically while the serving path re-reads that file on every single decision

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:1067** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-failure`

The trainer writes in place: `path.write_text(json.dumps(artifact, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")` (train_treatment_models.py:1067) — truncate-then-write, no temp file, no rename. The sibling trainer gets this right: `tmp = out.with_suffix(out.suffix + ".tmp"); tmp.write_text(...); tmp.replace(out)` (train_propensity.py:389-391). On the read side there is no caching whatsoever: engine.py:305 calls build_scorer per decision, which for the 'estimators' name calls models.build (scoring.py:614), which calls load_reach/load_timing/load_uplift (models.py:846), each doing `p.read_text()` + `json.loads` (models.py:439). Three file reads and three JSON parses per decision, on the book sweep and on the audio path.

**Impact.** A training run concurrent with a live sweep is read mid-truncate and produces a JSONDecodeError. models.load_artifact degrades to the EV priors (models.py:443-445) — correct — but `_warn_once` (models.py:93-104) logs the reason exactly once per process, so the fleet can serve priors for the rest of its life having said so a single time, and nobody is told when it recovers. Separately, at book-sweep volume this is millions of synchronous file reads and JSON parses a day inside the decision path, and on a container with the model directory on a network mount it is an availability dependency nobody declared.

**Fix.** Make train_treatment_models.py write tmp-then-os.replace, matching train_propensity.py:389-391. Cache the loaded artifact keyed on (path, st_mtime_ns, st_size) with a short TTL so a promotion is still picked up without a restart but a decision does not pay three file reads. Emit a gauge for 'estimators currently loaded' rather than relying on a once-per-process warning, and check the registry's artifact_sha (registry.py:430) at load time so a drifted file is refused rather than served.

### `mt-reco-decision-stamped-with-process-tenant` — offer_decisions.tenant_id records the process, not the borrower

**backend/agent_core/reco/decisions.py:82** · data-model · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-multitenancy`

`"tenant": db.current_tenant(),` (reco/decisions.py:82) is the only source of tenant_id for the row. The treatment engine does the opposite and says why — `tenant_id=features.tenant_id` (engine.py:360), sourced from `c.tenant_id` on the customer row (features.py:453,503). reco.features never selects customers.tenant_id at all: `"SELECT dnd, segment, risk, risk_score, preferred_window FROM customers WHERE id = :id"` (reco/features.py:266-269).

**Impact.** The assumption 'the process tenant is the customer's tenant' is true on a one-tenant install and false everywhere else. When it breaks, the failure is silent and permanent: a decision describing Bank B's borrower is filed under Bank A, so B's own scoped reads (reco/policy.py:279,294) cannot see the offer that was made to their customer, A's audit trail contains a borrower A has no relationship with, and the propensity trainer inherits the mislabelling. Because offer_decisions has no propensity, policy_version or explore_kind column either (unlike treatment_decisions), there is no second field that would betray the inconsistency.

**Fix.** Select customers.tenant_id in reco.features, carry it on CustomerFeatures, and pass it into decisions.record the way engine.py:360 does. While there, take tenant_id as a parameter in mark_presented/record_response/attach_lead and add it to the UPDATE predicates (reco/decisions.py:117-121, 139-143).

### `mt-reco-observability-unscoped` — The offer-engine health dashboard has no tenant predicate on any of its ten queries

**backend/agent_core/reco/observability.py:101** · privacy · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-multitenancy`

Ten aggregates over offer_decisions whose predicates are mode and window only: `FROM offer_decisions WHERE mode = ANY(:modes)` (observability.py:103-105), and the same shape at 122-124, 136-139, 153-156, 165-168, 181-184, 199-202 (joined to products and leads), 219-222, 244-247 (joined to interactions), 318-323. None mentions tenant_id, although offer_decisions.tenant_id is NOT NULL (0051:193-195) and reco/policy.py one module over does scope its reads correctly (`AND d.tenant_id = :tenant`, policy.py:279,294,313,319).

**Impact.** Same cross-tenant disclosure as the treatment scoreboard, over a table that names products and links to leads and interactions. It also makes the freshness alarm (`MAX(created_at)` at observability.py:102) lie: tenant A's engine can be silently dead while B's traffic keeps the dashboard green.

**Fix.** Copy the predicate from reco/policy.py into every query here and take the tenant as a parameter rather than reading it inside. The fact that two modules in the same package disagree about this is the tell that it was never a decision.

### `mt-capacity-plan-is-env-only` — Agent hours, field slots and rail capacity are one set of env vars for the whole deployment

**backend/agent_core/treatment/allocate.py:308** · integration · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-multitenancy`

```
def capacity_plan() -> dict[str, float]:
    out: dict[str, float] = {}
    for resource in RESOURCES:
        raw = (os.getenv(f"TREATMENT_CAPACITY_{resource.upper()}") or "").strip()
``` (allocate.py:308-332). The docstring concedes the ownership problem — 'agent hours and field slots belong to a floor manager, not to this repository' (allocate.py:311-313) — but the shape does not admit more than one floor manager. persist() writes per tenant (allocate.py:347-372, ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, plan_date, resource)), so the storage is per-tenant while the input is not.

**Impact.** Two portfolios collected by two different vendor floors — the norm in Indian collections, where early buckets are in-house and late buckets are agency — share one agent-minute budget. The Lagrangian solve then prices scarcity that does not exist for one of them and throttles a book that had capacity to spare. Since the price feeds every local decision (allocate.py:19-30), the error is not local: it is the whole ladder shifting down for a constraint borrowed from someone else's floor.

**Fix.** Read capacity from a table keyed on (tenant_id, product_id NULL-able, resource, plan_date) — the capacity_duals row already has the right key shape — and fall back to env when no row exists. Solve once per tenant per day rather than once per process.

### `mt-claim-due-spans-tenants` — The executor claims due plans across every tenant with no scoping, ordering fairness, or per-tenant pause

**backend/agent_core/treatment/decisions.py:359** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-multitenancy`

```
SELECT * FROM treatment_decisions
WHERE enacted IS FALSE
  AND mode <> 'simulated'
  AND suppression_reason IS NULL
  AND outcome IS NULL
  AND chosen_action IS NOT NULL
  AND chosen_action <> 'wait'
  AND scheduled_at IS NOT NULL
  AND scheduled_at <= now()
  AND created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'
ORDER BY scheduled_at ASC
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT :limit
``` (decisions.py:361-382). enact.process_one wraps it with a single process-wide mode gate — `if config.mode() != config.MODE_LIVE: return False` (enact.py:866) — and bot_worker.py:126 drains it without binding any tenant. followthrough.attribute_outcomes is the same shape (followthrough.py:98-133).

**Impact.** Strict `ORDER BY scheduled_at` across tenants means one bank's morning backlog is head-of-line blocking for every other bank's time-critical dials — a bank whose plans are all scheduled at 09:00 starves a bank whose plans are at 09:05, and the SLA nobody can meet is invisible because the queue depth metric is also un-tenanted. There is no way to pause one tenant (an onboarding freeze, a regulator's stop-notice, a client asking for outreach to halt) without stopping the executor for everyone. Every by-id write it then performs — mark_enacted (decisions.py:295-299), record_outcome (decisions.py:342-345), claim_by_id (decisions.py:394-399) — is keyed on id alone with no tenant check, so a bug that hands the wrong id across tenants has nothing to stop it.

**Fix.** Add tenant_id to the claim predicate and drain tenants round-robin (or weighted by book size), binding tenant_context for the duration of each claim so every downstream read inherits it. Add `AND tenant_id = :tenant` to mark_enacted/record_outcome/claim_by_id as the cheap backstop. Add a per-tenant enabled flag so one bank can be paused.

### `mt-insights-window-aggregates-have-no-usable-index` — The scoreboard's window aggregates have no created_at-leading index and will sequentially scan the whole corpus

**backend/agent_core/treatment/decisions.py:436** · scale · missing-for-production · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `L-multitenancy`

Four of the five insights() aggregates filter on the window alone - `FROM treatment_decisions WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '{window}'` (decisions.py:436-437, 445-446, 466-467) and the outcomes variant at 475-477 - with no `mode` predicate to anchor a composite index. The complete index set on the table is: [tenant_id] (0069:210-212), (customer_id, created_at) (0069:213-217), (mode, created_at) (0069:219-223), a partial on (scheduled_at) (0069:225-232), a partial on (customer_id, trigger_ref) (0085:130-134), a partial on (mode, variant, created_at) (0085:138-142) and idx_treatment_decisions_attribution (20260821_0091:56). No index leads with created_at, so `created_at >= …` alone cannot be served by any of them.

**Impact.** This one bites the single-tenant install the report otherwise treats as safe. GET /treatment/insights is an ANALYTICS_READ route (authz.py:443) that a dashboard will poll, and it runs five unindexed aggregates plus a jsonb LATERAL in the sibling metrics report (metrics.py:147-157). At 225 rows it is instant; at 50k-2M accounts producing decisions daily it is a repeated sequential scan over the largest table in the schema, competing with the executor's FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED claim on the same table inside a 15s statement_timeout. The failure mode is a dashboard that times out exactly when the book is large enough for anyone to care.

**Fix.** Add (created_at DESC) - or, when the tenant predicate lands, (tenant_id, created_at DESC) - and reorder idx_treatment_decisions_mode_created so the window is servable without a mode filter. Cap the window server-side and consider a materialised daily rollup: none of these five numbers needs to be computed from raw rows on every dashboard poll.

### `mt-enact-by-id-reads-unscoped` — The executor resolves the borrower, the bounce, the promise and the pay-link by id with no tenant check

**backend/agent_core/treatment/enact.py:164** · security · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-multitenancy`

`SELECT id, tenant_id, name, phone_primary, phone_alt, language, assigned_user_id FROM customers WHERE id = :id` (enact.py:167-171) — it selects tenant_id and does not filter on it. `SELECT status FROM payment_events WHERE id = :id` (enact.py:184) and `SELECT status FROM promises WHERE id = :id` (enact.py:189) in _resolved_since. `SELECT id, pay_url, amount FROM payment_intents WHERE customer_id = :cid AND (...) AND status IN ('created','sent','opened')` (enact.py:206-215) — a live payment link with a public token, fetched with no tenant predicate. Compare agent_core/connectors/first_party.py:34-38, which joins customers and filters `c.tenant_id = :t` for the same kind of read.

**Impact.** Ids are globally unique so nothing crosses tenants today, but this is a live outbound path — the value fetched at enact.py:206 is pasted into an SMS as `Pay securely here: {pay_url}` (enact.py:265). Defence in depth on the read that produces a payment URL in a borrower-facing message is not optional in a bank, and every one of these queries already has the tenant either in the row it selects or one join away.

**Fix.** Filter customers on tenant_id, and join payment_intents/payment_events/promises to customers with `c.tenant_id = :tenant`, taking the tenant from the claimed decision row (treatment_decisions.tenant_id is already selected by `SELECT *` in claim_due).

### `mt-features-read-by-id-without-tenant` — The feature builder assumes a globally-unique customer id is sufficient scoping

**backend/agent_core/treatment/features.py:450** · security · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-multitenancy`

`FROM customers c LEFT JOIN consent_records cr ON cr.customer_id = c.id WHERE c.id = :cid` (features.py:450-463) — the tenant is *read out* of this row (features.py:503) but never used to constrain it, and the twenty-odd downstream reads then key on customer_id alone (features.py:597,664,703,732,781,800,811,845,854,865,875,906,932,958,1056,1145,1173,1186,1210,1220,1262,1277). features.py:1099-1101 even joins customers for the timezone and still adds no tenant predicate. reco/features.py:266-269 and contact_policy.py:288-300 share the pattern.

**Impact.** The assumption holds only while (a) customer ids are globally unique and (b) every entrypoint validates ownership. (a) is true in this schema. (b) is true for GET /treatment/next (db_treatment_holds.py:298-305) and for the sweep, and untrue for the executor and the followthrough loop. When a bank ingests customers from a core banking system that reuses account-number-derived ids per entity — a normal thing for a group with two lending entities — (a) stops holding too, and the engine silently builds one borrower's vector from two borrowers' rows.

**Fix.** Add `AND c.tenant_id = :tenant` to the base read and raise LookupError on a miss (the code path for a missing customer already exists at features.py:464-465). Pass the tenant in from the caller rather than discovering it, which also makes the entrypoint contract explicit.

### `mt-estimator-artifacts-reparsed-per-decision` — Switching to the fitted scorer re-reads and re-parses three JSON artifacts on every decision

**backend/agent_core/treatment/models.py:846** · scale · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `L-multitenancy`

`build_scorer` is called once per decision - `scorer = build_scorer((arm.scorer if arm and arm.scorer else None) or config.scorer_name())` (engine.py:305) - and for the fitted names it calls `scorer = models.build(EVScorer())` (scoring.py:609-614), whose body is `reach, timing, uplift = load_reach(), load_timing(), load_uplift()` (models.py:846). Each of those calls load_artifact, which does `p = Path(path)` then `raw = json.loads(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))` (models.py:437-439) with no cache, no mtime check and no module-level memo anywhere in the file.

**Impact.** Latent only because TREATMENT_SCORER=ev today, so models.build is never reached - which is precisely why this will be discovered on the day the fitted uplift model is promoted to serve, i.e. the highest-attention change the engine will ever make. At that point every scored account costs three file opens and three JSON parses of artifacts containing a segment ladder (uplift n=14331), inside a book sweep of BATCH=50 accounts per worker iteration. The regression will look like the model being slow rather than the loader being uncached, and the natural rollback is to abandon the model.

**Fix.** Memoise on (resolved path, mtime, size) at module level and invalidate on change - the mtime check is what keeps `registry.promote`'s file copy taking effect without a restart, which is the property models.py currently buys by re-reading. Do it in the same change that gives the path a tenant/product dimension, so the cache key is the resolved path rather than the target name.

### `mt-holds-read-unscoped-inside-engine` — The engine reads treatment_holds without a tenant predicate that its own screen accessor applies

**backend/agent_core/treatment/policy.py:516** · security · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-multitenancy`

`SELECT kind FROM treatment_holds WHERE customer_id = :cid AND released_at IS NULL AND starts_at <= now() AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > now())` (policy.py:513-524), repeated in features.py:1173-1177. treatment_holds carries tenant_id NOT NULL (0069:131,180) and the screen accessor scopes it properly: `where = ["c.tenant_id = :tenant_id"]` over `FROM treatment_holds h JOIN customers c ON c.id = h.customer_id` (db_treatment_holds.py:60-62, 86-87).

**Impact.** A hold is the mechanism that stops outreach to a borrower in hardship, in dispute, or under a regulator's instruction. It is the highest-consequence veto in the engine and it is read on the weakest predicate in the engine. Same latent-only status as the enact reads, and the same argument for closing it: the module one directory up demonstrates the correct query.

**Fix.** Join customers and add `AND c.tenant_id = :tenant`, sourcing the tenant from AccountFeatures.tenant_id, which both call sites already have in scope.

### `mt-sweep-only-ever-sweeps-the-process-tenant` — The book sweep decides exactly one tenant's book and reports nothing about the rest

**backend/agent_core/treatment/sweep.py:89** · correctness · hidden-assumption · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `L-multitenancy`

`tenant = _tenant(conn)` (sweep.py:89) resolves to `return dbmod.current_tenant()` (sweep.py:125-131), and that single value is then the only tenant the claim can see: `WHERE c.tenant_id = :tenant AND a.status = 'active' AND a.dpd > 0 AND a.id > COALESCE(:after, '')` (sweep.py:144-159). The resume cursor is read and written under the same one tenant (sweep.py:221-235). There is no loop over tenants anywhere - grep for tenant in sweep.py returns only these sites - and `current_tenant()` falls back to the process constant because nothing binds a tenant (db_core.py:123).

**Impact.** This is the mirror image of every leak in the reader's report and it is worth stating separately because it fails in the opposite direction: a second tenant on the same deployment is not over-served, it is silently never served. Its delinquent accounts are never claimed, no treatment_decisions rows are ever written for them, and every scoreboard the operator looks at - which aggregates across all tenants (decisions.py:436) - keeps showing healthy volume from the first tenant. 'The engine is running' and 'the engine is running on your book' are indistinguishable from the outside. For a lender onboarding a second portfolio as a second tenant, the first symptom is a bucket that quietly stopped being worked.

**Fix.** Enumerate tenants (or the tenants with a sweep-enabled flag) and round-robin the cursor per tenant, binding tenant_context for each pass so downstream reads inherit it. Emit a per-tenant accounts-claimed counter so a book that is producing zero decisions is visible rather than inferred.

### `mt-hot-indexes-carry-no-tenant` — Every hot-path index on treatment_decisions is tenant-blind, so adding the predicate will not be free

**backend/alembic/versions/20260814_0069_treatment_engine.py:224** · scale · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-multitenancy`

`CREATE INDEX idx_treatment_decisions_due ON treatment_decisions (scheduled_at) WHERE enacted IS FALSE AND chosen_action IS NOT NULL AND chosen_action <> 'wait'` (0069:225-232); `idx_treatment_decisions_customer ON (customer_id, created_at)` (0069:213-217); `idx_treatment_decisions_mode_created ON (mode, created_at)` (0069:219-223); `idx_treatment_decisions_sweep ON (customer_id, trigger_ref)` (0085:131-135); `idx_treatment_decisions_ope ON (mode, variant, created_at)` (0085:137-142); `idx_accounts_delinquent ON accounts (id) WHERE status = 'active' AND dpd > 0` (0085:151-153). The only tenant index is the bare single-column `idx_treatment_decisions_tenant_id` (0069:210-212), which is useless as a leading column at low cardinality.

**Impact.** The sweep's account claim already scans a global delinquency index and filters the tenant afterwards via the customers join (sweep.py:144-160), so on a shared deployment every tenant pays to walk every other tenant's delinquent book. When the missing tenant predicates above are added, each one lands on an index that cannot serve it, and the scoreboard queries — which are unbounded aggregates over a corpus growing 19-42 rows/day/tenant today and orders of magnitude faster at real book size — degrade to sequential scans.

**Fix.** Rebuild the five hot indexes with tenant_id as the leading column: (tenant_id, scheduled_at) partial, (tenant_id, customer_id, created_at), (tenant_id, mode, created_at), (tenant_id, customer_id, trigger_ref) partial, (tenant_id, mode, variant, created_at) partial. Make idx_accounts_delinquent (tenant_id, id) by denormalising tenant onto accounts or indexing the join. Do it in the same migration that adds the predicates, or the fix will be measured as a regression.

### `mt-propensity-trainer-pools-tenants` — The offer propensity trainer pools offer_decisions and leads across tenants

**backend/scripts/train_propensity.py:69** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-multitenancy`

```
FROM offer_decisions d
LEFT JOIN leads l ON l.id = d.lead_id
WHERE d.presented IS TRUE
  AND d.chosen_product_id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY d.created_at DESC
LIMIT :lim
``` (train_propensity.py:71-87). No tenant predicate on either side, and the join to leads pulls a second tenant-scoped table in unscoped.

**Impact.** The same cross-tenant data-use problem as the treatment trainer, plus a specific pathology: the label depends on `leads.stage`, so one lender's sales-pipeline hygiene (how promptly they mark a lead won/lost) becomes a feature of another lender's propensity model. The current artifact already has only 1335 simulated samples; the first real deployment will be tempted to pool, and this query makes pooling the default rather than a decision.

**Fix.** Same as the treatment trainer: mandatory --tenant, predicate on d.tenant_id, and stamp the tenant into the artifact so models.load can refuse one fitted for someone else.

### `mt-trainer-disables-statement-timeout-on-the-live-db` — The trainer removes its own statement timeout and reads the entire corpus from the OLTP database

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:117** · reliability · missing-for-production · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `L-multitenancy`

`def _lift_timeout(conn: Any) -> None: ... conn.execute(text("SET statement_timeout = 0"))` (train_treatment_models.py:104-117), called first thing in `_rows` (train_treatment_models.py:120-121) before the unbounded `SELECT ... FROM treatment_decisions WHERE mode = ANY(:modes) AND feature_schema_version = :schema ORDER BY created_at ASC` (train_treatment_models.py:126-138). The docstring explains the reasoning - the 15s budget 'is not a budget, it is a guarantee of failure at any real book size' - and notes it is session-scoped, but there is no LIMIT, no chunking, no cursor, no lock_timeout, and no separate read connection: it runs on `db.engine`, the same pool the audio path uses.

**Impact.** The reasoning for lifting the timeout is sound; the absence of any replacement bound is the defect. On a real book this is a single statement holding a connection and a snapshot for an unbounded time against the live collections database, materialising every decision row with its per-action feature vectors into Python memory in one list comprehension. It pins autovacuum's xmin horizon on the hottest table in the schema for the duration, and it takes a pool slot from a fleet that also dials borrowers. An SRE would not sign off a batch job with no timeout, no chunking and no read replica against the transactional database; a training run that OOMs or bloats the table is an outage caused by a governance task.

**Fix.** Keep the statement_timeout lift but add a server-side cursor or keyset chunking on created_at, an explicit idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and lock_timeout, and a --max-rows guard. Point the trainer at a read replica or a restore where one exists, and record the row count and elapsed time into the artifact metadata so a run that read more than expected is visible in the model card.

### `no-bulk-insert-path-for-decisions` — Every decision is a single parameterised INSERT with two correlated subqueries in the VALUES list

**backend/agent_core/treatment/decisions.py:96** · scale · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-scale`

`active.execute(text("""INSERT INTO treatment_decisions (...) VALUES (..., (SELECT a.id FROM accounts a WHERE a.id = :account_id), (SELECT i.id FROM interactions i WHERE i.id = :interaction_id), ...)"""), {...})` (decisions.py:96-166) — one round trip and two extra index lookups per row, with the ~12 KB JSON payload serialised in Python at 144-146.

**Impact.** 2M single-row INSERTs a day, each carrying a large JSONB payload and two subqueries, is 2M round trips and 2M WAL records of a size that will dominate WAL volume and replication lag. There is no executemany or COPY path.

**Fix.** Batch the sweep's inserts with `executemany`/COPY per batch (the FK-safety subqueries can become a pre-batch existence check), and keep the single-row path only for the event-driven triggers where latency matters.

### `features-legal-notice-lookup-unbounded` — The legal-notice feature scans every decision ever made for the borrower, with no time bound and no supporting index

**backend/agent_core/treatment/features.py:1217** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-scale`

`SELECT enacted_at FROM treatment_decisions WHERE customer_id = :cid AND chosen_action = 'legal_notice' AND enacted IS TRUE ORDER BY enacted_at DESC LIMIT 1` (features.py:1217-1227). The only usable index is `(customer_id, created_at)` (0069:213-217), which does not cover chosen_action or enacted_at, so Postgres reads every row for that customer and sorts.

**Impact.** With one decision per account per day and a three-account borrower, that is ~1,100 rows per customer per year, read and sorted on every decision, for every account, for the life of the deployment. Multiplied by 2M decisions a day it is a meaningful share of the sweep's cost, and it grows every day the system runs.

**Fix.** Add `CREATE INDEX idx_treatment_decisions_legal ON treatment_decisions (customer_id, enacted_at DESC) WHERE chosen_action = 'legal_notice' AND enacted IS TRUE`, and bound the lookup to the statutory relevance window.

### `model-artifacts-reparsed-from-disk-per-decision` — Three model artifacts are read from disk and JSON-parsed on every single decision

**backend/agent_core/treatment/models.py:846** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-scale`

`reach, timing, uplift = load_reach(), load_timing(), load_uplift()` in `models.build` (models.py:840-849), which is called from `scoring.build_scorer` (scoring.py:614), which engine._decide calls per decision at engine.py:305. `load_artifact` does `json.loads(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))` (models.py:437-439) with no caching, no mtime check and no memoisation. The current artifacts are 4.0 KB, 4.0 KB and 9.5 KB; the uplift one grows with the segment ladder because the full `segmentLadder` report is embedded in `metrics` (train_treatment_models.py:688, 480-485).

**Impact.** 6M file opens and ~36 GB of JSON parsing per day at 2M decisions, all on the worker's critical path — and the same code runs on the audio path of a live call, where models.py:39-41 explicitly cites keeping the serving image light as the design rationale.

**Fix.** Cache the parsed artifacts in module state keyed on (path, mtime, size), refreshing only when the file changes. Strip `metrics.segmentLadder` from the shipped artifact and keep it in a sibling report file, so the serving artifact stays small.

### `offer-decisions-lacks-window-and-mode-indexes` — offer_decisions inherits every treatment-log scale problem and starts with fewer indexes

**backend/alembic/versions/20260731_0051_upsell_nbo_engine.py:264** · data-model · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-scale`

The table gets only `(customer_id)`, `(interaction_id)`, `(lead_id)` and `(customer_id, chosen_product_id, created_at DESC)` (0051:264-270). There is no `(created_at)`, no `(mode, created_at)`, no partial index for un-responded rows, no partitioning and no retention — and it carries the same three JSONB columns (0051:220-232). train_propensity's extraction filters on `d.presented IS TRUE AND d.chosen_product_id IS NOT NULL` (train_propensity.py:72-86), which nothing indexes.

**Impact.** The reco engine has 16 rows and 0 responses today, so none of this hurts yet. The moment RECO_MODE=live runs across a real inbound call volume it reproduces every finding above without even the partial indexes the treatment log has.

**Fix.** Bring offer_decisions to parity before it is switched on: created_at index, mode index, partial index for the trainer's predicate, monthly partitioning, and the propensity/policy_version columns treatment_decisions already has.

### `policy-rules-cache-key-defeats-the-cache` — The policy-rule cache is keyed on the resolution instant to the minute, but the engine resolves at future slot times — so it never hits and thrashes

**backend/policy_rules.py:315** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-scale`

`key = (str(tenant_id or ""), str(product_id or ""), instant.replace(second=0, microsecond=0).isoformat())` (policy_rules.py:312-316), justified at 438-440 by 'The keys are minute-stamped, so the working set is small'. But engine._generate passes the *planned slot* instant (`at=slot.at or now`, engine.py:534) through policy.veto -> contact_policy.evaluate -> `_rules_for(conn, customer, instant)` (contact_policy.py:76-88, 116). Every account x action yields a different minute. `_cache_put` then wipes the entire cache with `_CACHE.clear()` every 512 inserts (437-441), under a global lock.

**Impact.** ~12M distinct keys a day on a 2M book: the rule-set join (policy_rules.py:336-358) runs once per candidate action instead of once per minute, and the lock is taken and the cache wiped ~23,000 times a day. In the multi-threaded API process the global lock becomes a contention point.

**Fix.** Key on the *validity window* the rule set resolves to, not on the query instant — resolve once and cache under (tenant, product, effective_from, effective_to), so any instant inside the window is a hit. Replace the clear-everything eviction with an LRU.

### `trainer-disables-statement-timeout-on-shared-pool` — The trainer sets statement_timeout = 0 on a connection borrowed from the application's shared engine

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:117** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-scale`

`conn.execute(text("SET statement_timeout = 0"))` (train_treatment_models.py:117), applied to a connection from `db.engine` (1022) — the same QueuePool the API and workers use (db_core.py:169-181, pool_size 5 + overflow 10). The docstring at 113-116 argues it is safe because the setting is session-scoped, which is true, and says nothing about the connection itself being shared capacity.

**Impact.** A training run holds one of a very small number of pooled connections open with no timeout while it scans the whole decision log. Under contention the live call path is starved of connections by an offline job, and there is nothing to kill the runaway query.

**Fix.** Build a separate engine for batch jobs with its own small pool, its own credentials and a generous but finite statement_timeout, and point it at a read replica.

### `interaction-id-not-ownership-checked` — The offer engine reads a transcript and its KB events by a caller-supplied interaction id with no check that the interaction belongs to the customer or the tenant

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:541** · security · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-security-privacy`

reco/features.py:541-549: `SELECT speaker, intent, sentiment_delta, text FROM interaction_transcript WHERE interaction_id = :id ORDER BY turn_index` — bound only on the id. reco/features.py:565-573 does the same against `interactions` for ptp_captured/upsell_presented/primary_intent, and _kb_topics_queried at features.py:663-680 does the same against activity_events (`WHERE entity_type = 'interaction' AND entity_id = :id`). reco/engine.py:163-169 passes interaction_id straight through from the caller with no validation, and reco/engine.py:225-233 then writes the resulting signals into offer_decisions.features['call'] and offer_decisions.interaction_id. Compare db_treatment_holds.py:302-305, where the treatment route asserts tenant ownership of both customer_id and account_id before running the engine.

**Impact.** Any path that lets a caller choose the interaction id — the voice session extra, a sandbox scenario, a future API — mixes one borrower's conversation signals into another borrower's offer decision, and persists them in the second borrower's decision row. The row then trains the model. In a multi-tenant deployment it crosses the tenant boundary as well, because interaction ids are opaque and enumerable. The consequence is not just a wrong offer: it is one borrower's sentiment, intents and hardship flag written into another borrower's permanent record.

**Fix.** Resolve the interaction once with an ownership join — `SELECT id FROM interactions WHERE id = :iid AND customer_id = :cid` — and drop the call signals (falling back to CallSignals(channel=channel)) when it does not match, logging the mismatch. Do the same in treatment's feature builder for its interaction_id parameter.

### `decision-features-are-a-retained-profile-with-sensitive-inferences` — The PII-minimised feature snapshot is still an identified profile containing inferred income timing and hardship/bereavement state, retained indefinitely for a purpose the borrower was not told about

**backend/agent_core/treatment/features.py:323** · privacy · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-security-privacy`

features.py:323-328 claims the log "must not become a second copy of the customer record" and delivers on the direct identifiers. But the same dict carries `"salaryCreditDay": self.salary_credit_day` and `"salaryTimingGapDays": self.salary_timing_gap_days` (features.py:358-359) — inferred income timing; `"holds": list(self.holds)` (features.py:383), whose values come from HOLD_KINDS = ("hardship", "dispute", "complaint", "bereavement", "legal") (db_treatment_holds.py:38); `"mandateLastReturnReason"` (features.py:356) — a bank return code; `"riskScore"`, `"exposure"`, `"outstanding"`. Every row is keyed by customer_id and account_id (features.py:332, and the customer_id column itself). reco carries the parallel `hardshipMentioned` (reco/features.py:196) and `disputeOpened`. features.py:325 states the retention purpose plainly: "The log is retained for training and for the regulator".

**Impact.** This is a profile under any reading, and it is retained for model training — a purpose distinct from the servicing purpose the data was collected for, and one no borrower notice in an Indian lending flow currently describes. The inference that a named borrower is in hardship or bereavement, derived from what they said on a call and stored as a durable feature, is the single most sensitive artefact the platform produces. The engineering is right and the governance around it is absent: no purpose field, no notice text, no DPIA, no retention clock.

**Fix.** Treat this as a documentation-and-governance deliverable shipped with the code, not as a code change: a model card per artifact listing every feature and its derivation, a DPIA covering the training purpose, and notice language the client bank can adopt. In code, add the `purpose` column (see no-retention-no-partial-erasure) and consider dropping the hold *kind* from the feature vector in favour of a single hasHold boolean plus a permits-statutory-notice flag — the scorer's use of it (policy vetoes) does not need to know whether the reason was bereavement.

### `llm-rerank-exports-borrower-context-with-no-processor-controls` — When the rerankers are enabled, borrower financial context leaves the bank for Azure OpenAI with no per-tenant gate, no consent basis recorded, and an operator-controlled string reaching the prompt

**backend/agent_core/treatment/rerank.py:130** · privacy · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-security-privacy`

rerank.py:130-143 sends `Account context: {json.dumps(context)}` — bucket, dpd, promises kept/broken, touches today, open disputes — plus expectedValueInr and chanceOfReaching per action (rerank.py:104-115) to azure_openai.chat_complete (rerank.py:146-152). reco/models.py:452-462 sends product names, reason codes and suggested amounts along with the caller's intents. Both are off by default (config.py:79-80 `env_bool("TREATMENT_LLM_RERANK", False)`; reco/models.py:544-545 `env_bool("RECO_LLM_RERANK")`), and neither has a per-tenant flag, a consent check, or a record on the decision row beyond the recommender name. reco/models.py:445 puts `"productName": o.name` — a value an operator edits in the products table — into the prompt payload.

**Impact.** The stated target is on-premise inside a bank. A flag flip sends per-borrower delinquency data to a hosted US-region service, which is a cross-border transfer decision (DPDP s.16) and an RBI outsourcing decision that belongs to the bank's board, not to an environment variable. There is no data-processor record, no DPIA hook, and no way for the DPO to enumerate which decisions were LLM-assisted beyond parsing the recommender string. Separately, products.name reaching the prompt is a second-order injection channel — mitigated for ranking by the id allowlist (reco/models.py:480-486), not mitigated for the free-text `why` on the treatment side, where _safe_why (rerank.py:175-193) checks invented digits but not injected instructions.

**Fix.** Gate both rerankers on a per-tenant configuration row rather than a process env var, and refuse to enable when the tenant's deployment profile is on-prem. Add a boolean column (or a candidates-JSONB field) recording that an external model saw this decision, so the DPO can enumerate them. Sanitise products.name into the prompt (strip control characters and JSON delimiters, cap length), and extend _safe_why to reject a rationale containing imperative-sounding directives, not only invented figures.

### `decision-tables-outside-the-by-id-tenant-guard-allowlist` — treatment_decisions and offer_decisions are absent from the by-id tenant-ownership allowlist, so no guard exists for the code paths that address a decision by id

**backend/db_core.py:239** · security · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-security-privacy`

db_core.py:239-256 `_CUSTOMER_SCOPED_TABLES` lists accounts, callbacks, consent_records, conversations, disputes, document_requests, interactions, leads, payment_plans, promises, treatment_holds and authority_decisions. Neither decision table is in it, so `_assert_tenant_owns(conn, "treatment_decisions", id)` cannot be called. The by-id paths that consequently run unguarded: decisions.py:389-404 claim_by_id, clerk.py:119-131 _defer_hitl_plan (`UPDATE treatment_decisions SET scheduled_at = ... WHERE id = :id`), clerk.py:168-171 (`SELECT enacted, enacted_ref FROM treatment_decisions WHERE id = :id`), db_workspace.py:373-379 (`WHERE trigger_ref = ANY(:ids)`), and decisions.mark_enacted/record_outcome, which UPDATE by id alone. db_core.py:290-299 explains why by-id leaks are the worse kind: "the by-id paths leak one record at a time, to a caller who supplies the id — which is the worse of the two, because it is the shape someone probes deliberately".

**Impact.** No externally reachable exploit today: clerk jobs are enqueued only from payment_events and promise_fulfillment, never from a route. But the guard the codebase built for exactly this shape has a hole where its newest and most sensitive tables should be, so the next route that takes a decisionId — a supervisor approve/override screen is the obvious one — ships without it and nothing fails.

**Fix.** Add treatment_decisions and offer_decisions to _CUSTOMER_SCOPED_TABLES (both carry customer_id, so the existing join works unchanged) and call _assert_tenant_owns from every by-id path, starting with clerk._defer_hitl_plan and decisions.claim_by_id. Extend tests/test_object_visibility.py to cover them.

### `arm-probability-is-a-marginal-design-share-not-a-conditional-probability` — config.arm_probability returns the configured split share as pi(arm | x), but assign_variant makes the arm a deterministic function of the customer, so there is no overlap between arms within any borrower

**backend/agent_core/treatment/config.py:480** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

config.py:480-495 `arm_probability` returns the share from `ab_split()`. config.py:498-523 `assign_variant` hashes the customer id with blake2b and buckets deterministically -- the docstring at :501-506 correctly explains why. explore.py:96-108 then multiplies that share into the logged propensity, documenting it as 'P(this borrower is in this experimental arm)'. Conditional on x (which includes the borrower's features and, through the vector, effectively their identity), that probability is 0 or 1, not 0.8 or 0.2. There is no borrower for whom both arms are possible.

**Impact.** This is fine and standard if the estimand is defined over a randomly drawn customer, and it is the reason the deterministic hash is the right design. It becomes a hidden assumption the moment anything conditions on borrower-level features -- which the uplift T-learner does by construction. Positivity fails at the level the model is fitted at: no stratum defined by borrower covariates contains both arms except by the accident of the hash, and with 20 customers the hash is a single fixed partition. In a bank with segment-level reporting ('what is the effect in the secured book?'), every segment-level causal claim is resting on which side of a hash boundary a handful of customers fell.

**Fix.** State the estimand explicitly in ope.py and metrics.py: this is a population-average effect over borrowers, valid only when the arm partition is exchangeable with respect to outcomes, and it needs enough customers for that to hold. Add a covariate-balance check across arms (standardised mean difference per vector feature) and refuse to publish a causal number when any feature is imbalanced beyond 0.1 SMD -- with 20 customers it will fail, which is the correct answer.

### `outcome-label-depends-on-when-the-worker-got-to-the-row` — Attribution runs 25 rows per worker tick behind five other queues, and because the paid/ptp lookback is unbounded, a row examined late is more likely to be labelled a success than an identical row examined on time

**backend/agent_core/treatment/followthrough.py:81** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

followthrough.py:81 `BATCH = 25`; `process_one` (:502-528) runs `attribute_outcomes(conn)` and returns True the moment it labels anything, so `open_cases` re-decision is starved whenever attribution has a backlog. bot_worker.py:131 places `treatment_followthrough` as one stage of a single-threaded round-robin behind bot_jobs, whatsapp_outbound, promise_reminders, bounce_voice, call_closer, cadence, campaigns and treatment_enact. Because `_paid_since` / `_promised_since` have no upper bound (see previous finding), a row the worker reaches at day 6 has had six days of payment exposure where a row reached at hour 8 has had eight hours.

**Impact.** The label is a function of queue depth. Two decisions with identical features and identical borrower behaviour receive different labels depending on how busy the worker was, and the noise is not random -- it correlates with load, which correlates with book activity, which correlates with delinquency. At 19-42 decisions/day the queue keeps up; at a 50k book with a daily dpd_tick sweep it will not, and the corpus will acquire a systematic positive bias in exactly the periods the book is busiest.

**Fix.** Bound the label window explicitly rather than implicitly: pass an evaluation cut-off (`created_at + OBSERVATION_WINDOW`) into `_paid_since` and `_promised_since` as an upper bound, so the label is a function of the decision's own clock and not the worker's. Separately, give attribution its own worker or a larger batch, and make `process_one` do attribution *and* attempt one re-decision rather than returning early.

### `ips-clipping-bias-and-ess-floor-are-undocumented-planning-figures` — MAX_WEIGHT, MIN_ESS_FRACTION and MAX_UNSUPPORTED_FRACTION are round numbers with no sensitivity analysis, and the bias the clipping introduces is counted but never bounded

**backend/agent_core/treatment/ope.py:62** · statistics · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

ope.py:62 `MAX_WEIGHT = 50.0`, :67 `MIN_ESS_FRACTION = 0.10`, :71 `MAX_UNSUPPORTED_FRACTION = 0.35`. `_weights` counts clipped rows (:202-205) and `Estimate.clipped` is reported (:150), but nothing estimates how much the estimate moved because of it. `trustworthy` (:129-140) turns three arbitrary constants into a boolean that `registry.check` (:242-249) treats as a promotion gate. The docstrings are honest that these are trades made explicitly -- they just are not calibrated to anything.

**Impact.** A bank's model validation function will ask for the sensitivity of the promotion decision to each of these three constants, and the answer is not derivable from the code or the logs. With TREATMENT_GREEDINESS=0.7 on a short candidate list the minimum within-arm propensity is on the order of 0.1-0.2, so MAX_WEIGHT=50 will rarely bind today and will bind hard the moment greediness moves toward 0.9 -- meaning the gate's behaviour changes silently with an env var nobody associates with it.

**Fix.** Report the estimate at two or three clip levels (e.g. 10, 50, unclipped) so the sensitivity is on the same screen as the number, and add the standard self-normalised clipping-bias bound. Derive MIN_ESS_FRACTION from the effect size the gate needs to detect rather than fixing it at 0.10 -- ESS is only meaningful relative to the MDE, which power_control_arm.py already knows how to compute.

### `preprocessing-statistics-fitted-on-the-holdout` — Imputation means and standardisation scales are computed over the whole dataset before the split, so the holdout leaks into the fit

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:509** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

train_treatment_models.py:509 `X, y, means = _design(samples, names)` where `_design` (:345-362) averages over all `samples`; then :510 splits, and :516 `scales = _scales(X, mu)` uses the full X. Only the coefficient fit at :518 is restricted to `train_idx`. The uplift path is the same: :592 `X_t, y_t, means = _design(treated, names)` and :600 `scales = _scales(X_t + X_c, mu)` over everything, before the split at :604.

**Impact.** A mild optimism on top of the much larger split defect above. It matters more in this codebase than usual because mean imputation is load-bearing -- models.py:176-179 fills an absent feature with the training mean rather than zero on purpose, and several vector fields are frequently None (`ptp_keep_rate`, `risk_score`, `salary_timing_gap_days`, `days_overdue`, `connect_rate_channel`). A holdout row whose feature is absent is imputed with a mean that saw that row's own value.

**Fix.** Compute `means` and `scales` from the training indices only, and pass them into the holdout transform. It is a five-line change: split first, then `_design` over the training slice, then apply the resulting means/scales to the test slice.

### `reco-presented-and-response-escape-the-caller-transaction` — mark_presented and record_response open their own engine transaction instead of the caller's connection, so an offer can be recorded as pitched after the surrounding interaction rolls back

**backend/agent_core/reco/decisions.py:114** · reliability · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `L-time`

`with db.engine.begin() as conn: conn.execute(text("UPDATE offer_decisions SET presented = true, presented_at = now() WHERE id = :id AND presented IS FALSE"), {'id': decision_id})` (reco/decisions.py:113-121), and the same pattern in `record_response` at :135-143. Neither function accepts a `conn` parameter. This contradicts the discipline `recommend` states for the very rows they update: '``conn`` is required. The decision-log row is written on it, so a caller that rolls back does not leave an offer asserting a pitch that did not happen' (reco/engine.py:103-105). The treatment engine's equivalent takes the caller's connection — `record_outcome(decision_id, outcome, *, conn: Any | None = None)` with `with _writer(conn) as active` (agent_core/treatment/decisions.py:328-348).

**Impact.** The offer row is written on the caller's transaction and the presentation flag is written on a different one, so the two can disagree. A call whose enclosing transaction rolls back — a constraint failure later in the turn, a dropped session — leaves `presented = true, presented_at = now()` on a decision whose surrounding interaction never committed. Those are exactly the rows `_offer_history` reads to compute `offers_30d` and `last_offer_at` (reco/features.py:440-446), so a phantom presentation consumes the borrower's cross-sell frequency budget and, through the declined/family cooldowns, suppresses real offers. It also opens a connection per call on the audio path of a live conversation.

**Fix.** Give both functions the same `conn: Any | None = None` parameter and `_writer`-style helper the treatment engine uses, and pass the caller's connection from every call site. Where a caller genuinely has no transaction, let it open one explicitly rather than having the leaf function do it silently.

### `reco-presented-uses-created-at` — Offer frequency is counted from decision-creation time, not from when the offer was actually presented

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:441** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`if r.get('presented'): at = r.get('created_at')` (reco/features.py:440-441) — the row's `presented` flag is read but its `presented_at` column is not. `offer_decisions.presented_at` is written by `mark_presented`: `UPDATE offer_decisions SET presented = true, presented_at = now()` (reco/decisions.py:117).

**Impact.** `offers_30d` and `last_offer_at` are the inputs to the cross-sell frequency cap and to the cooldowns above. Measuring them from decision time rather than presentation time understates the recency of an offer that sat in a queue, so a customer can be pitched again inside the intended cooldown. Small today (16 rows) and structurally wrong at volume, where the gap between decision and presentation is a queue depth rather than milliseconds.

**Fix.** Select and use `presented_at`, falling back to `created_at` only where it is NULL for rows written before the column existed. While there, replace the mixed app-clock `cutoff` (line 416) with a SQL-side `count(*) FILTER (WHERE presented_at > now() - interval '30 days')` so one clock decides.

### `db-now-mixed-with-app-now` — Four decision-critical predicates use Postgres now() while the rest of the pipeline uses the injected app clock, mixing two clocks inside one decision

**backend/agent_core/treatment/policy.py:587** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`AND occurred_at >= now() - CAST(:window AS interval)` (policy.py:587, the ladder-memory window) and `AND enacted_at >= now() - CAST(:window AS interval)` (policy.py:598) inside `last_rung_used`, which is called from engine._decide with `within=LADDER_MEMORY` but never with `now` (engine.py:291-293). Also `starts_at <= now() AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > now())` in features._holds (features.py:1176-1177), in policy.suppresses_upsell (policy.py:519-520) and in enact._open_pay_url (enact.py:211).

**Impact.** Two clocks. In a container fleet, app and DB clock skew of even a few seconds silently moves the boundary of a 30-day ladder window; in a replay or backfill the skew is months. The concrete correctness bug is the ladder: `last_rung_used` decides whether the engine may escalate to a field visit, and it answers 'has this borrower been called in the last 30 days' against the DB's now rather than the decision's — so a replayed March decision sees August's contact history and refuses to escalate, or escalates on evidence that did not exist. For a bank running a parallel-run before go-live, the parallel-run's numbers are not the numbers the engine would have produced.

**Fix.** Bind the instant: pass `now` to `last_rung_used`, `suppresses_upsell` and `_holds`, and change the predicates to `>= :now - CAST(:window AS interval)` / `starts_at <= :at AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > :at)`. Postgres `now()` should appear only where the row's own write time is being stamped (decisions.py:296, 343), never where a decision's inputs are being filtered.

### `sweep-cursor-not-day-scoped` — The resume cursor is not scoped to the local day, so a midnight rollover mid-scan leaves the earlier half of the book undecided until the cursor happens to wrap

**backend/agent_core/treatment/sweep.py:99** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

The cursor is a bare account id, `_write_cursor(conn, tenant, accounts[-1]['id'])` (sweep.py:106), reset only when a batch returns empty: `if cursor: _write_cursor(conn, tenant, '')` (sweep.py:99-100). `_local_day` is recomputed per account at the moment it is processed (sweep.py:169-172), so a batch spanning midnight writes some rows under yesterday's date and some under today's.

**Impact.** At 23:50 IST the cursor sits at account id 'ACC-500000'. At 00:05 the local day rolls over: every account below that id is now undecided for the new day, but `_claim`'s `a.id > COALESCE(:after,'')` will not revisit them until the scan reaches the tail. On a book large enough that a full pass takes longer than a day — which is precisely the two-million-account case sweep.py:24-28 says the cursor exists for — the first half of the book is never decided again. The failure is silent: `process_one` reports work done and the daily-coverage metric counts only accounts that were reached.

**Fix.** Store the local day alongside the cursor in the same work_runtime_jobs payload and reset the cursor to '' whenever the stored day differs from the current one. Better, key the sweep on a per-tenant business date computed once at the start of the pass rather than per account, so one pass has one definition of 'today' regardless of how long it takes.

### `statutory-window-not-applied-to-non-voice` — Absent a published rule set, the statutory window bounds voice only; SMS, WhatsApp and email fall back to the 09:00-20:00 borrower default and are permitted for the hour past the statutory cut-off

**backend/contact_policy.py:494** · compliance · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `L-time`

`window = rules.calling_window(channel) if rules is not None else None; if window is None and channel == 'voice': window = (RBI_VOICE_START, RBI_VOICE_END); if window is not None: start_h, end_h = window; if now_local.hour < start_h or now_local.hour >= end_h: return REASON_HOURS` (contact_policy.py:494-500) with `RBI_VOICE_START = 8` and `RBI_VOICE_END = 19` (:70-71). For a non-voice channel with no published rule the statutory branch is skipped entirely, and the only remaining bound is the borrower default: `hours = _preferred_hours(customer) or contact_window.window_hours(None)` (:517), i.e. `DEFAULT_START_HOUR = 9, DEFAULT_END_HOUR = 20` (contact_window.py:32-33). The comment at :491-516 is explicit that this default 'is deliberately the borrower-preference default (09:00-20:00) rather than the statutory voice window'. The gap is one hour, 19:00-20:00. The breach auditor cannot see it either — metrics.py:354 filters `AND ce.channel = 'voice'`.

**Impact.** On a fresh install, or any tenant that has not published a rule set into the regulatory-rules table (the fallback path the constants at :67-69 exist for), a dunning WhatsApp or SMS at 19:30 IST is admitted, logged as `allowed`, and counted as compliant. RBI DOR.MCS.REC.No.199 is written about communication with borrowers, not about voice alone, so a digital dunning message after the cut-off is the same conduct finding as a call — and it is the channel a collections floor sends the most of. Because the auditor is voice-only, the breach rate reported to compliance stays zero while it happens.

**Fix.** Apply the statutory fallback to every outreach channel, not just voice: drop the `and channel == 'voice'` condition and let `rules.calling_window(channel)` override per channel where a tenant has published one. Keep the 09:00-20:00 borrower default as the separate, tighter preference check it already is. Extend metrics._breaches to every channel at the same time, or the fix is unverifiable.

### `naive-scheduled-at-read-as-utc` — A naive scheduled_at string is coerced to UTC before the IST hour is read, so an IST wall-clock slot is judged five and a half hours early

**backend/contact_window.py:69** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`at = datetime.fromisoformat(scheduled_at); if at.tzinfo is None: at = at.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc); hour = at.astimezone(IST).hour` (contact_window.py:65-70). Reached from `db._callback_dnd_active(customer_dnd, dnd_registry, preferred_window, scheduled_at)` (db.py:1605-1613) and from the code-mode script `outside_preferred_window(date, str(window))` (agent_core/skills/scripts.py:40), both of which receive an operator- or model-supplied string.

**Impact.** A UI or an LLM tool call that emits `2026-09-06T09:30` (no offset) — the natural rendering of an IST wall-clock slot — is read as 09:30 UTC, i.e. 15:00 IST. A callback the agent booked for 09:30 IST is judged against 15:00, so a 09:00-13:00 window is falsely reported as out-of-window and a 14:00-18:00 window is falsely reported as in-window. tests/test_contact_window_shared.py:95 pins the coercion as intended behaviour, so the drift is locked in.

**Fix.** Treat a naive timestamp as IST (or as the resolved customer zone once finding 1 and 3 are fixed) rather than UTC — the column is written in local wall time by the UI, and the module's own docstring says 'Windows in this product are written in IST'. Better, reject naive input from the API boundary and require an offset; a silent default here is a five-and-a-half-hour error with no error message.

### `preferred-window-two-timezones` — The same preferred_window column is judged in fixed IST by one half of the system and in the borrower's own zone by the other

**backend/contact_window.py:70** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`hour = at.astimezone(IST).hour` where `IST = timezone(timedelta(hours=5, minutes=30))` (contact_window.py:29, 70), reached from db._outside_preferred_window (db.py:1588), db._callback_dnd_active (db.py:1612), db_inbox.py:214, followups_db.py:1603 and agent_core/skills/scripts.py:40. The treatment gate reads the same column through `_preferred_hours` and compares against `now_local.hour` where `local = instant.astimezone(_zone(customer['timezone']))` (contact_policy.py:517-520, 553-554).

**Impact.** This is precisely the bug contact_window.py exists to close — its docstring opens 'the rule was copied there instead of shared, and the copy drifted' and 'the same date, two verdicts, decided by which copy happened to run' — reintroduced along the timezone axis instead of the bounds axis. For any borrower whose zone is not IST, the callback board shows a slot as in-window while contact_policy.admit refuses to dial it, or vice versa. An agent books a callback the dialler will not make and nobody finds out until the borrower complains that they were promised a call that never came.

**Fix.** Change `outside_preferred_window` to take the resolved zone (or the customer row) rather than assuming IST, and route every caller through one helper that takes `customer_id` and does the lookup. If the window strings really are always IST wall-clock regardless of borrower location, then contact_policy._veto is the side that is wrong and must compare in IST too — but pick one and delete the other. Add a test that asserts the two paths agree for a customer whose timezone is not Asia/Kolkata; there is no such test today (tests/test_contact_window_shared.py only exercises IST).

### `promise-fulfillment-hardcodes-ist` — The whole promise lifecycle — due date, break date, reminder hour, link expiry — is hard-coded to IST while the treatment engine uses the borrower's own zone

**backend/promise_fulfillment.py:29** · compliance · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`IST = ZoneInfo('Asia/Kolkata')` (promise_fulfillment.py:29), then `_promised_date_ist` (115-118), `_intent_expiry` (121-129), `_due_reminder_at` returning `datetime(day.year, day.month, day.day, 8, 15, tzinfo=IST)` (132-134), `today = datetime.now(timezone.utc).astimezone(IST).date()` (369), and in SQL `(promised_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date = (now() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date` (877-878) and `< (now() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date` (900-901). `customers.timezone` is never consulted anywhere in the file.

**Impact.** For a Gulf or US-resident borrower the PTP is judged broken on the Indian calendar — a promise for 'the 6th' is auto-broken at 18:30 on the 5th their time, before their day has ended, and the broken-PTP trigger fires a treatment decision against a borrower who has not yet defaulted. The 08:15 IST due reminder lands at 22:45 the previous evening in New York, outside both the statutory window and any consent window. Both are conduct issues a DPO and the grievance officer will see as harassment. The assumption is true for today's seeded book and false the moment a real NRI portfolio is loaded, which for most Indian NBFCs is a meaningful slice of the gold-loan and home-loan book.

**Fix.** Take the zone from `customers.timezone` via `contact_policy._zone` / `safe_tz_sql` (the SQL helper is already written and handles the dirty label form). Replace the literal `'Asia/Kolkata'` in both settle_promises statements with `SQL_SAFE_TZ` bound per row, and pass the resolved zone into `_promised_date_ist`, `_due_reminder_at` and `_intent_expiry`. Keep IST only as the fallback constant.

### `broken-ptp-trigger-age-always-zero` — The broken-PTP trigger is stamped with the moment the sweeper noticed, not the moment the promise fell due, so trigger age is structurally zero

**backend/promise_fulfillment.py:837** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`trigger=Trigger(kind='broken_ptp', at=datetime.now(timezone.utc), ref=promise['id'])` (promise_fulfillment.py:837), inside the loop that has just discovered the promise's IST day is already past (lines 893-910). `Trigger`'s own docstring says '``at`` is when the *event* happened, not when we got round to it. The gap between the two is the delay this whole product exists to close, so the scorer reads it directly' (features.py:128-130).

**Impact.** `Trigger.age_hours` (features.py:143-147) is logged on every decision as `ageHours` and read by the scorer's urgency term. For `broken_ptp` it is always ~0, so the engine cannot distinguish a promise broken an hour ago from one broken while the settle worker was down for two days, and it never learns that a stale broken promise is worth escalating. The feature is present, populated, and carries no information for this trigger — worse than absent, because the model will fit noise to it.

**Fix.** Stamp `at` with the end of the promised day in the borrower's zone (the instant the promise actually broke), which `settle_promises` already computes to select the row. Audit the other trigger sites for the same pattern — `sweep._decide_account` (sweep.py:180) passes the sweep instant, which is correct for `dpd_tick`, and `followthrough.advance` passes the original `created_at` (followthrough.py:441), which is correct.

### `uplift-control-half-sees-holdout` — The T-learner's control half is fitted on all control rows including the holdout, so tau is evaluated on data one of its halves trained on

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:606** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`t_idx, t_test = _split(len(X_t), holdout, seed)` then `zw_t, zb_t = fit_logistic([Z_t[i] for i in t_idx], ...)` (lines 603-604) — but the very next line is `zw_c, zb_c = fit_logistic(Z_c, y_c, seed=seed + 1)` (line 606), with no split applied to the control arm at all. `control_rate = sum(y_c) / len(y_c)` (line ~617) is likewise the full-sample rate.

**Impact.** tau = p_treated - p_control is the quantity the engine would allocate on. Its control half has memorised every control row, including the ones used to report `holdoutAuc`. Any lift the segment ladder reports for a fine-grained segment is partly the control model recalling that segment's own rows. On a corpus with controlN=3668 simulated rows this already inflates the ladder's verdicts; on a real book of 97 control rows it would be pure memorisation. Compare with train_segment_uplift at lines 802-803, which correctly splits both arms — so the codebase already knows how, and train_uplift is the outlier.

**Fix.** Apply `_split` to the control arm too, with its own seed, and fit `w_c, b_c` on `c_train_idx` only. Report holdout AUC and the ATE on the held-out portion of both arms. Add an assertion that no index appears in both a fit set and an evaluation set for either half.

### `day-counter-no-zone-provenance` — contact_day_counters records a local_date with no record of which timezone produced it, and no tenant scope

**backend/sql/03_consent.sql:79** · data-model · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS contact_day_counters (customer_id ..., local_date DATE NOT NULL, ..., PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, local_date))` (sql/03_consent.sql:79-83; alembic/versions/20260813_0066_contact_events.py:116-125). The date is computed in Python as `local.date()` from `_zone(customer.get('timezone'))` at reserve time (contact_policy.py:917, 973) and read back in SQL with a different zone resolution in ledger_usage (contact_policy.py:1056-1060).

**Impact.** The daily contact cap is enforced against a row whose meaning depends on a mutable column. Edit `customers.timezone`, or re-run the seed (which contact_policy.py:172 warns 'a re-seed puts them back'), and the resolved zone changes; the borrower's 'today' shifts by up to a day and the daily cap silently re-arms mid-day, permitting a second full quota of contacts. Because the cap is the enforcement mechanism for the harassment limit, that is a compliance event caused by a data edit with no audit link between the two. The missing tenant_id also means the PK cannot be reasoned about in a shared-schema multi-tenant deployment.

**Fix.** Add `tz_name TEXT NOT NULL` and `tenant_id` to the table and include tz in the reserve/read predicates, or compute local_date in SQL only (via SQL_SAFE_TZ) so there is exactly one resolution. Either way, changing a customer's timezone should be an explicit operation that reconciles or archives the affected counter rows rather than silently reinterpreting them.

### `migration-0051-runs-unbatched-full-table-updates` — 0051 backfills closed_at with two unbatched full-table UPDATEs joined against the entire activity_events audit trail, inside the migration transaction

**backend/alembic/versions/20260731_0051_upsell_nbo_engine.py:53** · reliability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

`UPDATE leads l SET closed_at = e.at FROM (SELECT entity_id, MAX(at) AS at FROM activity_events WHERE entity_type = 'lead' AND kind IN ('lead_updated', 'lead_created') GROUP BY entity_id) e WHERE ...` (0051:53-67), then `UPDATE leads SET closed_at = captured_at WHERE stage IN ('won','lost') AND closed_at IS NULL ...` (0051:71-74). No batching, no LIMIT, no progress, and the whole migration is one transaction.

**Impact.** activity_events is the audit trail — the largest table in the schema — and this aggregates all of it with no index guarantee, then updates every closed lead, holding row locks on leads for the duration. On a bank's data that is a deployment window that either runs for an unbounded time or hits the DBA's statement timeout and rolls the whole migration back, taking the schema changes with it. Separately the backfill's semantics are approximate by admission (0051:68-70) but nothing marks the approximated rows, so 'average time to close' is silently wrong for history with no way to tell which rows are estimates.

**Fix.** Move backfills out of the schema migration into a separate, resumable data migration that updates in batches of N by primary key with a cursor, committing between batches. Add a boolean `closed_at_estimated` column so the approximate rows are identifiable in the aggregates.

### `set-null-fks-rewrite-an-append-only-log` — ON DELETE SET NULL on the columns that say what was offered and to which account silently rewrites decisions that the same migrations call append-only

**backend/alembic/versions/20260731_0051_upsell_nbo_engine.py:236** · data-model · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

offer_decisions: `chosen_product_id ... sa.ForeignKey("products.id", ondelete="SET NULL")` (0051:233-238) and `lead_id ... ondelete="SET NULL"` (0051:247-249). treatment_decisions: `account_id ... ondelete="SET NULL"` (0069:182) and interaction_id likewise (:183-185). mandate_presentations.decision_id is ON DELETE SET NULL too (0085:235), which 0085:32-37 calls 'the load-bearing column'.

**Impact.** Retiring a product from the catalog silently blanks chosen_product_id on every historical offer decision, so the log can no longer say what was offered. Closing an account blanks account_id on its treatment decisions. Deleting a treatment decision (which the customer CASCADE above can do) orphans the mandate presentation that was its only proof of attribution — the exact edge 0085:32-37 says makes represent_mandate unevaluable. None of this raises, warns or leaves a trace.

**Fix.** Denormalise the identity onto the log row: store chosen_product_code / product_name and account_number_last4 as plain text alongside the FK, so the decision remains readable when the referent is gone. Change ON DELETE SET NULL to RESTRICT for chosen_product_id and mandate_presentations.decision_id, and soft-delete products via is_active (which already exists, 0051:89-92) rather than deleting them.

### `hold-reason-is-sensitive-free-text-shown-to-every-reader` — treatment_holds.reason carries hardship, bereavement and legal narrative in plaintext, is returned to every COLLECTIONS_READ actor unfiltered, and is copied a second time into activity_events

**backend/alembic/versions/20260814_0069_treatment_engine.py:50** · privacy · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

`sa.Column("reason", sa.Text(), nullable=True)` (0069:50) beside kind IN ('hardship','dispute','complaint','bereavement','legal') (0069:87-90). GET /treatment/holds has no kind filter and no redaction (main.py:4827-4836), and list_treatment_holds returns `"reason": r["reason"]` to any COLLECTIONS_READ holder (db_treatment_holds.py:60-120, authz.py:447). create_treatment_hold then writes the same free text into the activity feed: `record_activity(conn, "customer", ..., "hold_placed", ..., payload.get("reason"), ...)` (db_treatment_holds.py:199-207), and release does the same (:236-244).
