**Impact.** A bereavement hold's reason field will contain a death; a hardship hold's will contain a job loss or an illness; a legal hold's will name a proceeding. That is sensitive personal data under DPDP, visible to every collections agent on the floor rather than to the specialist the schema already models (specialist_user_id, 0069:54). Copying it into activity_events duplicates it into a table with its own separate retention and its own export paths, so an erasure or a redaction applied to holds does not reach the copy.

**Fix.** Restrict reason on the list endpoint to the placing user, the named specialist and a supervisor permission; return a redacted marker to everyone else. Record only the hold kind in activity_events, not the free text. Run the reason column through the existing PII redaction inventory, and consider structuring it (a closed sub-reason vocabulary plus an optional specialist-only note).

### `mandate-pii-added-under-a-deferred-encryption-control` — 0085 introduces bank account identifiers (UMRN, bank name, account last4) in plaintext while PII column encryption is an explicitly deferred control

**backend/alembic/versions/20260820_0085_decision_intelligence_p0.py:180** · privacy · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

`umrn TEXT` (0085:167), `bank_name TEXT`, `account_last4 TEXT` (0085:180-181), all plaintext, plus mandate_presentations.return_code / return_reason which record why a borrower's account could not be debited ('insufficient_funds', 0085:226-228). main.py:420-424 lists `"PII column encryption / Vault secret refs"` among _DEFERRED_HARDENING_CONTROLS and refuses to boot in prod without ALLOW_UNHARDENED_PRODUCTION.

**Impact.** A UMRN plus bank name plus account last4 is a financial identifier triple, and 'insufficient funds on the 5th of every month' is a direct inference about a borrower's finances. Under DPDP these are personal data requiring purpose limitation and security safeguards; inside a bank they are also subject to the bank's own data-classification policy, which will not permit them unencrypted at rest in an application schema. The migration adds them without touching the deferred-controls list, so the boot-time gate does not know its scope grew.

**Fix.** Bring these columns into whatever encryption scheme the deferred control lands (pgcrypto column encryption or application-side envelope encryption with a Vault key ref), and until then extend _DEFERRED_HARDENING_CONTROLS to name the mandate columns so the boot refusal message is accurate. Add mandates/mandate_presentations to the redaction inventory.

### `registry-promoted-by-is-unauditable-free-text` — The model-promotion ledger records the promoter as free TEXT with no FK, no approver, and no closed vocabulary on the corpus column that gates simulated models

**backend/alembic/versions/20260821_0089_model_registry.py:66** · compliance · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

`promoted_by TEXT` (0089:66) — no `REFERENCES users(id)`, unlike published_by_user_id on policy_rule_sets (0085:290). `corpus TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'live'` (0089:57) with no CHECK, while the whole simulated-vs-live serving gate hangs on that word (models are gated by TREATMENT_ALLOW_SIMULATED_MODELS and the artifacts all say corpus: simulated). No approved_by / approved_at column, and no CHECK that status='champion' implies promoted_at IS NOT NULL.

**Impact.** The migration's own thesis is 'This is the gate given a memory... "why is this model deciding whether to call people?" is answerable from the database rather than from whoever remembers' (0089:12-17). A free-text promoted_by answers 'who' with an unverified string. A bank's model-risk function (and RBI's model governance expectations) requires an identified approver distinct from the developer — four-eyes on promotion. And a typo in `corpus` ('Live', 'live ', 'simulated_v2') silently changes which side of the simulated-model gate an artifact falls on.

**Fix.** Add `promoted_by_user_id TEXT REFERENCES users(id)`, `approved_by_user_id TEXT REFERENCES users(id)` with a CHECK that they differ, `CHECK (status <> 'champion' OR (promoted_at IS NOT NULL AND approved_by_user_id IS NOT NULL))`, and `CHECK (corpus IN ('live','simulated','mixed'))`. Backfill promoted_by into the new column.

### `registry-is-per-tenant-but-serving-is-one-file` — The champion ledger is keyed (tenant_id, target) while the serving path reads one process-global file per target — one deployment can never serve two tenants' champions

**backend/alembic/versions/20260821_0089_model_registry.py:74** · data-model · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... uq_treatment_model_champion ON treatment_model_registry (tenant_id, target) WHERE status = 'champion'` (0089:72-78) against models.load_reach() reading `_path("TREATMENT_REACH_MODEL_PATH", "models/treatment_reach.json")` (agent_core/treatment/models.py:606-608), with load_timing and load_uplift the same (:613, :628). registry.verify(conn, tenant_id=...) compares the on-disk sha to that one tenant's champion (registry.py:399-441).

**Impact.** The whole registry design argument (0089:26-30) is that the ledger must not be able to hold a state the serving path cannot express. In the tenant dimension it does exactly that: promote a challenger for tenant B and tenant A's borrowers are now scored by B's model, or the promotion writes a ledger row that serving never honours — and registry.verify will report a sha mismatch for whichever tenant lost, with no way to resolve it. This is a hidden assumption that one deployment equals one tenant, which is true on this dev book and false for a bank running multiple entities.

**Fix.** Either make serving tenant-aware (artifact path keyed by tenant, e.g. models/{tenant}/treatment_reach.json, with a per-tenant cache) and keep the per-tenant champion index, or drop tenant_id from the champion uniqueness and state explicitly in the migration and the deployment docs that one process serves one tenant. Do not leave the two disagreeing.

### `model-registry-version-string-is-not-an-identity` — Two different artifacts may register under the same version string, so the version logged on a decision does not identify the coefficients that decided it

**backend/alembic/versions/20260821_0089_model_registry.py:80** · compliance · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS uq_treatment_model_version ON treatment_model_registry (tenant_id, target, version, artifact_sha)` (20260821_0089:80-83) — uniqueness is on the four-tuple including the sha, so (tenant, 'uplift', 'v3', shaA) and (tenant, 'uplift', 'v3', shaB) are both accepted. treatment_decisions records recommender_version as a bare TEXT column (20260814_0069:140) and registry.verify reports `record["version"]` alongside a sha comparison (registry.py:425-443), but nothing forbids the collision in the first place.

**Impact.** The migration's stated purpose is that 'why is this model deciding whether to call people?' be answerable from the database (0089:12-17). With version strings non-unique per target, a decision row naming version 'v3' cannot be resolved to one set of coefficients without also knowing which registry row was champion at that instant — and the registry does not record the interval over which a row was champion (promoted_at exists, retired_at exists, but nothing links a decision to the row in force). A model-risk committee reconstructing a past decision has to guess.

**Fix.** Make the version unique per (tenant_id, target) and keep artifact_sha as the integrity check rather than part of the key; or stamp the registry row id (not the version string) onto treatment_decisions so the join is exact. Add a CHECK that a champion has promoted_at, and record the champion interval so 'which model decided this row' is a lookup rather than an inference.

### `treatment-cases-uses-offset-pagination-over-a-correlated-scan` — /treatment/cases groups the whole decision log, filters with an untenanted correlated NOT EXISTS, then pages with LIMIT/OFFSET

**backend/db_treatment_holds.py:368** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

The open_only predicate is `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM treatment_decisions r WHERE r.customer_id = td.customer_id AND r.trigger_kind = td.trigger_kind AND r.trigger_ref = td.trigger_ref AND r.outcome IN ('paid','ptp'))` (db_treatment_holds.py:368-373) — evaluated per candidate group, with no tenant predicate and no index on (customer_id, trigger_kind, trigger_ref, outcome). The outer query GROUP BYs five columns over the join and then applies `LIMIT :limit OFFSET :offset` (:405).

**Impact.** Deep pagination re-aggregates the whole corpus for every page, and the correlated subquery has no supporting index, so the floor lead's most-used screen is the slowest query in the system and gets slower every day. Under the API's 15s statement timeout it will start returning 500s at a book size the demo never reaches.

**Fix.** Materialise the case view (a table or matview keyed on (tenant_id, customer_id, account_id, trigger_kind, trigger_ref) maintained on decision write), or at minimum add a supporting index on (customer_id, trigger_kind, trigger_ref) INCLUDE (outcome), scope the subquery by tenant, and switch to keyset pagination on (last_decided_at, customer_id) instead of OFFSET.

### `no-route-records-an-offer-response` — The offer engine has columns for presented / response / responded_at and no API surface that sets them — 16 decisions, 0 responses, and the whole funnel in /offers/health reads zero

**backend/main.py:1101** · integration · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

The only /offers routes are `GET /offers/tuner-suggestions` (main.py:1094-1098) and `GET /offers/health` (main.py:1101-1116). The writers exist but are internal: `mark_presented` (agent_core/reco/decisions.py:107-117), `record_response` (:126-139), `attach_lead` (:148-159). /offers/health then reports `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE presented)`, `FILTER (WHERE response = 'interested')`, `FILTER (WHERE response IS NOT NULL)` (agent_core/reco/observability.py:115-118) over columns nothing on the API path writes.

**Impact.** The offer engine has no label. Every conversion metric on the dashboard is structurally zero, propensity.json cannot be retrained on anything but the simulated 1,335 samples it already has, and an agent or a bot who hears 'yes, tell me more' has no way to say so. Distinct from a bug: this is a missing half of the loop, and it is why the whole reco engine is a recommender that never learns.

**Fix.** Add POST /offers/{decisionId}/response (COLLECTIONS_WRITE) accepting {presented, response, leadId} and wire it to the existing reco/decisions writers; call mark_presented from the voice/WhatsApp path when the offer is actually spoken or sent. Add the route to authz.ROUTE_PERMISSIONS. Until responses exist, have /offers/health report 'no labelled outcomes' rather than a funnel of zeros.

### `get-treatment-next-mutates` — GET /treatment/next writes a decision row, is gated on read permission, and has no idempotency key or rate limit — so retries, prefetch and dashboards inflate the corpus

**backend/main.py:4764** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

`@app.get("/treatment/next")` (main.py:4764) calls `_handle_write(db.next_treatment, ...)` (main.py:4777-4779), which opens `engine.begin()` and runs recommend_treatment, writing a treatment_decisions row (db_treatment_holds.py:302-311). authz maps it to COLLECTIONS_READ with the reasoning at authz.py:438-441. The docstring acknowledges it: 'The decision row is written either way — a supervisor asking "what would you do here?" is exactly the kind of question the shadow corpus should be built from' (main.py:4772-4775).

**Impact.** GET is safe and idempotent by contract, and the intermediaries in a bank's network act on that: a browser prefetch, a corporate proxy retry, a load balancer replaying a timed-out request, or a React screen re-rendering on focus all write extra decision rows. Those rows carry propensities and enter the off-policy corpus, biasing the estimator toward whichever borrowers a supervisor happened to open twice. Combined with the propensity-weighted estimators this is a silent statistical contaminant, not just noise. It is also an unrated write available to every read-only user.

**Fix.** Split the concerns: keep GET /treatment/next as a pure preview that does not log, and add POST /treatment/decisions (COLLECTIONS_WRITE) for the logging call the sweep and the bots make. If the preview must be logged, mark those rows with a distinct trigger_kind ('preview') and exclude them from every estimator, and dedupe on (customer, account, trigger, minute).

### `treatment-routes-have-no-response-model` — None of the eight /treatment/* routes declares a response_model, so the payload shape — including what PII rides in it — is unspecified and unenforced

**backend/main.py:4764** · maintainability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

main.py:4764, 4782, 4792, 4809, 4818, 4827, 4839, 4851, 4860 — every /treatment route returns a bare dict or list with no response_model, in a file where the neighbouring routes do declare one (`response_model=OfferHealthResponse` at main.py:1101, `response_model=DashboardResponse` at :1080). TreatmentHoldCreateRequest / TreatmentHoldReleaseRequest exist for input (schemas.py:3316-3342) but there is no output schema.

**Impact.** Three consequences in a bank. (1) The OpenAPI contract the client team and any integrating LMS build against says 'object'. (2) Nothing bounds what leaves: next_treatment returns result.to_payload() plus the action contract (db_treatment_holds.py:312-332), so any field a future engine change adds to the payload — a feature vector, a rationale quoting the borrower — ships to the browser with no review step. (3) The DPO cannot answer 'what personal data does this endpoint return' from the schema, which is a standard DPDP processing-record question.

**Fix.** Declare response models for all eight routes and make the decision payload an explicit allow-list of fields rather than a passthrough dict. Add a test asserting every route in authz.ROUTE_PERMISSIONS has a response_model, matching the totality property authz already proves for permissions.

### `field-prerequisites-can-be-loosened-by-a-tenant` — policy_rules declares a 'field_prerequisites' kind that _tighten has no branch for, so a client rule set replaces the statutory one instead of intersecting it

**backend/policy_rules.py:280** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

The kind is declared in the CHECK at 0085:326-327 ('field_prerequisites') and as KIND_FIELD_PREREQS at policy_rules.py:67, but _tighten (policy_rules.py:200-280) has branches only for calling_window, daily/weekly/mandate caps, cooling_off, visit_intimation, recording_retention, bucket_actions and mandate_return. field_prerequisites falls to the default `merged = {**current, **incoming}` / `return merged` (policy_rules.py:210, 280) — later layer wins. The module docstring claims the opposite: 'a later layer may only ever make the rule *stricter*. That is enforced per kind rather than asserted' (policy_rules.py:15-23), and 'A client who could widen the statutory window by adding a row would be a client who could delete the regulation, and "we only document that they shouldn'\''t" is not a control.'

**Impact.** Field visits are the most regulated action in the space. RBI DOR.MCS.REC.No.199/01-01-039/2026-27 requires prior intimation of a visit; the schema models that as a policy rule and then lets a tenant-scope row overwrite it. A client rule set publishing `{"requireIntimation": false}` for field_prerequisites is accepted by the CHECK, accepted by the resolver, and silently governs every subsequent field_visit decision — with policy_version on the decision row still naming the statutory set (policy_rules.py:393-394), so the audit trail asserts compliance with a rule that was overridden.

**Fix.** Add an explicit _tighten branch for field_prerequisites (boolean requirements OR together toward stricter, numeric notice periods take the max, allowed-reason lists intersect), and make the default branch REFUSE rather than replace: for any kind with no branch, log and keep `current` (the earlier, statutory layer). Add a test that asserts every value in the 0085:324-329 kind vocabulary has a _tighten branch, so a new kind cannot ship with replace-semantics.

### `policy-tie-break-is-not-implemented-at-any-layer` — The documented 'latest effective_from wins' tie-break is discarded by the Python regrouping — the SQL ORDER BY it lives in never reaches the fold

**backend/policy_rules.py:379** · correctness · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

The resolver's SQL carries the rule as a comment and an ORDER BY: 'Latest effective_from wins within a scope. Overlapping windows are not prevented by a constraint (that would need btree_gist), so the tie-break is stated here and is deterministic' / `ORDER BY s.effective_from ASC, s.version ASC` (policy_rules.py:351-354). The rows are then regrouped into by_set (:365-377) and re-sorted on a completely different key: `sorted(by_set.values(), key=lambda e: (SCOPE_ORDER.index(e["scope"]) ..., e["version"]))` (:379-383), which never reads effective_from. The fold at :389-401 then applies _tighten to every set in that order, and statutory_version is overwritten by the last statutory entry in version order (:393-394) rather than the latest-effective one.

**Impact.** Two statutory sets in force at once do not resolve to the later one as documented; they are intersected, and the version stamped on the decision is whichever has the higher version integer — which need not be the one with the later effective_from. So the one place the code claims to state a deterministic conflict rule states it in dead SQL. When the RBI 2027 window is published alongside the incumbent, the engine silently becomes stricter than either published set and treatment_decisions.policy_version names a set that did not solely govern the call. This is the mechanism behind the overlapping-windows finding, and it means fixing the schema alone (an exclusion constraint) leaves the resolver still not doing what its comment says.

**Fix.** Either implement the stated rule — within a scope, keep only the set with the greatest effective_from (ties broken by version) and fold across scopes only — or delete the claim and document the intersection semantics honestly. Either way, sort by effective_from in the Python key so the SQL ORDER BY is not load-bearing-looking-but-inert, and stamp the resolved rule-set ids on the decision rather than a single integer.

### `hold-datetimes-are-unparsed-strings` — slaDueAt and expiresAt are typed str and passed straight into timestamptz binds, so a malformed value is an unhandled 500 rather than a 400

**backend/schemas.py:3335** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

`slaDueAt: str | None = None` and `expiresAt: str | None = None` (schemas.py:3335-3336) with no validator, forwarded verbatim to the INSERT binds (db_treatment_holds.py:195-196). _handle_write catches KeyError, PermissionError, ValueError and IntegrityError (main.py:819-840); psycopg's DataError for an invalid timestamp is none of those, so it escapes as a 500.

**Impact.** A bot or an integrating LMS sending '2026-09-31' or '15/09/2026' gets an opaque 500 with no indication which field was wrong, and — because the hold was the thing being placed — the borrower is left uncovered while the caller believes it had a server-side failure to retry. It also puts a raw driver exception on the error-tracking path.

**Fix.** Type both as `datetime | None` (pydantic parses and rejects at the edge, returning 422 with the field named) and add the expires_at > starts_at check from the hold-expiry finding. Add DataError/DBAPIError to _handle_write mapped to 400 as a backstop.

### `reco-readme-entry-point-omits-required-conn` — The README's documented entry point omits the required conn keyword, so the only call example in the operator/integrator docs raises TypeError

**backend/agent_core/reco/README.md:41** · integration · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `R01-engine-config`

README.md:38-50 is the module's sole usage example: `result = recommend(customer_id='vikram-rao', interaction_id='IX-123', channel='voice', live=CallSignals(...))`. engine.py:84-94 declares `def recommend(*, customer_id: str, conn: Any, interaction_id: str | None = None, ...)` — conn is keyword-only with no default, and that is a deliberately locked invariant: tests/test_locked_engine_conn.py:90-92 `def test_recommend_requires_conn(): with pytest.raises(TypeError): recommend(customer_id='x')` and test_locked_engine_conn.py:99-108 assert `inspect.signature(fn).parameters['conn'].default is inspect.Parameter.empty` across all four engines. engine.py:103-105 explains why. The README documents the pre-lock signature and was never updated.

**Impact.** The README is what an integrator reads to wire a second channel or a batch/campaign path. Copying its example fails immediately with a TypeError, and the obvious repair — opening a connection inside the helper — is precisely the transaction-ownership bug the lock exists to prevent (engine.py:160-162: 'Opening a second one here is how a rolled-back caller used to leave an offer_decisions row behind'). A doc that teaches the shape the test suite forbids is worse than no example, and this is the same README that carries the 'Guarantees worth not breaking' section a reviewer will cite.

**Fix.** Update README.md:38-50 to show the real call inside `with db.engine.begin() as conn:` with `conn=conn`, and add one line under 'Guarantees worth not breaking' stating that the caller owns the connection and why. Add a doc test that execs the README snippet, or at minimum asserts every parameter in the example is in inspect.signature(recommend) and that no required parameter is missing from it.

### `reco-readme-env-table-incomplete` — The operator-facing config table omits a third of the knobs, including the second-largest penalty weight and every A/B control

**backend/agent_core/reco/README.md:60** · maintainability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

README.md:56-77 promises 'All read from the environment at call time' and then lists 15 variables. Missing: RECO_W_EXIT_INTENT (config.py:114, default 0.15 — larger than credit, sentiment, campaign and fatigue), RECO_FAMILY_COOLDOWN_DAYS (config.py:293), RECO_LOG_VECTORS (config.py:79), RECO_VARIANTS (config.py:189), RECO_AB_SPLIT (config.py:212), RECO_MODEL_MAX_AGE_DAYS (models.py:242), RECO_HYBRID_RULE_WEIGHT (models.py:534), RECO_LLM_RERANK (models.py:544). .env.example:404-429 has the same gaps. The README table also lists RECO_W_FATIGUE without noting it is subtracted after normalisation (config.py:95-96) while the others are averaged.

**Impact.** The README is the artefact the bank's ops team will be handed. An operator tuning from it cannot see the exit-intent penalty that is silently suppressing offers to customers who pulled a no-dues certificate, cannot discover that an A/B mechanism exists at all, and cannot find the switch that stops the propensity model going stale. The gap between documented and actual configuration surface is where production incidents live.

**Fix.** Generate the table from config.py rather than maintaining it by hand — a small module-level registry of (name, default, meaning, bounds) that both weights()/policy() and a doc test read, so a new knob cannot be added without appearing in the README and .env.example.

### `reco-readme-rollout-vs-reality` — The documented rollout has been skipped: the engine is live with 16 decisions, zero responses, and a propensity artifact trained on synthetic data

**backend/agent_core/reco/README.md:87** · maintainability · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

README.md:87-96 prescribes shadow for two weeks watching coverage/score distribution/suppression breakdown, then live capped with guardrails, then 'once ~2-3k labelled leads exist in offer_decisions, train a PropensityScorer'. Reality (established): RECO_MODE=live, offer_decisions has 16 rows and 0 responses ever, and backend/models/propensity.json is 1335 SIMULATED samples. The engine's own default is shadow (config.py:60, .env.example:410) — production overrode it.

**Impact.** The rollout document that a bank's change-advisory board would be shown does not describe what actually happened, and the guardrail metrics it names (complaint rate, AHT, sentiment delta, escalation rate) have no owner, no threshold and no implementation in observability.py. There is also no path to step 3: with 0 responses, the labelled-lead counter is not advancing, and nothing alerts on that.

**Fix.** Either revert to shadow until a holdout and a response-capture path exist, or rewrite the rollout section to state the real position and add the four named guardrail metrics to observability.py with thresholds. Add an alert for 'live for N days with zero responses recorded' — the response loop is the thing the whole engine depends on and it is currently dead.

### `reco-ab-split-silently-renormalises` — RECO_AB_SPLIT drops unknown arms and then renormalises the survivors, turning a typo into 100% control with only a log line

**backend/agent_core/reco/config.py:224** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

config.py:224-238: `if key not in known: logger.warning('RECO_AB_SPLIT names unknown variant %r — dropped', key); continue` ... `total = sum(share for _, share in buckets)` ... `return [(name, share / total) for name, share in buckets]`. So `RECO_AB_SPLIT="control:50,challengr:50"` yields `[('control', 1.0)]`. The warning goes to a logger that, per this deployment, has no handler on the API/voice roots.

**Impact.** The experiment silently does not run. Two weeks later the team reads a report showing 100% control, concludes the challenger 'made no difference', and ships or kills a change on data that never existed. The same mechanism hides a dropped holdout arm, which is the arm the whole 'does the engine help or merely reallocate' question depends on.

**Fix.** Return the parse outcome, not just the buckets: expose `ab_split_health()` with the dropped names, surface it in observability alongside the existing engine alerts (observability.py:419-440), and fail the split closed — if any named arm is unknown, return [] and run pure process defaults rather than a silently reweighted experiment. Also refuse a split whose weights do not sum to ~100 without an explicit opt-in.

### `reco-ab-hash-unsalted` — Bucketing hashes the customer id alone, so the same customers land in the same position in every experiment forever

**backend/agent_core/reco/config.py:258** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

config.py:258 `digest = hashlib.blake2b(customer_id.encode('utf-8'), digest_size=8).digest()` and config.py:259 `position = int.from_bytes(digest, 'big') / float(1 << 64)`. There is no experiment name, salt or epoch in the hash input. The treatment engine's split has the same shape (TREATMENT_AB_SPLIT=control:80,null_treatment:20), so a customer whose position is 0.9 is in the tail of BOTH engines' splits.

**Impact.** Carry-over bias. Every experiment ever run assigns the same low-hash customers to the first-listed arm; a customer who was in the holdout of experiment 1 is in the holdout of experiments 2, 3 and 4, so 'holdout' becomes a permanently under-contacted cohort with a genuinely different balance and delinquency profile, and the estimated uplift picks up that cohort difference. It is also unfair in the collections sense: the same 20% of the book is systematically never offered anything, which the bank's conduct-risk review will ask about. Invisible on a 20-customer book; structural on 200,000.

**Fix.** Hash `f"{experiment_id}:{customer_id}"`, where experiment_id comes from a new RECO_AB_EXPERIMENT (or a hash of the split string itself so it rotates when the split changes). Do the same for the treatment engine, and use a DIFFERENT salt per engine so reco's holdout and treatment's null arm are not the same people.

### `reco-policy-caps-unclamped` — Policy caps and cool-downs accept negative and zero values; RECO_MAX_OFFERS=0 still returns one offer

**backend/agent_core/reco/config.py:283** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

config.py:283-300 reads every field with bare `_env_int` / `_env_float`. `RECO_MAX_PER_CALL=-1` makes `signals.offers_presented_this_call >= policy.max_offers_per_call` true immediately, silently suppressing every offer forever. `RECO_MAX_OFFERS=0` is defeated downstream by `keep[: max(1, policy.max_offers_returned)]` (arbitration.py:115) — the shortlist floor is 1, undocumented in README.md:65. `RECO_DECLINE_COOLDOWN_DAYS=-30` would look backwards into the future. The simulator already relies on the unguarded zero path (`os.environ['RECO_DECLINE_COOLDOWN_DAYS'] = '0'`, simulate_offer_decisions.py:98-99).

**Impact.** The two knobs an operator reaches for in an incident — 'set max offers to zero' and 'set the cool-down long' — behave unexpectedly. Zero is not a kill switch; the kill switch is RECO_MODE=off, and nothing says so at the point of use. A cool-down set negative re-pitches a product the customer refused, which is a conduct issue, not a tuning one.

**Fix.** Clamp in policy(): counts to >= 0, day windows to >= 0, min_score to [0,1], sentiment_floor to [-1,1]; warn on clamp. Make max_offers_returned=0 mean zero (drop the `max(1, ...)` in arbitration.py:115) and document RECO_MODE=off as the kill switch in the README table.

### `reco-no-latency-deadline` — 'Never blocks for long' is a hope: nothing in the engine or the connection enforces a deadline

**backend/agent_core/reco/engine.py:10** · reliability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

engine.py:9-11 states the contract — 'It never blocks for long. Everything is a handful of indexed reads; the caller runs it in a thread so the pipeline is not stalled either way.' The only enforcement is the caller's `asyncio.to_thread` (voice/tools.py:1988), which does not cancel the thread and does not time out. Latency is measured at engine.py:221 and reported, never enforced. `grep -n 'statement_timeout|pool_timeout|connect_args' backend/db.py` returns nothing.

**Impact.** A lock on offer_decisions, a bloated candidates query, or a saturated connection pool turns 'no offer' into 'no turn': the customer hears silence, and the thread stays parked holding a pooled connection, so the next call queues behind it. On a live voice channel this is the failure that reaches the collections head as 'the bot went dead mid-call', and the never-raises design guarantees there is no exception to page on.

**Fix.** Set `statement_timeout` (e.g. 250ms) via connect_args on the engine used for the offer path, wrap _recommend in a deadline that short-circuits to suppressed='deadline_exceeded' after N ms, and have the caller pass a remaining-budget parameter. Emit the deadline breaches as a counter, not just a p99.

### `reco-roi-handed-to-the-model` — to_tool_payload hands the model the product ROI and an indicative amount, then the prompt tells it never to promise rates

**backend/agent_core/reco/engine.py:73** · compliance · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

engine.py:66-81 emits `"suggestedAmount": o.suggested_amount` and `"roi": o.roi` into the model-facing payload, justified as 'Compact, model-facing shape. Scores and feature internals stay out: the model's job is to phrase the offer, not to second-guess the rank' (engine.py:64-65) — scores are withheld, the rate is not. The voice caller then instructs 'mention this ONE product ... with the indicative amount ... Never promise approval, rates or limits' (voice/tools.py:2052-2056). The WhatsApp instruction (bot_tools.py:499-501) omits even that caveat.

**Impact.** An interest rate placed in an LLM's context on a collections call is a rate that will eventually be spoken, and an ROI quoted without the Key Fact Statement / annualised-rate disclosure required for retail credit in India is a mis-selling exposure — on a recorded call, with the recording retained six months under the incoming RBI circular. The control is a negative instruction to a generative model, which is the weakest control in the system, and it contradicts the very field being supplied.

**Fix.** Drop `roi` from to_tool_payload. If the rate must be communicated, do it through the deterministic talk_track (already generated in talk.py and already in the payload) with the mandated disclosure wording, or through a follow-up SMS/KFS link. Add a post-generation guard that blocks a bot turn containing a numeric rate on a product the payload did not authorise.

### `reco-simulated-rows-transit-through-live` — The engine has no 'simulated' mode, so the corpus simulator writes rows as mode='live' and retags them in a second transaction

**backend/agent_core/reco/engine.py:113** · data-model · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

config.py's _MODES is {off, shadow, live} (config.py:28) — there is no MODE_SIMULATED, unlike the treatment engine (scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py:605 passes `force_mode=config.MODE_SIMULATED`). scripts/simulate_offer_decisions.py:178 therefore passes `force_mode='live'` and then, in a separate `db.engine.begin()` block, runs `UPDATE offer_decisions SET mode = :m WHERE id = :id` (simulate_offer_decisions.py:184-191), with the comment 'adding a fake value to it would leak this tool into production config'.

**Impact.** There is a window — and a crash path — in which synthetic decision rows are committed as mode='live'. If the retag transaction fails, the rows stay 'live' permanently and are indistinguishable from real decisions in every downstream report and training query. The simulator also mutates process env (`os.environ['RECO_DECLINE_COOLDOWN_DAYS']='0'`, simulate_offer_decisions.py:98-99), which the never-cached config reads immediately — anything else running in that process is affected.

**Fix.** Add MODE_SIMULATED to _MODES (the DB CHECK already permits 'simulated' after migration 0052) and let the simulator pass it directly, so provenance is written atomically with the row. The 'leaks into production config' worry is addressed by keeping it out of the RECO_MODE env validation path, not by writing the wrong value first.

### `reco-mode-off-arm-logs-nothing` — A variant whose mode is 'off' produces zero decision rows, so an arm configured that way is unanalysable and invisible

**backend/agent_core/reco/engine.py:116** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

engine.py:116-119 returns before any INSERT: `if mode == config.MODE_OFF: return RecommendationResult(suppressed=True, reason='engine_off', mode=mode, variant=arm_name)`. config.py:169-171 accepts 'off' as a valid variant mode (`if mode is not None and mode not in _MODES`, and MODE_OFF is in _MODES), so `RECO_VARIANTS={"dark":{"mode":"off"}}` plus `RECO_AB_SPLIT=control:50,dark:50` is configurable and silently produces an arm with no data. The intended no-offer arm, 'holdout', correctly uses shadow (config.py:146).

**Impact.** An operator who reasons 'off means we make no offers, which is what a holdout is' loses the entire negative-class arm — no rows, no counterfactual, and the A/B report shows only the control arm's volume, which looks like the split is misconfigured rather than that half the book is dark.

**Fix.** Reject 'off' as a variant mode in _parse_variants with a warning pointing at 'holdout', or log a row (mode='off', suppression_reason='engine_off') before the early return. The second is better: the off path is currently the only invocation of the engine that leaves no trace at all.

### `reco-error-paths-are-invisible` — Every degradation path reports only through logger.exception, which in this deployment goes nowhere, and leaves no row

**backend/agent_core/reco/engine.py:133** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

engine.py:133-142 `except Exception: logger.exception('recommendation failed for customer=%s', customer_id); return RecommendationResult(suppressed=True, reason='engine_error', ...)` — no metric, no counter, and (unlike every other outcome) no offer_decisions row. Identical shape at engine.py:303-305, 322, 345, 362, 389 and decisions.py:103, 123, 145, 171, plus every config warning (config.py:38, 49, 62, 156, 159, 165, 170, 176, 206, 225, 230). The api and voice_insurance root loggers have no handler in this deployment, so logger.exception emits nothing. observability.py's engine alerts (419-440) key on decision COUNTS, so a path that writes no row cannot trigger them.

**Impact.** The engine can degrade to 100% 'engine_error' — every borrower silently gets no offer — and every dashboard shows a clean, quiet engine rather than a broken one. observability.py:426-433 will report 'no offer decisions in this window', which reads as 'an idle bot', the benign case it explicitly names. The quietest possible failure is exactly the one this design produces.

**Fix.** Emit a counter (engine_error, eligibility_error, treatment_hold_unreadable, decision_log_failed) alongside every logger.exception, and write a decision row with suppression_reason set for the error paths so the existing count-based alerts can see them. Independently, attach a handler to the api/voice root loggers — the never-raises design is only safe if the swallowed exceptions are actually readable somewhere.

### `reco-no-config-snapshot-per-decision` — Config is re-read three times within one decision and none of it is recorded, so a decision cannot be reproduced

**backend/agent_core/reco/engine.py:157** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

Mode is read at engine.py:113, `policy = config.policy()` at engine.py:157, and the scorer name and weights at engine.py:190-192 — three independent os.environ reads inside one call, by design ('read from the environment at call time (not import time) so a running process picks up a change without a restart', config.py:8-10). None of the resolved values reaches decisions.record (engine.py:224-244); only `recommender` and `recommender_version` do.

**Impact.** A decision written at the moment someone edits the environment can be scored under one min_score and arbitrated under another. More damagingly, no historical row can be re-derived: asked in an audit 'why was this borrower offered a top-up on 12 March', the answer requires knowing the weights and caps in force at that instant, and they were never written down. The tuner (tuner.py:27-46) proposes weight deltas against a moving baseline for the same reason.

**Fix.** Resolve config ONCE at the top of _recommend into an immutable snapshot object, pass it down, and persist it (or a stable hash of it, as policy_version) on the decision row. This also fixes the mid-decision drift and costs nothing on the audio path.

### `reco-feature-snapshot-retention` — Every invocation writes a full customer financial feature snapshot plus per-candidate model vectors, with no retention bound and no minimisation

**backend/agent_core/reco/engine.py:234** · privacy · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

engine.py:234 `features={**features.to_log(), "call": signals.to_log()}` and engine.py:289-306, which additionally writes a rounded model vector per candidate into the same JSONB (`row['vector'] = {k: (round(v, 6) ...)}`). offer_decisions has no expiry: the DDL (alembic 20260731_0051:189-262) has created_at and no retention column, and the only DELETE anywhere is the simulator purging its own `mode='simulated'` rows (simulate_offer_decisions.py:126-131). The engine is written on the shared caller connection for every call, live and shadow alike.

**Impact.** Under the DPDP Act a data fiduciary must not retain personal data beyond the purpose, and this table accumulates DPD, payment punctuality, affordability headroom and behavioural signals for every borrower on every call, indefinitely, in a table nobody has classified. The RBI circular's six-month recording retention sets an expectation for call-derived data that this table quietly exceeds. It is also the highest-value table in the system for an internal-abuse scenario, with no field-level access control described anywhere in the module.

**Fix.** Define a retention policy on offer_decisions (e.g. vectors and raw features purged at N months, keeping the decision skeleton for audit), implement it as a scheduled job, and document it in DATA_MODEL.md next to the treatment_decisions entry. Minimise `features.to_log()` to what the trainer actually consumes, and add the table to whatever DPO data-inventory exists.

### `reco-explanation-dropped-from-log` — The one human-readable rationale the scorer produces is thrown away before it reaches the decision log

**backend/agent_core/reco/engine.py:289** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

engine.py:289 `rows = [o.to_log() for o in scored]`, and ScoredOffer.to_log (scoring.py:56-65) emits productId/score/suggestedAmount/reasonCodes/pConvert/expectedValue/components — but not `explanation`, which scoring.py:42-44 describes as 'One sentence for the rep and the audit log: why this ranked where it did, in terms a compliance reviewer can check.' It is computed and discarded.

**Impact.** The field written for the audit log never reaches the audit log. A reviewer asking 'why this product for this borrower' gets a dict of per-signal contribution floats, which is a reconstruction exercise rather than an explanation. Reason codes help but are terse. For a bank that will eventually need adverse-action-style reasoning on automated offer decisions, the sentence is the artefact that matters and it is being dropped at the last step.

**Fix.** Add `explanation` to ScoredOffer.to_log() (it is a short string; the row-size argument that gated vectors does not apply), and surface it in the ops screens next to the score.

### `reco-swallowed-db-errors-poison-caller-tx` — Fail-soft exception handling on a connection the engine does not own converts a transient query error into the caller's failed COMMIT

**backend/agent_core/reco/engine.py:322** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

engine.py:317-323 `try: ... return treatment_policy.suppresses_upsell(conn, customer_id) / except Exception: logger.exception(...); return 'treatment_hold_unreadable'`; the same pattern at engine.py:342-346 and 357-364, and decisions.py:102-104 `except Exception: logger.exception('offer decision log failed...'); return None`. All four run `conn.execute` on the CALLER's connection. In PostgreSQL any failed statement inside a transaction block puts it in the aborted state (25P02) and every subsequent statement fails until ROLLBACK. Swallowing the error therefore does not make the pipeline resilient — it makes recommend() return a plausible-looking result on a connection that can no longer do anything, and the real exception surfaces later at the caller's COMMIT, outside recommend()'s try. voice/tools.py:1975-1999 happens to wrap its `with db.engine.begin()` in try/except; bot_tools.py:454-472 does not.

**Impact.** The advertised 'never raises' guarantee is exactly inverted under partial database failure: instead of degrading to 'no offer', the WhatsApp tool path raises out of the tool handler, and on any caller that shares a transaction with real work (a PTP write, a payment capture) the swallowed error silently kills that work too. This is the failure mode that shows up on the first Postgres failover or lock-timeout in the bank's environment, and it presents as an unrelated outage.

**Fix.** Stop swallowing DBAPI errors on a borrowed connection. Either (a) run each optional read inside a SAVEPOINT (`conn.begin_nested()`) so a rollback to the savepoint restores a usable transaction, or (b) catch only non-DB exceptions and let sqlalchemy.exc.DBAPIError propagate to the caller. For the decision-log INSERT specifically, use a savepoint and, if it fails, mark the result `log_failed=True` so the caller can refuse to speak.

### `reco-present-before-speech` — present() is called before the model actually speaks, so 'presented' over-counts and every response rate is biased low

**backend/agent_core/reco/engine.py:372** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

engine.py:372-376 `def present(decision_id, product_id=None) -> None: """Mark a logged decision as actually spoken, and consume campaign quota.""" ... decisions.mark_presented(decision_id)`. The voice caller invokes it at voice/tools.py:2033-2034, before returning the payload whose `say` instruction (voice/tools.py:2052-2056) is what causes the model to speak — the comment there admits the timing is an assumption: 'The offer is about to be spoken, so this is the moment it counts as presented'. bot_tools.py:496 does the same. Nothing later corrects the flag if the model does not mention the product, the customer talks over it, or the call drops in the intervening turn.

**Impact.** `presented` is the denominator of every conversion metric the engine reports and of the tuner's declined/presented ratio (tuner.py:44-58). Systematically inflating it makes the recommender look worse than it is, which pushes the weights in the wrong direction, and makes 'presented but no response' — the largest bucket — uninterpretable: it mixes 'we pitched and they ignored it' with 'we never actually pitched'. Campaign quota is consumed for offers that were never made, so a capped pre-approved pool under-delivers against a commitment to the product team.

**Fix.** Split the two events: mark `offered_to_model` at the current call site, and mark `presented` from the transcript/turn observer once the product name or talk track actually appears in a bot turn. Reserve campaign quota on the second event. Failing that, add a reconciliation job that clears `presented` when no bot turn in the interaction mentions the product.

### `reco-present-ignores-quota-exhaustion` — reserve_campaign_quota's return value is discarded, so an exhausted campaign is still pitched

**backend/agent_core/reco/engine.py:387** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R01-engine-config`

engine.py:385-388 `campaign = conn.execute(_campaign_lookup(), {'pid': product_id}).fetchone(); if campaign: arbitration.reserve_campaign_quota(conn, campaign[0])` — no assignment, no branch. arbitration.py:126-133 is explicit that the boolean matters: 'Returns False when the campaign just ran out — the conditional UPDATE is the check, so two concurrent calls cannot both take the last slot.' The atomic check exists and its answer is thrown away.

**Impact.** The race the conditional UPDATE was written to win is won and then ignored. Under concurrency — several agents and bots on the same campaign — the last slot is correctly awarded to one caller and the losers pitch anyway. For a pre-approved offer pool with a funded cap (a common structure in Indian retail lending), that means offers made beyond the approved limit, with the decision row still saying the campaign was in force.

**Fix.** Capture the boolean. On False, do not mark the offer as presented for that campaign: record `suppression_reason='campaign_quota_exhausted'` against the decision, emit a metric, and (since present() runs before the model speaks) return a signal the caller can act on by suppressing the pitch. Change present()'s signature from `-> None` to a small result object so the caller can react at all.

### `features-nonnullable-zero-defaults` — Eleven counters default to zero, so 'never happened' and 'not readable' are the same vector value

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:65** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`account_count: int = 0` (l.65), `prior_leads_won: int = 0` (l.78), `prior_leads_lost: int = 0` (l.79), `offers_last_30d: int = 0` (l.82), `open_dispute_count: int = 0` (l.85), `document_requests_90d: int = 0` (l.90), `closure_documents_90d: int = 0` (l.91), `dnd: bool = False` (l.94), `sentiment_current: float = 0.0` (l.156) — directly against the module rule at l.10-13.

**Impact.** Six of these feed the vector as hard zeros (vectorize.py:78, 80-81, 84, 91) with no way to distinguish absence. In a bank the disputes table, the document-request desk and the lead CRM are frequently separate systems that are onboarded on different dates; a deployment where document_requests is not yet integrated reports closure_documents_90d=0 for everyone, exit_intent=0.0 (scoring.py:224-226), and the engine cheerfully cross-sells to customers who filed a foreclosure request last week. `dnd: bool = False` is the dangerous one: a failed customers read at l.263-273 yields `{}` and `bool(customer.get("dnd"))` is False — fail-open on a DND flag.

**Fix.** Make every counter `int | None` and every flag `bool | None`, defaulting to None; add a `sources_read: frozenset[str]` recording which subsystems answered. Fail closed on dnd specifically: if the customers row is empty, treat DND as True and record a suppression reason rather than defaulting to False.

### `features-no-vector-recovery-when-logging-off` — to_log() cannot reconstruct the vector, so RECO_LOG_VECTORS=false permanently destroys those rows' trainability

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:105** · observability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

to_log (l.105-139) omits minimum_due, last_offer_at, open_lead_product_ids, held product affinities and every candidate-side field (affinity, margin_score, campaign_priority, ticket bands). engine.py:286-288 notes 'RECO_LOG_VECTORS=false turns it off... the consequence is simply that those rows cannot be trained on', and train_propensity.py:145-147 counts them as skipped['no_vector'].

**Impact.** The escape hatch offered for row-size pressure is irreversible: the vector cannot be rebuilt from the logged features because the candidate half was never logged and several customer fields are absent. A bank that flips the flag during a storage incident silently burns its entire training corpus for that period, and discovers it only when the next retrain reports a smaller n. Given the corpus is already 16 rows with zero responses, losing any period is material.

**Fix.** Make to_log a faithful superset of the vector inputs (add the missing customer fields and the per-candidate catalog facts) so a vector is reconstructible, or replace the boolean flag with a sampling rate so degradation is graceful and measurable. Emit a metric counting rows logged without a vector.

### `features-to-log-exact-amounts` — The decision log claims 'money bands only' and writes exact rupee amounts and risk scores, retained indefinitely

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:118** · privacy · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

Docstring: 'Ids and money bands only... The log is retained for model training, so it must not become a second copy of the customer record' (l.106-111). Body: `"outstanding": self.outstanding` (l.118), `"sanctionedAmount": self.sanctioned_amount` (l.119), `"dpdWorst"` (l.121), `"onTimePaymentRatio"` (l.124), `"riskScore": self.risk_score` (l.138), `"consentByChannel"` (l.134). No banding function exists in the module.

**Impact.** offer_decisions rows carry customer_id (sql/06_sales.sql:102) plus this jsonb, and the same vector is duplicated per candidate in `candidates` (engine.py:299-302). Under the DPDP Act this is personal financial data held for a purpose (model training) with no stated retention period, no banding, and no deletion path — a data-fiduciary obligation the DPO will have to answer for, and one the code claims to have already met. There is also no purge on erasure request: nothing in decisions.py or features.py references redaction, while db_redaction.py exists for other paths.

**Fix.** Either implement the claimed banding (log outstanding/sanctioned as decile or log-scale bands and drop riskScore) or correct the docstring and register offer_decisions.features as personal data with a retention TTL and an erasure hook. Note that the *vector* — which is what training actually needs — is already normalised to 0..1 and carries far less identifying detail than the raw `features` blob, so the raw blob can largely be dropped.

### `features-no-feature-drift-instrumentation` — Nothing measures feature availability, null rates, latency per source, or drift against the training distribution

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:213** · observability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

PostgresFeatureProvider (l.213-618) emits no metrics: no timing per query, no counter for how often on_time_payment_ratio came back None, no comparison of the live vector distribution against the artifact's recorded means (models.py:85, populated at train_propensity.py:371). The only observability is `logger.debug` on three failure paths (l.434, l.505, l.679).

**Impact.** The two most common production failures of a feature pipeline are silent: a source table stops being populated (null rate for one column goes to 100% and imputation quietly takes over) and covariate drift (the live distribution moves away from training). Neither is detectable here. In a bank, model monitoring is a standing obligation, not a nice-to-have — the model-risk function will require PSI/null-rate reporting per feature before the model is allowed to serve, and the code offers no hook to produce it. The artifact already carries the training means, so the reference distribution exists and is simply not compared against.

**Fix.** Emit per-source latency and per-column null-rate counters from _build_on, and add a scheduled job that computes PSI of the last N days of logged vectors against the artifact's means/scales, alerting on drift. Surface a per-decision `imputed_count` so a low-information score can be recognised at serve time and fall back to the rule scorer.

### `features-no-tenant-predicate` — Not one feature query carries a tenant predicate; isolation rests on globally-unique ids and an RLS layer that is not switched on

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:266** · security · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`SELECT dnd, segment, risk, risk_score, preferred_window FROM customers WHERE id = :id` (l.266-267) — and the same pattern at l.296-298 (products), l.310 (leads), l.324-326 (leads), l.339-341 (disputes), l.359-362 (document_requests), l.424 (offer_decisions), l.455 (activity_events), l.494-497 (ledger_entries), l.545-546 (transcript), l.569-570 (interactions), l.643 (products), l.669-674 (activity_events). Meanwhile offer_decisions, products, activity_events and customers all carry tenant_id, and decisions.record does pass `db.current_tenant()` on write (decisions.py:82). rls.py:19-22 records that the app connects as a BYPASSRLS role and rls.enable is reachable only from scripts/rls.py.

**Impact.** Reads are safe today only because ids are globally-unique TEXT primary keys. Two situations break that in a bank: (1) a multi-entity deployment (bank + its NBFC arm) that ingests core-banking CIFs, which are unique per source system and collide across them; (2) any table where the id is not the tenant-scoped key — activity_events.entity_id is a bare TEXT with no FK (sql/12_crosscutting.sql:5), so `ae.entity_type='customer' AND ae.entity_id=:cid` matches any tenant's row with that id. The write path is tenant-aware and the read path is not, which is the asymmetry auditors look for.

**Fix.** Either (a) make RLS the enforced default — provision a non-BYPASSRLS application role, run rls.apply/enable at deploy, and add a startup assertion that rls.status()['enforcing'] covers every table features.py reads — or (b) thread tenant_id through every query in this module explicitly. Do not rely on id uniqueness; document it as a deployment precondition if it is load-bearing.

### `features-doc-regex-underscore-and-language` — The closure-document regex normalises hyphens but not underscores, and is English-only

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:357** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`WHERE lower(replace(doc_type, '-', ' ')) ~ '(noc|no dues|foreclos|closure|settlement|restructur)'` (l.357-358). Compare scoring._norm, which replaces BOTH separators: `str(value or "").strip().lower().replace("-", " ").replace("_", " ")` (scoring.py:109-110). The comment at l.347-349 explicitly anticipates free-text doc_type across deployments.

**Impact.** A deployment whose document catalog uses snake_case — 'no_dues_certificate', 'foreclosure_quote' happens to survive on the 'foreclos' stem but 'no_dues' does not — silently reports closure_documents_90d=0. exit_intent then collapses from 0.6+ to docs/12 (scoring.py:224-226) and the engine pitches a top-up loan to a customer who requested a no-dues certificate: the precise scenario the field was added to prevent (features.py:86-89). Indian deployments also use vernacular and abbreviation-heavy doc types ('NDC', 'settlement letter Hindi') that no stem here matches.

**Fix.** Use `lower(regexp_replace(doc_type, '[^a-z0-9]+', ' ', 'gi'))` and widen the stem list ('ndc', 'no objection', 'pre ?clos', 'takeover', 'balance transfer'). Better: add a `doc_type_class` enum column populated at request time by the document desk, and keep the regex only as a fallback for un-classed legacy rows.

### `features-simulated-rows-pollute-real-fatigue` — Synthetic 'simulated' decisions are read back as real offer history

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:424** · data-model · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`WHERE customer_id = :cid AND created_at > now() - interval '180 days'` (l.424) — no `mode` predicate. offer_decisions.mode is constrained to ('live','shadow','simulated') (sql/06_sales.sql:130) and the schema comment says simulated exists 'so every dashboard, the trainer and the replay harness can exclude it with one predicate' (sql/06_sales.sql:107-110). scripts/simulate_offer_decisions.py:203 calls `decisions.mark_presented(result.decision_id)`, so simulated rows carry presented=true.

**Impact.** Running the corpus simulator against real customer ids — which is exactly how this codebase bootstraps a training corpus — writes phantom presented offers and phantom declines onto live customers. Those inflate offers_last_30d (suppressing real offers via fatigue) and populate declined_product_ids, which candidates.py:152-155 turns into REASON_DECLINED_COOLDOWN. A product a customer never refused becomes un-offerable. The feature-provider layer is the one place that reads the log back, and it is the one place that ignores the provenance column the schema added for this purpose.

**Fix.** Add `AND mode <> 'simulated'` at l.424 (and make it an explicit allow-list, `mode IN ('live','shadow')`, so a future mode value defaults to excluded). Add a regression test that a simulated presented row does not affect offers_last_30d or declined_product_ids.

### `features-offer-history-limit-200-truncates` — LIMIT 200 newest-first silently drops older declines on any customer with real contact volume

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:427** · scale · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 200` on offer_decisions (l.425-427) and `ORDER BY ae.at DESC LIMIT 200` on activity_events (l.458-459), both over a 180-day window, with the declined set built from whatever survives the truncation (l.437-446, l.464-474).

**Impact.** The engine logs a decision on EVERY invocation, including shadow runs and every close-probe within a call (engine.py:224-244, and it is reachable from four call sites in voice/tools.py, bot_tools.py and voice/workers/insurance.py). A customer contacted twice a week with two probes per call generates ~300 rows in 180 days. Past 200 the oldest rows fall out of the window, and with them the declines they recorded — so the engine re-pitches a product the customer already refused, which is both an irritation and, on a recorded line, a complaint. The failure is silent and gets worse the more engaged the customer is. On a 20-customer book with 16 rows total this can never fire.

**Fix.** Do not truncate the decline set. Run two queries: an aggregate `SELECT DISTINCT chosen_product_id, MAX(responded_at) ... WHERE response='declined'` (unbounded within the window, tiny result) and a separate bounded count for frequency. Or materialise the per-customer summary table proposed under features-activity-events-unindexed-on-audio-path.

### `features-decline-cooldown-never-expires` — declined_product_ids carries no per-product timestamp, so any recent offer re-arms every old decline

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:476** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`return declined, offers_30d, last_offer_at` (l.476) — `declined` is a bare set over 180 days and `last_offer_at` is the max over ALL presented offers of any product (l.444, l.472). candidates.py:152-155 then does `if pid in features.declined_product_ids and features.last_offer_at: if features.last_offer_at > cooldown_cutoff: excluded[pid] = REASON_DECLINED_COOLDOWN`.

**Impact.** The decline timestamp used for product X is the timestamp of the most recent offer of ANY product. On any actively-contacted book — weekly or fortnightly contact is normal in collections — last_offer_at is always recent, so every product declined in the trailing 180 days stays excluded permanently, no matter what decline_cooldown_days is configured to. The catalog silently shrinks per customer until candidate generation returns nothing and the engine reports 'no eligible products' with no operator-visible cause. Symmetrically, the family cooldown (candidates.py:157-166) inherits the same wrong clock.

**Fix.** Change declined_product_ids to `Mapping[str, datetime]` (product_id -> declined_at) built from `offer_decisions.responded_at` and the offer_declined event's `at`, and have candidates.py compare per product. Keep last_offer_at for frequency only. This is a feature-schema change, so bump SCHEMA_VERSION.

### `features-payment-window-hides-worst-payers` — The 365-day ledger window turns the worst payers into 'unknown', and months_since_last_payment can never exceed 12

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:496** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`AND le.posted_at > now() - interval '365 days'` (l.496) then `if not row or not row.get("payments"): return None, None` (l.508-509). The docstring one line above claims 'an unknown payer is not a good payer' (l.482).

**Impact.** A borrower who last paid 14 months ago is the single most delinquent profile in the book. This code reports on_time_payment_ratio=None and months_since_last_payment=None, models.py:112 imputes both at the training mean, and the customer scores as an average payer. Simultaneously the derived feature is structurally crippled: months_since is bounded at 12 by the window but normalised by 24.0 (vectorize.py:79), so the column's range is [0.0, 0.5] and the upper half of the feature is dead weight in the coefficient fit. A model-risk reviewer will fail this on the range check alone.

**Fix.** Split the two questions. Recency = `MAX(posted_at) FILTER (WHERE type='payment')` with no time bound (indexed lookup, cheap). Punctuality = a windowed rate that reports its own denominator. Emit an explicit `has_payment_history: bool` so 'never paid' and 'not observed in window' are different vector positions, and raise the months_since cap to 60 or use log scaling.

### `features-transcript-and-catalog-refetch-per-call` — Every invocation re-reads the whole transcript and the whole active catalog, then does an O(products x transcript) Python scan

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:540** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`SELECT speaker, intent, sentiment_delta, text FROM interaction_transcript WHERE interaction_id = :id ORDER BY turn_index` (l.541-547) — no LIMIT. `SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE is_active IS TRUE` (l.643) — no LIMIT, no tenant predicate, executed inside _product_mentions on every call. The match loop (l.648-653) is a nested scan over every active product against the concatenated transcript.

**Impact.** recommend() is called repeatedly within a single call (four call sites, and the close probe can fire several times). At turn 300 of a long call the engine re-reads 300 rows of transcript text and the full catalog every time. A bank catalog is not 8 products — a mid-size NBFC runs 60-200 active SKUs, and a large bank's product master is in the thousands. That is thousands of Python substring searches against a growing string, synchronously, on the audio path, with an explicit 150ms budget. Latency grows quadratically over the life of a call, which is exactly when the customer is most engaged.

**Fix.** Read only new turns (`AND turn_index > :last_seen`) and keep CallSignals accumulating in the session, or bound with `ORDER BY turn_index DESC LIMIT 40`. Cache the active-product name list per tenant with a short TTL rather than re-querying. Replace the nested substring scan with a single precompiled alternation regex built once per catalog version.

### `features-dominant-intent-nondeterministic` — dominant_intent ties break on set iteration order, so replay is not reproducible across processes

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:579** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`dominant = max(set(intents), key=intents.count)` (l.579). max() over a set returns the first maximal element in iteration order; Python string hashing is randomised per process by default, so a 2-2 tie between 'upsell_opportunity' and 'hardship' resolves differently in different workers.

**Impact.** scoring.intent_match returns 0.8 when dominant_intent == 'upsell_opportunity' and 0.25 otherwise (scoring.py:207-214), a 0.55 swing on a 0..1 sub-score that is also a vector column. Two workers scoring the same call rank different products; scripts/replay_offers.py cannot reproduce a logged decision; and the offline-evaluation claim that shadow mode measures what live would have done (engine.py:246-248) is weakened. Ties are common early in a call when only two or three intents have been observed.

**Fix.** `dominant = max(sorted(set(intents)), key=intents.count)` or use collections.Counter with an explicit tie-break on last-seen (most recent intent wins, which is also better semantics for a live call). Add a test that runs the same intent list through the function under two hash seeds.

### `features-live-merge-falsy-not-none` — The live/transcript merge tests truthiness, so a genuine zero loses, and transcript-only escalation/dispute signals are dropped

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:604** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`sentiment_current=(live.sentiment_current if live.sentiment_current else merged.sentiment_current)` (l.604-606), `sentiment_trend=live.sentiment_trend or merged.sentiment_trend` (l.607), and `escalation_flagged=live.escalation_flagged` / `dispute_opened=live.dispute_opened` (l.612-613) which take the live value unconditionally and never consult the transcript.

**Impact.** Same absent-vs-zero confusion as elsewhere, but in the one place the docstring claims live is authoritative (l.532-535). More seriously, when `live is None` — the replay harness (scripts/replay_offers.py), the WhatsApp path, any provider that does not construct CallSignals — escalation_flagged and dispute_opened are permanently False even though the transcript may carry an escalation intent. An offline replay therefore scores a call as calmer than it was, and any evaluation built on replay overstates the engine.

**Fix.** Make the overridable CallSignals fields `bool | None` / `float | None` and merge with `x if x is not None else y`. Derive escalation_flagged and dispute_opened from the transcript intents the way hardship_mentioned already is (l.591), then OR with live.

### `features-build-features-typeerror-swallow` — The compatibility shim catches TypeError from anywhere inside the provider and re-runs the whole build

**backend/agent_core/reco/features.py:727** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`try: return target.build(customer_id, ..., conn=conn) except TypeError: ... return target.build(customer_id, interaction_id=..., channel=..., live=live)` (l.719-733). The except cannot distinguish 'this provider's signature has no conn parameter' from a TypeError raised 200 lines deep inside a working provider.

**Impact.** A genuine bug inside a custom FeatureProvider — `float(None)`, a None concatenation — is caught, silently downgraded to a debug log ('feature provider %r does not accept conn'), and the entire feature build is re-executed. That doubles every query on the audio path at the worst possible moment, and if the second attempt raises the same TypeError it propagates with a misleading breadcrumb pointing at a signature problem that does not exist. Since PostgresFeatureProvider itself does accept conn, the shim only ever fires on customer-written providers — i.e. on exactly the integration code a bank writes and this seam exists to support.

**Fix.** Inspect the signature once and cache it: `accepts_conn = 'conn' in inspect.signature(target.build).parameters`, decided at provider registration, and let any TypeError from inside build propagate. Failing that, re-raise unless the exception's traceback depth is 1.

### `vectorize-missing-channel-segment-risk-hardship` — The vector omits channel, risk grade, segment, bucket and in-call hardship — the axes a bank actually underwrites on

**backend/agent_core/reco/vectorize.py:55** · statistics · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

The returned dict (l.55-93) has no key for `signals.channel`, `features.risk`, `features.segment`, `features.bucket`, `features.held_categories`, `signals.hardship_mentioned`, `signals.escalation_flagged`, or the offer's own suggested amount / ticket size. All of these are collected — CustomerFeatures carries risk, risk_score, segment, bucket (features.py:100-103, 73) and CallSignals carries hardship_mentioned (l.164).

**Impact.** A voice offer and a WhatsApp offer produce byte-identical rows, though their conversion rates differ by an order of magnitude — the model averages them and is wrong on both. risk/segment/bucket are the bank's own underwriting grades and the first thing a credit head will ask about; their absence means the model cannot express 'high-risk customers do not convert on unsecured top-ups'. hardship_mentioned being absent means the model has no representation of the one signal that should collapse propensity to near zero; it is handled only by the arbitration hold, so if that hold is ever bypassed the model itself has no opinion. There is also no encoding scheme for categoricals anywhere in the module, so adding them is not a one-line change.

**Fix.** Add one-hot columns for channel and for a small fixed risk-grade ladder (the risk column is already CHECK-constrained to critical/high/medium/low, sql/02_customer_account.sql), a bucket ordinal, and boolean hardship_mentioned / escalation_flagged. Add ticket_min normalised, since offer size drives conversion. Bump VECTOR_VERSION and retrain; the loader already refuses the old artifact correctly.

### `vectorize-caps-saturate-the-collections-tail` — Every normalisation cap is set for a small, healthy dev book and saturates on real distributions

**backend/agent_core/reco/vectorize.py:75** · statistics · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`_norm(features.dpd_worst, 180.0)` (l.75), `_clamp01(features.utilization)` (l.76), `_norm(features.relationship_months, 120.0)` (l.77), `_norm(float(features.account_count), 5.0)` (l.78), `_norm(features.months_since_last_payment, 24.0)` (l.79), `_norm(float(features.open_dispute_count), 3.0)` (l.80), `_norm(float(features.offers_last_30d), 5.0)` (l.81), `_norm(float(signals.customer_turns), 30.0)` (l.91). _norm clamps to 1.0 (l.34-42).

**Impact.** In a collections book the tail IS the population. DPD 180 vs 400 (written-off) are the same number, though they are entirely different propositions. Utilization is clamped at 1.0, so an over-limit cardholder — a strong distress signal in Indian cards — is indistinguishable from one at exactly the limit. relationship_months caps at 10 years, collapsing a bank's most valuable tenure segment into a single value. months_since_last_payment can never exceed 0.5 because its source is bounded at 12 months (features.py:496), wasting half the column. account_count caps at 5, which a mass-affluent customer exceeds routinely. Saturated features carry no gradient, so the fitted coefficients describe only the middle of the distribution and the model is blindest exactly where the decisions are hardest.

**Fix.** Replace linear caps with log or quantile scaling fitted from the corpus and stored in the artifact (the artifact already carries `means`; add `scales`). Where a cap is genuinely right, emit a companion `*_at_cap` boolean so the model can distinguish 'at the ceiling' from 'above it'. Keep utilization uncapped-but-log-scaled so over-limit is visible.

### `vectorize-three-densify-implementations` — as_row is dead in production — the serving path and the trainer each carry their own copy of the imputation rule

**backend/agent_core/reco/vectorize.py:121** · maintainability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`def as_row(features, signals, candidate, names=FEATURE_NAMES, means=None)` (l.121-142). Grep across the backend finds callers only in vectorize.py itself and tests/test_reco_models.py:110,123. Production scoring uses models.ModelArtifact.predict's inline comprehension (models.py:111-114) and training uses train_propensity.densify (train_propensity.py:168-171).

**Impact.** The module's entire premise is 'training and serving cannot disagree' (l.1-7), yet the shared helper is the one no production path calls, and the two that do serve are copy-paste twins. They agree today by coincidence. The tests that assert imputation-from-means-not-zero (test_reco_models.py:108-123) validate the unused copy, so a divergence introduced in models.predict or densify would ship green. In a bank this is a model-implementation-verification finding: the tested artifact is not the deployed artifact.

**Fix.** Make models.ModelArtifact.predict and train_propensity.densify both call vectorize.as_row / a shared `densify(vec, names, means)` helper, delete the duplicates, and repoint the tests at the shared function.

### `vectorize-default-mean-half` — The fallback imputation value 0.5 is a specific, often-bad claim about the customer, not a neutral one

**backend/agent_core/reco/vectorize.py:140** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R02-features-vectorize`

`value = means.get(name, 0.5)` (l.140), mirrored at models.py:112 and defended in train_propensity.py:158-160 as 'the midpoint of every bounded feature in the vector, and the least opinionated thing to substitute'.

**Impact.** 0.5 is only neutral if the coefficient is zero. On dpd_worst (cap 180) it asserts 90 days past due; on fatigue it asserts a customer who has been pitched 1.5 times this month; on exit_intent it asserts six document requests. For a customer whose ledger is unreadable, the model is told 'assume 90 DPD' — which will either suppress a good offer or, if the coefficient is positive, do the opposite. The trainer's own column_means (train_propensity.py:161-165) fall back to the same 0.5 for any column never observed in the corpus, so a feature the dev book never exercises gets an assertion rather than an abstention.

**Fix.** Fall back to the population mean recorded in the artifact and, when a column has no recorded mean, drop that column from the dot product entirely (equivalent to abstaining) rather than substituting a value. Record `imputed_features` on the decision row so an operator can see how much of a score was made up.

### `reco-comparable-score-ceiling-biases-the-blend` — comparable_score cannot exceed 1/(1+base_rate) = 0.85, so the hybrid blend is structurally tilted toward the rule term

**backend/agent_core/reco/models.py:121** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R03-scoring-models`

`return max(0.0, min(1.0, p / denominator)) if denominator > 0 else 0.0` with denominator = p + base_rate. At p = 1.0 and base_rate 0.1772 the result is 0.849. RuleScorer's `final = _clamp01(raw - penalty - exit_penalty)` reaches 1.0. HybridScorer then does `final = self._w * rule_score + (1.0 - self._w) * offer.score` (models.py:386) across the two.

**Impact.** At the top of the distribution — the offers that actually get presented — the rule term contributes up to 1.0 and the model term at most 0.85, so at w=0.5 the model is systematically discounted by roughly 7.5 points of headroom exactly where the ranking matters. The annealing knob therefore does not mean what an operator thinks it means: w=0.5 is not a 50/50 blend of two comparably scaled opinions.

**Fix.** Rescale so the two share a range: divide by (1 + base_rate) is not enough at the bottom; prefer a rank-based or quantile mapping of p onto the rule score's observed distribution, computed from the artifact's own holdout and stored in the artifact. At minimum document the ceiling and assert it in a test.

### `reco-load-artifact-raises-on-bad-encoding` — load_artifact's 'never raises' contract is broken by UnicodeDecodeError, which turns every call into engine_error instead of degrading to rules

**backend/agent_core/reco/models.py:144** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `R03-scoring-models`

```
    try:
        raw = json.loads(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    except FileNotFoundError:
        ...
    except (OSError, json.JSONDecodeError) as exc:
```
UnicodeDecodeError subclasses ValueError, not OSError or JSONDecodeError, so a truncated multi-byte write or a file replaced by a binary blob propagates out of load_artifact -> load_propensity -> build_scorer into engine._recommend, where the blanket handler returns reason='engine_error' (engine.py:135-143).

**Impact.** The stated failure mode ('Returns None (never raises) on any fault', models.py:135) is what keeps a corrupted model file from taking the offer channel down. Instead every recommendation in the process fails outright rather than falling back to the rule scorer, and the suppression reason blames the engine rather than the artifact — so the on-call SRE looks at the engine, not at the file that changed.

**Fix.** Widen the except to `(OSError, ValueError)` (JSONDecodeError is a ValueError anyway), and add a defensive try/except around the whole of build_scorer's resolution that returns RuleScorer on anything unexpected.

### `reco-unknown-feature-names-silently-imputed` — Feature names this build does not emit are imputed to the mean with no count and no ceiling
