The contrast is inside this same codebase: enact._copy (enact.py:243-253) refuses to send at all when the footer is missing - `footer = compliance_copy.written_footer(compliance_copy.tenant_contacts(tenant_id)); if footer is None: raise NoExecutor(compliance_copy.NO_GRIEVANCE_CONTACT)` - with the docstring citing RBI ¶100AA and the Digital Lending Guidelines. The page the borrower is then sent to has less disclosure than the message that sent them, and '/pay' is a public, unauthenticated route (main.py:269, main.py:886).

**Impact.** The hosted page is the collections communication the borrower actually reads and transacts on. A demand for money with no identifiable grievance route is the specific omission ¶100AA addresses, and it is the artefact an ombudsman or an internal compliance review will pull. The asymmetry is also a maintenance trap: the disclosure discipline was centralised in compliance_copy for messages and never applied to the one surface that renders HTML.

**Fix.** Render compliance_copy.written_footer(tenant_contacts(intent['tenant_id'])) into the page and refuse to render the page (or render a contact-us variant) when no grievance officer is on file, matching enact._copy's fail-closed behaviour. Include the loan/account reference the message already quotes.

### `workrt-signal-silently-noops-off-parked-state` — approve / reject return 200 and change nothing unless the job is exactly 'input_required'

**backend/work_runtime/adapter_pg.py:114** · correctness · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `W03-workers`

adapter_pg.signal (adapter_pg.py:94-130) always inserts the signal row, but the state transition is guarded: `if name in {"approve","reject"} and row["status"] == "input_required":` (adapter_pg.py:114). For any other status the function falls through to `got = query(job_id); return got` and the caller gets HTTP 200 with the unchanged job. main.py:1501-1510 only validates that the signal name is approve or reject and returns whatever comes back; nothing tells the operator the signal was ignored.

**Impact.** A supervisor who rejects a field visit or a legal notice on a job that has already moved on - approved by a colleague seconds earlier, or completed - receives a success response and believes the action is stopped. In a maker-checker control the difference between 'your rejection was recorded' and 'your rejection was discarded' is the whole control. It also makes the Floor's approvals list racy with no feedback.

**Fix.** Return the applied transition explicitly (or 409 when the job is not in 'input_required'), and surface it on the Floor. Record the signal outcome, not just the signal, in work_runtime_signals.

### `suppression-has-no-decision-id-in-payload` — A suppressed recommendation reaches the model with no decision id, so 'why did the bot stay quiet' is not traceable from the transcript

**backend/agent_core/reco/engine.py:79** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

to_tool_payload returns `"suppressed": self.suppressed, **({"suppressionReason": self.reason} if self.reason else {})` (engine.py:79-81) — decisionId appears only inside per-offer offerId strings (engine.py:69), of which there are none when suppressed. Contrast the treatment engine's payload, which carries decisionId, propensity, policyVersion, mode, variant, latencyMs, alternatives and excluded (customerInsights.ts:93-112, schemas.py TreatmentSnapshotResponse).

**Impact.** Suppressions are the majority outcome and the compliance-relevant one — 'we did not pitch because DND'. With no id in the payload and no result_preview on the voice audit row, the only link between a call and the suppression that governed it is a timestamp correlation against offer_decisions. That is not an audit trail a bank's compliance function will accept.

**Fix.** Always emit decisionId at the top level of to_tool_payload, alongside suppressionReason. It costs one key and makes every offer decision — including the silent ones — addressable from the transcript.

### `offer-nba-carries-no-decision-id` — The offer NBA row exposes leadId but not the offer decision id, unlike the treatment row beside it

**backend/customer_insights.py:117** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

_offer_nba returns `{"id": "nba-offer", ..., "leadId": policy.get("leadId")}` (customer_insights.py:117-125). The policy snapshot has the id available — `"decisionId": row.get("id")` (policy.py:189) — and _treatment_nba does surface it (`"decisionId": treatment.get("decisionId")`, customer_insights.py:208, 226). The response model allows it on any item (schemas.py:211).

**Impact.** Two decision rows sit side by side on the same card and only one is traceable. Any future outcome-capture work (see nba-no-outcome-feedback-loop) can close the loop for treatment and not for offers, which is exactly the engine with zero responses in its history.

**Fix.** Add `"decisionId": policy.get("decisionId")` and `"source": "reco_engine"` to _offer_nba, and mirror it in the TS type so both engines are addressable through one code path.

### `ev-priority-bands-saturate` — The engine row's priority thresholds are ₹50 and ₹10, so on a real book every recommendation is 'high'

**backend/customer_insights.py:222** · ux · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

`"priority": "high" if (ev or 0) >= 50 else "medium" if (ev or 0) >= 10 else "low",` (customer_insights.py:222), with the rationale 'A rupee figure a collections head can argue with decides the priority ... The thresholds are planning figures like every other number in this engine' (customer_insights.py:219-222).

**Impact.** Fifty rupees of expected value is below the cost of a single SMS. On a dev book of small synthetic balances the bands may separate; on a real book where a contact attempt's expected value is routinely in the hundreds or thousands, every engine row is 'high' and the band conveys nothing. Since priority also drives the sort among case-handling items, a saturated band silently reorders the whole card.

**Fix.** Derive the thresholds from the book — percentiles of the recent expected-value distribution, or a multiple of the modelled contact cost — and make them configurable rather than literals. Show the rupee figure (which is already rendered in the title) and drop the band, or band relative to the customer's own outstanding.

### `duplicate-case-handling-ladder-remains` — The contact ladder was de-duplicated; the case-handling ladder was not, and the two copies have already drifted

**backend/customer_insights.py:246** · maintainability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

customer_insights.build_nba:246-327 and customerInsights.ts buildNba:256-336 are line-for-line reimplementations of the same four rules (open dispute / upcoming PTP within 3 days / broken promises / no statement sent), with identical ids and copy. The module docstring still claims they mirror each other (customer_insights.py:3), and they already differ in seven ways — see the invariant. Concrete drift: paymentStreak breaks on any non-'paid' status in Python (customer_insights.py:84-88) but only on partial/overdue/upcoming in TS (customerInsights.ts:178-182), so a 'waived' or 'skipped' installment produces different streaks server-side and client-side for the same customer.

**Impact.** The exact failure the treatment work was undertaken to eliminate — 'two copies of one ladder, drifting, where the divergence only ever surfaces once somebody compares a queue against a decision log' (customer_insights.py:161-165) — is still present, one layer down. A rep on a slow connection sees the TS ladder; a rep on a fast one sees the Python ladder; they disagree about the same borrower and neither knows.

**Fix.** Reduce the offline path to a single hardcoded 'Recommendation unavailable' item (it already builds one, customerInsights.ts:269-278) and delete the client-side case-handling rules. If a genuine offline mode is required, generate the TS from the Python rule table at build time so drift is a compile error. Fix the docstring in the same change.

### `reco-not-consulted-on-customer-360` — Customer 360 runs the treatment engine live but only replays a historical row for the offer engine

**backend/db.py:962** · integration · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

In get_customer_insights, `offer = policy.snapshot(conn, customer_id=customer_id, tenant_id=_tenant())` (db.py:962-964) — a read of the last decision (policy.py:89-101) — while `treatment = _treatment_snapshot(conn, customer_id)` actually invokes recommend_treatment (db.py:970, 996-1004). The offer engine is never asked what it would do now for this borrower.

**Impact.** The two engines are surfaced on the same card under the same 'next best action' heading with radically different freshness guarantees, and nothing on the card says so. With 16 offer decisions in the corpus's entire history, the offer row is absent for nearly every customer, which reads as 'nothing to offer' rather than 'never asked'. It also means the reco engine gets no shadow corpus from browsing — the growth mechanism the treatment engine has (and which, per the finding above, needs bounding rather than copying wholesale).

**Fix.** Decide deliberately and document it: either run the reco engine in shadow on the card (with the same trigger-kind tagging and dedup recommended for treatment) so both rows are live, or label the offer row with its createdAt so a rep can see it is historical. Do not leave two engines with different semantics under one heading.

### `insights-read-endpoint-writes-a-decision` — GET /customers/{id}/insights mints a treatment decision row on every card open

**backend/db.py:998** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

_treatment_snapshot: `result = recommend_treatment(customer_id=customer_id, trigger=Trigger(kind="manual"), conn=conn)` (db.py:998-1003), reached from `insights = db.get_customer_insights(customer_id)` behind `@app.get("/customers/{customer_id}/insights")` (main.py:1060-1062). The docstring is explicit that this is intended: 'recommend_treatment writes a decision row, and that is deliberate — the shadow corpus should be built from the questions people actually ask' (db.py:988-991). The frontend refetches on a 30s staleTime (customers.$customerId.lazy.tsx:111) and invalidates on every refreshCustomer (line 117).

**Impact.** On a 20-customer book with a handful of viewers this yields the observed 19-42 rows/day and looks harmless. On a floor of 200 agents each opening 60 files a shift, it is ~12,000 synthetic decision rows a day, all trigger kind 'manual', none enacted, none with an outcome — swamping the enacted rows the uplift model actually needs, and biasing the propensity distribution toward whichever customers reps happen to browse. It is also unbounded write amplification on what the API contract calls a GET, so an aggressive UI refresh or a bot crawling the customer list becomes a write storm.

**Fix.** Either (a) make the browse path a genuine shadow read that does not persist, and keep persistence for triggers that represent a real intervention decision, or (b) keep persisting but stamp a distinct trigger kind ('agent_view') and deduplicate per (customer_id, day, trigger_kind); then exclude that kind from every training query and from the propensity/exploration statistics.

### `mesh-bus-publisher-keeps-the-env-identity-fallback` — The activation publisher still substitutes a process-wide env var for the caller identity, in the same function whose docstring calls that the bug

**backend/voice/mesh_bus.py:148** · privacy · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

`"customerId": customer_id or os.getenv("MESH_CUSTOMER_ID") or "",` (voice/mesh_bus.py:148) inside the BusActivateWorkerMessage args published when the insurance role is activated (137-155). The function's own docstring, twenty lines above, says: '``customer_id`` is per-call: the process-wide MESH_CUSTOMER_ID env fallback made every concurrent call activate the insurance worker against the same customer, so a second caller's sidecar answered with the first caller's CRM context.' (mesh_bus.py:124-127). The consumer has the identical fallback (insurance.py:75-78), so the value is reachable from either end.

**Impact.** The documented fix is only half applied. If customer_id is ever None at an activation site — voice/bot.py:1115-1122 and 1528-1533 both pass session.customer_id, which is None on an unbound inbound leg — the sidecar is activated against whatever borrower MESH_CUSTOMER_ID names, and every eligibility read and lead write in that activation lands on that account. The failure is invisible because the resulting lead is perfectly well formed. Cross-customer processing of personal data is reportable under the DPDP Act, and a control whose own docstring describes the removed defect while the line below reinstates it will not survive an internal audit.

**Fix.** Delete the `or os.getenv("MESH_CUSTOMER_ID")` on both sides (mesh_bus.py:148 and insurance.py:75-78) and refuse to publish an activation with no customerId — log and return, the way publish_role_change already returns early when the mesh is disabled. If a demo path is needed, gate it on an explicit non-production flag that the container refuses to start with when DB_PROCESS_ROLE indicates a real deployment.

### `mesh-worker-shared-activation-state` — The mesh worker falls back to instance-level activation args in a single process serving all concurrent calls

**backend/voice/workers/insurance.py:65** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

`args = getattr(params, "activation_args", None) or getattr(self, "activation_args", None)` (insurance.py:65-67). One InsuranceWorker instance is registered per process (insurance.py:189, 230-231) on a single shared bus channel (insurance.py:205).

**Impact.** If params ever lacks activation_args — a bus message shape change, a retry, a bridged frame — the worker reads whichever call last set instance state. That is a cross-call identity bleed with exactly the same consequence as the MESH_CUSTOMER_ID fallback: eligibility read and a lead written on the wrong borrower. This is the same bug class the main tools module already fixed for RTVI tasks, with the same reasoning ('a single module-level set meant every concurrent call shared one bucket', voice/tools.py:50-55).

**Fix.** Drop the instance-level fallback and require per-invocation activation args; refuse the tool when absent. Add a session/call id to the args and assert it matches on every tool call in the activation.

### `mesh-redis-silent-inprocess-fallback` — A missing REDIS_URL silently downgrades the sidecar to an in-process bus that no other process can reach

**backend/voice/workers/insurance.py:199** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `W04-reco-callsites-nba`

`if not url: from pipecat.bus.local.async_queue import AsyncQueueBus; logger.warning("REDIS_URL unset — insurance worker using in-process AsyncQueueBus"); return AsyncQueueBus()` (insurance.py:196-200).

**Impact.** The container starts, logs 'Insurance LLMWorker registered — waiting for activate_worker' (insurance.py:232) and reports healthy, while being permanently unreachable from the collections pipeline in another process. Every activation is dropped, product questions go unanswered, and the only evidence is one WARNING at boot. In a bank's change-controlled deployment, a misapplied config map produces a silently degraded specialist that passes smoke tests.

**Fix.** Fail to start when REDIS_URL is unset and DB_PROCESS_ROLE indicates a real deployment. Keep AsyncQueueBus behind an explicit VOICE_MESH_LOCAL=1 opt-in for tests.

### `capacity-price-read-failure-is-cached-as-zero` — A failed dual-price read installs an empty price map in the cache for a full TTL, with no counter

**backend/agent_core/treatment/allocate.py:440** · reliability · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `X01-tests-di`

allocate._todays_prices wraps the query in try/except and, on any exception, logs and sets `prices = {}` (allocate.py:436-439). The cache write `_CACHE = (now, prices)` at allocate.py:440 sits outside the try, so the empty map is installed and served for `_CACHE_TTL = 60.0` (allocate.py:443). price_for_action then returns 0.0 for every action (allocate.py:385-397). The module docstring for price_for_action at allocate.py:388-390 says 'Zero when dual pricing is off, when no solve has run, or when nothing is scarce — which are three different situations that all correctly produce the same answer'; a failed read is a fourth situation, and it is not one where zero is correct. The only test of the failure path, p2:275-289, asserts `price_for_action("human_call") == 0.0` and then calls reset_cache, so it never observes the caching.

**Impact.** A transient database problem silently disables the capacity optimiser for a minute at a time, and a persistent one disables it indefinitely, with no metric and only an exception line in a log the api and voice services discard. The optimiser exists to keep the day's plan inside the floor's agent-minutes and field-slot capacity; running unpriced means the engine commits the whole book to the most valuable actions and the floor discovers the oversubscription when the queue does not drain. Failing to zero is the right availability choice — a missing price must not stop a borrower being contacted — but doing it invisibly is not.

**Fix.** Cache the failure with a short negative TTL distinct from the success TTL, increment a counter (or set a `stale` flag on the returned map) so a silent disable is observable, and surface it in the monitor report alongside `converged`. Add a test that a raising engine leaves the cache unpoisoned for the full TTL and that the disable is counted.

### `arbitrate-without-a-chooser-records-certainty` — The default arbitrate() path records propensity 1.0 even inside a randomised arm

**backend/agent_core/treatment/arbitration.py:168** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X01-tests-di`

arbitration.py:168 `propensity, kind, distribution = 1.0, None, {}` — set before the `if chooser` branch. p0:230-242 exercises exactly this default with no chooser and asserts 1.0 for a suppressed verdict; nothing exercises the non-suppressed default. arm_probability is threaded into _hold (arbitration.py:192-200) but not into the unsuppressed default.

**Impact.** The engine always passes a chooser, so this is latent — but arbitrate() is a public function that the simulator and any future caller can reach, and the failure is silent: rows land with propensity 1.0 inside an 80/20 split, which is precisely the corruption P0 exists to prevent and which no estimator can detect after the fact.

**Fix.** Default the non-suppressed propensity to arm_probability rather than 1.0, and add a test calling arbitrate(arm_probability=0.2) with a surviving action and no chooser asserting 0.2.

### `propensity-floor-differs-between-explore-and-storage` — Three propensity floors exist and the test only knows about one

**backend/tests/test_decision_intelligence_p0.py:169** · data-model · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X01-tests-di`

p0:169 `assert choice.propensity >= explore.MIN_PROPENSITY` where MIN_PROPENSITY = 1e-6 (explore.py:67). arbitration.py:200 writes `propensity=max(1e-9, min(1.0, arm_probability))`. decisions.py:157-159 stores `max(1e-9, min(1.0, float(propensity)))`. engine.to_payload rounds to six decimal places (engine.py:156).

**Impact.** explore.py:64-66 claims the clip at logging time means 'every downstream consumer inherits the bound'. It does not: any caller that bypasses explore — arbitration's suppressed path, a future scorer, the simulator — can land 1e-9 in the column, producing an importance weight of 1e9 that ope.MAX_WEIGHT then silently caps and counts as one clipped row. The corpus's guarantee is only as strong as its weakest writer.

**Fix.** Import explore.MIN_PROPENSITY into arbitration and decisions and use it as the single floor, then add a test asserting decisions.record refuses (or floors to MIN_PROPENSITY) a propensity of 1e-9.

### `skip-guards-become-silent-passes` — Five DI tests degrade to a skip when the seed data is not what they expect

**backend/tests/test_decision_intelligence_p0.py:309** · testing · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X01-tests-di`

p0:309 `pytest.skip("seed has no early-bucket account with a phone number")`, p0:658 `pytest.skip("seed has no delinquent account")`, p1:393 and p1:429 `pytest.skip("no seeded customer")`, p3:785 `pytest.skip("no low-DPD account to price a waiver against")`. Contrast p3:1004 and p3:718, which correctly use `assert account, "no account in the fixture book"`.

**Impact.** In a client's CI, where the database is provisioned from their own migration set rather than the dev seed, these five tests — which include the control-arm exclusion test and the waiver-ceiling test — report as skipped and the suite reports green. The two tests that carry the most compliance weight are the ones most likely to skip.

**Fix.** Follow the pattern the same file already uses elsewhere: register the row the test needs inside the fixture transaction (as p3:1008-1028 does for the mandate) and assert rather than skip. Reserve skip for a genuinely absent capability, not for absent data.

### `rule-cache-invalidation-and-failure-storms-untested` — A published rule takes effect after a TTL nobody tests, and a failing resolver is re-queried once per decision

**backend/tests/test_decision_intelligence_p0.py:623** · reliability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `X01-tests-di`

p0:623-634 asserts only that a broken resolver returns EMPTY. policy_rules.resolve caches on (tenant, product, minute) with CACHE_TTL_SECONDS (policy_rules.py:307-329) and, on exception, `return EMPTY` before reaching `_cache_put` — so failures are never cached. reset_cache() exists but no test asserts a newly published rule set is picked up, or how long that takes.

**Impact.** Two operational surprises. First, a compliance officer who publishes a tightened window sees it apply somewhere between immediately and the TTL, and nothing in the suite states which — an awkward answer to give a regulator. Second, when the database is degraded every decision on a 2M-account book issues its own failing rule query, turning a slow database into an unavailable one at exactly the moment the fallback is supposed to be protecting availability.

**Fix.** Cache the EMPTY fallback for a short negative TTL and emit a counter when it is served. Add tests for both: publish-then-resolve within the same second returns the new version after reset_cache, and two consecutive resolves against an exploding connection issue one query, not two.

### `claim-due-test-asserts-only-absence` — The one test guarding a generated borrower from a real outbound message can pass while claiming nothing

**backend/tests/test_decision_intelligence_p0.py:687** · testing · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X01-tests-di`

p0:687-689: `claimed = decisions.claim_due(db_tx, limit=50); modes = {c["mode"] for c in claimed}; assert config.MODE_SIMULATED not in modes`. decisions.claim_due (decisions.py:359-385) is `ORDER BY scheduled_at ASC ... LIMIT :limit` over the whole table with no tenant or probe filter. The test never asserts its own MODE_LIVE row was claimed.

**Impact.** On a dev database with 225 decisions and any backlog of older due rows, the fifty claimed rows need not include either probe. The test then asserts the absence of simulated rows from a set that contains neither probe — green, and testing nothing. This is the file's self-declared 'entire safety story' (p0:646-648).

**Fix.** Assert both halves: `assert any(c['trigger_ref'] == f'claim-probe-{config.MODE_LIVE}' for c in claimed)` and `assert not any(c['trigger_ref'] == f'claim-probe-{config.MODE_SIMULATED}' ...)`. Narrow the claim by trigger_ref rather than relying on ordering.

### `models-build-test-is-coupled-to-the-checked-in-artifacts` — 'With no artifacts the scorer is the EV scorer' runs in an environment that has three artifacts

**backend/tests/test_decision_intelligence_p1.py:230** · testing · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X01-tests-di`

p1:230-232: `base = scoring.EVScorer(); assert models.build(base) is base`. models.build (models.py:846) calls load_reach()/load_timing()/load_uplift(), which read models/treatment_{reach,timing,uplift}.json from the repository. All three exist. The assertion holds only because all three say corpus:simulated and TREATMENT_ALLOW_SIMULATED_MODELS is unset in the test environment.

**Impact.** The day a client trains real artifacts — the entire objective of the programme — this test starts failing for the correct system reason, and the cheapest fix under time pressure is to delete it. Worse, it means the suite currently has no test of the state the client will actually be in: estimators loaded and serving.

**Fix.** Point the model paths at tmp_path via monkeypatch so 'no artifacts' means no artifacts, and add its mirror: with three loadable artifacts on disk, models.build returns an EstimatorScorer whose name records all three.

### `snips-and-dr-assertions-are-nearly-tautological` — Three of the six OPE tests assert properties that hold for reasons unrelated to the code under test

**backend/tests/test_decision_intelligence_p2.py:64** · testing · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X01-tests-di`

p2:71-73: every observation has reward 1.0, so `ope.snips(...).value <= 1.0` is guaranteed by SNIPS being a weighted mean of identical rewards regardless of the propensity arithmetic. p2:47-62: every logged action is 'whatsapp' and the policy picks 'whatsapp', so SNIPS equals the baseline for any set of positive weights — the test cannot detect a wrong divisor. p2:139-142 asserts only `est.value > 0` for doubly robust on a single 100%-unsupported observation.

**Impact.** The arithmetic sanity check the file calls load-bearing ('if this drifts, nothing downstream means anything', p2:48-50) would not catch an inverted weight, a missing arm factor, or a dropped clip. OPE is the number that gates a rollout; its tests need to be able to fail.

**Fix.** Give the observations differing rewards and differing propensities, and assert the estimate against a hand-computed value. For DR, assert value, ess, unsupported and trustworthy together on the same fixture.

### `allocate-persist-to-price-roundtrip-untested` — The solve-persist-price loop is never closed, and its two ends disagree about what 'today' means

**backend/tests/test_decision_intelligence_p2.py:275** · integration · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `X01-tests-di`

p2:265-289 tests only the two failure paths (pricing off, database exploding). allocate.persist (allocate.py:347-382) stamps `plan_date = allocation.plan_date`, which solve() defaults to `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` (allocate.py:215, :292). allocate._todays_prices (allocate.py:430) reads `WHERE tenant_id = :tenant AND plan_date = CURRENT_DATE`. No test writes a row and reads it back.

**Impact.** For an Indian deployment the two clocks diverge for five and a half hours every day: a solve run at 20:00 IST stamps the previous UTC date, and if the database session is IST, CURRENT_DATE will not match it — prices read as zero and the optimiser silently switches itself off for the evening shift, which is peak calling time. The 60-second cache (allocate.py:418-419) also swallows a transient read failure for a minute with no metric.

**Fix.** Add a db_tx test: solve, persist, reset_cache, price_for_action('human_call') > 0. Make the plan_date explicit and tenant-local on both sides, and count cache misses caused by exceptions so a silent disable is visible.

### `usage-table-has-no-exhaustiveness-guard` — A new action that consumes agent time would be free forever, and no test would notice

**backend/tests/test_decision_intelligence_p2.py:292** · maintainability · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `X01-tests-di`

p2:292-300 asserts three specific entries of allocate.USAGE. Compare p2:404-411, which does exactly the right thing for the card: `for action in A.ALL: assert action in _TREATMENT_ACTION_KIND, action`. There is no equivalent loop over A.ALL for USAGE or for a declared-zero set.

**Impact.** Adding an action to actions.py — a doorstep PTP collection, a branch appointment — silently costs zero of every scarce resource, so the optimiser will assign it to the entire book the moment agents are priced. The design doc calls the dual price 'the point'; an action outside the usage table is invisible to it.

**Fix.** Add `EXEMPT: frozenset` naming actions that genuinely consume nothing, and a test `for action in A.ALL: assert action in EXEMPT or any(action in usage for usage in USAGE.values())`.

### `negative-tau-is-clamped-and-therefore-unobservable` — 'Contacting this stratum makes things worse' is asserted to produce the same score as 'no effect'

**backend/tests/test_decision_intelligence_p3.py:170** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X01-tests-di`

p3:170-171: `assert base.predict({"dpd": 20.0}) == pytest.approx(0.381, abs=0.01)` and `assert with_segment.predict({"dpd": 20.0}) == 0.0`. models.ModelArtifact.predict returns `max(0.0, tau)`, so a blended tau of -0.476 and a blended tau of 0.0 are the same number to every consumer.

**Impact.** The EV formula cannot distinguish an action that is harmful from one that is merely worthless. Both fall to a value determined only by cost, so a harmful contact still outranks 'wait' whenever its cost is low — WhatsApp, SMS. In a bank the one finding a collections head most needs ('stop dunning this stratum, it is driving them to the ombudsman') is the one the scorer structurally cannot express.

**Fix.** Keep the clamp for the rupee multiplication but carry the unclamped tau on the ScoredAction and in the candidate log, and add a veto that excludes an action whose estimated tau is significantly negative. Add a test asserting that a harmful-segment borrower gets 'wait' rather than the cheapest contact.

### `drift-silently-drops-thin-features` — A feature with fewer than thirty observations disappears from the drift report without being named

**backend/tests/test_decision_intelligence_p3.py:357** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X01-tests-di`

p3:357-372 supplies forty identical rows so every feature clears the bar. monitor.py:249-252: `n = counts.get(name, 0); if n < 30: continue` — the feature is not added to `findings` and not added to `unmeasurable` (which is reserved for zero-sigma features at monitor.py:258-262). The report returns available:true with the feature absent.

**Impact.** The features most likely to be thin — mandate return codes, salary-timing gaps, the very columns p1:295-321 argues are 'the single most diagnostic thing known about a delinquent account' — are the ones that vanish. A drift report that is green because it measured nothing is the failure mode the P3 header explicitly warns about at p3:5-7.

**Fix.** Add thin features to a named `insufficientData` list with their counts, and add a test with twenty rows asserting the feature is reported as insufficient rather than omitted.

### `compliance-and-breach-metrics-are-not-tenant-scoped` — The compliance scoreboard counts every tenant's contacts and no test names a tenant

**backend/tests/test_decision_intelligence_p3.py:557** · privacy · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X01-tests-di`

p3:557 `out = metrics.compliance(db_tx, days=30)` — no tenant argument exists on the function. metrics.compliance (metrics.py:266-276) and metrics._breaches (metrics.py:345-390) query contact_events and optout_events with no tenant predicate, while every other DI entry point (registry.check, policy_rules.resolve, sweep._claim) is tenant-scoped.

**Impact.** In a multi-tenant deployment one client's compliance report includes another client's denial rate, opt-outs and window breaches. That is both a wrong number and a disclosure of another bank's conduct metrics; a DPO would treat the second as the more serious. The tests cannot catch it because none of them pass a tenant.

**Fix.** Add tenant_id to compliance() and _breaches() and thread it from the caller. Add a test that writes contact_events for two tenants and asserts each tenant's report sees only its own.

### `hold-reason-has-no-human-label` — The offer engine's most consequential suppression reason - `hold:hardship` - has no entry in the label map and reaches the rep as a raw identifier; two tests each prove half of the path and nothing joins them

**backend/agent_core/reco/policy.py:35** · ux · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X02-tests-engine-reco`

test_treatment_wiring.py:209 asserts `result.reason == "hold:hardship"` is what the offer engine produces for a held borrower (produced by policy.suppresses_upsell at policy.py:530 `return f"{HOLD_PREFIX}{kind}"`, plus `"treatment_hold_unreadable"` at reco/engine.py:323). reco/policy.py:35-51 `_SUPPRESSION_LABELS` contains none of the `hold:` family and none of `treatment_hold_unreadable`; humanize_suppression (reco/policy.py:79-86) falls through to `reason.replace("_", " ")`, which for 'hold:hardship' is the identical string. test_offer_policy.py:79 is the only test of the label path and it uses `hardship_stated` - the one code family that is in the map.

**Impact.** A rep on a live call opens the customer screen and sees 'hold:hardship' where the design promises a sentence. For hardship specifically that is the worst place to fail: the rep needs to be told not to pitch and why, in words, and instead gets a code they may not recognise as blocking at all. The unreadable-table case is worse - 'treatment_hold_unreadable' shown verbatim during an outage tells the rep nothing about whether to proceed.

**Fix.** Add `hold:*` handling to humanize_suppression mirroring narrate.humanise (narrate.py:102-103), plus an explicit entry for treatment_hold_unreadable. Then add the test that closes the loop: for every reason string either engine can emit, assert humanize_suppression returns something structurally different from the code (not merely de-underscored) - see weakness humanise-fallback-defeats-its-test for how to make that assertion real.

### `worker-queues-are-tenant-blind` — Every worker-facing queue query is tenant-blind and globally ordered, so on a multi-portfolio install one portfolio's volume starves another's and there is no per-portfolio dialler or attribution budget

**backend/agent_core/treatment/decisions.py:359** · scale · hidden-assumption · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `X02-tests-engine-reco`

claim_due (decisions.py:356-385) selects `ORDER BY scheduled_at ASC FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT :limit` with predicates on enacted, mode, suppression_reason, outcome, chosen_action, scheduled_at and created_at - and no tenant_id. attribute_outcomes (followthrough.py:99-131) selects `ORDER BY outcome_checked_at ASC NULLS FIRST, created_at ASC LIMIT :limit` with BATCH = 25 (followthrough.py:81) and no tenant_id. open_cases (followthrough.py:376-394) is a DISTINCT ON over 30 days of decisions ordered by `latest.enacted_at ASC NULLS LAST`, followed by an N+1 `_case_still_open` lookup per returned row (followthrough.py:396), and takes limit=1 from process_one (followthrough.py:509). The columns exist and are populated - decisions.py:100/109/133 writes tenant_id on every decision row - so the omission is in the readers, not the schema.

**Impact.** A bank running two or three portfolios in one install gets a single global FIFO. A large portfolio's overnight sweep fills claim_due and the small portfolio's due plans sit behind it, with no way to say 'this portfolio gets 200 dials a minute and that one gets 20' - which is how collections capacity is actually contracted and budgeted. On the attribution side 25 rows per tick across all tenants means the label corpus for a quiet portfolio advances only when the busy one is drained, and the follow-through loop advances exactly one case per tick for the whole install. At 50k-2M delinquent accounts none of these keeps up, and the failure is silent: the worker reports success every tick.

**Fix.** Give every queue reader a tenant predicate and drive it from a per-tenant scheduler with a configured share, so the dialler budget is expressed where operations can set it. Make BATCH and the open_cases limit configurable per tenant. Add an EXPLAIN-backed test that claim_due and open_cases use an index rather than a scan at book scale, and a throughput test asserting attribution clears N rows in a bounded number of statements.

### `suppressed-attempt-ledger-is-voice-only` — A contact-gate refusal is recorded as a suppressed attempt only for voice; a refused WhatsApp or SMS plan leaves no ledger row, so the denial rate the comment promises is voice-only

**backend/agent_core/treatment/enact.py:139** · observability · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `X02-tests-engine-reco`

enact.py:133-142 carries the comment 'Recording it as a suppressed attempt is what makes the denial rate a query over one table rather than a join between a log file and an intention -- and it is the row that answers "why did nobody call this borrower on Tuesday" with a reason instead of a shrug' - but the call is guarded: `if action == A.VOICE_BOT: _record_suppressed_dial(decision, customer, admitted.reason)` (enact.py:139-140), and _record_suppressed_dial itself (enact.py:425-456) returns early when there is no phone number and goes through outbound.reserve/outbound.suppress, which are voice-attempt constructs. For A.SMS and A.WHATSAPP - the two rungs the engine actually uses most - the refusal leaves only `record_outcome(decision_id, "cancelled")` (enact.py:141), which by the cancelled-collapses-eight-causes finding carries no cause at all.

**Impact.** The denial rate by channel is unanswerable for digital. A supervisor asking 'why did the WhatsApp ladder go quiet on Tuesday' gets a pile of undifferentiated cancelled rows, and the DPDP/consent story is weaker for exactly the channels where consent expiry and opt-out are most common. It also skews the one metric that would show the contact policy is over-tight: voice denials are visible and digital denials are not, so a cap set too low on messaging looks like the engine simply choosing not to send.

**Fix.** Record the refusal in contact_events (or the equivalent attempt ledger) for every channel with the gate's reason attached, not only for voice, and drop the phone-number early return for channels that do not need one. Assert it in the executor test that already fakes a daily-cap refusal (test_treatment_engine.py:1155-1178) by checking the persisted row rather than only the returned note.

### `prod-config-never-under-test` — The autouse fixture pins away every stochastic dial the deployment actually runs, so no test in these seven files exercises the shipped configuration

**backend/tests/conftest.py:217** · testing · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `X02-tests-engine-reco`

conftest.py:217-220: `monkeypatch.setenv("TREATMENT_GREEDINESS", "1.0")` / `monkeypatch.delenv("TREATMENT_AB_SPLIT", raising=False)` / `monkeypatch.delenv("TREATMENT_SWEEP", raising=False)` / `monkeypatch.setenv("TREATMENT_SCORER", "ev")`. The live deployment runs TREATMENT_GREEDINESS=0.7, TREATMENT_AB_SPLIT=control:80,null_treatment:20, TREATMENT_SWEEP=1. Every one of the 4,034 lines under review therefore runs argmax, no arm, no sweep. The docstring's own justification is honest - 'Enabling the engine broke eleven tests at once, all of them asserting a specific chosen action' - but the consequence is that the interaction the deployment depends on (ranked exploration inside arbitration's chooser, a null_treatment arm suppressing discretionary action, and sweep cases coexisting with bounce cases) has no coverage in the engine, followthrough or wiring specs at all.

**Impact.** The bank's change-control evidence pack will show 216 green tests for a configuration nobody ships. The first regression in exploration, arm assignment or sweep/bounce interaction reaches production with no test standing in front of it. A model-risk reviewer who reads conftest.py will (correctly) refuse to accept the suite as validation of the deployed policy.

**Fix.** Keep the determinism fixture for the pure-layer tests, but add a parallel `live_config` fixture that restores the deployment's env exactly, and duplicate the arbitration, ladder-walk and executor tests under it with assertions written on distributions and invariants (an action was drawn from the approved set; propensity is in (MIN_PROPENSITY, 1]; a null_treatment borrower gets no discretionary contact) rather than on a specific chosen action. Add a test that reads .env and asserts every treatment/reco env key it sets is one the code knows about, so a typo in the deployment cannot pass silently.

### `offer-policy-tests-assert-instead-of-skip` — test_offer_policy.py hard-asserts on seeded data where every sibling file skips, so a fresh customer install fails the suite as if the code were broken

**backend/tests/test_offer_policy.py:25** · testing · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X02-tests-engine-reco`

test_offer_policy.py:25 `assert row is not None` after a query for a lead in an open stage; line 58 the same for a DND-false customer with no open lead; line 99 `customer = db.get_customer(row["customer_id"])` will raise TypeError if the earlier query found nothing. Every other file in this set uses pytest.skip for the same situation - test_treatment_engine.py:903 `pytest.skip("seed has no early-bucket account with a phone number")`, test_reco_contracts.py:99 `pytest.skip("no eligible (customer, product) pair in the seeded data")`. The customer-selection query at line 41-51 also does not exclude customers with pre-existing offer_decisions, and _latest_decision breaks ties on created_at alone, so with Postgres now() frozen at transaction start a same-timestamp collision is nondeterministic.

**Impact.** The first thing a customer's platform team does is run the test suite against their own data. On a book with no open leads yet - which is every book on day one - three tests fail with assertion errors that look like defects in the offer policy. That is the worst possible first impression and it will consume a support cycle before anyone realises the suite assumes the demo seed.

**Fix.** Convert all three to pytest.skip with an explanatory message, guard the get_customer call, and either create the fixture data the test needs or select a customer that provably has no prior offer_decisions. Better: build the lead the test needs rather than finding one.

### `three-newest-actions-absent-from-engine-spec` — The file that presents itself as the spec for the pure layers omits represent_mandate, emi_date_change and self_service_plan entirely - the action excluded on every single live decision has no reachability test here

**backend/tests/test_treatment_engine.py:183** · testing · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `X02-tests-engine-reco`

The module docstring at test_treatment_engine.py:11-13 claims coverage of 'the pure layers (actions, timing, policy, scoring, arbitration, rerank)'. `grep -n represent_mandate tests/test_treatment_engine.py` returns exactly one hit, at line 183, inside a docstring. policy.veto dispatches to _mandate_veto, _emi_date_veto and _self_service_veto (policy.py:200-215) with twelve dedicated reason codes (policy.py:53-64) and none is exercised in this file; coverage lives only in test_decision_intelligence_p0.py. There is no test anywhere asserting that represent_mandate is *reachable* - that some constructible feature vector makes veto return None for it.

**Impact.** represent_mandate has been excluded on all 225 live decisions (124 no_mandate_on_file, 97 control_arm). The scorer prices it as the highest-ROI action in the book (RESOLVE_PRIOR 0.35 with no contact cost, scoring.py:60) and it has never once been a candidate. A reachability test - 'given a live mandate, an unpaid cycle and no recent return, veto returns None' - would have caught this on day one. Instead the engine has been running for weeks with its best action structurally dead and the suite green throughout.

**Fix.** Add a reachability test per action: for every key in A.ALL, construct the minimal feature vector that should permit it and assert veto returns None. Fail the build if any action has no such vector. Then add a monitor that alerts when an action's candidate rate is zero over a rolling window, which is the runtime version of the same check.

### `humanise-fallback-defeats-its-test` — test_every_suppression_reason_renders_as_prose cannot fail for any code containing an underscore, and it only walks arbitration's constants - not the veto codes or the contact reasons that actually dominate the log

**backend/tests/test_treatment_engine.py:803** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X02-tests-engine-reco`

test_treatment_engine.py:795-803 collects `[v for k, v in vars(arbitration).items() if k.startswith("SUPPRESS_")]` and asserts `narrate.humanise(code) != code`. narrate.py:107 returns `_SUPPRESSION_PHRASE.get(reason, reason.replace("_", " "))`, so a code with an underscore and no phrase passes. The 24 veto codes in policy.py:34-64 (BUCKET_DISALLOWS, DIGITAL_NOT_EXHAUSTED, NO_MANDATE, MANDATE_RETURN_BLOCKS, SELF_SERVICE_TOO_EARLY, ...) are surfaced to supervisors through `excluded` (asserted in test_treatment_engine.py:1040 and returned by the API at test_treatment_wiring.py:398) and none of them is in _SUPPRESSION_PHRASE or covered by this test. contact_policy.REASON_NO_PROMO_CONSENT ('no_promotional_consent', contact_policy.py:57) is likewise absent from _CONTACT_PHRASE (narrate.py:50-62).

**Impact.** The live corpus's dominant exclusion is `no_mandate_on_file` (124 decisions) and a supervisor reading the suppression breakdown sees 'no mandate on file' - passable - but 'mandate return blocks retry' and 'arrears not yet worth a plan' land as machine phrasing in front of a floor lead who must decide whether the queue is silent for a good reason. As new veto codes are added (three actions were added recently, bringing 12 new codes) the drift is unbounded and the guarding test will stay green throughout.

**Fix.** Change the assertion to explicit map membership: `assert code in narrate._SUPPRESSION_PHRASE`. Extend the collection to policy's veto constants and contact_policy's REASON_* constants against their respective maps. Keep the de-underscoring fallback for runtime safety but stop letting it satisfy the test.

### `rerank-tail-promotion-untested` — The rerank tests never build a shortlist longer than top_k, so the boundary that keeps a rank-4 action out of the model's reach is never exercised

**backend/tests/test_treatment_engine.py:829** · security · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `X02-tests-engine-reco`

rerank.LLMReranker defaults to `top_k: int = 3` (rerank.py:53) and splits `head, tail = base[: self._top_k], base[self._top_k :]` (rerank.py:74), returning `reordered + tail` (rerank.py:91) so the tail is structurally unreachable by the model. Every rerank test in the file builds its shortlist from `_two_actions()` (test_treatment_engine.py:829-832), which returns exactly two scored actions - so head is the whole list and tail is always empty. `_ask`'s allowed-set filter (rerank.py:166) is tested; the head/tail partition is not tested at all.

**Impact.** The design's central safety claim is that the model reorders an approved shortlist and cannot reach past it. If the partition regressed - an off-by-one, a top_k of 0, an accidental `base` instead of `head` - the model would be handed the full candidate list including actions the deterministic scorer ranked below the value floor, and no test would notice. In a bank the LLM layer is the component most likely to be scrutinised and most likely to be changed under time pressure.

**Fix.** Add a test that scores four or five actions, asks the model to promote the last one, and asserts the tail order is byte-identical and the promoted key was never in the prompt. Assert `_ask` was called with exactly top_k payload entries by capturing the prompt in the monkeypatched chat_complete.

### `attribute-helper-fails-on-book-size` — The attribution test helper caps itself at 8 passes of 25 rows and calls pytest.fail beyond that, so every test in the file fails once the book is larger than 200 pending decisions

**backend/tests/test_treatment_followthrough.py:172** · scale · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `X02-tests-engine-reco`

test_treatment_followthrough.py:172-181: `passes = min(int(pending) // followthrough.BATCH + 2, 8)` then `if pending > passes * followthrough.BATCH: pytest.fail(f"{pending} decisions are awaiting attribution, more than {passes} passes of {followthrough.BATCH} can reach. The dev database is carrying a backlog -- run scripts/simulate_treatment_corpus.py --purge...")`. With BATCH = 25 (followthrough.py:81) the ceiling is 200 pending rows. Fourteen tests in this file call _attribute.

**Impact.** The docstring concedes the backlog is 'hygiene rather than a property of the code', but the sizing is a property of the dev book. The corpus already grows 19-42 rows/day; a customer environment sweeping a real book will exceed 200 pending within hours and every attribution test in the file will fail with a message telling the customer's engineer to purge their production corpus. Worse, it reveals the real constraint: attribution is 25 rows per worker tick with roughly five queries per row, which on a book generating tens of thousands of decisions a day cannot keep up, and the follow-through loop advances exactly one case per tick (followthrough.py:506 `open_cases(conn, limit=1)`).

**Fix.** Give the tests their own decision namespace (a dedicated trigger_ref prefix or a test tenant) and make _attribute drain only that namespace, so the helper is independent of ambient volume. Separately, make BATCH and the open_cases limit configurable, add an index-backed query plan check, and add a throughput test that asserts attribution can clear N rows within a bounded number of statements.

### `ladder-ceiling-is-per-case` — The ladder ceiling is per case, the sweep opens a new case every local day, and the ladder tests deliberately record touches as not counted - so the only tested brake is one RBI does not measure

**backend/tests/test_treatment_followthrough.py:548** · compliance · hidden-assumption · 1/1 confirm · reader `X02-tests-engine-reco`

test_the_ladder_runs_out asserts `len(acted) <= config.policy().max_attempts_per_case` (test_treatment_followthrough.py:556) against arbitration.py:104 `if features.case_attempts >= policy.max_attempts_per_case`, default 5 (config.py:263). sweep.py:14-22 keys a case on `(customer, 'dpd_tick', local_date)`, so tomorrow is a new case with case_attempts back at zero. Meanwhile the ladder-walk helper inserts contact_events with `touch_counted: false` (test_treatment_followthrough.py:493), so no ladder test in this file ever consumes the borrower's daily contact budget. The sweep is deleted from the environment for every test by conftest.py:219.

**Impact.** RBI's persistent-contact test is about what the borrower experienced, not about our internal case key. A borrower with an open bounce case and a daily sweep case can legitimately receive up to five contacts on each, bounded only by contact_policy's daily cap - which the ladder tests never exercise. On a 20-customer dev book with the sweep disabled in tests this is invisible; on a real book it is the shape of a complaint. The suite currently proves a ceiling that does not bound the thing the regulator counts.

**Fix.** Add a per-borrower attempts ceiling alongside the per-case one, evaluated in arbitration from contact_events rather than from case_attempts, and test it with the sweep enabled and touch_counted=true so the daily cap and the ladder cap interact as they will in production. Rewrite _attempt to set touch_counted=true, which is what enact does, and let the tests discover which brake fires first.

### `insights-endpoint-asserts-keys-only` — The insights and next-action API tests assert shape and never value, so the endpoints could return zeros or another tenant's data and stay green

**backend/tests/test_treatment_wiring.py:408** · testing · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `X02-tests-engine-reco`

test_the_insights_endpoint_reports_the_suppression_breakdown (test_treatment_wiring.py:408-413) does `for key in ("decisions", "actionable", "coverage", "suppression", "byAction", "byMode"): assert key in body` - no assertion on any value, no `days` boundary check. test_the_next_action_endpoint_answers_with_a_plan (line 380-398) asserts the action is one of seven strings, the rationale is truthy, and 'excluded' is a key - it does not assert the action is the one the engine chose for that customer, nor that the response is scoped to the caller's tenant. test_the_next_action_endpoint_404s_on_another_tenants_borrower (line 401) uses 'nobody-at-all', an id that exists in no tenant, so it proves 'unknown customer 404s', not cross-tenant isolation.

**Impact.** The API is what the front end and any downstream integration consume. A regression that returns an empty suppression breakdown, or that drops the tenant predicate so a supervisor at one lender sees another's decisions, passes both tests. The cross-tenant case in particular is a DPDP exposure that the test's own name claims to cover and does not.

**Fix.** Assert values: create a known decision for the fixture customer and assert /treatment/next returns that action and that decision's rationale. For the 404 test, seed a customer under a second tenant and request it with the first tenant's key, which is the case the test name describes. Add a bound on the days parameter and a test for it.

## Low (180)

### `reco-has-no-holdout-and-no-response-loop` — Nothing in the reco engine detects that the response loop has never closed

**backend/agent_core/reco/decisions.py:126** · statistics · missing-for-production · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-failure`

`record_response` (reco/decisions.py:126-145) and `attach_lead` (148-171) both open their own transaction, swallow every failure, and are fire-and-forget from the voice thread (`await asyncio.to_thread(decisions.record_response, ...)` at voice/tools.py:2093-2095, inside a `try/except` that only logs, voice/tools.py:2106-2108). offer_decisions holds 16 rows and zero responses ever recorded, and there is no monitor equivalent to the treatment engine's monitor.report / alerts (treatment/monitor.py:544-584) that would notice.

**Impact.** The engine that decides what to sell a borrower has no label stream and no way to discover that it has none. Its propensity artifact is simulated, its scorer is the rule fallback, RECO_AB_SPLIT is unset so there is no holdout arm — and nothing in the system raises any of that. A model-risk reviewer will ask how the offer engine's performance is monitored, and the answer is that it is not.

**Fix.** Port the treatment monitor's alert shape to reco: presented-without-response rate, response rate by arm, and an alert when either is degenerate for a rolling window. Make record_response's failures visible (a counter, not just an exception line) since it runs detached from the call.

### `reco-present-opens-two-connections-on-audio-path` — Marking one offer as presented checks out two pool connections in sequence from the live audio path

**backend/agent_core/reco/engine.py:372** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-failure`

`present()` calls `decisions.mark_presented(decision_id)` (reco/engine.py:376), which opens `with db.engine.begin() as conn:` (reco/decisions.py:114), and then opens a second `with db.engine.begin() as conn:` of its own for the campaign quota (reco/engine.py:382-387). Neither shares a connection, and the module contract says the engine 'never opens its own connection' (treatment/engine.py:11-15, the same discipline reco's docstring at reco/engine.py:160-162 claims to follow).

**Impact.** Two pool checkouts per presented offer, on a path that runs while a customer is on the line, against a pool of five plus ten overflow shared with the API and the KB. Under concurrent voice sessions this is a plausible source of pool exhaustion, which surfaces as a timeout in the middle of a call rather than as an obvious database error.

**Fix.** Take an optional `conn` on present() and mark_presented, as the treatment module's decisions.py already does with its `_writer` helper, and do both writes in one transaction.

### `record-outcome-drops-unknown-labels-silently` — An outcome label the Python set does not know is dropped at WARNING, so the plan silently stays unterminated

**backend/agent_core/treatment/decisions.py:334** · observability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-failure`

`if outcome not in OUTCOMES: logger.warning("ignoring unknown treatment outcome %r", outcome); return` (decisions.py:334-336). The intent is sound — it mirrors the CHECK constraint so a typo costs one label rather than aborting a lent transaction — but the effect is that the caller believes the decision is terminated when it is not, and claim_due will re-claim it. The same pattern is in reco.decisions.record_response (reco/decisions.py:130-132).

**Impact.** A drift between OUTCOMES (decisions.py:310-325) and the database CHECK (extended by alembic 20260821_0087) turns into unterminated plans rather than a loud failure. Low today because the two agree, but the failure is silent by construction.

**Fix.** Return a bool from record_outcome so a caller can tell the difference between 'labelled' and 'ignored', and add a test that asserts OUTCOMES equals the CHECK's value list read from the live schema.

### `decided-today-and-planned-checks-unscoped` — The sweep's idempotency check queries treatment_decisions without a tenant predicate

**backend/agent_core/treatment/sweep.py:195** · data-model · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-failure`

`_decided_today` filters on `customer_id`, `trigger_kind` and `trigger_ref` only (sweep.py:198-207), inside a function whose caller has already resolved a tenant (sweep.py:92). Same shape in decisions.planned_actions (decisions.py:199-214) and already_planned (decisions.py:252-266).

**Impact.** Harmless while customer ids are globally unique, which they are today. It becomes a correctness bug the moment ids are namespaced per tenant or a tenant is migrated — and it fails toward *under*-contacting, which is the quiet direction.

**Fix.** Add `AND tenant_id = :tenant` and pass the tenant already in hand, so the query states the assumption rather than depending on it.

### `mt-allocate-price-cache-not-keyed-by-tenant` — The dual-price cache is keyed on time alone while the query it caches is tenant-scoped

**backend/agent_core/treatment/allocate.py:445** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-multitenancy`

`_CACHE: tuple[float, dict[str, float]] | None = None` (allocate.py:445) and `_todays_prices()` returns `_CACHE[1]` whenever `now - _CACHE[0] < _CACHE_TTL` (allocate.py:416-419) — the key is a timestamp. The query underneath is correctly scoped: `WHERE tenant_id = :tenant AND plan_date = CURRENT_DATE` with `{"tenant": dbmod.current_tenant()}` (allocate.py:428-433). Contrast policy_rules._CACHE, keyed `(tenant_id, product_id, minute)` with a bounded size and an explicit comment that a per-tenant key is a memory leak if unbounded (policy_rules.py:79-83, 312-316).

**Impact.** The moment anything binds a per-request or per-job tenant — which is the whole point of tenant_context, and the obvious next change — the first tenant to warm the cache sets the capacity surcharge for every other tenant for 60 seconds. That surcharge feeds `costs.for_action` (config.py:165-167), which feeds the expected value of every action, which decides whether a borrower is contacted at all. A bank whose vans are idle would have field visits priced at another bank's scarcity and would stop sending them, with nothing in any log to say why. It is dormant today only because nothing binds a tenant.

**Fix.** Key the cache on the resolved tenant, bound it, and evict the way policy_rules does. One line of key construction; it should not wait for the tenant binding to land.

### `mt-followthrough-attribution-spans-tenants` — Outcome attribution batches across every tenant with a shared batch budget

**backend/agent_core/treatment/followthrough.py:98** · reliability · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-multitenancy`

`SELECT id, customer_id, account_id, trigger_kind, trigger_ref, chosen_action, enacted, enacted_at, created_at FROM treatment_decisions WHERE outcome IS NULL AND mode <> 'simulated' AND chosen_action IS NOT NULL AND created_at >= now() - interval '30 days' ORDER BY outcome_checked_at ASC NULLS FIRST, created_at ASC LIMIT :limit` (followthrough.py:99-132). No tenant predicate; the BATCH limit is a single global budget.

**Impact.** The labelling loop is what turns decisions into training data. A large tenant's unlabelled backlog consumes the whole batch budget and a small tenant's corpus never acquires outcomes — its uplift model never fits, and the failure looks like 'not enough data' rather than 'starved by a neighbour'. The module's own docstring records a previous deadlock of exactly this family (followthrough.py:118-127), which shows the loop's fairness is fragile and under-instrumented.

**Fix.** Scope the claim by tenant and rotate, or at minimum make the ORDER BY include tenant_id so the round-robin is structural rather than accidental. Emit per-tenant labelled/inconclusive counters.

### `reco-decisions-open-their-own-transactions` — The reco log's outcome writers each open a fresh connection, unlike the treatment log which reuses the caller's

**backend/agent_core/reco/decisions.py:114** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-scale`

`with db.engine.begin() as conn:` in mark_presented (114), record_response (136) and attach_lead (155) — none of the three accepts a `conn` parameter. treatment/decisions.py:41-51 does the opposite, and states the reason: 'The engine is called from inside other people's transactions... opening a second connection there would be a deadlock waiting for load.'

**Impact.** Three extra pool checkouts per offer outcome, on the live-call path, against a default pool of 5 + 10 overflow (db_core.py:149-150). Under concurrency the caller can be holding a connection and block waiting for one, which is the deadlock the treatment module documents. The reco engine has 16 decisions today; this bites the moment RECO_MODE is live at any volume.

**Fix.** Give all three an optional `conn` parameter with the same `_writer` contextmanager treatment/decisions.py already implements, and pass the caller's connection through.

### `sweep-decided-today-unscoped` — The sweep's once-per-day check is not tenant-scoped even though the claim query it guards is

**backend/agent_core/treatment/sweep.py:195** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-security-privacy`

sweep.py:144-160 _claim correctly scopes: `WHERE c.tenant_id = :tenant AND a.status = 'active' AND a.dpd > 0`. sweep.py:195-208 _decided_today does not: `SELECT 1 FROM treatment_decisions WHERE customer_id = :cid AND trigger_kind = :kind AND trigger_ref = :ref LIMIT 1`. The same asymmetry appears in decisions.py:199-217 planned_actions and :249-270 already_planned, which the engine consults on every decision.

**Impact.** Only bites where customer ids collide across tenants, which is unlikely with the current id scheme. If it happens the failure is silent under-contact: tenant B's borrower is skipped for the day because tenant A's identically-numbered borrower was already swept, and nothing logs it. Worth fixing while the surrounding queries are being scoped rather than as a separate exercise.

**Fix.** Add `AND tenant_id = :tenant` to _decided_today (the tenant is already in scope at sweep.py:89) and to planned_actions/already_planned as part of the same pass that fixes the analytics queries.

### `hold-interaction-id-written-without-an-ownership-check` — POST /treatment/holds stores a caller-supplied interactionId with no tenant-ownership check and no foreign key, even though 'interactions' is already in the by-id guard allowlist

**backend/db_treatment_holds.py:192** · security · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `L-security-privacy`

db_treatment_holds.py:148-152 guards the two ids it thinks matter — `_assert_tenant_owns_customer(conn, customer_id)` and, when present, `_assert_tenant_owns(conn, "accounts", account_id)` — and then db_treatment_holds.py:192 writes `"interaction_id": payload.get("interactionId"),` straight through. `interactions` IS in db_core.py:247 _CUSTOMER_SCOPED_TABLES, so `_assert_tenant_owns(conn, "interactions", interaction_id)` was available and simply not called. The column takes no foreign key either: alembic/versions/20260814_0069_treatment_engine.py:51 is `sa.Column("interaction_id", sa.Text(), nullable=True)` and the table's constraint list adds none for it. schemas.py:3335 `interactionId: str | None = None` applies no validation.

**Impact.** A COLLECTIONS_WRITE holder can attach another tenant's (or another borrower's) interaction id to a hardship or bereavement hold. The wrong-tenant id then travels onto every screen that renders the hold (db_treatment_holds.py:107 returns it) and into any future join that resolves it, which is how a bereavement hold ends up pointing at a stranger's call. Small blast radius, trivial fix, and it is the same class as the reco interaction-id gap — the two together are the pattern, not the instance.

**Fix.** Call `_assert_tenant_owns(conn, "interactions", payload.get("interactionId"))` inside the same transaction as the customer and account guards, and add the FK (ondelete="SET NULL", matching treatment_decisions.interaction_id at 0069:183-185) so the database enforces existence even for writers that bypass this function.

### `engine-error-detail-in-api-constraint-log` — The API's constraint-violation handler logs the raw psycopg error, which carries offending row values

**backend/main.py:839** · privacy · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-security-privacy`

main.py:835-840: `except IntegrityError as exc: logger.warning("write rejected by a database constraint: %s", exc.orig)`. psycopg's DETAIL line typically reads `Key (customer_id)=(CUST-100012) is not present in table "customers"`, and for a unique violation it echoes the conflicting values. The HTTP response is correctly generic (`detail="constraint_violation"`).

**Impact.** Low in the API process, because RedactingFilter is installed there (main.py:453) and will mask anything matching a PII pattern — but a customer id or an account id is not a PII pattern, so it passes through. The same code shape in a worker would be uncovered entirely (see worker-process-has-no-log-redaction). Mostly worth noting because it is the second instance of the same class and the first one is a blocker.

**Fix.** Log `exc.orig.__class__.__name__` and the constraint name (available as `exc.orig.diag.constraint_name` on psycopg) rather than the full error string. Setting hide_parameters=True on the engine addresses the SQL/parameters half of it globally.

### `metrics-causal-and-monitor-disagree-on-null-variant-rows` — A decision with no arm assignment is counted in neither arm by the SQL and as treated by the Python, so the two dashboards describe different populations

**backend/agent_core/treatment/metrics.py:76** · observability · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `L-statistics`

metrics.causal's treated counter is `count(*) FILTER (WHERE variant <> :arm AND ...)` (metrics.py:74-81). In SQL three-valued logic `NULL <> 'null_treatment'` evaluates to NULL, so a row whose `variant` is NULL is counted in neither the treated nor the control bucket. monitor.uplift_calibration does the same test in Python: `arm = str(row.get("variant") or "")` then `if arm == control_arm: ... elif chosen_action not in ("", "wait"): treated_n += 1` (monitor.py:415-426), so a NULL-variant row becomes `""` and lands in the treated bucket. `config.assign_variant` returns None -- leaving variant NULL -- whenever `ab_split()` is empty or `customer_id` is falsy (config.py:513-514). ope.observations handles the same case explicitly and correctly: `(variant IS NULL OR variant <> ALL(:excluded))` (ope.py:475).

**Impact.** Small today because TREATMENT_AB_SPLIT is set and every row carries an arm, but it is a live trap for the operational sequence a bank will actually run: turn the split off after the measurement window and metrics.causal silently reports `available: false` forever while monitor.uplift_calibration keeps reporting a `measuredAte` computed over the entire book as if it were a treated arm. Two panels on the same scoreboard then disagree, and the one that is wrong is the one that still shows a number.

**Fix.** Make the arm test explicit and identical in all three places, following the pattern ope.py:475 already uses: treat NULL as 'not randomised' and exclude it from both arms, in the SQL (`variant IS NOT NULL AND variant <> :arm`) and in monitor's Python (`if not arm: continue`).

### `segment-heterogeneity-z-tests-against-a-nested-population-estimate` — The segment gate divides (segment ATE - population ATE) by the standard error of the segment ATE alone, ignoring both the population estimate's own variance and the correlation from the segment being inside it

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:878** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-statistics`

train_treatment_models.py:875-878: `se = _ate_stderr(p_t, len(rows_t), p_c, len(rows_c))` then `z = abs(ate - population_ate) / se if se > 0 else 0.0`, where `population_ate` is passed in at :660 as `treated_rate - control_rate` computed over the full sample the segment is a subset of. `_ate_stderr` (:723-729) is the SE of a single difference of two proportions. The correct denominator is SE(ate_segment - ate_population), which for a nested subset is neither SE(segment) nor SE(segment) + SE(population).

**Impact.** The shipped artifact's promoted segment cleared the bar at z = 2.817 against z_required = 2.498 -- a margin of 0.32. A denominator that is wrong by even 15% flips that verdict either way. Combined with the clustering correction (which would inflate the SE by ~1.7x on this corpus), the promoted segment almost certainly does not clear a correctly computed threshold, and the two rejected-for-no-heterogeneity segments would be even further from it.

**Fix.** Compare the segment against the complement rather than against the whole: compute the ATE on rows outside the segment and difference two independent estimates, so `SE = sqrt(SE_in^2 + SE_out^2)` is correct by construction. That also makes the Bonferroni correction at :202-217 the right correction for the right family of tests.

### `explore-seed-repeats-within-a-case` — The exploration seed deliberately excludes the clock, so successive rungs on the same case draw the identical arm and logged propensities are not independent

**backend/agent_core/treatment/explore.py:199** · statistics · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`return '|'.join([customer_id, trigger_kind, trigger_ref or '', ','.join(actions)])` with the docstring 'Excludes the clock, so the same decision replays to the same answer' (explore.py:199-209). `_draw` is a deterministic function of that seed (explore.py:180-190). For `bounce` and `broken_ptp` the `trigger_ref` is a fixed event id, and `followthrough.advance` re-decides the same `(customer, kind, ref)` (followthrough.py:436-446).

**Impact.** Whenever the candidate set is unchanged between two rungs of one case — common, since the ladder often re-offers the same feasible actions — the explorer draws the same index every time. The exploration that is supposed to generate the corpus is degenerate within a case, and the `propensity` column stored on each row is the marginal arm probability, which the IPS and doubly-robust estimators in ope.py treat as an independent draw. It is not: the draws within a case are perfectly correlated, so the variance of every off-policy estimate is understated and the confidence intervals are too narrow. Established fact: propensity is present and non-degenerate on all live rows, which is exactly why nobody would notice this from the data.

**Fix.** Add an attempt counter to the seed — the case's `case_attempts` (already a feature, features.py:1287) or the decision's own sequence number — so successive rungs are independent draws while a single decision still replays identically. Note the change in the artifact and in ope.py's assumptions.

### `sweep-cursor-advances-past-rows-another-worker-locked` — The resume cursor is advanced past accounts that SKIP LOCKED silently omitted, so with more than one worker those accounts are dropped for the whole pass

**backend/agent_core/treatment/sweep.py:106** · scale · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `L-time`

`_claim` uses `FOR UPDATE OF a SKIP LOCKED` (sweep.py:156) so an account held by a peer worker simply does not appear in `rows`. The caller then writes the cursor from the last row it did see: `_write_cursor(conn, tenant, accounts[-1]['id'])` (sweep.py:106), and the next claim filters `a.id > COALESCE(:after, '')` (:153). An account whose id sorts below that value and was locked at claim time is never revisited until the cursor resets at the tail (:99-100). The module docstring at :30-36 presents SKIP LOCKED as the concurrency design ('two workers cannot hold the same account'), which is true for correctness and untrue for coverage.

**Impact.** Harmless on the single-worker deployment running today. The moment the sweep is scaled horizontally — which is the only reason a 2M-account book finishes in a day, and the case the cursor exists for per :24-28 — every account a peer happened to hold is skipped for the pass, silently and without a metric, and the skip rate rises with worker count exactly when coverage matters most.

**Fix.** Advance the cursor to the highest account id the claim query *considered* rather than the highest it returned — for example by selecting the id range first and writing the range end, or by partitioning the book across workers on a hash of the account id so no two workers contend and SKIP LOCKED never fires. Emit a per-pass counter of accounts skipped so the gap is visible either way.

### `local-midnight-replace-on-dst-zone` — The weekly-cap window is built with .replace(hour=0) on a zone-aware local datetime, which silently picks the wrong instant where local midnight does not exist

**backend/contact_policy.py:367** · correctness · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `L-time`

`local = now.astimezone(tz); start = local.replace(hour=0, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0) - timedelta(days=6); start_utc = start.astimezone(timezone.utc)` (contact_policy.py:366-368), repeated verbatim in `_refresh_used_this_week` (contact_policy.py:850-851).

**Impact.** India has no DST so this is inert today. In zones that transition at midnight — several South American and Middle Eastern zones an NRI book would contain — 00:00 local does not exist on the transition date, and ZoneInfo resolves the fold silently rather than raising, shifting the seven-day cap window by an hour. The weekly cap is then computed over 6 days 23 hours or 7 days 1 hour. Low impact, but it is the one place in this module where the codebase does the naive thing that timing._first_instant_in_window explicitly warns against (timing.py:110-112).

**Fix.** Compute the boundary from the date and re-localise: `datetime.combine((local.date() - timedelta(days=6)), time.min, tzinfo=tz)`, and if exactness matters use `fold=0`/`fold=1` deliberately. Or take the seven-day boundary in SQL with `date_trunc('day', now() AT TIME ZONE tz)`, which is already the pattern used by ledger_usage.

### `standardisation-fitted-on-the-full-sample` — Feature means and scales are computed over the whole corpus before the train/holdout split, so the holdout leaks into every model's preprocessing

**backend/scripts/train_treatment_models.py:509** · statistics · defect · unverified (verifier-added) · reader `L-time`

`X, y, means = _design(samples, names)` then `train_idx, test_idx = _split(len(X), holdout, seed)` then `mu = [means[n] for n in names]; scales = _scales(X, mu); Z = _standardise(X, mu, scales)` (train_treatment_models.py:509-517) — `_design` and `_scales` both see every row, including the holdout, and `means` is additionally the imputation value for missing features. The same ordering is in train_uplift: `X_t, y_t, means = _design(treated, names)` at :589, `scales = _scales(X_t + X_c, mu)` at :599, split at :603. The artifact then ships those full-sample means (`'means': {k: round(v, 8) ...}`, :466) as the serving-time imputation.

**Impact.** The holdout AUC is optimistic by a small, unquantified amount, because the centring, the scaling and the imputed value for every missing feature were all chosen with the holdout rows in view. On its own this is minor; stacked on the random rather than out-of-time split it is a second reason the reported .73/.81/.72 cannot be taken at face value, and it is the kind of thing an MRM reviewer asks about by name.

**Fix.** Compute `means` and `scales` from the training indices only, apply them to both splits, and keep shipping the training-set means as the serving imputation. State in the artifact which rows the preprocessing was fitted on.

### `product-relations-has-no-tenant-and-no-self-relation-guard` — product_relations permits a product to relate to itself and reaches its tenant only through products, unlike its sibling product_campaigns

**backend/alembic/versions/20260731_0051_upsell_nbo_engine.py:105** · data-model · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`

product_relations (0051:105-134) has product_id and related_product_id both FK to products with a unique triple index (:135-140) and a relation CHECK (:130-133), but no `CHECK (product_id <> related_product_id)` — so a product may 'exclude' or 'require' itself. It also carries no tenant_id, while the table created immediately after it, product_campaigns, does (0051:150-153).

**Impact.** A self-'excludes' row makes a product permanently ineligible for every customer with no visible cause; a self-'requires' row is a trivially unsatisfiable precondition. Both are silent — the recommender simply stops offering that product. The missing tenant_id also means the complementarity graph is global, so a shared product catalog cannot carry per-tenant affinities.

**Fix.** Add `CONSTRAINT ck_product_relations_not_self CHECK (product_id <> related_product_id)`. Decide explicitly whether the relation graph is global or per-tenant; if per-tenant, add tenant_id NOT NULL and put it first in the unique index.

### `treatment-decisions-lacks-an-interaction-index` — treatment_decisions is the only one of the three decision logs with no index on interaction_id, though it carries the column and screens join on it

**backend/alembic/versions/20260814_0069_treatment_engine.py:210** · scale · defect · 1/1 confirm · reader `M01-migrations-routes`
